Uniform Title: Suprabhedāgama Main Title: Suprabhedāgama (Kriyāpāda and Caryāpāda) Description: Transcribed from the Devakottai series.
Notes: Transcribed by the staff of Muktabodha under the direction of Mark S. G. Dyczkowski. Revision 1: Reformatted April 13, 2007. Publisher: Śivāgama Siddhānta Paripālana Saṅgham.

Now, in the Kriyāpāda of the well-differentiated Śivamaya, this is the chapter on the procedure for questions.
Seated upon the peak of Kailāsa, surrounded by throngs of sages,
as well as by gods, yakṣas, gandharvas, siddhas, and vidyādharas.
Seeing that the Lord of Gods was surrounded here by Brahmā, the Moon, the Sun, and the World-Guardians, Vighneśa bowed and spoke these words: ||| 1-2 ||
O Blessed One, Lord of the gods of gods, Protector of the worlds, Master of the universe!
With a mind focused on nothing else, please declare the supreme knowledge of Śiva.
Having attained which, all men reach absolute liberation;
the knowledge, yoga, ritual action, and conduct have been previously explained in detail. (1.4)
For the sake of favoring men, you should speak briefly:
tell us something of the origin of the tantras, and how the mantras originated.
O Lord, what is the purification, the sipping of water (ācamana), the bathing, and the rite of the sacred ashes?
What are the limbs of worship, the ritual adoration, and what is the characteristic of the mudrās?

What is the procedure for the food offering (naivedya) and the fire ritual (agnikārya), and how is the oblation into the sacrificial pit (agnikuṇḍabali) performed? What is the rite for the festival (utsava), and what is the rite for the ceremonial bath (snapana)?

O Lord, what is the characteristic of the cold-water jar (śītakumbha), and what are the features of the fresh food offering (navanaivedya)? What is the rite of the lamp during Kārttikī under the asterism Kṛttikā, and what is the rite of filling (pūraka) in the month of Āṣāḍha?
The manner of the ripening of fruits, the characteristics of the teacher, the characteristics of the instruments, and how villages and so forth are formed—O Lord, [please explain these]. (1.9)
What is the determination regarding dissolution, or what is the procedure for plowing?
What is the procedure for the foundation of a house, and what is the procedure for the site of a dwelling? (1-10)
What is the procedure for laying the first brick? How is the rite for depositing the embryo performed? What is the rule for the fingers, and what is the characteristic of a temple? (1–11)
What is the procedure for the eight-fold rite (aṣṭakāvidhāna) at the summit? Or what is the characteristic of the liṅga?
What is the characteristic of the image (pratimā), or what is the characteristic of the ritual sowing of seeds (aṅkurārpaṇa)? || 1-12 ||
Furthermore, what is the installation of the *liṅga*, and how is the installation of the *sakala* [form] performed?
What is the installation of the *śaktis*, or what are the characteristics of the retinue (*parivāra*)? (1.13)
p. 2) Now, [I shall explain] the separate installation of the eight retinues, the consecration of Indra and the others, and how the installation of Āditya is performed. (1-14)
And how is the consecration of the field-protector performed, and how is the installation of the trident?
And how is the consecration of the King of Weapons, and how is the installation of the Teacher? (1-15)
O Lord, what is the procedure for restoring a dilapidated [shrine], or how is the procedure for expiation?
And how, in the section on ritual action (kriyāpāda), are the various Tantras integrated together?
O Lord, how did the Caryāpāda and the Śaivas arise?
What is the prescription for the distinction of castes, and how is the mandala formed, O Lord? (1.17)
Tell me the path of initiation established in the Caryāpāda for those Ādiśaivas and Anuśaivas; or how are the sixteen ritual acts [performed]? (1.18)
What are their vows and practices? How is the ascent of the sacred thread performed? And how is the weighing against gold (tulā) conducted for consecrated kings, O Svarṇagarbha?

What is the procedure for the Hiraṇyagarbha and the Tulābhāra rites? What is the ritual for the fire sacrifice (dahanavidhi)? What is the ordinance for the ancestral sacrifice (pitṛyajña), and what is the Piṇḍīkaraṇa rite? 1-20.
And how is the ritual for the Aṣṭakā, and what is the procedure for atonement?
How is the channel-wheel (nāḍīcakra) in yoga, and what is the wheel of time (kālacakra) like? (1–21)

O Mahādeva, everything concerning the relationship between the support and the supported has been proclaimed in the Yoga-pāda; but how is the sequence of Śiva’s creation described in the Jñāna-pāda? (1.22)
The Lord created the emanation of the *paśu*s; how is the sixfold path (*ṣaḍadhvan*) characterized?
These questions and other questions have been asked by me in their entirety. (1-23)
"You ought to speak to me, O God, for I am worthy of your favor, O Lord.
The Blessed One said: "Excellent, excellent, O one of great wisdom, that you have made this inquiry!"
This Tantra of pure Śaivism should not be given nor revealed,
except to one who is initiated, wise, and devoted to Śiva.
It is indeed worthy of being heard, for its exposition elsewhere is not praised;
this Tantra, endowed with four quarters, is the cause for the attainment of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
O Vināyaka, this tantra is the essence of essences and is well-differentiated;
out of affection for you, I shall speak it all—listen to it in due order.
The Śaiva, Pāśupata, Soma, and Lākula systems constitute the fourfold [division].
Among these, the Śaiva is supreme and gentle, while the Pāśupata and others are fierce. (1.28)
Furthermore, Śaivism is fourfold: Vāma, Dakṣiṇa, Miśra, and Siddhānta; among these, the Siddhānta is the most excellent.
"Listen to the Siddhānta in its twenty-eight divisions according to the truth.
Thus ends the first chapter, on the procedure for inquiry. || 1 ||
Now follows the chapter on the procedure for the introduction of the tantra.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the supreme origin of the tantras:
the *tantra* spreads manifold misfortunes that rely upon mantras. (2.1)
And because it provides protection for men, it is known as Tantra;
[namely] Kāmika, Yogaja, Cintya, Kāraṇa, and likewise Ajita. (2-2)
Dīpta, Sūkṣma, Sahasra, Aṃśumān, Suprabhedaka, Vijaya, Niśvāsa, Svayambhuva, and Anala.
Vīra, Raurava, Makuta, Vimala, as well as Candrajñāna, Bimba, Prodgīta, and Lalita. (2–4)
The Siddha, the Santāna, the Sarvokta, the Pārameśvara, the Kiraṇa, and the Vātula—these constitute the twenty-eight Saṃhitās. (2–5)
I shall speak as the respondent to the speaker of all tantras,
having quickly divided the single knowledge into eighteen compendia.

After the creation, for the sake of liberation as declared by me, [I shall explain] the *Kāmika* [Tantra] of the one named *Praṇava*, consisting of a number of granthas for the benefit of others. (2.7)
The one with two parts is said to be the *praṇava*, and from that, Hara arises with three parts;
these are the three sub-divisions, which declare the supreme Bhairava.
The three [mantras] of Kāmika are said to be Nārasiṃha and Vaivatsa;
however, that which is born of Yoga for the one called Sudhā is declared to consist of a hundred thousand [recitations]. (2.9)
From the one named Sudhā, he obtained the sacred ash (bhasma); thereafter, the Lord gradually attained Vīṇāśikha, Uttarantāra, and Sudhāsantati.
And the self-yoga—these five are the divisions of the Yoga Tantra.
That which is called the "Well-Illuminated" (Sūdīpta) is said to consist of one hundred thousand [verses]. (2-11)
From Dīpta he reached Gopati; from him, Ālikā was obtained—[the lineage] that is well-reflected upon, auspicious, leftward-turning, the destroyer of evil, and born of the gods.
And the Amṛtavidratantra is proclaimed to be sixfold; it is declared in ten million verses as the source of that which is called Kāraṇa. (2-13)
From the *Kāraṇa* [Purāṇa], Śarva-Rudra attained the status of Prajāpati;
the *Kāraṇa*, the *Pāvana*, the *Daurga*, the *Māhendra*, and the *Bhīmasaṃhitā*. (2.14)
Then follows the sevenfold method for their slaying;
and the Ajita, known as the Śiva, consists of a hundred thousand verses.
From the one named Suśiva, Śiva was attained; from that Śiva, Acyuta [was attained];
and from him, Prabhūta, Parodbhūta, Pārvatī, and Padmasaṃhitā. (2-16)
In this tantra, this [tantra] is proclaimed to be fourfold;
that which is renowned as the *Dīpta* of Īśa is said to consist of one hundred thousand verses.
From Īśa, Trimūrti was obtained; from him, Hutāśana was obtained—immeasurable, unclouded, innumerable, and of boundless splendor.
Bliss, that which arises from Mādhava, the marvelous, and likewise the immortal—these are declared to be the ninefold radiance through the study of the Sūkṣmatantra. (2-19)
The subtle [teaching] of the Subtle One was proclaimed in that book, which numbered as many verses as lotuses;
thereafter, Kālabhīma attained it, just as Bhīmādharma had done.
It is past, stainless, pure, and immeasurable, yet it possesses birth;
it is awakened, enlightened, the ornament of the hand, and the excellent awakener.
These ten numbers are proclaimed as belonging to the Thousand-fold Tantra;
that which is designated as Ambu-saṃjña is proclaimed by means of five hundred thousand.
From Agra and Ambusaṃjña, the Sun (Ravi) then attained Agra;
[he received] the Vidyāpurāṇa, the Tantra, the Vāsava, and the Nīlalohita.

The *Prakaraṇa*, the *Bhūtatantra*, the *Ātmālaṅkāra*, the *Kāśyapīya*, the *Tama*, the *Aindra*, the *Brāhma*, the *Vāsiṣṭha*, and the *Īśānottaratantra*—these twelve are remembered as the *Aṃśumat*. (2.24, p. 5)
This Tantra of the Lord of Ten is proclaimed as the *Suprabheda*. || 2-25 ||
From Vighneśvara to Udaśeśa, ten [lineages] were obtained from Bṛhodara;
they are said to number thirty million, and no further division exists therein.
From ritual action up to knowledge, everything is clearly seen right here;
therefore, this scripture is remembered as being well-distinguished by this very [text]. (2-27)
The division of Śiva has thus been declared; now the division of Rudra is being told:
the supreme tantra called Vijaya, belonging to Rudra who is known as Anādi (the Beginningless). 2-28.
Then the Supreme Lord attained [the scriptures] numbering three crores of granthas:
Vijaya, Udbhava, Saumya, Aghora, and Mṛtyunāśana. (2.29)
The Kubereśa, the Mahāghora, the Vimala, and the Vijayāṣṭaka—
these are said to constitute ten million recitations of the Niśvāsa of the Ten-Syllable [Mantra].
From Daśārṇa, Śailajā was obtained; these are proclaimed as having eight divisions:
Niśvāsa, Uttara-niśvāsa, and the emergence of the face of Niśvāsa.
Niśvāsa, Naya, Niśvāsakārikā,
and the one known as Ghora— thus the Guhya is declared to be eightfold.
The self-arisen [portion] of the Nidhana is proclaimed to be half of three koṭis;
from the Nidhana, the self-arisen [portion] was heard by Śrutavān, and from it arose the Udbhava. (2.33)
The lotus [system] of Prajāpati is threefold, namely that of Svāyambhuva;
then there is that of Āgneya, and thus the number of granthas is thirty million.
In this way, the Āgneya Tantra was thus obtained;
likewise, the Fire-god [Hutāśana] attained the singular Āgneya as well as the Āgneya Nāda.
The *Tejasa* is proclaimed as having one million verses;
from that, the *Prajāpati* was obtained in thirteen divisions.
The pure, blossoming mat of awakening, which awakens one to awakening;
the state of non-delusion during the time of delusion; the cart and the driver of the cart.
Halaṃ, Vilokharaṃ, Bhadraṃ, and Vīra—these thirteen are for Vīra;
Raurava belongs to Brahmaṇeśa, with a number equal to eight lotuses (sixty-four).
Then Nandikeśa arrived; six divisions are thus established:
Kāladāha, Kalātīta, Raurava, and Rauravottara. (2–39)
The Mahākālamata, the Aindra, and the Raurava are proclaimed as the six;
while that called the Śiva-makuṭa consists of one hundred thousand [verses].
Then Mahādeva attained [the distinction], and there would be a twofold division;
the Makuṭottara and the Makuṭa are thus prescribed as being of two kinds.
Vīrabhadra then received the pure [teaching] concerning the one whose self is everything, consisting of three hundred thousand verses; there are exactly sixteen divisions. (2.42)
Ananta, Bhoga, Ākrānta, Vṛṣa, Liṅga, Praśodara, Praśodbhūta, Sudanta, Raudra, and likewise Bhadravidhi. (2–43)
The Tantra known as Ārevata, Atikrānta, Aṭṭahāsa, Alaṅkṛta, Ajita, Māraṇa, and Vimala—these are indeed sixteen. (2.44)
The Candrajñāna of Ananta consists of thirty million verses;
from that, Bṛhaspati obtained fourteen divisions. (2.45)
Sthira, Sthāṇu, Mahānta, Nandīśa, Nandikeśvara, Ekapāda, Purāṇa, Śaṅkara, and Tūlarudraka. (2–46)
The Śrībhadrakalpa-bheda, the Śrīmukha, the Śivaśāsana, the proclaimed Śivaśekhara, and likewise the Devyāmata; || 2-47 ||
The Tantra of Candrajñāna consists of fourteen types;
the face-reflection of the Tranquil One [is] numbered in the hundreds of thousands. (2.48)
The sage Dadhīci attained fifteen divisions:
the Great Yoga of the Four-Faced One, the Stobha, and the Pratibimbaka.
The Arthālaṅkāra, the Vāyavya, the Toṭaka, the Tuṭinikara, the Pratyaya, the Catulāyoga, the Kuṭṭima, and the Paṭṭiśekhara. (2.50)
The Great Vidyā, the Great Saura Bimba, consisting of exactly fifteen [syllables],
has been proclaimed as the hymn of the Wielder of the Trident (Śūlin), recited three hundred thousand times.
Then, sixteen divisions indeed were obtained, known as the Kavaca;
namely, the Kavaca, the Vārāha, and the Piṅgalāmata. (2.52)
(7) [He sees] one bound by nooses, one holding a staff, and one bearing a *kuśa* grass bow;
as well as Śivajñāna, Vijñāna, Śrīkāla, and Jñāna itself. (2.53)
He taught Āyurveda, Dhanurveda, and the science of piercing all types of fangs;
and he taught Gīta, Bharata, and Mātodya, as well as Protgīta, by means of the sixteenth [digit].
The *Lalitasahasranāma* is said to belong to Lalitañcala himself;
having attained the *lalita* from the *ālaya*, it is the *lalita* with a graceful belly (*lalitodara*). (2.55)
The Kaumāra and the Vighneśa [tantras] are proclaimed as the threefold [division];
this tantra, established from the Bindu, consists of a number of fifty million times ten million.
From the one known as Bindu, another connection, Caṇḍeśvara, is obtained;
then there is Sārottara, and likewise Aiśānottara.
The Śālābheda, the Śaśimaṇḍa, and the Siddhatantra—these fourfold [tantras] constitute the lineage of one established in Śiva, numbering six thousand in total. (2.58)
In the Śaiva [tradition], the wind (Vāyu) subsequently attains a sevenfold division:
from Liṅga comes Adhyakṣa; from Surādhyakṣa comes Śaṅkara;
Amaleśvara, Asaṅkhya, Anila, Dvaṃdva, and Santāna—thus it is declared as sevenfold.
That which was spoken by Somadeva in its entirety consists of exactly two hundred thousand [verses] in number.
Nṛsiṃha obtained [the knowledge] from Soma; there may be a fivefold division.
Likewise, there is the Śivadharma, the Dharmānta, and the Vāyuprokta. (2.61)
Then the Īśāna [tantra], sung by Śarva and strung with the divine, is prescribed;
and the supreme Pārameśvara is proclaimed by the illustrious Goddess.
That [treatise] consists of twelve hundred thousand verses and has been transmitted in seven ways;
it was received by the sage Uśanas from the illustrious Goddess in due order.
The Mātaṅga, the Yakṣiṇī, the Padma, and the Pārameśvara,
as well as the Puṣkala, the Suprayoga, the Haṃsa, and indeed the Sāmānya.
It is said that there are five crores of rays for Garuḍa;
from him, the Saṃvartakas are obtained, and their divisions are indeed nine.
Gāruḍa, Nairṛta, Nīla, Rutvin, Bhānuka, Dhenuka, Prabuddha, the one called Buddhakāla, and likewise the ninth, Aṅkiraṇa. (2.66)
The *Vātula* scripture of Śiva is said to consist of one hundred thousand verses;
Mahākāla then obtained it, and indeed twelve divisions were proclaimed. (2.67)
The Vātula, the Uttara, the Kālajñāna, and the Prarohita—
all of which are universal, consisting of all things, supreme, eternal, pure, and of great extent.
The Viśva and the Viśvakara, as well as the Vātulī, are recorded as the twelfth;
thus, the number of tantras among the twenty-eight is proclaimed. (2.69)
The pair of feet should be Kāmika, as well as the knees and shanks, which are Yoga;
having meditated upon them, the toes are declared to be Kāraṇa, and the shank likewise.
The region of the knees is Ajita, the root region is Dīpta;
the secret seed-syllable is Sūkṣma, and the surface of the hips is Sahasra. (2-71)
Aṃśumān is the portion of the back, Suprabheda is the navel;
Vijaya is the region of the belly, and Niśvāsa would be the heart.
The Svāyambhuva [Tattva] is the two breasts, Anala is the eye,
Vīra is the region of the throat, and Raurava is the ear.
The *Makuṭa* is the crown, the *Tantra* is the limbs and minor members, the *Vimala* is said to be the arms, and the *Candrajñāna* is the region of the chest. (2.74)
The Bimba-tantra is Suvaḍana, the Protgīta is known as Jihvā,
the Lalita is Kapolatala, and the Siddha is indeed Lalāṭaka.
The *santāna*, *kuṇḍala*, *jyotis*, the sacred thread (*upavītaka*) spoken by Śarva, the *hāra* of the Supreme Lord, and the *kiraṇa* adorned with jewels; || 2-76 ||
The wind of the Supreme Lord is Vātula; through that, indeed, without hesitation, [one attains] the Kalpa, the conjunction of the Sūtras, and the anointing with the Śiva-dharma.
The Lalita, the Puṣpamālā, the Siddhānta, and the Nivedana;
likewise, the Tantrakāya is embodied by the mantra which consists of vital breath.
Through these divisions and subdivisions, [the Lord] remains embodied within the state called Sādākhya;
this is the Śaiva division of the Tantra, consisting of eighteen and ten compendia (saṃhitās).
Like a wish-fulfilling gem, it appears as one yet can manifest in many ways;
just as the speaker may be one while the listeners are many. (2.80)
(9) One should perform within that same tantra by which [the rite] was begun—from the plowing up to the worship—and one should not cause another tantra to be performed. (2.81)
One should perform [the rite] according to another tantra, for it has not been specifically stated therein.
The introduction to the tantra has been explained; now hear the extraction of the mantra.
The second chapter on the introduction to the Tantra. || 2 ||
The Chapter on the Extraction of Mantras:
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the supreme method for extracting mantras, which brings about all accomplishments, is most excellent, and bestows all desired objects. (3-1)
It is called *mantra* because its nature consists of both *manana* (reflection) and *trāṇa* (protection): reflection upon all that is to be known, and protection from the ocean of saṃsāra. (3-2)
One should likewise worship Śiva, the Brahmās, the Aṅgavidyeśas, the Gaṇeśas, the Lokapālas, the Astras, the Vidyāṅgas, as well as the Bījārṇa and the Kṣurikā.
The seeds beginning with Earth, the previously mentioned Seed-Brahman, the Piṇḍa-mantra, the Kalā-mantra, the Pañcabrahman, and the Rudraka; || 3-4 ||
I shall explain this in detail; listen to it, O Gajānana!
He is that God who is both supreme and non-supreme, the omniscient one, all-pervading at all times.
The Supreme Brahman is indeed partless; from it, the two powers arise.
That pair is declared to be partless, and from that, the emergence of Nāda occurs.
Therefore, it arises from the *bindu*, and from that, the seed-syllable of the womb;
beginning with the letter *a* and ending with the *visarga*, that seed-syllable consists of sixteen syllables. (3.7)
The remaining sources are composed of thirty-three syllables and are of an imperishable nature;
within them the tantras have arisen, and within them the mantras have emerged. (3.8)
For him, there is no need for the expressive mantras, as he is [already] manifest through them;
this ten-seed mantra is said to be the essence among all mantras.
The syllable *oṃ* is the first seed-syllable, while *ā* is the second;
the third seed-syllable is *ī*, the cause that brings about all things.
The fourth seed-syllable is *ū*, the fifth is *vyo*.
The sixth would be *ma*, and likewise the seventh is *vyā*.
The eighth seed-syllable is *pi*, and the ninth is known as *e*.
The syllable Oṃ is the tenth seed-syllable, renowned as the very self of all.
This alone is to be understood as declared by Śiva;
this is proclaimed as the Śiva-mantra, and its characteristic is now stated.
Sadāśiva is established within that reality, manifest and facing in all directions;
there is a lotus born from the power of will (icchā-śakti), adorned with a thousand petals.
There, one should meditate upon Sadāśiva, situated upon a pericarp joined with filaments, possessing five heads, four faces, and endowed with twelve eyes. (3.15)
He has four faces, four noses, eight ears, and four necks;
he has ten arms, a single body, two feet, and is seated upon a lotus.
Resembling pure crystal, with a radiance equal to ten million suns, cool as moonbeams and snow, and adorned with all ornaments. (3.17)
The god wears white garments and a white sacred thread;
he holds the gesture of fearlessness, a trident, an axe, and a vajra-sword in his right hands.
In her left [hands], she holds a shield, a goad, a noose, a bell, and fire;
to her left is Manonmanī, situated in the midst of the fivefold enclosure.
Thus one should meditate upon Sadāśiva, who cuts away all sins;
this form should always be meditated upon, as it bestows the fruits of all actions. (3.20)
Listen indeed to this form of Umeshas, which is Sadashiva;
there is a division of my own forms, one with a single face and four arms.
The Śiva-mantra is thus renowned; now hear of the Brahmā-aṅgas.
Beginning with the first five seed-syllables, the Brahmā-aṅgas are indeed well-established.
White, red, dark blue, saffron-colored, and resembling milk—
these five colors of the five are here called the five Brahmans.
The limbs of Śiva are proclaimed to extend from the color of raw meat up to the color of mustard seeds; [the colors] are pale-white, smoky, slightly smoky, black, and resembling the sun. (3.24)
(11) Its nature is darkness (*tamas*), it is easily recognized, and it is the auspicious weapon (*śivāstra*) of ten million suns.
Aghorāstra is proclaimed as a synonym for the weapon that is a limb of Śiva (*śivāṅgāstra*). || 3-25 ||
The weapon-mantra (astra) is joined with a single syllable, beginning with Oṃ and ending with Namaḥ, conjoined with the Visarga; the others are conjoined with the Bindu.
The remaining [syllables], joined with the *pluta* [protracted] vowels, are proclaimed as the limbs of Śiva;
and just as the limbs of Brahmā have been described, their forms are now stated here. (3-27)
Three-eyed, four-armed, and gentle, endowed with all auspicious marks,
adorned with necklaces and armlets, and decorated with every ornament.
Their form has been declared by me; now hear the characteristics of the Vidyeśas.
It is proclaimed that the names of the Vidyeśas begin with the second [vowel] and end with "namaḥ. (3.29)
Ananta has the luster of a hibiscus flower; Sūkṣma is blue in color; Śivottama is like a kunda flower; and Ekanetraka is the color of a bandhūka flower.
The [form] of Ekarudra has the luster of a lotus; Śrīkaṇṭha has the color of a red aśoka flower by means of his three forms; and Śikhaṇḍin has the brilliance of añjana, like a blue lotus. (3-31)
The eight Vidyeśvaras are remembered as beginning with Ananta and ending with Śikhaṇḍin;
for their heart-mantra and ritual service, there are indeed two Oṃkāras.
Their form is considered to be endowed with the characteristics previously described.
O lotus-faced one, I shall now declare the characteristics of Gaṇeśa; listen to that. (3.33)
The seed-syllable of the Gaṇeśas begins with the letter *e* and ends with the second [vowel, *ā*].
Caṇḍa, whose body is made of Jāmbūnada gold, is indeed like the sun. (3.34)
Nandīśa is the color of ruby; Kāla has the luster of emerald; Vṛṣabha has the hue of an autumnal cloud; and Gaṇeśa resembles a lotus.
Bhṛṅgīśa is white in color, while Ṣaṇmukha is red;
these lords of the Gaṇas, beginning with the Goddess and ending with Ṣaṇmukha, are to be known thus. (3.36)
Their heart-mantras should be known as previously described for the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśas);
O Gajānana, hear now the mantras of Indra and the other World-Protectors (Lokapālas).
Then the ten seed-syllables are proclaimed according to the sequence starting from the east:
Indra shall be yellow in color, and Pāvaka (Agni) shall be tawny in color.
Yama is said to be black in color; Nirṛti is smoke-colored;
Varuṇa is white in color, while Vāyu is indeed yellow in color. (3-39)
Soma, however, resembles snow; O Lord, he is like crystal.
His fire is like a flash of lightning, and that of Brahmā is like the wrath of Indra.
The form of those [mantras] has been explained individually; now hear the characteristics of mantras:
the first [syllable] ending with the tenth is uttered in sequence as the mantra. (3–41)
The vajra consists of various colors; the spear is radiant like lightning; the staff is a dark blue cloud; and the sword has the luster of a blue lotus. (3–42)
The noose resembles fire, the goad possesses the hue of a ruby,
the mace is the color of snow, and the trident is sapphire-blue.
One should visualize the Atasī flower, the discus, the lotus, and the radiance of the sun above the heads of the beings, and there one should arrange the weapons. (3.44)
In the center is this seed-syllable of Śiva, as well as the limbs of the Brahman-body of Śiva;
it is joined with the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśas), the Lords of Ganas (Gaṇeśas), and the world-protectors (Lokapālas) along with their weapons.
The mantra, its form, and likewise its color have been specifically declared as ten;
now hear from me, O Gajavaktra, the others that arise from the ten seed-syllables in their proper order. (3–46)
We shall describe the characteristics of the limbs of knowledge (vidyāṅga) as they are joined with the eyes;
[the measures] are seven, eight, and five mātrās respectively, according to the sequence of the qualities and syllables. (3-47)

The syllable *oṃ* at the beginning, joined with the word "namas" in the heart for the one who is profoundly peaceful; *oṃ*, O Soul of the *praṇava*, *namaḥ* again and again—[this is] the color [of the deity] resembling crystal in the head. (3-48)
The *śikhā* [mantra] begins with *huṃ* and the *praṇava*; the *śikhā* itself has the luster of collyrium.
Likewise, the *varma* consists of the syllable *huṃ* and resembles a lotus petal. (3–49)
The syllable *phaṭ* here shall be the weapon, possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns;
this is the Pāśupata weapon, with slightly terrifying fangs. (3.50)
Oṃ, the tongue is known as Saṃ; they know the eye to be of a reddish luster.
Their forms are as previously described; now hear the seed-syllable of their Śaktis.
Oṃ bhṛṃ jṛṃ kṣmṛṃ shall be the Śakti-mantra; the principal seed-syllable (bīja) is the deity.
Her form and characteristics are said to have the luster of molten gold. (3.52)
She has four arms and three eyes, is adorned with all ornaments, has broad hips, a slender waist, and elevated breasts. (3.53)
Thus endowed with these characteristics is the primordial power Manonmanī;
the characteristic of Śakti has been declared—now hear [the description] of the Kṣurikā weapon.
The supreme mantra of the razor, beginning with *ościpikhīcidakṣi*, is like pure crystal; the Razor-weapon (*kṣurikāstra*) has four arms. (3.55)
The Vidyāṅga weapon, the Śivāṅga weapon, and the Aghora weapon as the third;
the Śivāṅga weapon is indeed twofold, and likewise the Śiva weapon.
The heart of knowledge is the universal self, and that which arises from yoga is known as the limb of wisdom;
the terrible heart arises from the elements—thus the heart is threefold. (3.57)
One should emit [the breath] by means of that which is born of the elements, but one should withdraw it by means of that which is born of yoga;
this is declared by the wise to be the knowledge that bestows liberation. (3.58)
The seeds beginning with earth (la) are la, va, ra, ya, ha, and ka;
the name of Brahmā is as before, and Brahmā himself is likewise—listen to this now. (3-59)
The first is the seed-syllable of Brahmā, the second is the piṇḍa-mantra, and the third is the kalā-mantra; this is considered the threefold Brahmā. (3.60)
Among the Brahma-seeds, that which is the Brahman is here called the "Brahma-seed"; it extends from Sadyojāta up to Īśāna, according to the procedure to be described.
This should be known as the Piṇḍamantra; now hear the Kalāmantra from me:
Sadyojāta has eight kalās, and Vāmadeva has thirteen. (3.62)
The wise one should fashion the face [of Aghora] with eight, eight, and four *kalās* respectively; having divided Īśāna fivefold, he should likewise arrange it.
Thus, the thirty-eight *kalās* are indeed described; the *kalā* is said to be Brahman.
I shall now explain the *cakras* of Brahmā and Rudra according to the sequence of the syllables for their ritual placement (*nyāsa*).
There, the wise man should have a pavilion constructed measuring nine cubits,
or he should prepare a water-shed provided with twelve pillars.
One should especially construct a canopy adorned with banners and decorated with incense and lamps in the center of that pavilion, and therein a wheel.
One should drop the pair-line by means of the eastern and western paths;
likewise, one should drop the line by means of the southern and northern paths. (3-67)
The distance between [the two] should be known as seven finger-breadths; one should construct it according to the measurement-finger (mānāṅgula).
With a measurement of sixteen finger-breadths, one should fashion a circle in the center. || 3-68 ||
In the center of that is an eight-petaled lotus, and outside of that is one with sixteen petals;
having observed them, the wise man should rotate [the visualization] through the enclosure in successive order.
At the front of their doors, one should carve a trident with a space of five finger-breadths between them;
the wise practitioner should then install the thirty-three deities according to the external ritual procedure.
Having visualized the deities in the external site-plan (vāstu-pada),
one should indeed install the Vāstu-deities there in their proper order, equipped with swords and shields.

One should visualize there, surrounding [the central deity], gods resembling red in color with their hands joined in the *añjali* gesture at the heart, arranged one by one at intervals in sequence. (3.72)

One should extract the syllables of Brahmā from the great directions and the syllables of Rudra from the intermediate directions; O Brahmin, one should draw forth Brahmā in the directions starting from the east and ending with the north.
One should extract the Rudra-mantra from the southeast direction up to the corner;
listen now to the ritual placement (vinyāsa) according to the sequence of Brahmā and Rudra.
Thereupon, one should lay down the Brahma-thread with white powder;
then, using powder mixed with various colors, one should rotate [the lines] starting from the Brahma-thread.
One should indeed spread the letters of the *ra*-group with red-colored powder;
the seed-syllable that is the eighth from the *ya*-group is conjoined with the seed-syllable of fire.
Endowed with the fourteen vowels and accompanied by the *bindu* and *nāda*, the sin of killing a Brahmin and other such evils are destroyed by the mere recitation [of this mantra]. (3.77)
Having extracted this *prāṇada* [mantra] specifically into the pericarp (*karṇikā*),
one should place the *praṇava* on the eastern petal and the syllable *dyā* to its right.
He should immediately assign *sadyogaccha* upon an eight-petaled lotus;
then likewise *sadyojā*, *ta*, *pṛcchi*, and again *paś*.
And all these [syllables] beginning with *ja* should be placed upon the petals starting from the east;
likewise, one should place the syllable *ma*, the syllable *sa*, and the syllable *go*. (3.80)
And likewise for one who is born, this very creation of the stable [elements] occurs;
as do *bhā*, *ve*, *bha*, consciousness (*cetanā*), and likewise *atibha*. (3.81)

One should place the syllable *mi* in the eastern direction (Indra’s quarter) within the vessel, and the syllable *ga* in the western direction (Bhṛtināva); one should not indeed place the syllables *va*, *ta*, *ja*, *nya*, and *sa* in the sixteen petals of the directions.
Proceeding in this manner by way of circumambulation through the vowels and the consonants, there is the syllable *ja*, *bha*, as well as *pe*, *ma*, and *pya*, which is the syllable *tam*. (3.83)
The letter *kha* and the letter *vi*, the letter *kha* and likewise *mā*; *kā*, *pa*, and *poca*, and indeed *o* and *care kāra*. (3.84)
Muñcya, Drāca, Rudra, Śannota, and Pañcadhi, as well as Gāśca; [these are recited] starting from the east and proceeding clockwise. (3.85)
Twenty-four [deities] have been declared by me in sequence for the first enclosure:
Na, Mā, Sva, Vya, and Di, and then again— || 3.86 ||
Neither posterior nor likewise prior, neither moving nor even stationary;
intent on the affliction of the foolish, and indeed within the range of the wicked. || 3-87 ||
Sra, vi, ca, ka, kā, ra, ṣa, pi, and likewise ca; co, pra, and likewise dra, mu, pra, and śa as well. || 3-88 ||
And this second [syllable] is said to consist of thirty-two phonemes;
that *visarga* is indeed the letter *ma*, for they say there are thirty-six letters in its resonance. (3.89)
Outside of that, on the sixteen petals, are *bha*, *mo*, *ca*, *ya*, *eva*, *ca*, *pā*, *ca*, *rū*, *ca*, *kva*, *kā*, *ra*, *ca*, *ri*, *kā*, *ra*, and *ca*. (3.90)
Ba, ca, mo, ca, tathā, na, ca, ma, ca, pāma, tathaiva ca; the syllable mo, and also ma, together with the visarga. || 3.91 ||
The syllable *ret*, *niśca*, as well as *tathādyāśca* and *niścayaśca*, then *ta āyataḥ*, the letter *śi*, the *praṇava*, and likewise *yāccadaśca*. (3.92)
Then, in the third enclosure, there is the letter *ka* with the visarga (*khaḥ*), as well as the three *dha*s and the *prapañca*; thus, thirty-six syllables are said to be [located] there. (3.93)
The letter *na* and *vāca*, then *dīpa*, *nādhā*, *praśca*, and also *jane*; *vyāścarvaśca* and *samau*, *praśca*, the letter *la*, and indeed *bhukti*. (3.94)

The *niścaya* (consonant) and likewise the *drā* (vowel), the *oṣṭhya* (labial) and the *ekāra* (e-vowel), as well as the *savisarga* (with visarga) ending in *ka*, and *ma*, *ca*, *sa*, and *ca*—these are long (*āyata*). (3.95)
Ṇya, cara, as well as hi, mocana, and dha; likewise, the form *tya*, *na*, *kā*, *ī*, and *ta*. (3.96)
Ta, bhu, and navaubhāni; likewise va, śca, and bha—these constitute the forty-four syllables here in the fourth enclosure.
And *ya*, *va*, *ca*, *ta*, *da*, *ma*, *dya*, *vā*, *śca*, and likewise *tathaiva ca*; *pā*, *do*, *hā*, *mā*, *śca*, *ya*, *śca*, *eva*, *vā*, *kā*, *ra*, *śca*, and *śi*. || 3-98 ||
That [syllable] with the visarga and the letter *ma* is not the syllable *ka*; from that comes the *praṇava*.
Just as there are sounds such as *ya*, *dha*, *u*, *na*, *ā*, *dha*, *ba*, *da*, and *śa*, so too is that which possesses the visarga and *ma*.

Then there is *ta*, *ca*, *ṇa*, and *ca*; *vi*, *rū*, *kā*, *ra*, *u*, *hū*, *kā*, *ra*, *ba*, *śca*, *yaḥ*; then *ta*, *taḥ*; *hyā*, *kā*, *rau*, *sa*, *rvva*, *kā*, *rau*, *ca*, *śaḥ*, *ca*, *raḥ*, *śca*, *ta*, *ā*, *ya*, *taḥ*. || 3-100 ||
Furthermore, *tu*, *he*, *secca*, *kāra*, *lakāra*, *na*, *eva*, *ca*, *lakāra*, *nikāra*, and likewise *svarādyo* and *heviḥ*. (3-101)
Repha, pūrva, upakāra, tu, saḥ, ca, dyauḥ, api, eva, ca; nyā, akarot, iti, śāḥ, ca, eva, tyāḥ, ca, śaḥ, ca, vaḥ, eva, ca. || 3-102 ||
The syllables va, ka, ra, vi, u, bha, vya, u, bha, and finally the syllable ka—
these sixty-eight syllables are thus declared for the fifth enclosure.
The letter *jye*, as well as *mo*, *na*, *dāpa*, *dapā*, and likewise *yat*, *pākṛti*, *pacca*, *kāne*, and the first vowel; || 3.104 ||
And that which is *āyasakāra* and *hārgasā* is with the *visarga*;
likewise, *na*, *ca*, and *jo* are *tejas*, and *kāra* is indeed born [from them]. (3-105)
The letter *ai*, the letter *vi*, the letter *ū*, and likewise again the letter *re* followed by the letter *śa*, and then again *sacca*. (3-106)
First is the letter *repha*, then the long vowel, then *spa* and *caṇe*, and after that *virū*;
then *na hyorve ghotatīṃ tāśā*, and then again *tāścaśā*. (3-107)
Then the long *repha*, the letter *pa*, and the letter *ra*—these are the fifteenth [syllables].
Then the nasalized (*ṇāmin*) *nābhi*, *śliṃ*, *śīṃ*, and likewise the syllable *ślīṃ*.
Then the *praṇava*, the letter *śa*, *deśāt*, *ettā*, and then *jā*.
The letter *a*, the letter *ṣa*, the letter *ru*, as well as *pūṣau* and *rūpa*. || 3-109 ||
And sixty-six [deities] are proclaimed in sequence in the sixth enclosure:
*tadha*, *ṣāṣ*, *śevi*, and *pāca*, and then again [the same]. (3.110)
Rūcadra, likewise Raucaya, Nāśāviri, Ghna, Viścarvasa, Yākāra, and Taru. (3.111)
The letter *ca* preceded by *repha* (r), as well as *ru*, *caṇḍa*, and *gadha*;
likewise *ḍā*, *gaṇa*, *carūḍā*, and *rāvasā*—these also [occur] in the *caraṇa*. (3.112)
Rū, stau, stai, mā, and śca; pro, vā, and eva; sva, rā, dyo, vi, sa, and visargayuk; ta, śca, va, śca, śi, ma, stā, ca, va, śca, śi, and bha. || 3-113 ||
*Tara*, *ghoma*, *gara*, *rāścaiva*, *saścaraścaśca*—these are the three; likewise, there are the three *hrīṃ*s of the lamp and the three *hrikāra*s. (3-114)

The three syllables are the *huṃ* sounds; likewise, there are three *praṇavas* and three *phaṭ*s. There are also the illuminators (*dīpaka*) and the parts (*aṃśas*); these constitute the seventh enclosure, numbering eighty. (3.115)
Drau, caru, and likewise mocana; cara, carupī, and likewise ya; caṣṭā, and likewise daṃ; tū, ca, vaś, and likewise lipī. || 3-116 ||
Li, Ki, Lipī, Li, Hi, Tanti, Punar, Nāmādā, Dvaṃścaṇa, Rūlā, Cadrū, and likewise [the others]. (3-117)
Yaścala and likewise Mūcaṇa, as well as Rujāśva, Bījāya and Bīcaivaṇa, and also Berudra. (3.118)
When the syllable *ma* is not accompanied by the *visarga*, it is not [the word] *namaḥ*;
therefore, the vowels are considered to be with the *visarga* in the word *namo*. (3-119)
Then *vīrya*, *pauṣṇa*, *hyatāmra*, *vanāścantā*, and *canaḥ*;
likewise, the two *aphaṭkāra*s, *huṃ*, and again the *praṇava*. (3-120)
The six, the two *v*s, and the six again, as well as *svāc* and *hā*;
*svāścastiḥ*, the letter *sa*, with the two *visargas*, and likewise *manaḥ*. (3.121)
Furthermore, in the eighth enclosure, eighty-eight syllables are proclaimed; these include the letter 'ma' with the visarga, as well as the letters 'na', 'ya', and 'ya'. (3.122)
Those which are *nir*, *ve*, *dha*, *māḥ*, *sāḥ*, *ca*, *juḥ*, *cagyaḥ*, *ca*, *ṛ*, *eva*, *ca*, *śvaḥ*, *ca*, *hvā*, *ca*, likewise *jīṃḥ*, *ca*, *graścanoca*, and *ha āyataḥ*. (3-123)
Likewise, there are the Līpas, the Pāśas, and the various Lāpas;
also the Monayas, the Piśas, and those who are long-extending Rudrapās. (3.124)
Then there are Drāpaṇa, Pitatārū, Laśca, Nāyau, and Calā; furthermore, those with the form of Nāka, Rūrāṃśca, and Rudrāśca. (3-125)
*Rā*, *cara*, *ruś* and likewise *tat*, as well as *praṇava* and *hya*, *eva*, *ca*, *paśca*, *iś*, *tathā*, *adya*, *ca*, *api*, *carva*, and *sa*—these indeed [constitute it]. (3-126)
The letter *ma* with the visarga, and from those two, *ta* and *ya*;
again, *tava*, *gopte*, and *gauyau*; and likewise *hyā* and *gu*. (3.127)

Then, from that [source], there arose *ma*, *na*, *hu*, *prā*, *śca*, *ha*, *śca*, *sma*, *śca*, *vraṃ*, *śca*, *nāṃ*, *ta*, *taḥ*, *ta*, *hā*, *ca*, *tathā*, *svā*, *ca*, the letter *ya*, and the long *ra*. (3-128)
And *ya*, *bhi*, *bhū*, *ma*, *preca*, *ha*, and *āyata*; and *sā*, *ya*, *rā*, *ya*, *ja*, and *va*. (3-129)
Hā, ca, svā, ca, talī, ca, jva, su, and da—
these are declared as the syllables in the ninth enclosure, numbering one hundred and eight.
And that which is *lā*, *ca*, *tathā*, *kā*, *ca*, *vyāli*, *kali*, and *kiṃ*—what is there from that?
And that which is *ya*, *ca*, *tā*, *ca*, *tathā*, *śva*, *śā*, *ca*, *yaśca*, and *va* extended (*āyataḥ*). (3-131)
Dhra, cya, and likewise tā, tā, śrī, ā, and again caya;
tā, ca, nā, ca, svarācchādya, yaḥ, antāḥ, and na indeed. (3-132)
The letter A and the letter Ma, likewise Namaṇa and Pitā;
La and Pa, Ya and again Lācabha. (3.133)
Ṇecapiśca, likewise Rūca, Pañcapuśca, and Yaeva; Ṣvāca, Puśca, likewise Ṇa, and Viśvarūparbhaga. || 3-134 ||
And Bhā, Gha, Ca, Cha, and Ṣva;
Caru and Pu; Dyo and Ātma; and Vyocana—these indeed are they. (3.135)
Cecanā, and likewise taśca, ceceva, and today's vowels; yaścarā, and likewise paśca, raścaya, and likewise yaśca. || 3-136 ||
The letter *me*, the letter *ca*, the letter *pa*, and likewise *pā*; *parū*, *niścadyo*, and those which are *ta* and *paścatiṇāccivāḥ*. (3-137)
The letter *na* and the vowel to be uttered, *ra*, *pa*, and *ca* as well as *ndra*;
likewise *ru*, *ṣṇu*, and *pi*, then *ā* and *pu*, and finally *ra* and *ka*. (3-138)
The syllables *sya*, *naiḥ*, *tathā*, *sā*, *carvaḥ*, *saḥ*, *daḥ*, *eva*, *ca*, *praḥ*, *khaśca*, *sutau*, *hū*-kāra, *carvaḥ*, and *eva* [are the seed-syllables]. || 3-139 ||
In the tenth enclosure, one hundred and twelve [deities] are proclaimed;
Ka, Cha, Ma, along with the Visarga, and Naya, Īśa, Cara, and Āyata. (3.140)
The letter *yā*, likewise the letter *kā*, the letter *rā*, and the letter *ha* are long;
*na*, *cch*, *dhyā*, as well as *ne*, *gi*, *tyā*, *tyo*, and *ni* are likewise short. (3.141)
Tā, ca, sthi, ca, tathā, sa, ca, ma, ca, pī, ca, ga, eva, ca; yo, balaṃ, ca, nayau, nā, ca, ṇe, ca, vi, ca, tathā, punaḥ. || 3-142 ||
Then there is the syllable *ru*, likewise *no*, *ma*, and *secanama*; after that, *ṇe*, *virūtau*, and again *re*. (3.143)
The others are *vi*, *ru*, *ntā*, *śca*, *na*, *śca*, *ya*, *eva*, *ca*; then *ta*, *śca*, *na*, *śca*, *akāra*, *tma*, *śca*, *vi*, *śca*, *vadhū*, and again *punaḥ*. (3-144)
Agni, Svara, Ādya, Upaśvarūpa, Nityojas, Savisarga, and likewise the Mathas once again. (3.145)
Then *praśca*, *viśca*, as well as *rūnau* and *viśvarūca* were formed;
likewise *vyā*, *viśca*, *vyomin*, *smāca*, and *praścati*. (3-146)
Śikṣa, kṣmā, and likewise sūc, śabda, and also śaścan; jña and ga, and likewise piṃ, ga, ta, and also paru. (3-147)
One should specifically place *tu*, *ṣi*, *sā*, *ta*, *sthi*, *carva*, *pūta*, *stu*, and *anau*. (3.148)
In the *Daśaikāvaraṇa*, sixteen syllables of one hundred [units] each are taught:
the letter *ka*, *vi*, *lau*, and likewise *a* with the head of *ya*. (3.149)
The letters gha, ma, na, and ya; ja, ña, ca, and ṣa;
as well as ra, pa, ta, and ya—these indeed are the *pagas* for the sake of the *śī*. || 3.150 ||
The letter *ja*, the syllable *yaś*, the syllable *nāś*, and the letter *ī* are the initial syllables;
then follows the *praṇava* with its *visarga*, and thereafter the expansion of the letter *ma*.
Pāruti, kṛkāra, praścaṇa, and virūrakas; haṃsa, abhyasvara, and that which moves from ka to āyata. (3.152)
The letter *a* at the beginning, the vowels (*svarāḥ*), and likewise again the *ṇecavi*;
the *rurthau* at the beginning, the vowels, and the letter *yartha* at the beginning. (3-153)
At the great festival, there are many [mantras], as well as the *praṇava* itself;
likewise, the syllable *rū* with the *visarga*, and again the *praṇava*.
The four *sū* syllables, as well as the four *nā* syllables; likewise, *na* after *denādeḥ*, and *na* at the end of *akāra*. || 3-155 ||
The letter *a* and the letter *sma*, the letter *a* at the end and *ar* as well; *ā* and the vowel *o*, and likewise *ma* and *u* and *śi*. (3.156)
And likewise ṣāṃ, śāṃ, vāṃ, lāṃ, and yāṃ; and also with okāra, as well as ne, vi, cavyā, and ma. || 3-157 ||
Vyokāra, likewise ūca, raca, and ākāra; praṇava, vaya, maśca, naccama, and eva. (3.158)
Śi, śca, ḍa, rca, va, sau, caiva, rva, śa, śca, va, and eva—
these are declared in the twelfth enclosure, numbering one hundred and twenty in sequence.
Ya, Ca, Na, and likewise Ra, Vāca, Pāca, and Eva; Ya-kāra, Hyāguvā, and Devamāyā as well. (3.160)
And *noḥ*, *paścāt*, *prayadyuḥ*, *vidham*, *drāk*, *eva*, *kāḥ*, as well as *vaḥ*, *siḥ*, *yathā*, *daḥ*, *bhūyaḥ*, *bhyaḥ*, and *ca*—and indeed *ca*. (3.161)
Reca, Ghoṇe, Virudra, Viścaya, Āyata, Viścaṇe, Piśca, Rūpaddha, and then Śuyau. (3-162)
And those which are *gu* and *tathā*, likewise *ṇecaru* and *māyā*, as well as *yathau*; and likewise *mācaṇe*, *rūti*, and again the letters beginning with *ka*. (3.163)
The vowels *deya* and *vyā*, the first [vowel] *e*, *va*, *ca*, *bha*, and these two [consonants];
then *vācamā*, *vākane*, *kāne*, and the first vowel thereafter. (3-164)
Then *tryaṃ* and *saś*, followed by *dīpa* with the *visarga*, and *va* with the *visarga*; likewise, the syllable *ta*, the *praṇava*, and *na* with the *visarga*. (3.165)
The letter *ja* is the illuminator, and the letter *ha* with the visarga is the agent;
likewise, the letter *ma*, the *praṇava*, and the *praṇava* with the visarga [are also so]. (3.166)
The Praṇava, and likewise Dā, Saśca, Tuśca, Tapa, then Ta, Bhāva, Svākāra, and Ma with the Visarga. (3-167)
Na, ca, pe, ca, as well as bha, pra, śca, gaccha, and eva; likewise, the letter ma with the visarga, tā, and pa. || 3-168 ||
Na-kāra and śā-drau, kṣaṃ-kāra joined with the visarga of kṣavi;
tvaiṃ and cakṣūṃ, likewise kṣaṃ, tvāṃ, kṣāṃ, and also hāṃ and hāḥ. || 3.169 ||
In the thirteenth enclosure, one hundred and twenty-eight [deities] are proclaimed:
Ya, Cma, Oś, Ca, Ru, Va, Cka, and Āy.
*rā*, *cayā*, *ktyā*, *śa*, *ca*, *diśca*, *mākāra* itself, *eva*, *ca*;
likewise *laye*, *ktā*, *tathā*, *mūca*, *taśca*, *jādyo*, and *sa* itself. (3-171)
Candra, Naścadhārā, Viśvasu, Aṣṭha, Riścava, Aṇya, Reca, Carava, and likewise Caravau. (3-172)

The letter *ya*, the letter *gha*, the letter *ya*, and the letter *a*; then again, the letter *ra*, the letter *śca*, the letter *agni* (the letter *i*), as well as the letter *la*, the letter *kā*, and the letter *ma* joined with the visarga.
And *niyavāśi*, *haukāra*, and likewise *praṇava* in an instant; *pi*, *rū*, *vī*, and then *śidāsā*. (3-174)
Pā, śi, dā, sā, ca, ṇe, kā, raḥ, pi, śca, ru, ya, na, e, va, ca; yā, nā, śca, ma, hi, mau, dhī, ye, vā, śca, śi, śca, ta, tha, i, va, ca. || 3-175 ||
Dāsa, Sarva, Cauca, Śiścava, Ha, Eva, Noyani, Na, Dhanis, and Adyasvara. (3-176)
The syllables *maṃ*, *pa*, *dhā*, *ta*, *tī*, *ra*, followed by a vowel;
and *na*, *ca*, *ma*, *sa*, *no*, *sa*, *śā*, *nti*, *śā*, *yā*—these are the illuminators (*dīpaka*). (3.177)
Then one should place the letter *śa* together with the *visarga* and the letter *va*;
then, by means of the letter *ma* together with the *visarga*, one should lead [the letters] *na*, *ya*, and *pa*. (3.178)
*Drāc* and *ruś* with the visarga, as well as *ma*, *ka*, *na*, and *ca*; likewise, *mṛś* and *aś* with the visarga, as well as *ma*, *ka*, *na*, and *ca*. (3.179)
The letter *ma*, the letter *va*, and the letter *sa* together with the *visarga*;
likewise *ma* again; and *na*, *na*, and *ne*, and furthermore *ātman*. (3.180)
That [syllable] with the visarga, the letter *ma*, and the letter *na*—
these are then declared in the fourteenth enclosure as the thirty-sixth and the hundredth syllables.
Having thus arranged the phonemes, one should begin the extraction;
I shall now describe the form of Saudha, endowed with five faces.
He should be joined with fifteen eyes and adorned with ten arms;
his hands should display the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and he should be endowed with eight weapons.
Clad in garments of fine silk and adorned with all ornaments, seated upon a lotus throne—this is called the Prāsāda [form]. || 3-184 ||
He should have one face and three eyes, four arms, and a beautiful form;
he is the god wearing divine garments and adorned with divine ornaments.
Thus, having been described as Brahmā, the characteristics of Rudra are now stated:
he has four faces, eight arms, and is endowed with twelve eyes. (3.186)
His hands should display the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness; he should hold a trident and a goad, be adorned with all ornaments, and wear a white sacred thread.
One should especially meditate upon his red form, clad in linen garments,
during the transit of the sun, at the equinoxes, at the solstices, and under one's birth asterism.
At the conclusion of initiation and consecration, during famine, when there are ill omens, during an earthquake, a conflagration, or when afflicted by fever, Āryās, and other such calamities; (3.189)
One should bathe Śiva with cow’s milk, or scented water, or ghee, or honey, or even coconut water, while reciting the Rudra mantra. (3.190)
The sin committed over seven lifetimes by the patron is destroyed;
this mantra of all the gods is thus considered to be twofold. (3.191)
In one's own name, however, the first letter of the *ṛc*s is that which belongs to Agni;
joined with the *bindu* and the *nāda*, it is the root mantra for all. (3.192)
For thus the limbs would be long; indeed, they are proclaimed as being six limbs.
The Astra-mantra is joined with the Visarga, while the five Brahmans are indeed short vowels.
Just as the color, so too is the form; this is what is enjoined in this mantra.
Indeed, this is the mantra for all of them, for Śiva, the Supreme Self. (3-194)
This extraction of the mantra, which bestows all accomplishments and should be employed in every rite, has been declared; now listen to the rules for purification and sipping water (ācamana).
Thus ends the third chapter, concerning the extraction of the mantra.
(p. 23) Now begins the chapter on purification and ritual sipping (ācamana).
Hereafter, I shall fully explain the characteristics of purification and ritual sipping for the benefit of practitioners who follow the duties of the four stages of life (āśrama). 4-1.
During the Brāhma-muhūrta, the wise man should indeed contemplate Śiva with his mind; for three quarters of that hour—lasting three ghaṭikās—are radiant day after day.
The *muhūrta* known as Brāhmya is declared among my reckonings;
having risen and gone outside the village, one should perform the purification of impurity.
Having placed the sun to his right, he should discharge feces and urine;
at night, facing south, he should place a blade of grass upon the ground.
A wise man should place the sacred thread either on his hand or at the root of his ear;
having wrapped it around his head there, he should remain upright without causing it to sag.
Facing the sun, or toward water, fire, the moon, a cow, or a Brahmin;
or near a temple, at a well, in a cow-pen, or in ashes. (4–6)
In a field, in the shade of a tree, in a river, or even within a lake; near a sacred tree (caityavṛkṣa), or at the shore of the ocean. (4.7)
A man should not perform both [actions] at a crossroads or in the midst of a planetary assembly.
Holding the penis with the left hand, he should take a lump of clay in the right hand. (4.8)
Having approached pure water, one should thereafter perform purification;
the penis [should be cleansed] once with earth, to the extent of the measure of an akṣa fruit.
Having thus applied [the earth] everywhere,
one should afterwards apply it to the feet ten times with the left hand, and seven times with both hands.
One should always purify [the teeth] with water; this is prescribed for householders.
It has been stated that for students (brahmacārins), this [period] is double that of householders.
For those who have renounced, the quantity [of water] should be threefold, or fourfold for ascetics;
one should practice purification to whatever extent there is purity of mind. (4.12)
Having risen from that place, one should indeed perform the sipping of water (ācamana) elsewhere;
having washed both hands and feet in the sequence beginning with the right. 4-13.
He should perform all ritual acts with his hand holding the purifier (pavitraka);
on land, he should place his right foot forward and his left foot in the water.
Having neither looked at the navel nor the directions, and having formed the hand like a cow’s ear, one drinks there the water that is silent and which has submerged a *māṣa* bean. (4.15)
Just as one should touch the mouth with the thumb after drinking the three [substances], so too,
having touched the face with the hand, there should be sprinkling with water on the feet.
A wise person should touch the two eyes with the thumb and the ring finger.
Then, one should touch the nose again with the thumb and the index finger.
One should touch the two ears with the thumb and the little finger;
when that triad is drunk, it serves for the satisfaction of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas.
For the sake of laughter at the Atharvavedin, one should touch his mouth twice;
then, having sprinkled both feet, [one does so] for the satisfaction of the seven seers.
[He placed] the head, the face, the two eyes, the two ears, and the supreme moon with his eye;
likewise, the two arms, the navel, the heart, Indra, Viṣṇu, and Agni.
When one is near food, phlegm, or excrement, perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) immediately;
after touching the thumb to the nose, the wise man should then perform the ācamana.
Thus has the ritual of invocation been declared; now hear the procedure for the bath.
Thus ends the fourth chapter on purity and ritual sipping of water.
Now begins the chapter on bathing.
Hereafter, I shall fully describe the supreme bathing that removes sin;
there are five types of baths for Brahmins for the sake of the purification of those who are deficient.
Bathing is of five kinds: that of Varuṇa, that of Agni, the celestial, that of Vāyu, and the mental.
Bathing with water is the bath of Varuṇa; it becomes the bath of Agni when performed with ashes.
Having seen the divine [water] with heat, [the wind], and that which is from dust and cows,
and having performed the measurement with mantras as it has been taught— these are proclaimed as the five baths.
I shall describe the Vāruṇa and Āgneya [rites]; listen to that truth, O Gajānana.
They are of four kinds: performed at a river, a pond, a lake, or even a well.
(25) O lotus-faced one, one should not perform bathing in a well when it is possible to do so in a step-well or similar body of water;
nor should one bathe in a tank when a river is available. 5-5.

A tank is ten times more meritorious than a well; a river is ten times more meritorious than a tank; and rivers that flow toward the ocean are ten times more meritorious than those [ordinary] rivers. (5–6)
The preceptor should proceed toward the east or the north for the purpose of bathing;
bathing while facing the east is said to yield a hundredfold merit.
Even there, the southern bank brings infinite fruit;
so too does water, whether pure or impure, when it is near a temple of Śiva.
One should know that [river] as Śivagaṅgā because of its water being the abode of Śiva;
having approached their sacred ford (tīrtha), one should especially perform a ritual bath there.
Seated comfortably in a clean place, facing either the east or the north, one should perform the cleansing of the teeth using the wood of the *plakṣa*, *udumbara*, or *nimba* trees. (5.10)
Having first performed the cleansing bath (malasnāna), one should thereafter perform the ritual bath (vidhisnāna);
then, using substances that cause whiteness, such as chalk and the like, one should rub the limbs and minor parts of the body.
This is declared to be the impure bath; now hear about the mantra-bath.
[It is performed] with fish, frogs, snakes, and other such aquatic creatures. (5.12)
Therefore, one should always consume water, especially that which is free from defects;
however, for the sake of pacifying any remaining faults, one should prepare a *śivatīrtha* (an auspicious bathing place).
The practitioner should take pure earth, measuring one cubit on all four sides and purified with the syllables *huṃ phaṭ*. (5.14)
The mantra-practitioner should establish [the vessel] with Sadyojāta, sprinkle it with Vāmadeva,
touch it with Aghora, and divide it into three parts with Puruṣa.
With the mantra of Īśāna, one should consecrate each [of the four] individually: first with the eastern, then the southern, likewise the northern, and finally the northeastern.
Having recited the Brahmaśiva weapon-mantra, one should perform the placement (nyāsa) in the sequence starting from the east;
furthermore, one should cast that portion over which the weapon-mantra has been recited into the ten directions.
One should cast that portion which was recited for Śiva into the midst of the sacred bathing place (tīrtha),
consecrated with the mantra "phaṭ" and by means of the application of the Nārāca weapon.
(26) The subtle defects that exist in the water shall be eradicated;
by half of the *brahmajapta* [mantra], one should draw [the power] into one's own limbs. (5-19)
Having touched the head, face, heart, feet, and private parts respectively with half of the remainder, and having bathed, he should pierce [the body] again and again.
Having sipped water, one should then bathe in the midst of the Śiva-tīrtha;
for there are indeed five sacred sites (tīrthas) in both hands of the twice-born.
The Brahma, Agni, Pitṛ, Deva, and Ṛṣi tīrthas are fivefold:
the Brahma-tīrtha is at the base of the thumb, and the Agni-tīrtha is in the middle of the fingers. (5.22)
The space between the forefinger and the thumb is called the ancestral (paitraka) tīrtha;
at the base of the fingers, however, the divine (daivika) tīrtha is said to be located.
One should assign the Ṛṣitīrtha on the tip of the finger, and the five deities:
Agni, Vāyu, Prajāpatyadhyakṣa, Tīkṣṇaraśmi, and Purandara. (5.24)
The wise one should place [the mantras] in order, established upon the thumb and the other fingers;
he should drink with the *brahmatīrtha* and perform sprinkling with the *agnitīrtha*.
With the ritual honors due to a universal monarch, using fragrant *āmalaka* fruits and other such items,
one should consecrate the face with the "face-seal" (*vaktramudrā*) at the conclusion of the water-play.

Having performed the ritual bath with the limbs of Śiva-Brahman and the limbs of Vidyā, the wise one should perform the *aghamarṣaṇa* rite with the five Brahmans, the limbs of Śiva, and the three-footed mantra.
Having closed one's eyes within the water, one should not show any part of the body at all;
then one may show the sacred bathing place (tīrtha), or else show the face while submerged.
That which is called "submerged in the mouth" (mukhamagna) becomes one hundred and fifty in sequence;
half-an-aṅga is one thousand and a half, while a nimnagā is said to be ten million.
Having gone forth while engaged in meditation and having performed the ritual rinsing (ācamana) according to the true method in due order,
one should then recite "Sūrya" in the morning, and at midday, one should utter "Āpaḥ."
Having recited "Sāye 'gniśca," one should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) in the prescribed order;
then, having sprinkled [the body] with the verse "Āpo hi ṣṭhā," one should pour water while reciting the Sāvitrī.
Having stood, one should perform the twilight worship (saṃdhyopāsana) in the morning with pure palms joined;
standing during the midday [worship] for one who is seated, and seated during the evening [worship].
One should recite [the mantra] at least once, as much as possible, up to the limit of breath-control (prāṇāyāma);
however, one should always recite the Sāvitrī eight times during the periods of the twilights (saṃdhyā). (5.33)
"O Mitra, come to this [place] with truth"—thus is he constantly addressed.
With these three mantras, the wise one should perform worship at the beginning of the morning.
The wise man should satisfy the gods, the ṛṣis, and the ancestors with the Vāma, Aghora, and Sadyojāta mantras, respectively, in the east, north, and south.
Bathing at night is not recommended because the sun is not visible;
for the river at night is constantly flowing with the blood of Vṛtra.
Therefore, one should never perform bathing or drinking [of water] at night; however, one may indeed take it for the sake of the gods or for oneself.
The best of teachers should cause [the disciple] to purify gold either by looking at it, or by [immersing] water [in it], or even by performing three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma). (5.38)
O God, since water-purification is not possible for bathing at night, one should therefore take a lamp for the sake of the deity and indeed for oneself. (5.39)
One should always perform this practice in this manner and then recite the Śiva-mantra;
having touched water with the *ṛc*s that have been recited, one should sprinkle it in sequence from the head down to the feet.
The wise one should recite the Śiva-mantra according to his capacity along with the Brahma-aṅgas; then, by means of the mantra ending in *phaṭ*, he should withdraw the Śiva-tīrtha.
Having taken up a clean cloth, one should discard the wet garment;
then, one should proceed to the abode of Śiva and perform a circumambulation.
Having prostrated like a staff upon the ground before Śiva, the supreme cause,
wherever a pair of door-panels is desired at the opening of the mouth— || 5-43 ||
In each of those door panels, one should worship nine deities;
one should arrange the serpent and the bird in order, above and below.
Having specially established that [deity] in the center of the *skandha*-board, one should worship it with its own initial syllable and with perfumes, flowers, and so forth. (5.45)

Having performed the opening of the door with the weapon-mantra (astramantra) up to the end of the visualization (atimāna), one should display the mudrā and enter toward the pavilion (maṇḍapa). (5.46)
Then, having bound the *śodhanī* [mudrā], one should purify with the syllable *huṃ*.
This is declared to be the water bath (*jalasnāna*); now hear about the ash bath (*bhasmasnāna*).
Thus ends the fifth chapter, on bathing.
Now begins the chapter on the ash-bath (bhasmasnāna). Hereafter, I shall fully explain the supreme procedure for the ash-bath,
which brings prosperity, is purifying, and serves as a necklace and ornament.
This merit, which brings mastery over the world and destroys sin day by day,
[is such that] by the will of Śiva, cows have descended from the city of Śiva to the fivefold earth.
From the Ocean of Milk, the best of seas, as it was being churned by the gods and the asuras,
five cows were born, who are the mothers of all the worlds.
Nandā, Subhadrā, Surabhi, Suśīlā, and likewise Sumanā;
Kapilā, Kṛṣṇā, Śvetā, as well as Dhūmrā and Raktā. (6.4)
This description of those beginning with Nandā and ending with Sumanā has been proclaimed for the benefit of all the world and for the propitiation of the gods. (6.5)
The mother-cows stood upon the earth for the purpose of bathing Śiva;
[they provided] the cow-dung, the yellow pigment (rocanā), the urine, the milk, the curd, and the ghee of the cows.
Indeed, the six limbs are pure and bring about all accomplishments;
through cows sacrifices proceed, and the gods are established in cows. (6–7)
The Vedas, along with their six auxiliary limbs and the methods of Pada and Krama recitation, were vomited forth by the cows;
at the base of the cows' horns, Brahmā and Viṣṇu are eternally stationed.
At the tip of the horn are all sacred fords, both stationary and moving;
in the middle of the head am I, surrounded by those beings together with me.
O child, the Tattva-brother is especially situated on the forehead;
the two Nāgas, Kambala and Aśvatara, are stationed in the nostrils. (6.10)
The Aśvinī deities are in the two ears; the Moon and the Sun are in the two eyes;
the Marut deities are in the teeth; and Varuṇa resides in the tongue.
Sarasvatī resides in the *huṃ* syllable; Yama and Yakṣa are in the two cheeks;
the two twilights are in the two lips; and the Moon is situated in the neck.
The Gandharvas are in the centers of the city, and the five [elements] are at the front of the city.
In the western corners of the ancient [city], there was likewise a lake called Gaṇāhya.
The Rudras reside in the channels, while the Vāyus are in all the joints;
the Pītas are situated on the hips, and Umā resides in the chest.
Prosperity is always present in the drinking of [cow's] urine; Dharma has taken refuge in the tail; the rays of the sun are the hairs; the Ganges herself is in the cow's urine. (6.15)
And likewise all the sages are stationed upon the tips of his body hairs;
O Gajānana, the earth has arisen within his belly, as have all living beings.
The four oceans are full of cows, which are the clouds; O Lord of all obstacles, you have resided among the cows just as [the world] is established therein.
Whatever is given, offered in sacrifice, consumed, or exists as the entire world of moving and non-moving beings—all that resides in cows.
One should take the cow's urine from a Kapila cow and the cow dung from a black cow.
Milk is prescribed for the white-colored [cow], and curd for the smoke-colored;
ghee is to be taken from the red-colored one, while yellow pigment (rocanā) is used for all colors.
From cow’s urine, guggulu was born—fragrant and pleasing to behold;
it is the food of all the gods, and especially of Śiva.
The glorious Bilva tree, beloved of Śiva, has arisen from cow dung;
the goddess Śrī dwells there with a lotus in her hand, and for that reason it is called the Śrīvṛkṣa (the Tree of Fortune).
The seeds of blue and red lotuses are born again from cow dung;
whatever seed there may be in the world should be known as originating from milk.
From curd all beings are born for the sake of auspiciousness and the attainment of their goals;
from ghee, nectar arose, which is most dear to the immortals.
Therefore, one should respectfully bathe Śiva with those [waters] and with the six ancillaries (ṣaḍaṅga).
Gorocanā is auspicious, purifying, and the granter of all desires.
Having thus reflected upon the cows, one should take even cow-dung from ashes;
or, if it has fallen upon the ground, the cow-dung should be taken with the *sadyojāta* mantra. (6.25)
One should indeed dry the lumps with the Vāma mantra, burn them with the Aghora mantra,
and consecrate them with the Puruṣa and Īśāna mantras.
One should place it, combined with *ketakī* flowers, into nine vessels;
or else, the wise should take the ashes from the *agnihotra* fires.
Having first performed the bath with water, one should thereafter perform the ash-bath;
however, when no water is available, the ash-bath is prescribed even before that.

One should perform the ash-bath (bhasmasnāna) with ashes consecrated by the recitation of the Śiva-Brahma-mantras; one should smear the head with the Īśāna mantra and the face with the Tatpuruṣa mantra.
The wise one, having sprinkled the heart with the Bahurūpa mantra and the navel with the Vāma mantra,
should sprinkle all the limbs with the Sadyojāta mantra.
Or, having slept, one should today wear clean garments;
having thoroughly cleansed one's feet and hands, perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) afterwards.
In the absence of smearing with ashes, the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) is prescribed;
all that constitutes sacrificial ritual (ādhvara-karma) is not to be performed without the triple mark.
One should apply the *tripuṇḍra* with the index, middle, and ring fingers;
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra are the presiding deities of the *tripuṇḍra*.
Brahmā himself is in the place of the head, as well as on the forehead and the shoulders;
Vināyaka is in the throat, and likewise Keśava is in the arms.
Īśvara is said to be in the heart, and Prajāpati in the navel;
the Aśvins are in the knees, and likewise the Pañcagaṇas are in the feet.
Whatever merit is gained from bathing at all sacred fords and whatever fruit is obtained from all sacrifices—
that fruit is accomplished, multiplied ten millionfold, by the bath of ashes.
This has been declared as the ash-bath; now hear the section on worship.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, the Chapter on the Ash-Bath.
(p. 31) Now follows the chapter on the ancillaries of worship (arcanāṅga-paṭala).
Therefore, I shall now fully explain the compendium of the ancillaries of worship:
water for the feet, water for sipping, the water-offering (arghya), fragrance, flowers, and incense. (7-1)
The lamp, the offering, and the dance of the Liṅga— these ten,
when combined with the ten limbs, constitute the most excellent worship of Śiva.

Worship ending with the lamp is declared [one type], while worship ending with the food offering (naivedya) is another; worship ending with the propitiatory rite (śāntika), the bali, and the dance is said to be the third kind of worship. (7.3)
Uśīra, sandalwood, dūrvā grass, and white mustard seeds—
this fourfold combination is declared to be the substance for the water for washing the feet (pādya).
Combined with cardamom, cloves, camphor, nutmeg, and the fruits of the *trapuṣa* plant, the five-limbed *ācamana* (sipping water) is accomplished by means of these substances. (7.5)
Water, milk, tips of kuśa grass, barley, white mustard seeds, rice, sesame, and grains— when combined, these are called the eightfold arghya.
They know that *akṣata* consists of barley, rice, white mustard, and *vrīhi* rice;
indeed, *akṣata* is proclaimed to be that which is joined with *vrīhi* rice grains.
Agallochum, sandalwood, costus, and saffron—
these should be combined with camphor in equal parts, or half-parts, or even one-quarter parts.
This has been declared as the fragrant substance; now listen correctly regarding flowers:
white, black, and likewise red correspond to the three qualities, beginning with sattva.
Flowers that are yellow in color, which are mixed with the qualities of *rajas* and *sattva*,
as well as those that are black— such as the blue lotus (*nilotpala*) and others— one should avoid as belonging to *tamas*.
The *nandyāvarta* is prescribed for the forenoon, the *karavīra* for midday,
the *mallikā* is said to be for the evening, and the *dvikarṇikā* for midnight.
The *droṇa*, the white lotus (*śvetapadma*), the *jātī* with many pericarp-filaments,
the *nandyāvarta*, the *śriyāvarta*, the *mandāra*, and the hundred-petaled lotus (*śatapattrika*).
The white Arka, Mālatī, Punnāga, and likewise Kurava—
such flowers as these one should designate as Sāttvika.
The red utpala, as well as the padma, the brhati, the dhurdhuraka, and the flowers of the pāṭalī and the raktapuṣpa— one should designate these as belonging to the rājasa type.
One should likewise prescribe the *karṇikāra*, *dhurta*, *sarala*, and *āragvadha*, as well as other such yellow and non-mishraka (unmixed) substances. (7.15)
The karañja, the vakula, the śirīṣa, and likewise the ketakī;
the lāṅgalī, the vihīta, the bandhūka, and the ḍāḍimī. (7.16)
One should avoid *kiṃśuka*, *madantī*, and water lilies (*kumuda*); nor should one worship the Lord with flowers that are overripe, unripe, or still in bud. (7.17)
One should avoid flowers that have fallen among hair or insects, those entangled in spiderwebs, those that have fallen on their own, and those that are stale. (7.18)
Śamī, bilva, apāmārga, kuśa, dūrvā, and likewise sahā;
nāganandī, rudraparṇī, and the leaves of dhātakī as well. (7.19)
One should especially worship with Bhadrī, Mahābhadrī, and likewise Droṇapatra; however, one should not worship with those that have a pungent odor or are scentless.
Among all species of leaves, the bilva leaf is praised;
likewise, among varieties of flowers, the lotus flower is declared to be the best. (7.21)

During festivals and the like, on processions, and during the acts of serving food, all [ornaments] are prescribed; however, those specifically forbidden must be avoided while those not so mentioned are to be accepted. (7.22)
Thus the flowers have been described; now the incense shall be fully explained. Black agallochum (kṛṣṇāguru) should indeed be used, and it should be prepared with double the [usual] amount.
Sandalwood mixed with a small amount of camphor is said to be "triguṇa";
this incense, named Śītāri, becomes purified when combined with honey. (7.24)
Thus, this incense is supreme, most excellent, and distinguished above all others;
it may be guggulu, or clarified butter, or molasses, or bilva-incense. (7.25)
One should burn well-prepared incense made from either kuṣṭha or sandalwood, or cow’s ghee, or oil, combined with camphor and a wick. (7.26)
The flame of the lamp is distinguished by a length of four or three finger-breadths;
for the Blessed One, Sadāśiva, the God of gods, is ever fond of the lamp. (7-27)
The procedure for the ancillaries of worship has been declared; now hear the procedure for the worship itself.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, on the ancillaries of worship.
(p. 33) Now begins the chapter on the procedure for the worship of Śiva.
Hereafter, I shall fully explain the sequence of the procedure for the worship of Śiva, which removes all sins, is divine, and brings happiness to all the worlds. (8-1)
It bestows prosperity, destroys all obstacles, and increases the kingdom of the king;
furthermore, it is said to be of two kinds: for one's own sake and for the sake of others. (8.2)

One should begin the worship for one's own sake at a momentary [image], a mobile liṅga, on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), in a maṇḍala, or even upon a painted image (kautuka) adorned with devotion. || 8-3 ||
Whether seen in a village or elsewhere in places constructed as abodes of Śiva, worship for the sake of others is prescribed at those stationary liṅgas. (8-4)
Sand, rice, cooked food, river-clay, cow-dung, as well as fresh butter, a rudrākṣa bead, ground sandalwood, and a brush made of kuśa grass. || 8-5 ||
A flower-garland, a finger-snap, and a movement—these are known as the twelve *kṣaṇikas*.
At the end of the worship, the *kṣaṇikas* should be discarded, and one should bring the reality (*tattva*) into one's heart.
The crystal, the one born of gems, the stone, the arrow-liṅga (bāṇaliṅga), and the metal-born are declared to be the movable liṅgas; the sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila) is made of rice grains.
Or, a mandala may be described as being measured by one cubit using sand;
having smeared that area with cow dung, one should draw it provided with eight lotus petals.
That which is known as the *maṇḍala* consists of the worship of twelve images;
that which is known as the *kautuka* is likewise a painting on a wall.

One who is renowned for performing sacrifices for one's own sake should worship according to the prescribed method; however, in the case of a sacrifice for another's sake, it may extend from the offering of lamps up to the final oblation.
This has been explained in general; however, for the sake of others, the specific [practices] are as follows:
the perpetual festival, the perpetual fire-sacrifice, and the worship of the sandals.
One should perform the lustration ceremony at night, as well as singing, dancing, and instrumental music,
to the best of one's ability, before those [images] known as stationary lingas.
When all those aforementioned [rites] have been performed, except for the perpetual festival,
one should perform the remaining rites for one's own sake, omitting the worship of the sandals.
One should perform worship for one's own sake for initiated twice-born men of anuloma birth, and for the sake of others for those who follow the Ādiśaiva tradition, or for their own sake as well.
Situated in the center of the fire-mandala, with flames arising from the seed-syllable of fire, one should burn [the body] like dry wood, starting from the big toe up to the crown of the head. (8-15)
Having contemplated that [the body] has been reduced to ashes, one should then gather it into a mass with the wind [mantra];
one should then visualize the previously mentioned nectar flowing into those ashes.
One should lead the self there with the heart-mantra of Sarvātman; one shall become a divine body, O God. Now hear the ritual placement upon the limbs (aṅganyāsa).
The emanation should proceed thus from the head downwards, while the withdrawal should proceed from the feet upwards;
the placement [of mantras] from the nose to the heart is proclaimed as the ritual of maintenance (sthiti).
Then, one should fashion the head with five [parts] each by means of the fifth [mantra];
therein, one should contemplate the four faces by means of the face-mantra.
There, the fifth face is the universal self by means of the heart;
otherwise, one should visualize it as terrible in the heart, the neck, the shoulders, and below the chest.

One should place those [syllables] on the navel, the belly, and the back, or alternatively, recite them ten times; likewise, one should apply them to the secret organ, the anus, the two thighs, the two knees, and the two shanks.
The wise one should then place the two buttocks, the waist, and the two sides in eight parts;
likewise, he should place the hands, feet, nose, and head on the exterior.
One should place the kṣurikā weapon on the right side of the hip;
then, in sequence, upon the head, the face, the heart, the private parts, and the feet.
One should perform the placement (nyāsa) of the Brahma-mantras, beginning with Īśāna and others, according to the path of emanation;
however, in the rite of placement, one should proceed from the feet upward, beginning with Sadyojāta and others, according to the path of reabsorption.
The placement from the navel up to the heart is proclaimed as the "placement of stability" (sthitinyāsa).
One should place the All-Self (Sarvātman) at the heart and Śiva together with [the other principles] upon the head.
Having placed Jvālinī at the crest-lock (śikhā), the armor (varman) in the middle of the body,
and the weapon (astra) in the regions of the hands, one should perform the five-limbed ritual (pañcāṅga) in the sky.
Having performed the placement of the auxiliary limbs of knowledge as before, one should apply the eye [mantra] to the eyes;
one should then place the principal seed-syllable upon the thirty-two locations of the joints.
One should place the Lord, endowed with thirty-eight digits (kalās), within the heart-lotus;
one should meditate upon the Lord as the Praṇava, unmoving and the size of a thumb.
One should worship with mental flowers, perfumes, incense, lamps, and offerings; indeed, purification of the self is proclaimed as occurring within the heart. (8.29)
Having worshipped the deities of the door in due order with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, one should worship Vāgdevī above the right door-post and Śrī on the left. (8.30)
Having worshipped Vighneśa in the center, the group beginning with Nandi to the south,
and Yamunā and Mahākāla to the left, each by their own names.
Having swept the site and sprinkled it with water, and having performed the binding of the directions (*digbandha*) with the *astra-mantra*,
one should dispel the obstacles (*vighnas*) situated on the earth, in the heavens, and in the intermediate space by means of the *hṛdaya-mantra*.
One should [visualize] those situated on the earth through the gaze of the vital breath (prāṇa), those moving in the intermediate space through the gaze of reality (tattva),
and those stationed in the directions through the gaze of knowledge (jñāna), by means of the mudrā designated by their respective names.
One should worship Brahmā at the station of Brahmā with flowers, perfumes, and so forth, using the *hṛdaya* mantra; thus the purification of the place is accomplished.
O Lord, now hear about the purification of the ritual materials (*dravya*).
