Then, having smeared [the ground] with cow dung, one should arrange the vessels for the ritual materials:
the arghya vessel, a shallow bowl (śarāva), and the vessels for water for the feet and for sipping.

One should wash the water-vessel and the vardhanī with the weapon-mantra (astra-mantra); then, having gazed upon them with the heart-mantra (hṛdaya), one should enclose them with the armor-mantra (kavaca). || 8-36 ||

Having taken up the *arghya* vessel and ignited its interior with the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*), and having touched it, one should meditate upon a white lotus within it, as well as the three mandalas. Recalling the three principles (*tattva*) within them—consisting of Ātman, Vidyā, and Śiva— 8–9. Having recollected those three principles, which consist of Ātman, Vidyā, and Śiva, [one should perform the ritual].
O Śivā, with auspicious water, indeed with the five unprecedented Brahmans.
Having consecrated the lumps consisting of the phonemes of the *kalās* in their proper sequence,
the knower of mantras should cast fragrant flowers and perfumes into the water.

Then, having dropped drop by drop from that water into all the vessels, including those for the ritual substances, everywhere, using kusha grass and the heart-mantra (hṛdaya-aṇu), [he should sprinkle them].
This shall be the purification of the substances; after this follows the purification of the mantras:
the mantras should be joined with the syllable *oṃ* at the beginning and the word of salutation (*namas*) at the end. (8.41)
First having uttered *śiva*, then both *brahmāṅgaka* and so forth, while reciting the *vidyāṅga*, the primary seed-syllable (*bīja*), and the *kṣurikā*. (8.42)
Having meditated upon them as endowed with their respective forms, as before for the purification of the mantra,
they are prescribed to be employed at the time of the ritual action, ending with *svāhā* during the oblation (*havana*).
The classes of mantras beginning with Mālā and those that have been brought forth—this is declared to be the purification of the mantra; hereafter follows the purification of the liṅga.
One should cause the great bell to be sounded with the mantra *huṃ phaṭ*. Having removed the concealing cloth, one should commence the purification of the liṅga. (8.45)
At the commencement of removing the floral offerings (nirmālya), at the commencement of the ritual bath, and at its conclusion;
at the time of incense, at the beginning of the sacrificial oblation (havis), and likewise at its end. || 8.46 ||
One should cause the great bell to be sounded at the conclusion of the perpetual festival, at the end of the dance,
at the time of removing the floral offerings (nirmālya), and especially at the end of the ritual bath.
One should perform [the ritual] at the beginning of the oblation (havis), at the end of the dance, and finally at the end of the earth;
likewise at the commencement of the bath, during the incense offering, and similarly at the conclusion of the oblation.
During times of constant festivals and the like, one should not remove the covering from the cloth-painting (paṭa).
One should offer the heart-offering (hṛdayārghya) that was previously presented to Śiva and then perform the ritual dismissal (visarjana).
The wise preceptor should take the flower with the thumb and forefinger;
he should discard it with the little finger, the ring finger, and the middle finger once it has become stale.
And at the time of dismissal, one should place a flower upon the head;
O best of gurus, the crown of Śiva’s head must never be deprived of a flower.
One should offer the floral remains (nirmālya) from the Piṇḍikeśa to Caṇḍeśa;
one should complete the purification of the Liṅga, ending with the Piṇḍa, in the proper sequence.
Having washed the *liṅga* with the *astra-mantra* and the pedestal with the *pāśupata-mantra*,
one should discard any lingering perfumes and the like from the right hand using water.
Having enumerated the five purifications, one should then perform the preparation of the seat;
having invoked the form upon the seat, these two [steps] are performed on the path.
Having understood [the sequence] through the relationship of the pervaded and the pervader, one should begin the creation:
the lotus arising from the power of will (icchā-śakti), extending from the earth up to Śiva. (8.55)
The egg of the earth is Skanda, and its stalk extends as far as the waters;
that stalk, reaching up to the principle of Pradhāna, is covered with thorns.
The Śambara mantra, beginning with the letter 'a' and ending with the letter 'kṣa', is known as the "thorn" (kaṇṭaka).
It is said that its stalk is dark-blue; this is remembered as the "stalk-thread" (nālasūtra).
From the principle of masculinity (puṃstattva) up to limited agency (kalā), it is endowed with the eight petals of the sacred seats (pīṭha);
indeed, it consists of the feet of Dharma, Jñāna, Vairāgya, and Aiśvarya.
(39) Following the sequence beginning with the southeast (Āgneya), they have fierce fangs in the form of lions;
they are white, red, yellow, and black, possess three eyes, and rest upon vajra-thrones. (8.59)
All of them, facing one another and joined by ten million lions,
possessing terrifying and yet non-terrifying prowess, should be stationed with the *bhārdra* mantra.
Indeed, those endowed with unrighteousness, ignorance, lack of dispassion, and lack of sovereignty are fixed in order from the east to the north, and they possess white radiance.
Having placed the upper cover and the lower cover upon the three qualities (guṇatraya),
O face-born one, the Great Māyā-knot is situated above the pedestal.

One should contemplate the pericarp of that [lotus] as consisting of the reality of Vidyā; indeed, one should contemplate the seed-syllables beginning with Icchā-śakti and the Vidyeśvaras as the petals.
Those mantras are said to be in the filaments; they are established within the Vidyā.
One should fashion the Śakti there with the principal seed-syllable in the filament.
One should know that the base, middle, and tip are white, red, and black respectively; the petal is white, and the pericarp has the luster of gold.
Having indeed sown twenty-five green seeds here, one should then place the array of Śaktis, which resembles molten gold.
And in the filaments and in the center, one should worship Vāmā and the others in order, starting from the east:
Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, Raudrī, Kālī, and Kalavikaraṇī. (8.67)
One should place the goddess Manonmanī in the pericarp—she who transforms power, who destroys power, and whose nature is the subduer of all beings. (8.68)
The solar mandala is in the cup, the lunar mandala is on the filaments,
and Manonmanī is situated upon the fire-mandala at the center of the pericarp.

The seat beginning with *icchā-śakti* and ending with *nāla* is called *anantāsana*; that which ends with the *guṇas*, such as *dharma*, *jñāna*, and so forth, is known as the seat named *siṃha*. (8.70)
O observer of noble vows, that is known as the yogic posture (yogāsana) of the Supreme Lord;
it is the lotus-seat beginning from the pericarp and ending at the filaments. (8.71)
Above the filaments, ending with the *śakti*, is the pericarp (*karṇikā*), the pure seat (*vimalāsana*).
Thus, one should arrange and worship the lotus-seat (*abjāsana*) by means of their respective names.
Having first formed the *mukulī* [mudrā], and after that the *padma* mudrā,
the Brahmin should display the *śaśakarṇī* [mudrā] up to the end of the pericarp (*karṇikā*).
(The image) upon the seat is Sadāśiva, the unsurpassed, endowed with five faces and fifteen eyes. (8.74)
Endowed with ten mighty arms and blazing with eight weapons, he holds in his right hands the gesture of fearlessness, the trident, the axe, the thunderbolt, and the sword. (8.75)
In the left [hands], he holds the boon-granting gesture, the goad, the noose, the bell, and fire;
he resembles clear crystal and consists of thirty-eight digits (kalās).
The supreme [deity] consists of the five Brahmā-limbs, the limbs of knowledge, and the ten seed-syllables;
he wears divine garments and bears matted hair marked with a vajra.
Seated in the bound lotus posture (baddhapadmāsana), with a neck like a conch shell and in the full bloom of youth,
he is endowed with three eyes representing will, knowledge, and action.
Having recognized the deity as the white sacrificial thread (yajñopavīta), both supreme and non-supreme,
and having meditated upon him endowed with all ornaments, one should then invoke him.
One should fashion the Manonmanī [liṅga] according to the circumference at the base of the liṅga;
however, when that [liṅga] is installed, Sadāśiva is indeed present in the mobile [liṅga].
Having thus meditated upon the conceptual form (saṅkalpyamūrti),
and then recollecting the mantra while filling his joined palms (añjali) with flowers, he [should invoke] by means of the vehicle-gesture (vāhanamudrā).
Once it has entered the tip of the heart, one should meditate upon the form of Śiva,
mentally uttering the *praṇava* (Om) and [contemplating him] as endowed with qualities such as omniscience.
He is liberated from all limiting adjuncts, the cause of causes,
inconceivable, immeasurable, the sustainer, and the immutable Lord.
The one of steady intellect should meditate on [the deity] arisen within the Bindu before the stable [Bindu];
the best of teachers should then place it within the center of the self of Sadāśiva. (8.84)
One should worship the Supreme Lord with devotion through the rites of invocation and so forth;
having invoked him with the Sadyojāta mantra, one should establish him by means of the Guhya mantra.
One should meditate upon the presence through the multiform [form], the cessation through the Puruṣa,
and the one complete in all limbs through Īśāna.

One should invoke [the deity] with the rite called *āvāhana* (invocation) and establish it with the *śānta-mudrā* (peaceful gesture). One should effect its presence (*sānnidhya*) with the *dhvaja-mudrā* (banner gesture) and perform the binding (*rodhana*) with the one called *niṣṭhura* (harsh).
Having offered water for the feet with the *hṛdaya-mantra*, then water for sipping (*ācamana*) with the *vaktra-mantra*,
and having offered the *arghya* with the *śiras-mantra* upon the five heads, the wise one [should proceed].
"O Gajānana, without performing the *karanyāsa* and without performing the burning and flooding (*dahanaplāvana*) therein, one should perform everything for the sake of purifying oneself. (8-89)
At the time of invocation, at the conclusion of the worship, and likewise during the rite of dismissal, the wise knower of mantras should offer the *arghya* oblation on these three occasions. (8-90)
One should apply the three fragrances to the *arghya*, the unguent, and the bath;
likewise to the invocation (*āvāhana*), the *arghya*, the water for the feet (*pādya*), the bath, the incense, and the unguent. (8–91)
In the offering of food (naivedya) and in the dismissal (visarga), one should employ eight flowers;
except for the invocation (āvāhana), one should employ water at the seven [other] times.
Having combined the fragrance with the flower, one should join the flower with the fragrance;
having combined the incense with the lamp, one should join the lamp with the lamp.
Having anointed the liṅga with oil produced from sesame seeds, or oil produced by means of a hand-press,
or indeed with cow's ghee, while reciting the *hṛdaya-mantra* (the Heart Sūtra).
One should massage [the area] with rice-flour paste or with turmeric powder,
using the Śiva-mantras, the Piṇḍa-mantras, the Kalā-mantras, and the Māna-mantras.
By means of the thousand-syllable mantra, the ten-syllable mantras pervading space,
the five limbs, the limbs of the Vidyā, and primarily the seed-syllables of the Kṣurikā.
One should consecrate [the image] with floods of water endowed with fragrant flowers;
one should apply cow urine with the Sadyojāta mantra, and cow dung with the Guhyaka (Vāmadeva) mantra.
Having bathed [the image] with milk by means of Bahurūpa, with curd by means of Puruṣa,
and with ghee by means of Īśāna, one should then prepare the pañcagavya all together.
Having taken up the prescribed number [of substances], one should bathe [the deity] with the ten-syllable mantra,
using honey, the juice of sugarcane, and coconut water.
One should bathe [the image] with waters mixed with the bile of a goat and ox while reciting the *hṛdaya* mantra.
Furthermore, regarding the aforementioned substances, if they are not available, one should employ whatever is at hand.
Having rubbed [the image] with turmeric powder, one should bathe it with fragrant water;
then, with the *hṛdaya-mantra*, one should offer clothing, water for sipping (*ācamanīya*), and the respectful offering (*arghya*).
One should worship with various garments such as those made of *dukūla*, *paṭṭa*, and cotton, as well as with fuel-sticks, flower garlands, and leaf-cuttings.
In prosperity, having adorned [the image] with various bodily ornaments such as gold bands and the like, and with golden flowers and white and black blossoms; || 8.103 ||
One should ask forgiveness from the God of gods, who is the limb consisting of consciousness, the substrate, and enjoyment;
likewise, one should perform recitation, praise, prostration, and meditation with faith. (8.104)
Dancing, singing, instrumental music, and the sounding of the great bell—
these are declared to be the components of rhythm (layāṅga) for the worship of the God of gods, performed daily.
One should worship the remaining limbs of enjoyment with the *layas* and *bhāgas*;
one should assign the enclosures (*āvaraṇa*) in sequence according to the path of the five enclosures.
Having worshipped Sadyojāta in the western vessel, Vāmadeva in the north, Aghora in the south, and Puruṣa from the eastern vessel; || 8-107 ||
Having placed Īśāna in the northeastern quarter, one should worship him properly;
likewise, one should separately provide bathing and lamps for those limbs according to their status as limbs.
Then, one should worship the *ātmatattva* (the principle of the self) in the pericarp,
the *vidyātattva* (the principle of knowledge) in the south, the *śivatattva* (the principle of Śiva) in the north, and [the *śaktitattva*] in the center.
One should worship the triad of principles— the self, the inner self, and the supreme self— in their respective places with white and black flowers offered from the heart.
The enclosure of the womb (garbhāvaraṇa) has been described; after that is the enclosure of the Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśāvaraṇa).
One should perform the sacrifice upon the lotus petals outside the enclosure of the womb.
Having worshipped Ananta in the east, one should worship Trimūrti in the southeast;
Sūkṣma in the southern part, and likewise Śrīkaṇṭha in the southwest.
Śivottama is in the western quarter, Śikhaṇḍin in the domain of the wind (the north-west);
likewise, Ekanetra is in the northern quarter, and Ekarudra in the north-eastern quarter.
Thus, having worshipped the second enclosure with the syllable Om and their respective names—
Umā in the north, and Vṛṣan in the eastern part— 8-114.
One should place Gajarāja in the south and Guha in the western direction;
likewise, Mahākāla in the southwest (Nirṛti) and Bhṛṅgīśa from the region of the wind (Vāyu).
Caṇḍeśa is in the direction of Īśāna, and Nandīśa in the region of Agni; [the deities] beginning with Umā and ending with Dikṣumukha are on the petals of the third enclosure.
One should worship Indra and the other guardians of the world in the directions beginning with the east;
one should worship Brahmā in the southern part and Viṣṇu in the north.
Lokeśa is between the two Gaṇas, and Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Umā are to the north;
such is the fourth enclosure. Now hear about the enclosure of the weapons.

In the eight directions, one should worship the excellent vajra and the other [emblems], the wheel, and the lotus in the north, along with the world-protectors and their retinues, using their respective mantras. (8.119)
One should display the seed-syllables and mudrās of the mantras of the womb-obscuration (garbhāvaraṇa);
one should display Kālakaṇṭha for the lords of knowledge (vidyeśas) and the lords of the gaṇas (gaṇeśas). || 8-120 ||
The trident mudrās of the lords of the world and of their weapons have been proclaimed;
at the time of worshipping the deities, the wise one should conceal [them] as follows. (8.121)
For those submerged in evil diseases, for those defiled by their own past actions, for the cruel, for the hunchbacked and others, and likewise for the emaciated; (8.122)

Likewise, it is traditionally taught that [this applies] to those who feign devotion, to revilers, to sinners, and furthermore, to those whose faults are seen and those whose faults are unseen. (8.123)
By the sound of the great bell, the rākṣasas and asuras,
as well as the brahmarākṣasas, piśācas, bhūtas, yakṣas, and lords of the uragas [were struck with fear].
By the sound [of the bell], they go far; by it, the gods come into close proximity.
Incense and lamps should be offered together with the ringing of the bell.
A person, holding a incense burner filled with glowing embers in the right hand and a bell in the left hand, [should proceed].
Always playing instruments that are beautiful and produce deep sounds, the Guru brings peace to the village through the resonance of the *adhūpakhaṇḍā* [flute]. (8-127)
There, the wise one should offer water for sipping (ācamana), and he should mentally or actually display a mirror, a discus, and chowries.

One should display to the God of Gods the seed-gesture (bījamudrā), the salutation-gesture (namaskāramudrā), the bud-gesture (mukulimudrā), the lotus-gesture (padmamudrikā), the one called the banner (dhvajākhyā), and the phallus-gesture (liṅgamudrā). || 8-129 ||
One should worship all the images as forms of Śiva according to the prescribed rule,
having performed the worship of the seat and the coverings, but excluding the worship of the door-keepers.
One should perform daily bathing except when free from greed, and bathe on every festival day;
one should worship the images of Caṇḍeśa and his attendants, excluding other images.
Having worshipped the attendants of Śiva according to the prescribed rule,
one should bathe Śiva and present him with offerings at the time of displaying the mudrās.
Beginning first with the head, and then on the right, left, and back,
as well as the upper part, the knower of mantras should present the fivefold arghya offering.
(On page 44: "With the *sadyoghora* mantra, O Revā, offer the *arghya* ending with the fifth [vowel];
this is declared to be the *apasavya-arghya*, which should be performed constantly at all times of worship. (8.134)
Having offered the *arghya* repeatedly by way of both the left and right paths,
one should offer the upward-facing *arghya* to the front and the back-facing *arghya* to the rear.

One should present the water for the guest-offering (arghya) facing forward with the dismissal of the body, and subsequently cause the food offering (naivedya) to be given facing away, according to the extent of one's resources.
Having offered foods to be chewed and eaten, as well as drinks, along with excellent fruits, clarified butter, and molasses,
and having presented that lamp, one should indeed worship Kamatha daily.

Once that Śiva-fire has been protected, having purified and kindled it on all sides, and having sprinkled it while worshipping with the heart-mantra (hṛdaya), the worship of the world-lords (lokeśas) is then performed according to the tradition.
Having worshipped Śiva in the lotus with the Brahmāṅga mantras below,
he should then offer oblations of ghee-mixed rice, or ghee alone, or even rice.
Either three times for each [deity] or even just once,
one should sprinkle [them] with the sprinkling mantra and then dismiss them.

In this manner, the wise practitioner should perform the daily fire-rite (agnikārya) in the middle, the lowest, and the highest [levels]; indeed, he should perform everything as prescribed for the fire-rite.
Having offered the *parivāra-bali*, one should discard the remains of the offerings (*nirmālya*) and food;
then, having given mouth-perfume and betel leaf, as well as the daily sacred thread (*nityapavitraka*).
Then, for the purpose of removing all defects, having fumigated and sprinkled [the site],
and having recollected the ten seed-syllables, one should place the purifying thread upon it.
When the time for worship has arrived, having removed the sacred thread from the top of the liṅga once the liṅga has been worshipped, one should bring that sacred thread back [to its place].
A perpetual festival should be observed as prescribed by the rules during the three junctions of the day; and the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) should be performed every night, especially so.
Having washed his feet and hands and prostrated with the eight limbs with devotion, having performed three circumambulations and recited the mantra, he should ask for forgiveness. || 8-146 ||
He who transcends the three times and the qualities (guṇas), the eternal Śiva whose nature is time;
he is the sole cause of merit, bringing about arising, persistence, and dissolution. (8.147)
O gracious one, may all my various ascetic practices, performed at all times according to the rules,
be fruitful, unfailing, and complete.
Having recited this mantra, the Guru should say to the Lord, "Forgive me.
This should be done daily at the end of the night, for three quarters of the time and three *ghaṭikās*. (8.149)
The "Brahma-muhūrta" is thus described;
it is said that one should awaken [the assembly] with a great sound in this manner for the sake of auspiciousness. (8.150)
Having performed purification such as bathing and having performed the worship of the Śaiva deities and others, one should begin in due order by looking [at the sun] before its rising.
One watch is the best junction, five nāḍīs is the middling;
the lowest would be half of the middling; one should act according to one's means. (8.152)
That one *ghaṭikā* is for bathing, two *ghaṭikās* for worship,
half a *ghaṭikā* for the food offering (*naivedya*), and then half a *ghaṭikā* for the sacrificial oblation (*bali*).
In that case, the time is prescribed as joined with one and a half *ghaṭikās*;
likewise for the daily festival, the ritual bath, the pure [rite], and the pure dance. (8.154)
Three and a half ghaṭikās are prescribed for worship performed with abundant materials; worship performed without such materials is said to be of middling or inferior duration.
When it is thus worshipped, everything moving and unmoving is worshipped.
Therefore, the worship of the Liṅga should be performed by the wise and the great-souled,
[even more so] than through celibacy, the Vedas, and various auspicious sacrifices.
By means of the Agnihotra sacrifices, by renunciations, and by the well-guarded stages of life (āśramas).

Whatever auspicious fruit is obtained by ascetics through all the triple-staff vows, the Pāśupata and other observances involving clarified butter, and through these and other such practices—[that fruit is attained here]. (8.158)
One who is devoted to the worship of the *liṅga* obtains that fruit well; for one person worships the *liṅga*, while another performs austerities. (8.159)
Between those two, however, he is the superior one who fully worships the Liṅga;
for he wanders through thousands of births among various wombs.
A man devoted to the worship of the Liṅga indeed attains liberation.
The procedure for the worship of Śiva has been declared; now hear the characteristics of the mudrās.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, the procedure for the worship of Śiva.
(p. 46) Now follows the chapter on the characteristics of the mudrās.
Hereafter, I shall fully explain the supreme characteristics of the mudrā; endowed with its proper characteristics, it should be employed at the time of performing rites such as worship. 9-1.
Astrīvaktrī, Mahāmudrā, Śodhanī, and Saṃhāriṇī; Pañcamukhī, Surabhi, Dravyā, and likewise Mukulī. || 9-2 ||
Padmā, Śaśakarṇī, and likewise Śaktibījā;
Āvāhanī, Śāntā, and likewise Manoramadhvajā. (9.3)
Niṣṭhurā, Liṅgamudrā, Gāyatrī, Kālakaṇṭhakā, Śūlamudrā, and Namaskārā—these twenty-three [mudrās] have been proclaimed. || 9-4 ||
Having joined the two fists together, one should quickly extend the hands;
this is known as the *astramudrā*, which strikes fear into all.
Having placed the left hand [on the lap], one should then contract all the fingers of the right hand and bind them with the thumb.
Having firmly pressed the fingers against the left thumb,
this is the mudrā called Vaktra, for the purpose of bathing the Preceptor.
One should touch the two feet with both hands and place both hands upon the head;
this is the Mahāmudrā among these, following the purification of the hands.
Having joined the bases of the hands together and then crossed them over at the region of the heart, one should strike [the palms]; this is the mudrā of the hand, which serves as a purifier.
Having extended the fingers of the right hand with the thumb placed upon the head, and having formed it constantly like a fist, this is known as the Saṃhāriṇī [mudrā]. || 9-10 ||
Having placed the fingers of both hands back-to-back with their tips interlocked,
one should place one finger across them and press down firmly with the two thumbs.
Having raised the middle finger above [the thumb] and the auspicious ring finger,
this is known as the five-faced mudrā of Śaṅkara.
Having formed the braid-bind (veṇībandha) with the hands, the two thumbs are placed together;
the index and middle fingers are joined, as are the little and ring fingers.
Thus, these four pairs, which rain down divine nectar, are called the Surabhi-mudrā for the purpose of purifying substances. || 9-14 ||
Having joined the palms with both hands, one should extend the remaining fingers while the thumbs and ring fingers are joined; this is the *mudrā* known as Dravyarūpiṇī. (9.15)
Having joined the two hands together on one side, with a hollow space in the middle,
one should display the *mukulinī* mudrā, which has the shape of a lotus bud.
That which was previously described as the *amukulī*, with the fingers extended from the region of the heart and opened out in the shape of a lotus, one should display it as the *padmamudrā*.
One should bend the two index fingers and place them at their tips;
the two thumbs should rest upon the heads of those [fingers], being even and thick in the middle.
Having placed [the hand] at the wrist of the left, one should likewise place it on the right;
this mudrā is to be known as the Śaśakarṇī in yogic practice. (9.19)
One should again bend a single index finger against the thumb;
this is renowned as the Śakti-mudrā, and one should employ it for the Śaktis.
Having placed the two hands palms upward, one should form the braid-binding (veṇībandha);
one should insert the two thumbs into the middle of the hollowed palms, which are thus concealed.
Likewise, having repeatedly extended the two little fingers,
one should display the seed-syllable mudrā (bījamudrā) joined with the thumbs at the tips.
This is proclaimed as the *śānti* [mudrā], with the tips of the index fingers joined to the thumbs.
Having formed the hands like a hollowed vessel, one should place the little fingers and the thumbs together. (9.23)
Having made the two root joints equal, this mudrā is known as Īśāvāridhi; the hands should be joined together with palms facing upward, and the little fingers should be raised.
The row of fingers on both hands should be known as *vāmāvalī*; the middle finger should also be curved, and the ring finger should be joined with the palm of one's own hand.
Having extended the two index fingers, one should place the two thumbs at their tips; indeed, those [thumbs] should be bent at their root joints. (9.26)
Known as Manoramā, O Śiva, she bestows union;
one should encircle the tip of the left index finger with the right hand. (9.27)
Having placed the thumb upwards, one should then apply it to the heart;
and one should encircle the left thumb with the three left fingers in succession.
The Dhvaja-mudrā is thus described; it should be employed in yogic rites by placing the two thumbs in the middle and pressing both [fists] together with the two fists.
Or, having joined both hands together, one should apply them firmly;
having formed fists, the two hands should have the thumbs raised and positioned [at the top]. (9-30)

This is the *mudrā* known as the *liṅga*; having performed it according to the instruction of the teacher, all [fingers] are interlaced with one another, joined at the tips of the backs of the hands. (9.30)
One should perform the syllables with the thumb and fingers within the space between the eyebrows;
in the rite of worship, one should employ the Gāyatrī mantra within the Gāyatrī.
Then, having formed a fist with the fingers joined in that position,
one should display the *kālakaṇṭhī* by joining the tips of the two thumbs together.
Having placed them so that they mutually overlap, one should join the palms with the backs;
having raised the two middle fingers, this is proclaimed as the *śūla-mudrā*.
The hands, with fingers constantly joined, should be placed against the region of the heart;
the binding of all [fingers] should be performed by pressing the thumbs together. (9.34)
It should be understood that one performs salutation; having formed the mudrā for the sake of fulfilling the ritual procedure, the instructors should cause all the rites to be performed.
The characteristics of the mudrās have been declared; now listen to the characteristics of the sacrificial oblation (havis).
Thus ends the ninth chapter on the characteristics of the mudrās. 9.
Now follows the chapter on the rules for sacrificial food (haviṣya).
Hereafter, I shall fully explain the supreme rule regarding sacrificial food:
wild rice (nīvāra), wheat, barley, and that which grows from bamboo.
Rice is declared to be the primary substance for the food offering (naivedya) to Śiva;
however, if the aforementioned grains are unavailable, it may be offered with śāli rice.
White rice, great rice, and likewise red rice; black rice, golden rice, and other varieties of rice as well. (10.3)
Having taken rice from either the *śāli* or *vrīhi* varieties for the purpose of preparing the grains,
one should likewise avoid those grains that are defective in color, fragrance, or taste, as they are unfit.
A woman born of the four castes who has sons and a husband, or one born from any one of them, or another woman for whom auspicious rites have been performed—[she should be the officiant]. (10.5)
(49) That preparation of rice, performed with proper devotion, consists of pouring grain into a mortar and heating it until scorched by the rays of the sun. (10.6)
Facing either the east or the north while threshing with a pestle,
one should remove the husks with a winnowing basket and discard the chaff and broken grains.
One should take unbroken grains of rice that are white in color and pure;
one should know that two guñjas make a māṣaka, and twenty māṣakas make a dharaṇa.
Eight *dharaṇas* make one *pala*, and a *pala* is said here to be a handful (*muṣṭi*). Four handfuls make a *pāda*, and four *pādas* make a *prastha*. || 10.9 ||
Four *āḍhakas* shall constitute one *droṇa*; four times that amount, intended for the *dhāmārgava*, one should prepare as the food offering (*naivedya*).
Having worshipped in the morning and evening, as well as at midday,
one should cook two *prasthas* of that [grain] at those times and offer it.
With a single lamp at two times, and two lamps here at night;
according to these stated measures, there are the inferior, mediocre, and lowest-inferior [levels]. (10–12)
At dawn and at midday, one should offer two *prasthas* of rice as an oblation;
in the evening, having worshipped the lamp, its number should be doubled.
One should present two *prasthas* at each of the three times of day.
The Dīpa is said to be fourfold, and those which are likewise doubled.

One should likewise avoid consulting with those of inferior conduct, as well as the sounding of musical instruments, during bathing, eating, traveling, or when wiping away with a concealed cloth. || 10-15 ||
At the time of dawn, one should also cause the sound of musical instruments to be made during the offering of the *bali*.
For the middle class, it is prescribed that at the lower level there be an *āḍhaka* of sacrificial food (*havis*) at midday;
at both times, there should be two *prasthas*, and the lamp should be twenty [in number].
But in the three middle [mandalas], the wise one [should perform it] accompanied by the sound of musical instruments. || 10-17 ||
Then, one should perform the offering of oblations (bali) at the Linga three times a day.
One should know that the middle [offering] is moderate; at the three times, there should be an *āḍhaka* of sacrificial food (*havis*).
At half a watch (*yāma*), it should be half of that, and there should be twenty-four lamps.
But that worship which takes place at midnight is said here to last for half a watch (ardhayāma).
One should perform the ritual baths up to the point of the offering (nivedya), omitting the bali and homa;
or alternatively, one may conclude with the Vāma [rite], having bathed and performed the worship while omitting [the other elements].

At the end of the third watch of the evening, the conclusion of the worship is declared; likewise, the bali offering is prescribed for the three times of day, as well as the flowers and water-offering (arghya) in their proper sequence. (10.21)
Accompanied by the sound of musical instruments and joined with conchs and trumpets,
the daily fire-oblation (nityahoma) at midday is performed while being endowed with the Śiva-mantra.

For the middle [type of vessel], three āḍhakas [of oil] should be used at each of the three times; for the best [type], three āḍhakas at each of the three times, and a lamp combined with seventy [wicks] every half-yāma.
There should be an offering of food three times a day; one should perform the fire-oblation twice a day;
and at all six periods of the day, one should cause it to be proclaimed accompanied by all musical instruments.
Where one should perform the sixfold [rite], there is no fixed calculation of time;
for the highest [deity], the lowest [offering] is prescribed by means of a *droṇa* at the three junctions of the day.
At the half-hour of the half-droṇa, there should be eight hundred lamps;
it is taught that offerings (bali) should be made at the three times of day, accompanied by fire oblations (homa) at those same three times.
There were twenty-four musicians equipped with all kinds of instruments,
thirty-four courtesans, and twenty-four elderly attendants.
One should perform dance at all three times of the day with women endowed with beauty and youth,
accompanied by five teachers and lasting for a period of one watch (yāma).
In that [rite], the best [oblation] is for the middle [class]; the fourfold oblation is for the three [classes].
However, according to the rule, one should offer milk-rice and other items, each with one *droṇa* of rice.
One should provide the stirring-in of the ingredients after having cooked each [portion] separately;
for each *droṇa*, one should offer two hundred lamps during the half-watch (*ardhayāma*). || 10-30 ||
The offering of oblations and fire-sacrifices performed at the three times of day is called the incense for the enemy of cold;
it is accompanied by thirty-four musical instruments and fifty courtesans.
The time for that has been declared; one should perform the dance during the three junctions [of the day].
Two ghaṭikās should be set aside for bathing, and one ghaṭikā should be for worship.
The offering for the purpose of [daily] sustenance should consist of three parts; likewise, the portion for the purpose of the journey should consist of three parts.
Beyond that, for three ghaṭikās, [the rite should proceed] with the auspicious sounds of conch shells and musical instruments.
During the remaining time, one should present the great oblation of foodstuffs and the like, serve them, provide entertainment, and engage in singing and other such activities. (10.34)
p. 51) At this point, at the conclusion of the worship performed during half a watch (yāma), one should perform the closing of the door;
however, the closing of the door may also be performed at other times. || 10-35 ||
That which is declared for the highest [grade] is said to be for the middle; that for the highest-middle is for the highest-middle.
With reference to the highest-of-the-high, the sequence of sacrificial offerings (haviṣya) is now described.
Five droṇas each of cooked foods such as milk-rice (pāyasa) and others should be offered;
for every half-watch (ardhayāma), there should be five hundred lamps.
Three times a day, there shall be offerings and fire-oblations accompanied by fifty musical instruments,
along with milk three times the quantity of rice and combined with plantain fruit.
This milk-rice (pāyasa) is said to consist of a fourth part of split mung beans, provided with eight finger-breadths [of seasoning];
now hear about kṛsarānna.
Having added a fourth part of sesame powder to the rice,
one should cook that ghee— which is a fourth part of the [mixture]— according to the prescribed rule.
This is declared to be *kṛsarānna*; now *gulānna* is described:
one should add twice as much milk as rice, half that amount of sugar, and half that amount of ghee;
this is called *gulānna*.
The wise man should add one-fourth part of mung beans to the rice.
One should carefully add half a portion of fine mung beans along with small coconut fruits;
now I shall describe the "Great Oblation" (mahāhavis), which is the lowest of the low, consisting of one droṇa of grain. || 10-43 ||
Twofold is declared to be the middling, and threefold the most excellent;
likewise, four, five, and sixfold are the three types of middling.
This triad of superior [consecrations] is multiplied by seven, eight, and nine respectively.
Thereafter, O lotus-faced one, I shall describe the *upadaṃśa* (adjuncts); listen to that truth. (10.45)
One should take exactly thirty-two parts of clarified butter;
one should collect sixteen parts of jujube paste and eight parts of curd.
One should offer well-ripened plantains, jackfruit, and mangoes.
Young men should also consume side-dishes; listen as I describe those side-dishes.
The plantain, the pumpkin, the cucumber, the patolika, the kośātakī, the carūpuṣpa, the tip of the cane, and likewise the likuca. || 10-48 ||

The best of teachers, having parched the three fruits (triphalā) of the *prastha* measure, [should likewise prepare] the "vine-spear" (*vallīśūla*), the "end-of-intestines" (*antrānta*), and all other [substances] in equal proportions. (10.49)
The bottle gourd, the coconut, the surana, and the kāravallikā;
likewise, other pure tubers, roots, and fruits that are flavorful. (10.50)
Likewise, pungent, sour, bitter, and sweet [flavors], as well as those with meat-bits, he cooks together with salt. (10.51)
Then, having washed the rice grains thoroughly with water and having purified them especially with the principal seed-mantra (bījamukhya-mantreṇa), || 10.52 ||
This water, measuring one thousand five hundred times the quantity of the rice,
he should place over the fire in the middle of the hearth and worship it with its own seed-syllable.
Upon that [altar], he should likewise place the vessel and kindle the fire with wood infested by worms and accompanied by sparks. (10.54)
Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, one should then wrap it with a cloth;
thereafter, one should kindle the fire with wood inhabited by termites.
One should avoid food that is undercooked, overcooked, or stale;
likewise, one should especially avoid bowls and dishes that have been externally cleansed. (10.56)
On the exterior of all those vessels, the wise man should apply the triple mark (tripuṇḍra) and,
with the mantra "Huṃ," should gradually raise them all up.
Having covered the opening with a cloth, the cook should lift them out;
having sprinkled the path all around, it should be provided with a parasol and a peacock-feather whisk.
Accompanied by the sound of conch shells, one should cause the garland to enter;
having placed it either in the northern or the southern part of the pavilion.
One should not pour the oblation into clarified butter used as a side-dish for the offering;
rather, it should be poured into a vessel made of gold, silver, copper, or even a plantain leaf.
The vessel should be made of pure bell-metal weighing one hundred palas;
it should be provided with three legs, standing upon them, and devoid of any base or support on the ground.
The great vessels, set upon pedestals and made of pure bell-metal, were uniform;
taking in his hand a ladle that was of the proper size and possessed the correct characteristics.
Then, in rites such as the *nābhicaryā*, one should fill the vessel with food;
a fourth part of the sacrificial oblation (*haviṣya*) should be offered to Śiva. (10.63)
Having a form like the full moon, it was covered with gulma and gulā liquor, as well as fruits, clarified butter, curd, or various side dishes.
One should thus offer the sacrificial oblation (*haviṣya*), which bestows all accomplishments, to Śiva alone;
having offered it according to the prescribed rule with the *hṛdaya* mantra. (10.65)
One should offer the bali-oblation with one part out of four parts;
one should perform the rite of homa with one part out of four parts.
The remaining beneficial food should be given to the preceptor alone;
having offered the water for rinsing the mouth with the *hṛdaya* mantra, one should present it to Caṇḍeśa.
Thereafter, one should cause betel to be offered, consisting of one leaf and one fruit;
the leaf should be four times the size of the fruit, mixed with oil and lime-powder.
One should cause the various offerings to be presented with the heart;
however, the remains of Sadāśiva’s offering are not food for human beings.
Or he may cast them into water, such as that of elephants and other animals;
or else, having burned them with fire, the wise man should bury them in the earth. (10.70)
For all [deities], however, the food offering (naivedya) is the meal for the attendants;
even that, when offered through sacrifices, brings no fault in the matter of eating. (10.71)
The characteristics of sacrificial offerings have been declared; now hear the procedure for the fire-ritual (agnikārya). Thus ends the tenth chapter on the rules for sacrificial offerings.
Now begins the chapter on the procedure for the fire-rite (agnikārya).
Hereafter, I shall fully explain the sequence of the fire-rite procedures:
the daily (nitya), the occasional (naimittika), the installation (pratiṣṭhā), and likewise the festival (utsava).
During an eclipse, at the equinox or solstice, upon the sighting of enemies, and during rites for pacification, nourishment, initiation, and the sacred thread ceremony; 11-2.
For those Śaivas, however, one should perform the fire-rites during the ceremonies beginning with conception (garbhādhāna),
as well as during cremation and at times such as the performance of expiatory rites (prāyaścitta).
Whether in a fire-pit (kuṇḍa) or on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), O child, in these two types of fire-offering rites,
the wise one should construct the pit according to the prescribed method of drawing.
(54) If, however, the sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍila*) consists of sand, it should be fresh and one cubit (*hasta*) in extent;
[the purification consists of] cleansing, washing, drying, and likewise heating. (11.5)
One should draw three lines pointing eastward and one line facing north;
the scraping [of the ground] is performed with the Astra-mantra, and the sprinkling with the Kavaca-mantra.
The three lines facing east are Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra;
the line facing north is Śivā—of this there is no doubt.
Having worshipped Śivāgni there with flowers and unbroken grains (akṣata), one should prepare it;
that which arises from a sun-crystal is best, or else that which is produced from wood.
One should bring the fire from a field or from the house of a Vedic scholar into a copper vessel, a clay bowl, or even one made of gold or silver. (11.9)
Or [he may do so] in a new earthen vessel, especially if one is not available;
having placed the fire right there, the best knower of the Tantras [should proceed] in the southeastern direction.
One should purify it with the weapon mantra (astra-mantra) and enclose it with the armor mantra (kavaca).
Having rendered it nectar-like with the principal seed mantra (bīja-mantra), one should meditate upon it.
The practitioner of mantra should worship the Kṣurikā with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings in due order;
he should then place a seat of Darbha grass upon either a sacrificial pit or a leveled altar.
Having specially established Vāgīśvarī in the midst of that [mandala],
the wise man, having bathed after her menses, should meditate upon her with self-restraint.
One should divide the fire-pit by three and deposit it according to the path of yoga;
having established it with the seed-mantra, one should provide purification and the ritual sipping of water (ācamana).

Having bathed [the image] with the *sadyojāta* mantra while recollecting it as being in the three stages of tranquility (*praśānta*), the rite of impregnation (*garbhādhāna*) is thus performed; thereafter follows the rite for the male child in the womb (*garbhapuṃsavana*).
Then one should worship Rudrāṇī with the Vāmadeva mantra;
thus the Puṃsavana rite has been described—now hear about the Sīmanta.
One should perform the birth-rite (jātakarma) with the multiformed *śiras* [mantra], accompanied by perfumes, flowers, and so forth, and with the *astra* mantra recited over the mouth.
It has two faces with the heart [syllable], two nostrils, six eyes, three girdles, three feet, four limbs, and two heads. (11.18)

Wearing the sacred thread (*upavīta*), with matted locks and a crown, mounted upon a bull, with a white face, seven arms, limbs brilliantly radiant, and surrounded by the seven tongues of flame. (11.19)
The tongues are proclaimed to be of seven kinds: golden, yellow, red, black, as well as the radiant (suprabhā), the protruding (atiriktā), and the multiformed (bahurūpā). || 11-20 ||

The tongue in the eastern direction is golden, the one in the west is variegated, and the one situated in the middle is like refined gold; the northern tongue should be red, and the one located in the southern direction is black.

Suprabhā should be the eastern tongue, extremely red and situated in the fire [quarter]; the locations of the tongues are proclaimed to be in the directions beginning with the east within the Bahurūpa [mandala]. (11.22)
This secret form of Agni is proclaimed for the sake of all-pervading peace;
constantly recollecting this form, one should perform the birth-rite (jātakarman).
One should worship that Puruṣṭuta with perfumes and other offerings belonging to Īśa;
this is known as the naming rite (nāmakarman) and is remembered as one of the five sacraments (saṃskāra).
One should strew kuśa grass with tips pointing eastward and northward around the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
Three enclosing sticks (paridhi) are prescribed for the west, south, and north.
If one desires to kindle the fire, one should place it upon the girdle;
to the south, one should prepare a lotus-shaped seat for Brahmā.
Having placed the *praṇītā* water-vessel in the north, with Viṣṇu as its presiding deity,
one should worship Brahmā and Viṣṇu with the primary seed-syllable mantra.
Likewise, the world-protectors (lokapālas) and the preceptor who instructs on the girdle (mekhalā) are to be honored;
as well as the vessel for clarified butter (ājyasthālī), the vessel for the sacrificial porridge (carusthālī), the praṇītā vessel, and the prokṣaṇī vessel.

The wise one should place the sacrificial materials and vessels on the left side upon *darbha* grass; likewise, the pairs for the deities should be arranged two by two, while those for the ancestors should be placed one by one.
The wise man should remove all the vessels and all the materials without exception:
fuel, clarified butter, sacrificial wood, milk, curd, honey, and the cooked rice offerings (carus).
Parched grain flour, sesame, mung bean, māḍhaki, and māṣa;
mustard, dhava, and nivāra; and fruit-cakes—these are the eighteen [items]. (11.31)
All these aforementioned [substances] should be offered in sequence during the daily rites and so forth;
for there are seven [materials], beginning with the daily fuel, used in the ritual of homa.
One should arrange all the sacred waters (tīrthas) in the auspicious vessel of purified water (praṇītā);
on the right, one should place the materials for the fire-oblation (homa) and the sprinkling-water (prokṣaṇī) in their proper order.
Facing either east or north, one should especially perform the fire oblation (*homa*);
thereafter, one should perform the purification of the clarified butter (*ājyaśuddhi*), followed by the circumambulation with fire (*paryagni*) and the sprinkling (*plavana*) in due order. (11.34)
One should perform the sprinkling with *kuśa* grass itself; one should place the tips of the *kuśa* blades there.
The sprinkling is performed everywhere with the mantra beginning with "adite nv ā. (11.35)
Having performed the touching with water, one should heat the flow [of the breath] in the fire;
the wise man should perform twenty-five exhalations while recollecting the seed-syllable of fire.
One should indeed cause the first feeding of solid food (annaprāśana) and other rites to be performed in this manner;
however, for the heart mantra, one should recite it seven times for each of the seven oblations.
One should perform all actions, such as the opening of the mouth and so forth, with the heart-mantra;
for it is thus that [the deity] is generated from the fire of Śiva. Afterwards, one should mentally prepare the sacrificial seat (viṣṭara).
Then, in the midst of the fire, the practitioner of mantra should visualize the lotus of the Lord;
having fashioned it as before, he should then invoke Śiva.
Then, having performed the rites beginning with the invocation according to the previously mentioned procedure,
one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) for Śiva with the ancillaries (aṅgas), the ancillaries of the Vidyā, and likewise with the Brahmans;
[and for] the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśas) and the Guardians of the Quarters (Lokapālas), together with their weapons and powers.
Having worshipped with incense, flowers, and so forth, the wise practitioner should perform the fire oblation (homa).
Having offered ten oblations to Śiva, there should be only one oblation for the others;
one should present all the materials combined into the mouth of Śiva.
Likewise, one should offer oblations of ghee and other substances into the limbs of Śiva-Brahman and the limbs of Vidyā, either a thousand times, half of that, or even half of that again. (11.43)
Having offered one hundred and eight, or twenty-five, or sixteen oblations of the materials at the end with the *vyāhṛtis*, one should then perform the sprinkling (*pariṣecana*).
In this manner, according to the prescribed sequence, the supreme practitioner should perform the fire sacrifice (homa).
He should carefully observe the color, fragrance, sound, smoke, and flame within the fire:
[the flame] having the luster of diamond, gold, or silver, and possessing a radiance equal to vermilion or the moon.
It has the luster of the rising sun and a radiance equal to yellow orpiment.
Resembling the luster of lapis lazuli and naturally tawny, they possess the brilliance of molten iron and gold; thus, ten colors are proclaimed.
Sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, kaccola, and nutmeg are fragrant; likewise, jasmine, trumpet-flower, and the sweet-smelling mandārava. || 11-48 ||
It is beautifully adorned with *uśīra*, *nāga*, *punnāga*, and *campaka* trees;
it resounds with the sounds of tree-trunk drums and the like, echoing with the thunderous roar of clouds and celestial drums. (11.49)
Now hear about the incense that brings about all prosperity, which has the appearance of a kunda flower, the form of dark lac, and is auspicious. (11.50)
The smoke may also take on the appearance of a parrot’s plumage; it may be excellent, shaped like a *svastika*, or rising upwards in the form of an umbrella.
If one’s sacrificial flame resembles a cresting peacock or has the form of a kadamba bud, then for him there is success in the homa; of this there is no doubt. (11.52)
Having understood such auspicious matters as these, the most excellent knower of the tantras should perform [the rite];
then the preceptor, having offered the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with the Śiva-mantra, [should proceed].
Having first dismissed Śiva here, one should afterwards dismiss the fire;
at the conclusion of the fire-rite, however, one should perform the Prāṇāgnihotra.
Beside that, in the fire-hall, the dining place is said to be located;
that place should be smeared with cow dung and especially purified. (11.55)
Having adorned it with flour-dust, provided with a canopy and lamps, [place it] in one auspicious vessel made of copper, bell-metal, or clay. (11.56)
Having combined the remnants from the vessels, one should worship Śiva residing within oneself;
for this very self is the sacrificer, and the intellect is known as his wife. (11.57)
And one should worship well within the fire situated inside the altar of the heart-lotus, having spread the darbha-grass of the body-hairs, [offering] the syllable Om conjoined with Śiva. (11.58)
Having recited [the mantra] and sprinkled [water] all around, the knower of mantras should then sprinkle his feet;
having especially drunk water with the mantra "amṛtōpa," he should proceed.
Joining the ring finger, middle finger, and thumb, one should slowly offer five oblations of food with the five *prāṇa* mantras. (11.60)
Having touched that vessel, the wise man should afterwards eat;
then, having sipped water according to the rule, he should remain facing the sun.
Then, one should touch the abdomen with the Śiva-mantra;
O Lord, [one should likewise touch] the right big toe and the right big toe of the foot. (11.62)
(58) Having recollected Śiva and reciting the heart-mantra, one should thus perform the *culukodaka* (water-sipping) rite for oneself, beginning from the base of the feet. (11.63)
This is perpetually proclaimed as the Prāṇāgnihotra;
by assuming the form of the Teacher, the Lord cuts through the floods of bonds.
Abiding in the *liṅga*, he accepts the worship; abiding in the fire, he accepts the oblation of clarified butter.
This is declared to be the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*); now hear the characteristics of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*).
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, the procedure for the fire-ritual. || 11 ||
Now begins the chapter on the characteristics of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
Hereafter, I shall fully explain the supreme characteristics of the pit;
at the time of the consecration and other festivals, the wise man should cause a pavilion to be constructed.
Especially during the consecration, one should specifically arrange [the deities] in front of the palace,
on the northeastern side, and on the eastern side.
The wise man should establish the kitchen in the southeast and the permanent fire-sanctuary in the south;
and in sacrifices for which no specific locations are mentioned, these prescribed places are ordained.
The pavilion is considered to be of three types: the best should be ten cubits, the middling nine cubits, and the lowest seven cubits. (12.4)
It should be provided with sixteen pillars or even twelve pillars,
extending toward the cardinal and intermediate directions, without any gaps, and possessing the excellence of the sky.
It should be provided with four gates and adorned with four archways;
its height should be equal to a palm tree or else six finger-breadths.
Having encircled it with garlands of *darbha* grass and adorned it with flower garlands,
one should cover it above with canopies and decorate it with strings of pearls.
One should fashion the altar in the center using one-third of that [measurement],
with a height of one cubit and resembling the surface of a mirror.
That [mandala] should be square in the east; in the southeast, it has the shape of the vulva (bhaga);
in the south, it is a half-moon; and in the southwest, it is a triangle.
In the west, a circular pit (kuṇḍa); in the northwest, a six-cornered one;
in the north, a lotus-shaped pit; and in the northeast, an eight-cornered one.
Between the directions of Indra and Śaṅkara (northeast), one should cause a circular *kuṇḍa* to be made;
the *kuṇḍa* for the daily fire-offering (*nityahoma*) should be one cubit in measurement. (12.11)
For fifty oblations, the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) should be the measure of a single handful;
for a hundred, it should be one cubit (ratni); and for a thousand, it should be the size of a span (karasaṃhita).
It should be two cubits for ten thousand oblations, four cubits for one hundred thousand,
six cubits for one million, and eight cubits for ten million oblations.
The width of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) is declared to be eight cubits above the wall;
one should perform the oblations in the pits according to the measurements stated for the unmentioned [types of] offerings.
Now hear the characteristics of the square sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa):
three lines facing east and likewise three facing north.
When laid out in this manner, there shall be a square of four parts;
for all sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas), beginning with the yoni-shaped, indeed originate from the square.
In the corner, one should take a fourth part and draw a circle with that portion;
likewise, one should rotate another [line] in sequence until reaching the limit of half the field.
One should lay down a line from the eastern direction [of the center] to the tip of the ear (the corner) measuring one-seventh of it;
from that point, one should extend two lines so that it becomes like the leaf of an *aśvattha* tree.
Having divided the field into ten parts and set aside two parts,
one should take eight parts in the middle and draw [the shape] like a half-moon.
Having divided the field into five parts, one should place two parts on each side.
With that same measure, one should [draw] two lines joined at their tips.
Having formed three lines there, that is called a triangle;
one should place a single part outside the field divided into eighteen parts.
Therefore, having grasped the center, one should rotate [the cord]; that is known as the circle.
Having divided that field into eight parts, one part on each side is placed outside.
Having first taken the midpoint between those two with a thread as before,
and having drawn six threads around it, a hexagon shall thus be formed here.
Having made it circular as before, one should place a single spoke in the center;
it should be joined with sixteen petals, and the tips of the petals should be shown outward.
This is declared to be the Lotus Pond (padmakuṇḍa), which accomplishes all desires and aims;
one twenty-fourth part [of the area] is situated outside in the cardinal directions.
Having taken [the cord] from the center to the corner, one should apply eight threads;
this is declared to be the "eight-cornered" [mandala], such is the certainty of the scripture. (12.26)
The measurement of the depression (ghāta) shall be equal to the extent of the width;
the girdle (mekhalā) of the pit (kuṇḍa) should be of the same form as the pit itself.
It should be made with three girdles or even with a single girdle;
its height and width should be four finger-breadths according to that measurement.

Thus, there may be a single girdle; now listen to the description of the three-girdled type. The upper part should be four finger-breadths [in width], the middle part should be three finger-breadths, and the lower part is said to be two finger-breadths; this indeed refers to both the width and the height.
One should place the yoni upon the girdle like a leaf of the aśvattha tree.
Its height shall be one finger-breadth, its width four finger-breadths,
its length seven finger-breadths, and its stalk one finger-breadth.
The characteristics of the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) have been declared; if it is an altar (sthaṇḍila), however, it is as described before:
four finger-breadths in height and resembling the surface of a mirror.
One finger-breadth in height and eight finger-breadths in width—such shall be the place for the *praṇītā* vessel; likewise, the *brahmasthāna* should be so.
One should place a square for the *praṇītā* vessel and a lotus for Brahmā;
or, even without these, having merely established them upon the ground, one should worship both.
If, however, the sacrificial ground consists of sand, one should make it one cubit in measure;
the characteristics of a pit (kuṇḍa) of one cubit are thus proclaimed in due order.
Having thus constructed sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) of two cubits and so forth, along with their girdles (mekhalā) and other features,
they should be equal in width and height, increasing by one finger-breadth (aṅgula) at each step.

Having made [the surface] perfectly level all around above the lip of the *kuṇḍa*, [one should fashion] the girdle (*mekhalā*) at a distance of one finger-breadth from the hand [of the altar], O slender-waisted lady. (12.37)
In cases where the measurements are excessive, one should construct [the structure] by increasing it finger-width by finger-width;
alternatively, for a measurement of eight cubits, one may increase it by six or four finger-widths.
The characteristics of the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) have been declared; now hear concerning the daily festival (nityotsava).
Thus ends the twelfth chapter on the characteristics of the sacrificial pits. 12.
(p. 61) Now follows the chapter on the procedure for the daily festival (nityotsava). Hereafter, I shall fully explain the sequence of the procedure for the daily festival.
It is declared that at the conclusion of the three daily worship sessions, an offering (bali) is made for the sacrifice (kratu).
One should also offer an oblation to all of them; therefore, it is remembered as "bali.
[This includes] the yakṣas, rākṣasas, piśācas, bhūtas, and likewise the nāgas. (13.2)
Upon merely hearing that sound of Bali, [the gods] immediately go outside;
therefore, a wise person should perform the daily festival with every effort. (13.3)
To the south of the pavilion, there is a square mandala;
the vessel is said to be made of gold, silver, copper, or bell-metal.
The thickness of the bowl should be four, three, or two barley-corns for the best, middling, and lowest types respectively;
its width should be one cubit, and the lip should be nine finger-breadths.

The solid [pedestal] should consist of nine units and four [units in height]; in the center of the vessel, a lotus is prescribed. One should not have the vessel made of bell-metal with a width of only one-third [of its height].
The elevation of that lotus should be made two finger-breadths, or even one finger-breadth;
outside of it, there should be a pericarp, and then eight petals, half [the size] of that.
Half of that height should be its width, and the tip of the petal should be nine units high;
the vessel should be made circular, measuring twenty finger-breadths in diameter at the center.
The width of the vessel for the lowest [grade] is said to be sixteen finger-breadths.
Having prepared the vessel of Bali in this manner, the wise one should place it within the maṇḍala. (13.9)
Then, the offering (bali) for the liṅga with food at the three times of day is excellent;
the wise know that the midday offering with food is the middling one.
O Gajānana, at midday one should offer food as the linga; this is the lowest [grade].
In the forenoon, one should offer flowers as the linga, and in the evening, rice grains alone.
One should cook rice in sequence such that for the best quality there is one āḍhaka, for the middling half of that, and for the lowest five quarters (pādas). 13-12.
The best of instructors should avoid food that is undercooked or overcooked, too hot or too cold, and that which is excessively sour or salty. 13-13.
Mixed with curds, ghee, and fruit, it should be firmly kneaded until very solid.
Its height should be sixteen finger-breadths, and its base should be twice that.
Above, the circumference should be three finger-breadths, decreasing gradually from there.
One should make the middle [part] twelve finger-breadths high and two finger-breadths wide.
The lowest [measure] is said to be eight finger-breadths, and the upper limit should be one finger-breadth more.
Having placed the Pāśupata weapon, one should contemplate its form there. (13–16)
Three-eyed, four-armed, and fierce, blazing with the tip of his crest-lock, he grants boons and fearlessness; his left hands hold an axe and a trident.
Having thus meditated upon the Pāśupata [deity], the preceptor should worship within the *baliliṅgas* and display the weapon-mudrā (*astramudrā*) and the scripture-mudrā (*śāstramudrā*).

Furthermore, the wise one should specifically display the mudrās of salutation and the lotus, and having worshipped that form with incense, flowers, and so forth, [he should contemplate] the image. (13–19)
In front, one should follow the image as it proceeds, carrying the cutting implements and other tools; the ten weapons should surround it, adorned with all ornaments. (13–20)
Having first performed the ritual bath, the attendants of the eightfold city—wearing white turbans and upper garments, and adorned with white garlands and unguents—[proceeded]. || 13-21 ||
With the sacred grass (pavitra) in his hand, observing silence, and holding a staff only a cubit long,
he was adorned with all ornaments and beautiful in every limb.
One should bear the liṅga upon one's head and especially perform circumambulation;
by the offering of oblations in the forenoon, there shall be delight for Brahmā.
Wearing a red turban and upper garment, and adorned with white garlands and unguents, one should always wear these at midday; this shall be pleasing to me. (13.24)
Wearing a yellow turban and an upper garment, he should offer an arrow for the pleasure of Viṣṇu;
then, facing south, he should sprinkle the disciple while reciting the Hṛdaya mantra.
Having offered incense and flowers, one should place the bowl upon the head, [carrying it] either on a palanquin, in a carriage, or even mounted upon an elephant. (13.26)
Alternatively, one should perform a circumambulation on foot,
accompanied by the sounds of kettledrums, maddala drums, jhallarī cymbals, and victory bells.
Accompanied by the sounds of trumpets, cymbals, conchs, lutes, and flutes, and provided with umbrellas, banners, and adorned with peacock feathers and chowries. (13.28)
It was provided with incense and lamps, adorned above with a canopy,
accompanied by dance and song, and graced by courtesans.
Together with other devotees, accompanied by the sound of hymns of praise, he should first stand with palms joined; then Bhṛṅgiṇī shall fall down. (13.30)
The third is Kadruvādya, and the fourth is Ḍhakkaka;
the fifth is Kayaṭa, and the sixth is Kuñcitāla. || 13-31 ||
The seventh blow should be [performed] there, while the eighth is cut at an irregular point;
having circumambulated the single external pedestal, one performs the circumambulation at the front of the temple.
The *śubhratāla* belongs to Indra, while the *bāddhāvaṇa* belongs to Agni;
the *dviguṇītāla* belongs to Yama, and the *mallatāla* belongs to Nirṛti. (13.33)
The *navatāla* is for Vāraṇī, the *vaināgatālaka* for Vāyu, the *kollikā* is said to be for Soma, and the *ḍhakkarī* for Īśāna. (13.34)
Having performed three circumambulations of the temple with these prescribed rhythmic beats (tāla),
and having thoroughly washed one's feet, one should begin the worship of the sandals (pādukā).
One should especially worship with water for the feet, water for sipping, respectful offerings, perfumes, flowers, and excellent incense, as well as with the first *bali* offering. (13.36)
Then, having dissolved it and subsequently placed it within the eastern maṇḍala,
the knower of mantras should worship it with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, using the heart-mantra.
The wise one should unite Śiva with the previously mentioned mantra for the setting [of the deity],
having worshipped the Lord of the gods with the mudrā known as *namaskāra*.
Having circumambulated three times by way of both the left and the right, one should then prostrate like a staff; this is remembered as the "staff" (daṇḍa) salutation. || 13-39 ||
Afterwards, that which is called the staff (daṇḍa) is heard; one should apply it with eight limbs:
the head, the two knees, the two ears, the chin, and the two arms. (13.40)
One should pay homage with eight limbs; hear now how that is done even with five limbs:
having placed the head, hands, two knees, and the body upon the ground. (13.41)
(64) This five-limbed [prostration] is thus remembered as the triple salutation;
it is declared to be the lowest [form], yet one should perform it according to one's ability. (13.42)
Then one should offer the flowers of the oblation to Caṇḍeśānī;
or else, one should cast the food-liṅga into the water or upon the outer pedestal.
At the conclusion of that, one should perform the *nṛtta* (dance) together with the prescribed ritual;
this is called its *upāṅga*, and it should be performed constantly at the end of the worship.
In a well-adorned pavilion decorated with various ornaments, she proceeded while drums and other instruments were played, [the sounds] being established as auspicious.
The dancer and the drummer are stationed on the right,
while the singer and the flute-player are positioned on the left.
The two teachers are traditionally held to preside over the southern and northern regions respectively;
having bathed well and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) properly, preceded by the application of fragrant substances and other offerings.
Clad in white garments and adorned with white garlands,
they were complete with every ornament and highly skilled in dance and song.
In the morning twilight, there is Gāndhāra; after that, the Ṣāḍava-pañcama.
At midday, there should be Naṭṭarāga, and after that, Kauśika.
If at evening one is instructed in the *ekaka* (single) form, then at midnight the fifth [form] is taught;
one should perform the transition (*sandhi*) according to the dance described by Bharata. || 13-50 ||
When this dance is performed, there will be abundance of food and peace for the world;
ill omens perish, and the obstacles that block men's fields vanish. (13.51)
The presiding deity of the letter Ka is also the bestower of enjoyment and liberation;
having secured the door-bolt, one should establish it within one's own home.
Thus has the perpetual festival been described; now hear about the [special] festival.
This is the thirteenth chapter, concerning the procedure for the perpetual festival. 13.
(p. 65) Now begins the chapter on the ritual for the festival of Śiva (śivotsavavidhi).
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the ritual for the festival of Śiva; listen.
A nine-day [festival] is declared to be the best, while a seven-day one is remembered as the middling.
The five-day festival is declared to be the minimum; thus, the festival is remembered as being of three kinds.
However, if that is not possible, festivals of three days or one day should likewise be performed.
One should begin the hoisting of the banner during the first and third [periods];
however, the hoisting of the banner is not prescribed during the second or during the festival.
Having tripled that day [counting from the start], one should raise the banner at its beginning;
or, being wise, having raised the banner at the beginning of that day doubled.
Or, preceded by the hoisting of the banner or the beating of the drum, the most excellent preceptor should cause [the rite] to be performed at a time threefold or twofold [in duration]. (14.5)
First, having performed the offering of the germinating seeds (aṅkurārpaṇa) at the beginning of the night,
and then having struck the drum, one should thereafter hoist the banner.
On the day following the festival, the most excellent day for the consecration (pratiṣṭhā),
one should commence the purificatory bath (avabhṛtha) in the evening at the time of morning.
"Whether it be night, evening, or morning—this is the certainty of the scripture.
On the ninth day there are eighteen offerings; on the seventh day, however, there are fourteen. (14.8)
In the three, five, and one lunar mansions, the offering consists of ten, six, and two [parts] respectively;
when this is done, the wise man becomes a bringer of peace to the world.
In the months beginning with Kṛttikā, the Śiva festival should conclude with Kṛttikā in the month of Kārttika;
in the months beginning with Mārgaśīrṣa, it should conclude with Ārdrā.
In the month of Pauṣa, it ends with Puṣyā; in the month of Māgha, it ends with Maghā;
in Phālguna, it should end with Uttarā; and in Caitra, it should end with Citrā. || 14-11 ||
In Vaiśākha, it extends to Viśākhā; in Jyeṣṭha, it reaches the end of Mūla;
in Āṣāḍha, it is Uttarāṣāḍhā; and in Śrāvaṇa, it ends with Śravaṇā. || 14.12 ||
Likewise, in the month of Pūrvābhādra, the conclusion of Pūrvābhādra is declared;
at the end of Āśvina, in the month of Aśvayuj, the wise man should perform the festival.
The Śiva festival should be performed in all months up to the Ārdrā constellation;
alternatively, it may be held on the sixth, eighth, or new moon day, or under any other auspicious lunar mansion.

When the king’s pride has dissolved and the commencement of battle is at hand, one should begin [the construction] with a tail equal in width to the main body, or with three tails, or two tails. (14–15)
In the center, having drawn a bull, whether standing or reclining,
it should be provided with a garland of *darbha* grass and adorned with excellent small bells.
Having performed a circumambulation of the village, or a circumambulation of the temple,
[he should offer] bamboo, or betel nut, or sandalwood, jātī, or bilva.
It may be made from *sāla*, *khadira*, *campaka*, *devadāru*, or even a *nālikera* tree; it should be well-polished and a very firm banner.

The length of the temple (prāsāda) should be three times [the width], or twice, or equal to it; this is considered the proper measure for the site of the bull (vṛṣabha), extending up to the boundary of the neck and the pinnacle (śikhara). || 14-19 ||
Likewise, the flagstaff (dhvajadaṇḍa) is prescribed to have a circumference of thirty-six finger-breadths, reaching up to two or three stories, or even to the top of the gate-tower (gopura).
O Lord, for a fine staff, the circumference should be thirty finger-breadths or twenty-four finger-breadths; thus should the measurement from the best to the lowest be taken.
It should be joined with three *ghaṭikās* in width, measuring eight *aṅgulas*;
its thickness should be four *aṅgulas* or perhaps three *aṅgulas*.
Its length should be twelve or sixteen finger-breadths;
having made a hole in the handle, it should be made as smooth as possible. (14.23)
Having placed three *ghaṭikās* [of clay],
one should make the tip of the bamboo tube level with the top of the staff, with that which is situated inside them.
Alternatively, one may fashion a staff that is perfectly steady and fits within the vessel;
the length of the bamboo staff is said to be twelve tālas.
Alternatively, a height of sixteen tālas, or even fourteen tālas,
or ten tālas may be adopted, with a circumference of twelve aṅgulas.
And half of that half again for the mother;
the wise man should bind it with an iron ring for the sake of the mechanism, or, if unavailable, it may be made of wood. (14.27)
At its end, having wound it around a cord, and having doubled it so that it rests upon the base,
one should strike it firmly with the middle finger using a thread.
One should fashion [the image] either between the pedestal (pīṭha) and the gateway (gopura), or in front of the bull,
or within the central necklace (madhyahārā), or even in the middle of the central part and so forth.
Having dug the ground to the depth of one's thighs, one should deposit [the object] right there during the winter season;
having first established a staff and surrounded it with a garland of *darbha* grass. (14.30)
The pedestal for the banner (dhvajapīṭha) is prescribed to be four tālas in width and two tālas in height, resembling the interior of a mirror.
The width should be five *tālas* and the height three *tālas* for the middle type of the highest-of-the-high (*uttamottama*) pedestal, measured from its upper base.
In the middle of those two, eight flag-pedestals (dhvajapīṭha) are prescribed;
there, the wise man should raise the flag by means of a rope-mechanism.
Standing facing the temple, having empowered it with the mantra of the Ghorāstra and having secured it with the flagpole, one should raise it according to the prescribed ritual.
One should construct a square pavilion in front of the temple;
there, one should prepare a sacrificial altar (sthaṇḍila) with pure rice grains.
One should place the trident, which consists of all the gods, upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila);
Rudra shall be in the central petal, and Brahmā in the southern petal.
Then, on the left petal, one should place Viṣṇu, the presiding deity of the three-petaled [lotus];
and on the left side, at the base of the trident, one should assign Jyeṣṭhā and Raudrī.
The *phalaka* has Āskanda as its deity; the *kumbha* there likewise has Varuṇa as its deity;
the *sthalī* has Agni as its deity; and for the *daṇḍa*, it is Sarasvatī.
Pārvatī is said to be the pedestal (pīṭha), and Vasundharā resides in the portion of the ground;
having worshipped [the pedestal] with perfumes and other offerings, one should place the water-pots (kalaśa) in front of it.
In the center, one should place [the image] accompanied by the Vidyeśvaras, with Vṛṣabha as its presiding deity,
together with the *kūrca* grass-bundles, the covers, the weapons, and the golden ornaments.
Having worshipped with perfumes and other offerings using their respective names,
one should place the drum, wrapped in cloth, upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) in front of that [deity].
The drum has Viṣṇu as its deity; the wind-instrument (suṣira) has Vāyu as its deity.
Sound is the form of Brahman, and likewise, the absence of form belongs to Īśvara.
Vāsuki is the leather cord, while Ravi and Candraka are the bracelets;
the Mothers are the seven stakes, and Skanda is the deity of the blows.

Having honored [the deity] with fragrant substances and so forth using the heart-mantra, the wise one should first worship the preceptor (ācārya), and immediately after that, the reciter (vādaka). (14.44)
The preceptor, having struck [the drum] three times with the Vāma mantra,
the player should then strike it, especially according to the *balitāla* rhythm.
One should play the *diśitāla* rhythm accompanied by song, dance, and the like:
"We know the one with the sharp horn; we meditate upon the one whose feet are the Vedas. (14.46)
May that Bull (Vṛṣabha) impel us. Having recollected this mantra and having especially offered salutations, [one should proceed]. (14.47)
One should bathe the image with water-pots containing its root-mantras and offer boiled green gram as an oblation;
