there, the declaration of a meritorious day (*puṇyāha*) should be performed, and then one should cause the sound of kettledrums to be made.
Resounding with the blasts of conchs and drums, filled with song and dance,
adorned with every ornament, and accompanied by a trident.
At the time of circumambulating the village, one should worship the deities of the junctions;
having invoked the guardians of the world (lokapālas), one should especially offer them oblations.
With a delighted mind, the teacher should cause [the disciples] to hear [the teachings] on the days of pilgrimage,
having daily worshipped the trident and the banner with offerings of sacrificial oblations.
Prior to the commencement of the festival, one should have the chariots and other vehicles prepared in due order,
as well as sturdy mechanical swings and likewise colorful mechanical theaters.
He saw mechanical temples and likewise pavilions for mantras;
he saw revolving elephants and mechanical chariots, as well as mechanical lions.
One should especially have a bull fashioned, as well as mechanical devices,
umbrellas adorned with various peacock feathers, and various types of fans.
One should likewise have various umbrellas, banners, and chowries made;
then, having adorned the temple both inside and out. (14.55)
Having arranged the placement of doorways and arches, adorned with plantain and betel-nut trees,
he should construct a very beautiful water-shed (prapā) in front of the temple.
Having gradually decorated the water-shed, which was covered with a canopy, adorned with strings of pearls, and provided with flower garlands; 14.57.
Having wrapped the pillars with cloths and provided them with fruits, flowers, and banners,
one should then construct the sacrificial hall on both sides of where the [central post] was previously excavated.
Or else, it should be performed in the north, or likewise in the northeast or the southeast;
or it should be firmly constructed in a pavilion provided with sixteen pillars.
One should arrange the altar in the center of one part out of nine parts.
One cubit in height, resembling the surface of a mirror.
One should prepare either several sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) or even just one;
having smeared this area with cow dung and scattered various flowers upon it.
With fine rice flour and various well-ground colored powders,
one should likewise fashion there a vajra-hook, a trident, and a wheel.

One should mark [the site] with a lotus, a blue-lotus-marked design, a *nandyāvarta*, a jar-like form, a central moon-like shape, and tree-shaped figures; or specifically, having adorned the left side or the city and its surroundings.
The paths and the side-paths are free from depressions and elevations. || 14-64 ||
Having leveled the ground by means of watering and smearing it, and having adorned it with banners, flags, and likewise with fluttering streamers; 14.65.
With plantain trees, incense lamps, door-pitchers,
and other vessels, along with pitchers containing sprouts and *pālikā* pots, [the area] was adorned on all sides.
One should adorn the pavilion with garments, perfumes, and garlands;
then, from the first day of the festival, one should perform the rite of sowing the germinating seeds (aṅkurārpaṇa).
One should perform it specifically in the same manner as prescribed for the depositing of the sprouts;
then, having prepared a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) made of rice flour in the center of the altar (*vedi*).
Having adorned it with six, five, or four *droṇas* of rice, and then [covered] over that with sesame seeds and *darbha* grass; 14.69.

One should place the Śiva-kumbha in the center, provided with its thread, richly adorned with a kūrca-grass mat and cloth, and endowed with the five jewels; to its left, one should place the Vardhana-vessel.
One should prepare [the vessel] equipped with a cloth and a kūrca, and adorned with gold;
having meditated upon the Lord Sadāśiva, one should place it within the Śiva-kumbha.
Having meditated upon the Manonmanīs, the wise practitioner should place them in the *vardhanī* vessel;
having placed eight jars around it, he should endow them with the Vidyeśvaras.
(70) One should worship the lords of the jars there with their respective mantras—jars provided with strainers, wrapped in cloth, accompanied by gold, and filled with water. || 14.73 ||
One should fashion the form of the image out of iron and so forth, or from wood and paint, using weapons in the tenfold sequence according to the method to be described.
One should worship the weapons all around the altar;
the wise practitioner should place the vajra and the others in the directions starting from the east, proceeding clockwise.
Having placed the wheel on the left and the lotus on the right,
one should worship the forms of the eight auspicious symbols outside the altar.
One should install the trident weapon (śūlāstra) there during the festival in the abode of Yoga;
then, having performed the fire-rite (agnikārya), either nine, five, or one [oblations] again.
For the Ekāgni rite, one should have all the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) constructed either to the east, the north, or the west of the altar; they may be circular or square. || 14.78 ||

Having performed the circumambulation with fire (paryagnikaraṇa), especially around the sacrificial hall, one should scatter barley with the Hṛdaya-mantra and white mustard seeds with the Sadyojāta-mantra.
Having offered sesame seeds with the Īśāna mantra, one should [offer] from the eyes upward;
at the end of the substances, having offered the Vyāhṛtis, one should offer the Pūrṇāhuti with the Mūla mantra.
At the conclusion of the worship, the wise one should indeed perform the fire-ritual as prescribed;
O child, he should perform the worship according to the rules every day, both morning and evening.
At the conclusion of the fire-oblation, the wise man should offer the *bali*, and at the conclusion of the *bali*, he should perform the festival;
first comes the *viśvarātra*, and second, the *bhūtarātra*.
The third should be the Ṛṣirātra, the fourth the Indrarātra, the fifth the Brahmarātra, and the sixth indeed the Viṣṇurātra. (14.83)
The seventh [night] belongs to Rudra, and the eighth to Īśvara;
the ninth belongs to Sadāśiva—these are the presiding deities for the nine-day rites.
Beginning from the night of the Ṛṣis and ending with the day of Sadāśiva,
this seven-day cycle should be employed, starting from Brāhmī and concluding with Sadāśiva.
The five causes should be applied from Rudra up to Sadāśiva;
the three causes and the one cause [should be applied] up to the station of Sadāśiva. (14.86)
(On page 71: "By means of the three causes, there shall always be a day of Sadāśiva on the Ekāha; and with oblations and lamps, [this occurs] constantly on these days. (14.87)
One should perform worship with special care, in accordance with one's wealth;
one should especially worship the presiding deities of the village as well. (14.88)
May this pure food mixed with curd, combined with sweetmeats and cakes,
and fruit mixed with jaggery, be pleasing to Gaṇeśa.

A full offering of *balaya*, *ajjanī*, clarified butter, rice, curd, and roasted barley flour is declared the "fierce offering for spirits" (*bhūtakrūrabali*); with that, one should present the offering to the spirits.
The five roots, kuśāgra, śālya rice, and ghee mixed together,
combined with plantain fruit, is said to be the offering for the sages (ṛṣis).
Indravallī, haridrā, and priyaṅgu, combined with ghee,
should be offered on the fourth day as the excellent oblation for Indra.
A lotus flower, along with turmeric, milk-rice, and parched grain, should be offered on the fifth lunar day; this is declared to be the bali offering for Brahmā.
On the sixth day, rice cooked with milk and mixed with ghee and the fruit of the *bṛhatī* plant should be offered; this is supremely pleasing to Viṣṇu.
One should indeed offer *kṛsarānna* mixed with coconut fruits on the seventh lunar day; this shall be pleasing to Rudra.
Combined with bamboo shoots and curd, and accompanied by plantain fruit,
this offering (bali) for Īśvara should likewise be presented on the eighth lunar day.
Pure food mixed with curd, combined with parched grain and cakes,
accompanied by plantains and jackfruit, and blended with jaggery and sugar-candy.
On the ninth day, however, food should be offered to Śiva, who is known as Sādākhya;
for all [of these forms], the food should consist of pure rice mixed with clarified butter and immersed in curd.
Or the preceptor should especially cause it to be given with the respective mantra;
he should cook one *droṇa*, or half of that, or even half of that again. (14.99)
Having offered separate oblations (bali) each the size of a wood-apple fruit,
one should likewise offer the village-oblation (grāmabali) in front of the festival procession.
Accompanied by the sound of musical instruments, provided with incense and lamps, adorned with banners and peacock feathers, and accompanied by hymns and auspicious recitations. (14.101)
Having placed the trident and the food-liṅga upon the sacrificial altar,
the best of preceptors should arrange the ten weapons around them.
In the absence of a sacrifice, however, all of that [should be offered] while being borne upon the head;
the preceptor, accompanied by his disciples and adorned with all ornaments, [should do so]. (14.103)
Adorned with all ornaments, wearing the turban and the upper garment,
he is a primordial Śaiva, serene in soul, and endowed with faith and devotion.
Having offered the bali-oblation to those beginning with Brahmā and ending with Īśāna, or indeed from Indra to Īśāna, one should do so especially in that village along with the gods.
One should offer the bali oblation in the evening and in the morning, especially at the conclusion of the fire sacrifice;
then one should commence the festival at its end, adorned with all ornaments.
Then, equipped with various weapons, they were preceded by those on elephants;
after them followed those mounted on horses, and after them those riding on elephants.
At the end of that were mechanical stages adorned with celestial women;
at the end of those were eternal mechanical structures, swinging machines, and pavilions.
Afterwards, accompanied by dance and song, they [should go] to the temple of the Yantra;
the first is declared to be the comfortable seat (sukhāsana), and the second is with Umā.
The third is Vṛṣārūḍha (Mounted on the Bull), the fourth is Tripuraghna (Destroyer of Tripura),
the fifth is declared to be Nṛtta (the Dancing One), the sixth is indeed Candraśekhara (Moon-crested),
the seventh is Ardhanārīśa (Lord who is Half-Woman), and the eighth is Hari (Half-Man).
The ninth is the wandering for alms, and the tenth is the destruction of the sense of time.
Ten and one [eleven] for the burner of desire (Kāmadahana), then the ancient Liṅga;
these twelve images are all endowed with every ornament.
Having placed [the image] with devotion upon a colored cloth, a palanquin, or a chariot,
the Ādiśaivas and Anuśaivas are considered to be the attendants of the gods.
After the Paśupatas, there are the Mahāvratadharas;
after them, the Kālāmukhas; and after them, in due order, the Brāhmaṇas.
In front of that [image] are the Rudra-prostitutes (rudragaṇikās), adorned with all ornaments;
after them, the singers are said to be placed, and after them, the dancers should follow.
(73) Then, accompanied by the Śakti, one should proceed slowly and gradually toward Īśvara, especially with women, tridents, and the like, and with lamps for the yantras. (14.116)
It was adorned everywhere with torches of weapons and torches of staffs, and it was beautified by canopies, lamps in the openings, and banners. || 14.117 ||
Caṇḍeśa, fully adorned, should walk behind everyone;
in front of him, all musical instruments should be sounded properly and in due order.
With *paṭaha*, *maddala*, *tāla*, *bherī*, *paṇava*, and *ḍuṇḍubha* drums; with *jarjharī*, *jhallarī*, *monta*, and likewise with the sounds of the *vīṇā* and the flute.
One should cause it to be proclaimed especially in front and behind;
at its conclusion, the Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and others should arrive endowed with devotion.
At the end of that [period], all castes shall then proceed in due order;
those who follow the gods with their inner self directed toward them.
At every step, men—whether old, young, or middle-aged, as well as women and men alike—obtain the fruit of the Aśvamedha sacrifice. (14.122)
They are liberated from all evil and become endowed with everything everywhere;
thus one should perform the circumambulation of either a village or a city. (14.123)
One should go slowly to the temple and offer the oblation upon the sacrificial pedestal;
having washed one's feet, one should enter the interior of the temple.
The god stood with his eyes cast down, together with all the hosts of deities,
while the great sound of drums and other instruments resounded before Śiva.
Namaka and Camaka are established in the south;
Gāndharvaka and Auśaka are established in the north.
The preceptor is on the right side, and the king is on his left;
on both sides of the deity, courtesans are prescribed.
In the presence of the God, one should especially perform a dance accompanied by song;
and during the festival of the God of gods, the rite of *nīrāñjana* (the ceremonial waving of lamps) should be performed.
One should place the ash, the flower, and the lamp within the vessels;
having first given water for sipping (ācamana), one should then place a flower upon the head.
Having placed the Acyuta [mantra] upon the head, one should especially offer fragrance;
then one should give water for sipping (ācamana) again and cause incense and a lamp to be offered.
Having ground [the substance], one should rotate it over the head of Śiva with a lamp placed upon it.
At the conclusion of that, one should cause the ashes to be given and show the mirror once again. (14.131)
Having carried him away by means of courtesans accompanied by the sound of musical instruments,
and having placed him on the edge of a seat, one should cast him outside the walls.
The foremost of practitioners should have this performed, and one should protect it in the evening;
moreover, clothing and other such items should especially be given to the devotees. (14.133)
For by observing this sequence of circumambulation, one destroys all sins;
one should perform it day after day until the festival of the deity is concluded.
One should offer the first of all the sacrificial portions for the satisfaction of the God;
thereafter, on the day preceding the holy pilgrimage site, one should commence the hunt.
By the power of the commencement of battle, the wise man should go to the village and perform a circumambulation; he should especially bind the *kautuka* (protective amulet) on that night.
Having placed upon the sacrificial mound either a golden, silver, or even a cotton thread, one should place a trident upon that sacrificial mound.

In the center of the sacrificial pavilion, having performed the tying of the auspicious thread upon the trident and not upon the heart, one should cause the declaration of the "meritorious day" (puṇyāha) to be made there.
Having fashioned an image for the festival and tied the *kautuka* (sacred thread) to its heart,
one should place it upon a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) together with nine water-pots (*kalaśa*).

Having worshipped [the lingas] with perfumes and other offerings— provided with covers, brushes, and cloths, and accompanied by Śiva and the Vidyeśvaras— one should perform the ritual bath using [water from vessels] ending in tridents.
One should perform the ritual bath in a river, a pond, a lake, or a pool;
or else, one may perform the remaining rites even without bathing in a river or similar waters. (14.141)
Having performed the fire-oblation, the bali-offering, and the festival in the morning,
one should then perform the powder-festival either in front of the temple, or to its south, or to its east.
Having smeared the ground with cow-dung and provided it with incense and lamps,
and having adorned it with *pālikā* vessels and other ornaments, one should prepare a sacrificial altar (*sthaṇḍila*) there.
The trident should be placed to the west, and then the mortar and pestle;
one should wrap the mortar with cloth and then encircle it again with darbha grass.

Having worshipped the trident and then the mortar with perfumes and other offerings, one should offer ghee upon the head [of the deity] along with gold, *dūrvā* sprouts, and unbroken rice grains. (14.145)
First, having thoroughly dried the turmeric, the preceptor should place it in the mortar with each successive portion of powder, and strike it with the Heart-mantra and the Astra-mantra three times.
Then, the most excellent teacher, having bathed the liṅga while reciting the Pañcabrahma mantras, should grind it together with his devotees using that powder. (14.147)
One should bathe the trident, together with the protective cord and oil, using the heart-mantra;
there, one should worship the preceptor with garments, gold, and rings.
One should quickly go clockwise around a village or even a city;
or, having prepared two sacrificial mounds on the bank of a river or a lake, [one should perform the rite]. || 14.149 ||
Having firmly established the trident (śūla) right there, one should place the previously mentioned water-pots (kalaśas) upon it;
one should worship both the trident and the pots with their respective mantras.
The Gaṅgā, the Yamunā, the Nardadā, the Sarasvatī,
the Sindhu, the Godāvarī, and the Kāverī— these are the seven.
Having invoked [the deities] into the central jar filled with fragrant water,
one should place the deities beginning with Ananta and ending with Śikhaṇḍin in the jars surrounding it.
One should cause the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha-vācana*) to be made, worship the deities with the spear-weapon (*śūlāstra*), and then perform worship;
afterwards, one should bathe [the deity] with water-pots and perform the ritual bath at a sacred ford (*tīrtha*).
Those men who perform their ablutions here at the Trinetra-tīrtha together with the Triśūla are liberated from all sins, just as serpents are freed from their sloughs.
In the sacrificial hall, one should again offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) into the fire of Śiva;
thereafter, one should properly perform everything situated above the homa as prescribed by the scriptures.
Thereafter, one should worship Yāgeśa with auspicious perfumes, flowers, and other offerings;
then, one should cause Śiva to be bathed there with consecrated jars.
One should cause garments and other articles to be given to the devotees and attendants;
first of all, one should especially perform the lowering of the banner (dhvajāvarohaṇa).
One should cause it to descend after three days, or five days, or seven days;
then, having performed a ritual bath, especially for the primary liṅga.
(76) One should also perform the ceremonial bathing of the festival images, as well as the trident and the banner, there with hymns and auspicious recitations. (14–159)
The wise one, at the conclusion of the worship, should offer an oblation of pure food with curcuma (haridrā) and side-dishes,
and then perform the lowering of the flagstaff.
Then, having performed a circumambulation, one should dismiss the deities of the junctions;
one should cause the materials used for the sacrifice to be presented to the preceptor.
In this way, whatever mortal performs a festival for Śiva shall deliver twenty-one generations of his lineage and attain the world of Śiva.
This has been declared as the Śivotsava; now hear about the ritual bathing (snapana).
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, the procedure for the Śivotsava. || 14 ||
Now begins the chapter on the procedure for the ritual bath (snāna).
Hereafter, I shall fully explain the sequence of the ritual for bathing [the deity]:
on the fifth, the ninth, the fourteenth, and on the two festival days (parvan).
On the transit of the sun, at the equinoxes, at the solstices, and likewise during an eclipse—
from the fifth lunar day until the end of the eclipse— it is excellent, with each subsequent period being ten times more meritorious than the preceding.

At the conclusion of initiation, at the conclusion of consecration, during sprinkling, at the end of a festival, at the end of a sacrifice, under an auspicious constellation, and during the rite of lighting the Kṛttikās; || 15-3 ||
It should be performed on one's birth-star, during auspicious rites, in the practice of mantras, at the time of a king’s consecration, at the end of life, or at birth. (15.4)
In cases of excessive rain, drought, famine, or ill omens;
during earthquakes, the conflagration of the quarters, or afflictions such as fever and māryā; || 15-5 ||
When all kinds of diseases have arisen, or even when there is affliction by enemies,
or at times such as for expiation and the like, the Guru should perform the ritual bathing of Śiva.
Listen now to the ninefold ablution there in brief, according to its sequence:
with five, with five, and likewise with twenty-five.
Listen now to the middle triad among the three groups of others:
one less than fifty, and then eighty-one. (15.8)
One hundred and eight is to be known here as the threefold middling [number]:
namely, sixteen, two hundred, and three hundred and eight. (15.9)
There are one thousand and eight [mantras], beginning with the supreme and ending with Ādiśiva;
the supreme is renowned as being threefold—now hear the ritual bathing for all of them. (15.10)
In front of the temple, one should construct a square pavilion measuring twenty, twenty-four, or twelve cubits.
It is recorded as being of nine types, measuring nine, eight, seven, six, and five cubits;
for the nine pavilions, the base is recorded as being eight thousand [units] in measure.
A structure endowed with thirty-six limbs is prescribed for the best [class of temples];
one endowed with sixteen pillars should be caused to be made for the middling [class]. (15.13)
One should construct for those of inferior status a structure joined with twelve pillars;
one may have it made as either a peaked pavilion (kūṭa) or a square pavilion (maṇḍapa), according to its own proportions.
It was provided with four gates, adorned with four archways,
equipped with canopies and banners, and beautified by garlands of *darbha* grass.
The offering of sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa) should be performed according to the procedure to be described;
thereafter, the primary Śaiva practitioner should take up the ritual jars (kalaśas) and consecrate them.
Whether made of gold, silver, or even copper, or with conch shells, mother-of-pearl, or even the horns of cows. (15–17)
Alternatively, [one may worship] with images made of clay, endowed with all the auspicious marks,
well-baked, resonant, glossy, and possessing the brilliance of a bimba fruit.
One should have the Supreme Lord bathed with these [substances] endowed with the prescribed characteristics;
the best [quantity] is a full *droṇa*, while the middling is half of that.

An *āḍhaka* is declared to be the minimum for all, or indeed an *āḍhaka* may be given to everyone; one should fill [the vessels] made of conch, mother-of-pearl, or horn according to their own respective measurements. (15–20)
Having wrapped it with thread and having performed the ritual of time (kālayitvā), one should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana).
Having applied a coating of cow dung, one should cast the lines of the mandala.
Furthermore, having established the deities of the Sūtras and the limbs beginning with Dharma,
one should likewise prepare a sacrificial mound there with pure *śāli* rice.
One should prepare separate jars of one āḍhaka or half of that;
half of those should be filled with rice, and half of those combined with sesame seeds.
(78) Listen now to the first seven-fold procedure among the nine types of ablutions:
within the pavilion, there is a lotus with four petals, provided with a pericarp. (15.24)
It is renowned as the *pañcakumbha*, adorned with great petals;
they know it to consist of nine squares by means of four lines drawn eastward and northward.
Having laid out eight equal lines facing east and north in succession, [one proceeds].
One should take the nine squares in the center and discard one outer row. || 15-26 ||
In the four directions beginning with Indra (the east), one should take a single step;
from Agni (the southeast) to Īśa (the northeast), there should be three steps by means of the [next] three [verses]. (15.27)
One should leave two squares for the purpose of the door on both sides of the great diagonal line;
having made twenty-five squares, one should establish the three lower [sections].
The distance from the feet [of the central point] should be one tāla; twelve lines are to be laid out.
Likewise, the north-south line is to be established, and one should then apply eight doors.
In the middle [line], one should abandon twenty-five squares and two squares that have been covered;
having made thirty-five squares, one should carefully select one among them.
Listen to these forty-nine and eighty-one squares;
having completed one square, one should leave the squares at the doors and other such locations. (15.31)
Thus, there are eighty-one squares; now hear about the middle from the middle.
There is a sixteen-fold thread with its tip pointing east, and likewise one with its tip pointing north. (15.32)
One should effortlessly include twenty-five squares at the ends and the center;
nine squares should be taken for the intermediate directions, and one should omit two squares because they constitute the doors.
In the four directions, within the squares of the lunar days (tithi), one should omit three in the third [square].
When this is done, there are exactly eight hundred squares, with Śiva being the preeminent one.
One should draw twenty threads, facing east and north respectively;
in their center, twenty-five [threads] are to be taken, with two on each side.
One should abandon the area consisting of eight doorways using cow dung and water,
as well as the cardinal and intermediate directions, proceeding step by step for twenty-five paces.
One should draw a lotus garland situated in the center of the Madhyamavyūha;
one who knows the ritual procedure should act in this way so that there may be two hundred and sixteen [petals]. (15.37)
The ninefold ablution has been declared; now hear of their respective substances:
diamond, emerald, lapis lazuli, and coral. (15.38)
One should place a pearl and the five gems into the Śiva-pitcher;
in the absence of gems, one should place gold, and for the nine [pitchers], gold alone. (15.39)

Water for the feet, water for sipping, the arghya offering, the five products of the cow, water with kuśa grass, milk, curd, and ghee—these they know as the first enclosure (prathamāvaraṇa). || 15-40 ||
One *prastha* of ghee is prescribed; two *pādas* of curd are mentioned;
three *pādas* of milk are stated; and one *prastha* of cow dung as well. (15.41)
Cow’s urine with six times as much milk is known as *pañcagavya*;
likewise, honey, sugarcane juice, and the fruits of the jackfruit and mango [are included]. (15.42)
The plantain, the coconut, mustard, and likewise sesame;
the wood-apple, the citron, and both varieties of orange. (15.43)
Yavanī, vāralāja, its powder, añgula, candana, laghu, kuṣṭha, kaccola, and puṣpapatraka—[these are the ingredients]. (15.44)
Camphor, Himalayan sandalwood, jaṭāmāṃsī, murantraṇa, śamī, dūrvā grass, white arka, bilva leaves, and campaka. || 15-45 ||
Śaṅkhapuṣpī, apāmārga, viṣṇukrāntā, dhūrtūra, nandyāvarta, white lotus, punnāga, and atipāṭalī. (15.46)
Along with the goddess Śatapatrī, Lakṣmī, Sthalāravindaka,
Dhātakī, Tulasī, Karavīra, and Kṛṣṇamallikā.
Mallikā, śatāvarī, gokṣuraka, kṛtāñjali, mahādroṇa, droṇa, bhadrī, and madhumadrikā. || 15-48 ||
Indravallī, rudrapāṇi, dhātrī, and haridrakī; vyāghra, navī, māñjiṣṭhī, sarala, and bhadrakāṣuka. || 15-49 ||
Fresh butter, liquid extract, and sajjantakola, as well as balā, atibalā, siṃhī, and priyaṅgu extracted from lodhra. || 15-50 ||
Nāgakeśara, jambūka, kapittha, aśvattha, guggulu, cardamom, cumin, and black cumin. (15.51)
Sesame oil, saffron, *megha*, *agaru*, black aloe wood, *śrīveṣṭaka*, fragrant resin, long pepper, and *hastapippalī*. (15.52)
Black aloe-wood, tagara, realgar, red sandalwood,
cloves, and turmeric— these are to be powdered and used as a decoction for the final cleansing.
One should prescribe a decoction made from the bark of the *pippala*, *udumbara*, *plakṣa*, and *vaṭa* trees;
as for the substances, one should indicate sesame seeds, the tips of *kuśa* grass, and likewise *mārjavya*. (15.54)
These substances have been described; bathing is of two kinds: cleansing and sprinkling.
All substances that are liquids are known as bathing substances. (15.55)
The wise one should fill all the vessels for cleansing substances—such as those containing fruit-powders, medicinal herbs, and so forth—with water, excluding those intended for liquids. (15.56)
The five juices, mixed with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), are prescribed for the five jars;
those ending in "ājya" are for the nine jars, while those ending in "vat" are for the five jars.
From *gulā* to *punnāga*, there are forty-nine;
and from *dravya* to *jātyala*, there are specifically eighty-one. (15.58)
The rites beginning with the water for the feet and ending with the ritual sprinkling (*mārjana*) shall number one hundred and eight;
these are known as the arrays (*vyūha*) of Adharma and the others, situated in the cardinal and intermediate directions.
For the middle [mandala], the array of Śiva (śivavyūha) is proclaimed as consisting of nine arrays;
one should worship it with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, and likewise strew it with *darbha* grass.
One should place the Śiva-pitcher in the center with the Śiva-mantra;
it should be filled with thirty-two, twenty-four, or sixteen prasthas [of water]. (15.61)
This is declared to be the Śiva-kumbha; the Vardhanī vessel is half its size.
It should be joined with five gems, provided with a tuft of grass (kūrca), and wrapped in cloth.

Having placed the Śiva-pitcher (śivakumbha) in the center of the Śiva-array (śivavyūha), one should place it either in the auspicious part of that array, in its very middle, or in the northern part of it.
Having placed the Vardhanī vessel— equipped with a spout, covered with cloth, and adorned with gold—
along with the Manonmanī [vessel], while recollecting the seed-mantra.

The wise one, having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings while reciting the heart-mantra, [should offer] the eight lords of the Vidyeshvaras, beginning with the water for the feet (pādya) and ending with the clarified butter (ghṛta). 15-65.
One should worship each of the presiding deities of the Śatarudra, beginning with honey and ending with the ritual sprinkling (mārjana); one should offer a garment to each of them.
One should worship with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, using each deity's own name in the dative case;
one should then install sixteen and two hundred [deities] in sequence as before.
The primary substances mentioned previously have been well proclaimed;
it should be beautifully adorned with uśīra, agaru, karpūra, and candana, as well as excellent flowers.
That by which water for rinsing the mouth is mixed with pure [substances] is known as *upasnāna*;
the number of such *upasnānas* is equal to the number of the seven sacred bathing places (*tīrtha*). (15.69)
Beginning from the lowest of the low and ending with the highest of the low, everything has been specifically described, including the deities and the ritual substances. (15.70)
O Gajānana, there are indeed three types of bathing—superior, middling, and most excellent—as well as the substances used, each with some slight distinction. (15.71)
There, six threads facing east and likewise threads facing north [should be laid out], with a measurement of five tālas, so that the arrangement of the squares is not forgotten. (15.72)
From here onwards, having returned, one should bypass eight squares.
Four types of obstacles are said to be located at the four great cardinal directions, occupying four squares each.
One should collect twelve words here within the four corners;
in each of those twelve squares, there are twenty-five [syllables]. (15.74)
Having established the nine squares by means of the specific central arrangement,
the best of installers should place [the deities] according to the path of the six enclosures.
The knower of mantras should place nine jars in the center of the arrangement as before; having consecrated the *vardhanī* vessel to its left, he should do so as previously described.
I shall describe the sequence of five rows, ending with the fifth enclosure:
in the first [row] are the seed-syllables, and in the second are the metals.
In the third [vessel] one should place jewels, and in the fourth, the sacred relics (dhātu);
in the fifth, however, these thirty-eight substances made from the five products of a cow (pañcagavya). (15.78)
Yavani, vāra-mudga, sesame, and mustard seeds; likewise white śāli, mahāśāli, and red śāli rice. (15.79)
Saugandhī and Hemaśālī are known as the ten seeds;
having filled twenty-two jars, one should place them in the first enclosure.
One should place as many [vessels] as required for the preliminary ablutions (upasnāna) and so forth,
namely forty-four jars, all around.
Having worshipped according to the prescribed rite while recollecting the seed-mantra, the first enclosure has been described; now hear about the second enclosure.
Cāmīkara, likewise hema, and thereafter śātakumbha; jāmbūnada and tapta—these seven types of gold are mixed with the first [type]. || 15.82 ||
One should place twenty-six threads together with water into the pitcher;
there shall be that same number of waters within those pitchers. (15.83)
Having placed fifty-two pitchers in the four corners of the second enclosure, the preceptor [should do so] with the Brahma-mantras.
The second enclosure has been described; now hear of the third enclosure:
ruby, lapis lazuli, diamond, and likewise topaz. (15.85)
Crystal, pearl, blue sapphire, and coral—
these nine gems [should be placed] in thirty excellent water-jars.
That same number shall be the water within those jars;
there should be sixty jars, having worshipped them with the limb-mantra and the vidyā.
The third enclosure has been described; now hear of the fourth enclosure:
yellow orpiment, red arsenic, collyrium, and realgar. (15.88)
Then, one should place rodhra, lead, and likewise red ochre, along with the seven metals and water, into thirty-four jars. (15.89)
For that duration, those waters within the jars should be taken;
specifically, there should be one hundred and eight, or sixty, jars.
One should worship each of those individually, especially with the limbs of the Vidyā;
now hear about the placement of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) in the fifth enclosure.
Cow’s urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and water with *kuśa* grass—
these six, beginning with cow’s urine, one should place into thirty-eight jars.
One should place the thirty-eight digits (kalās) of the five Brahmans in sequence;
for as many as there may be, each should be placed within water.
Having combined the substances in the jars, especially those of the Śatarudra,
one should place them individually in three hundred jars.
Having bathed and worshipped them according to the prescribed rite with their respective names, three hundred and eight [times] have been declared; now hear the highest of the high.
Having laid out one hundred and twenty-one lines, with twelve lines pointing eastward and likewise twelve pointing northward, O Vināyaka, one should establish the squares there.
At the four corners, the wise one should lay down four lines, beginning from the southeast (āgneya) and so forth, such that they are separated by a single square.
One should abandon the thirty-six [squares] joined with the limbs, which are situated at the positions of the limbs. Having left two squares at each door, forty squares remain. (15.98)
Having made a central square among them, one should then [divide] it into nine sections;
within each individual section, there are twenty-five [units].
Furthermore, having arranged eight, one thousand, and eleven jars—
having placed the jars known as Vidyeśa, Umā, and Śiva as before—
one should omit the Vidyeśa enclosure; hear now concerning those [arrangements] consisting of ten enclosures.
Seeds indeed in the first, and metals alone in the second.
In the third [vessel] one should place the jewels, and in the fourth the mineral elements;
in the fifth the five products of the cow, and in the sixth the water with fruits.
All fragrant substances and medicinal herbs should likewise be offered in the seventh;
earth in the eighth, and astringent decoctions in the ninth enclosure.
And in the tenth [day], listen to the flowers one by one in sequence;
the wise man should place the seeds and the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) as before.
The fifth enclosure has been declared; now hear about the sixth enclosure:
the plantain, the wood-apple, the mango, the citron, and the pomegranate. (15.105)
Coconut, orange, jackfruit, and breadfruit—these fruits and their juices are here designated as the sixty-two [types]. (15.106)
One should place those [mantras] individually within water inside the jars;
here, there are one hundred and twenty-four jars.
One should worship each of those individually with the mantra beginning "praśāntāya.
[Worship them] with perfumes and medicinal herbs; now hear about the seventh enclosure.
Uśīra, sandalwood, camphor, and jasmine; śaṅkhapuṣpa, the goddess Śrī, viṣṇukrāntī, and śatāvarī. (15.109)
One should know that there are eight perfumes and sixty-six minerals; such is the number to be understood according to the specific requirements of the secondary ablution (upasnāna).
In brief, one hundred and thirty-two [types] have been declared for herbs, creepers, and trees combined. (15.111)
One should collect fruits, flowers, roots, and so forth; this is declared as the seventh enclosure. Now hear about the eighth enclosure.
On the tip of a Darbha grass blade, on the point of an ivory peg, during the plowing by a boar, at an anthill, on the tip of a bull's horn, and likewise in a river or even on a mountain. (15.113)
The wise man, having taken earth from the ocean itself, should purify it;
in this manner, he should place seventy portions, one into each of the jars. (15.114)
Having filled it completely with water, that number within the water is proclaimed as one hundred and forty. (15.115)
One should worship with the water of the earth; now hear about the ninth enclosure:
the mango, the jackfruit, the banyan, and likewise the udumbara. (15.116)
One should place the powder of the eight trees—the aśvattha, śirīṣa, madhūka, and palāśa—along with water. (15.117)
Having filled each one individually, there shall be seventy-four of them;
that is the number of those waters for the subsidiary ablutions.
The wise one should worship the crest with forty-eight hundred [verses]— that is, one thousand and forty-eight— in sequence, using perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
The tenth enclosure has been described; now hear about the flowers:
lotuses, palāśa leaves, nandyāvarta, mallikā, karavīra, campaka, and the blue water-lily—thus is the group of eight.
Having cast them into the jars, they are recorded as being seventy-eight in number.
Having placed flowers in the jars and filled them with water,
one should arrange that same number of secondary ablution vessels (upasnāna).
Having thus established the ten vessels filled with scents, flowers, and unbroken grains (akṣata), one should carefully wrap each and every jar with cloths.
One should visualize the Śatarudras and the sacred waters (tīrthas) within the ritual substances;
the ninefold installation is prescribed there, and one should display the mudrās.
The wise one should thus establish the seat, the invocation, and so forth, with salutations at the beginning and end, and the beautiful seed-syllables in the middle.
Having performed the consecration with the fire as previously described, one should carry out the rite;
having especially performed the *puṇyāha* ceremony, one should worship the jars.

In that place, one should worship in due order a Śaiva preceptor who knows the ritual procedure and is born of a noble lineage; there, one should honor a single teacher who is conversant with the rules.
Having lifted up the Śiva-pitcher with garments, ornaments, flowers, a finger-ring, or sacrificial vessels, either with the hand or with the head. (15.128)
Having fanned the inner sanctum and standing facing north,
the knower of mantras should install the Lord of the Gods with the root mantra.
Having established the pedestals upon the *vardhanī* with the *Gaṇām-bika* mantra,
they should be installed again in their respective places, just as before, according to the sequence.
Having prepared the materials for the bath according to the rule, and likewise having performed the ritual rising,
one should bathe Sadāśiva with the mantra once he has been established.
Or, having placed the water-pot to the right of the great deity,
one should establish it with an unbroken stream of water, the size of the tip of a cow's horn.
One should release the jars that have been set out and employed; and at the conclusion of all the ablutions, one should [use] turmeric powders. (15.133)
Having bathed it, the wise one should worship it and prepare an abundant oblation;
even in the absence of seeds, however, one may use wild rice (*nīvāra*) or millet (*vāyava*).
If even metals are not available, one should place heated gold;
if even gems are not available, the preceptor should take a pearl.
But if even the minerals are not available, especially yellow orpiment [is used];
and if even the flowers are not available, the instructor should take a lotus. (15.136)
In this way, the mortal who acts likewise, endowed with devotion, sports eternally like the moon and is glorified in the world of Śiva. (15.137)
Having arrived by his own will alone, he shall become the sole sovereign of the earth.
Ninefold bathing has been proclaimed; now hear the procedure for the cold-water jar (śītakumbha).
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, the procedure for the ritual bathing.
(p. 86) Now begins the chapter on the ritual of the Cold Water Jar (śītakumbha).
Hereafter, I shall fully explain the characteristics of the Cold Water Jar [to be used] during drought, famine, and the invasion of a foreign kingdom. (16.1)
One should have a "cold-pitcher" (śītakumbha) constructed for the purpose of destroying fever and epilepsy, for the purpose of eliminating Vasurī, and for the purpose of destroying all diseases.
The image, complete with thirty-two marks and endowed with radiance,
should be wrapped with three threads at intervals of one barley grain or one finger-breadth.
Having prepared a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) before Śiva,
adorned with rice grains and provided with a pericarp, one should surround it with sesame seeds and darbha grass.
A wise person should have it prepared with eight *droṇas* of *śāli* rice, combined with half that amount of husked rice, and further combined with half that amount of sesame seeds. (16.5)
One should fill the auspicious water-pot with water filtered through a cloth,
combined with all fragrant substances and endowed with the five jewels.

He should place the pitcher, together with its cloth covering, its beard-like ornament, and its golden embellishment, upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), accompanied by perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
On the preceding day, there should be the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa); one should perform a vigil during the night.
One should engage in the study of sacred texts in all directions, especially while touching the water-pot (kumbha).
A peace-offering oblation (śāntihoma) should be performed, particularly in front of that [pot].
At dawn, a crest was fashioned upon the middle of the head of the God of Gods.
Having wrapped the limbs with garments, one should adorn them with flowers and garlands;
having placed a water-pot in the middle of that, one should place the aperture upon its back.
The tube shall be made of gold and equal in measure to the tip of an iron needle;
it should be twice as much for one who gives milk, and three times as much for one who gives honey.
The wise one, having placed the water-pot with effort while reciting the heart-mantra,
should likewise establish the secondary pot upon the sacrificial mound as before.
It may last for twenty-one days, or even fourteen days;
or for seven days, or five days, or especially for three days. (16.13)

The wise one should cause it to be heard continuously, having placed it upon the head; mindful of that which brings peace, he should perform the special daily worship at the appropriate times. (16.14)
One should worship there twice as much as possible, or at least to the best of one's ability;
then, having poured water from the small jar and risen as before, [one should proceed].
One should perform the fire oblation until the descent from the pitcher;
there, one should honor the preceptor with garments, rings, and other such gifts.
One should especially cause the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to be given to the preceptor;
at the end, the knower of mantras, having set aside the water-pot (kumbha), [should perform the rite] with the Vaktra-mantra.
Having offered abundant oblations according to the previously mentioned procedure,
one should also honor other devotees with food and drink.
This has been declared as the Śītakumbha; now hear about the nine-fold food offering (navanaivedya).
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, the Śītakumbha-vidhi-paṭala.
Now begins the chapter on the ritual for the ninefold food offering (navanaivedya).
Hereafter, I shall fully explain the characteristics of the ninefold food offering;
for by performing it with the names of the foremost [deities], victory shall surely ensue.
At an auspicious moment, a favorable conjunction, and under a propitious lunar mansion and karana,
accompanied by the sound of musical instruments and provided with a trident.
Then, adorned with all ornaments and accompanied by their devotees,
they entered their own field and took their positions in the northeast direction.
The wise one should offer an oblation of curd-rice to the protectors of that field,
having cast it with a needle while reciting the heart-mantra.
Provided with pure rice and husks, along with all kinds of side dishes,
one should perform a circumambulation of either a village or a city.
Adorned with all ornaments and accompanied by all kinds of musical instruments,
her attendants and elephants should likewise be led before her.
Having brought loads of awns from the end [of the field], and loads of rice immediately thereafter; having brought loads of side-dishes from the end, and then loads of husked rice. (17.7)
The musicians and the courtesans, adorned with all their ornaments, should proceed;
behind them all, the image should walk slowly.
Then all the devotees should depart again in due order;
having entered the palace, the minister should indeed establish the heaps of awns.
Having gathered the rice grains scorched by the rays of the sun into a mortar,
and having fashioned a circular mandala with the four corners, one should decorate it with various flour-dusts.
Having prepared a sacrificial mound with śāli rice, one should place a mortar there;
having bound the mortar with a cloth, one should then worship the pestle.
Having thoroughly agitated it with the primary seed, one should diligently extract the rice grains,
together with coconut and sugar-cane, and provided with black pepper and cumin.
One should offer [the gift] to the deity with devotion using the *hṛdaya* mantra;
for other images, however, one should cause it to be given again using the *hṛdaya* mantra.
Having bestowed the power of the retinue, one should offer it to Caṇḍeśa;
specifically, having offered betel-leaf there with the heart-mantra (hṛdaṇu), [one should proceed].
Having offered abundant oblations while conforming to the previously mentioned procedure,
he should then feed all his devotees with fresh grain.
The ninefold food offering has been declared; now hear about the Kṛttikā-lamp.
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, the ritual procedure for the ninefold food offering.
Now begins the chapter on the ritual procedure for the Kṛttikā-lamp.
Hereafter, I shall fully explain the characteristics of the Kṛttikā-lamp;
one should perform the rite of the lamp during the month of Kārttika, under the asterism Kṛttikā.
Having adorned the temple and gathered the requisites for the lamp-offering,
one should perform the ritual bathing there, in accordance with the wishes of the patron.
Having constructed gabled pavilions at the summit of the palace, specifically on all eight sides and provided with four corners; 18-3.
Having placed earth everywhere within the structural bonds (kūṭabandha), one should indeed place lamps there;
upon those [lamps], one should place the lamps of light (dīpastambha).
A vessel made of khadira wood or coconut is prescribed for the measurement;
having placed clarified butter or purified oil into the vessel, (one should proceed). 18-5.
Having placed [the substance] combined with cotton seeds and combined with a torn cloth into the midst of clarified butter, one should ignite it upon the top of a pillar.
One should decorate the palace here everywhere with lamps and garlands,
as well as on the small nose, the large nose, the pitcher, and the pigeon-hole.
One should well illuminate the *pālikā* and the *suguhā* there with lighting-machines, as well as upon the tops of palaces, in various regions, in pavilions, and at gate-towers. (18.8)
One should especially place lamps everywhere along the walls;
on the pillars, small vessels should be placed, which are completely surrounded by lamps.
One should place the lamp on its stand with the Aghorāstra mantra;
the "peak-lamp" (kūṭadīpa) is the best, while the "pillar-lamp" (staṃbhadīpaka) is middling.
After [installing] Dīpa, which is described as the lowest and merely a secondary measure,
one should subsequently have Bhavānī and the trident-bearing God of gods fashioned.
The wise man should perform the festival according to the rules for one day; however, he should not carry out the sequence of offerings and other rites within the house alone.
Having adorned a village, a city, or a dwelling with lamps, those best of men, filled with devotion, perform a circumambulation. (18.13)
Having performed a circumambulation of the village, which is enriched with such specific qualities, and then having entered the temple, one should proceed with the sequence of serving the food.
Having prepared abundant oblations for the God of gods with devotion,
[he should worship] with hymns, recitations, devotees, musical instruments, and even dances and other such performances.
Having fully gratified the Lord of Gods, one should properly perform the ritual action.
The offering of lamps during the Kṛttikā constellation has been described here; now hear concerning the rite of filling [the vessels]. || 18-16 ||
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, concerning the ritual procedure beginning with the Kṛttikās. || 18 ||
(p. 90) Now follows the chapter on the ritual procedure for the Āṣāḍha-pūrṇā festival:

Having performed the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa) on the previous day under the constellation preceding Āṣāḍhā, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) at night, diligently offering the sacrificial oblation (bali). || 19-1 ||
Having tied on the protective amulet (pratisara) at night, one should then worship the preceptor;
likewise, at dawn, there should be a special worship of the Lord of the Gods.
Having cast the *balī* right there and performed a circumambulation of the village,
one should collect parched rice flour and other items for the purpose of bathing Śiva.
Having established a water-shed on the riverbank, adorned with all ornaments,
one should worship the deity situated in its center with the heart-mantra.
It should be accompanied by parched grain flour, molasses, and mango fruits,
as well as plantains and jackfruit, and especially by cakes.
The wise one, having first offered each of the pure clay vessels to be accepted with devotion,
should then offer them with devotion while reciting the heart-mantra.
Then, having scattered parched grain flour before Śiva with the *hṛdaya-mantra*,
the preceptor should bathe the trident in that [mixture] with fresh water.
Having returned again to the Ālaya, one should then perform the ritual bathing;
having offered abundant oblations with the Hṛdaya mantra before Śiva. (19-8)
Having offered abundant oblations especially to Śiva,
one should also present oblations to the images of other deities.
Thus has the procedure for the ripening of the fruit been briefly declared; now listen.
This concludes the nineteenth chapter, the procedure for the Āṣāḍha-pūraka-rite. 19.
(p. 91) Now follows the chapter on the procedure for the ripening of fruits.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the supreme procedure for the ripening of fruits;
that man who, having seen Śiva from afar, pays him homage... (20.1)
Like a snake shedding its slough, the wise man, exhausted by the fatigue of a long journey, is liberated from all sins by performing a circumambulation. (20.2)
Even if there is affliction on the path, it shall become auspicious for the lord, and his sins are destroyed;
followed by people here in this world of mortals, he indeed lives. (20-3)
By performing circumambulation during a festival or at the time of an offering, a person obtains the fruit of a horse sacrifice at every single step. (20.4)
Having performed the salutation in this manner, he is honored in the worlds;
one should cast water or a beautiful flower toward the deity. (20.5)
That man on earth who has established a grove for the God of gods enjoys various pleasures adorned with diverse flowers. (20.6)
He alone is wealthy, glorious, and honored in these worlds;
such a master of yoga should give ten thousand [cows] to a learned Brahmin who has mastered the Vedas.
O Lord, bathing [the deity] with cow's milk is superior to [bathing with] cow-horn [water];
it is equal to bathing with the five products of a tawny cow (kapilā-pañcagavya) mixed with kuśa-water.
A man endowed with devotion who performs the ninefold bathing of the Lord of the Gods obtains a reward equal to that of bathing ten million cows.
Endowed with various enjoyments, he is glorified in the world of Śiva;
for whatever action exists on the ninefold path, its enjoyment likewise becomes ninefold. (20.10)
Having prepared the oblation in nine parts, one enjoys ninefold enjoyment;
he who gives a bell and a gem attains distinguished fame and prosperity.
Providing garments, ornaments, and so forth for the God of gods, with many well-filled garments as well as various ornaments. (20.12)
One who is honored here by the gods shall become the sole sovereign of the earth;
likewise, one who offers a lamp to the God of Gods even once at the proper time [attains the same]. (20.13)
In the world, however, he too is remembered as being like a lamp for the sake of all-knowingness.
That man who, with mind, action, or speech, aims toward Śiva— (20.14)
Or rather, whatever great fruit is obtained through all undertakings and applications, through all acts of giving, austerity, and sacrifice, [is attained] again from that very state. (20.15)
Therefore, one shall obtain that fruit as a preeminent excellence in heaven;
and by performing cultivation with this intent, one shall conquer all seven worlds.
Whatever man should build a dwelling with bricks,
stone, or iron, he is glorified in the world of Śiva by means of a golden celestial chariot.
When the celestial chariot is successfully completed, by installing [the deity] according to the prescribed ritual method,
one attains the world of Śiva, being eternally honored by the immortals.
Once the Śivaliṅga has been established, one subsequently attains proximity [to the deity];
moreover, one will come to possess the very form of the image that was installed. (20.19)
Having assumed various forms together with Īśa, the heroic one entered his world along with Īśa, finding its vulnerability and acting according to his will.
Whatever flowers, petals, fruits, seeds, and especially grains have been offered to Śivā; || 20–21 ||
Indeed, upon the completion of the Śiva-sacrifice through that performance, the embodied beings of the sacrificer go to the world of Śiva. (20–22)
In this way, for those twenty ancestors of his lineage who have passed away, ten preceding him and ten succeeding him are included in brief. (20–23)
For those born on the mother's side, that world is desired as their place; likewise for those who serve their wives, along with their sons and brothers. (20–24)
There shall be residence in the world of Śiva, which is unattainable even by the gods;
having enjoyed vast pleasures, when the dissolution of the universe has arrived— (20–25).
Having attained the yoga of knowledge, he is liberated right there.
By constructing walls and pavilions for the sake of the Lord, one would attain the desired heaven.
By diligently constructing step-wells, wells, and tanks dedicated to the Lord, [one attains the same].
He who performs this, becoming rich in abundant wealth, shall attain Śiva at its conclusion.
But that man who, though incapable of performing his duties, constantly remembers [the Lord], dies right there; for him, heaven is certain—of this there is no doubt. (20.28)
Having understood the true nature of the seat and the one who sits upon it, one should worship Śiva;
thus one shall gradually attain Sālokya, Sāmīpya, and Sārūpya [liberations].
Worship with fire leads to Sālokya, and likewise, through the offering of bali, the same result is achieved.
She has no proximity whatsoever to the festival; she is silver through the meditation on Rudra.
And that fool who, deluded by ignorance, should utter revilement against Śiva, goes to a terrible hell for seventy-three [kalpas]. (20.31)
If he is unable [to do so], he should strike him or go outside from there;
however, he who would give up his life for the sake of Śiva— || 20-32 ||
I am unable to describe the perfection of its fruit;
however, O Śiva, one will attain that union—of this there is no doubt. (20.33)
Devotion is indeed twofold: natural and artificial.
That devotion which is natural has been cultivated through previous births. (20-34)
That which is innate should be known as bestowing happiness both here and hereafter;
whereas that which is artificial, being produced by effort, bestows happiness only in the next world.
That devotion which is indeed innate as well as cultivated is imperishable;
one should contemplate that such a person is Śiva himself—that man is Śiva. (20.36)
A hundred cubits or half of that from the *liṅga* on all sides is the sacred field (*śivakṣetra*) of Śiva;
dwelling right there is the cause for [residing in] the world of Śiva.
In whatever place one meets their end (the five elements), that very spot becomes the cause for reaching the world of Śiva;
however, that which is a human-made linga is traditionally considered to be of the measure of a sacred field (kṣetra).
For a self-manifested [image], it should be one thousand; for one made by a ṛṣi, half of that.
All groves, ponds, and stationary or moving things [are likewise dedicated]. (20.39)
By the power of the Supreme Lord, they proceed to the divine realm without a doubt;
therefore, a dwelling should be constructed in the vicinity of a sacred field of Śiva.
For one's own sake, however, a wise person should perform worship to Śiva with all the ritual offerings;
therefore, [one may worship] with leaves, fruits, flowers, water, or even mentally.
Having made the mind of the nature of Śiva, one should always worship Śiva.
There has never been, nor will there ever be, a dharma superior to the dharma of Śiva. (20.42)
In other animal-like practices, heaven alone is indeed the fruit;
but this [practice] in the Śiva scriptures bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (20.43)
Having completely set aside all other scriptures, one should apply oneself to the scriptures of Śiva.
The procedure for the ripening of the fruit has been declared; now hear the characteristics of the teacher (ācārya).
Thus ends the twentieth chapter, concerning the method for the ripening of fruits.
Now follows the chapter on the characteristics of the preceptor (ācārya).
Hereafter, I shall fully explain the characteristics of the preceptor,
so that upon hearing the procedure for the ripening of the fruit, devotion to Śiva may arise.
Then the man’s delight in establishing the *liṅga* proceeds;
first he should seek out a preceptor (*ācārya*), and immediately thereafter, the guardians of the image (*mūrtipāḥ*).
Born of a family of the primordial Śaivas, established in the five spheres of experience,
he knows the true meaning of all scriptures and is proficient in the knowledge of Śiva.
One who knows the reality of the Śiva-siddhānta, who worships Śiva, the sacred fire, and the guru, and who is complete in all limbs and endowed with all auspicious marks. || 21-4 ||
One who is said to be between the ages of sixteen and seventy,
who wears a topknot or has his hair tied up, who is grateful, and of pleasing appearance— (5) || 21-5 ||

The householder should be known as the highest, even though he is a materialist, provided he has reached a firm conviction in the scriptures regarding everything from ritual action up to knowledge. (21.6)
In the Kriyāpāda one becomes skilled, which follows upon the Caryāpāda;
in the Yogapāda there is the practice of Kriyā, which colors the Jñānapāda. (21.7)

The knower of reality, established in the true meaning of reality, understands what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted; he knows the supreme, most excellent state, or rather, they know the supreme as fivefold.

The wise one who has been duly initiated for the sake of breaking the bonds of the body, who finds bliss in the nectar of the knowledge of Śiva, and who knows the method of reasoning and refutation, [attains liberation]. (21.9)
A learned man who is of such a nature as this, and who should cause the installations and other rites to be performed—
he alone, O Vatsa, is always the true installer of the Lord.
One should not have the installation and other rites performed by non-Śaivas and the like;
however, from the Kaṇvas onwards, those who follow Śaivism should perform everything up to the installation.
Otherwise, if it is performed for the king, the deities will bring about his destruction;
the Lord of Gods will not accept the prostration, and consequently no fruit arises from it.
If one should ever perform [this] out of delusion, it shall never bring proximity [to the goal].
Therefore, I shall now describe the image-bearers (mūrtipās) who are born of the lineage of the primordial Śaivas.

But in that treatise concerning the commencement of the Ācārya, those whose doubts have been dispelled [should act], for they know the reality of his intention and are favorable toward the Ācārya. (21.14)
A wise person should accept those who are well-known, perfectly composed, possessors of a physical form and its manifestations, and endowed with these qualities. (21.15)
Then, having recognized those who are dwarfish, one should avoid them with great effort;
likewise, one who observes the rules of his own scripture should avoid one who is deficient in limbs or minor members. (21.16)
An atheist, a miser, one afflicted by disease, one who is deaf, one who lives off interest, a physician who subsists on medical treatises, and likewise one who lives as a stage-player; || 21-17 ||
A slanderer, one engaged in cruel deeds, a coward, an adulterer, one who is arrogant toward his own priest, one devoid of truth, and an ungrateful person— || 21.18 ||
A renunciant, an astrologer, one who has fallen from his vows, one with emaciated limbs, a surgeon, one habitually slandering others, a lifelong celibate, and a skull-bearer; || 21.19 ||
One who is too short, too stout, too tall, or has a protruding belly; one with deformed teeth, a hunchback, or is bald—these indeed are [unfavorable]. (21.20)

One who is afflicted by *śipiviṣṭa* (leprosy), possessed of ulcers, with tawny beards, eyebrows, and eyes, as well as one suffering from abdominal tumors, large testicles, and hemorrhoids; || 21-21 ||

One who knows only a little of the *pratiṣṭhā-tantra*, who is enamored with the scriptures of the bound (*paśu*), who is devoid of instruction on the subtle body (*tanu*), and whose mind is distracted or absent-minded; || 21-22 ||
One with deficient limbs, one with redundant limbs, a rogue, one who lives by trade, a eunuch, a Guhyaka, a Nairgaka, and a Śvāpadantaka. (21–23)
A wise person should avoid such individuals who are excluded from all ritual acts;
if one should associate with them out of delusion, [the deity] will never be present.
Having properly accepted the preceptors and the image-makers as previously described, one should then, O dear one, look for an artisan born of a noble family.
One should direct everything concerning the master builder, the string-holder, the carpenter, and the woodworker, as instructed by the presiding architect and according to the treatises on the arts.
Furthermore, he who constructs palaces and such is known as the *hastapati* (master of craftsmen);
the *sūtragrāhin* (string-holder) is one who knows measurement; and the *vardhakī* is one designated by the name *druma*.
That which is capable of thinning [the material] is called *takṣaka*;
it should cut all things that are to be cut, and in the case of things to be split, it is the "splitter of substances.
In the case of things to be pierced, it should pierce the substances; thus, the work of the artisan is threefold.
The master builder and the cord-holder [should oversee] the temples, statues, and so forth. || 21-29 ||
One should perform the opening of the eyes and other rites; one should act with Takṣaka as one would with [other] serpents.
However, in that case, one should always avoid [the specific rites] regarding the mantra-practices for Śeṣa.
Even in the work of artisans, they must act under the direction of the master builder;
for in all artistic undertakings, the master builder acts according to the guidance of the Sthapati.
The master builder (sthapati) should be knowledgeable in the scriptures and practical work, accomplished in his craft, and of noble birth;
he must not have missing limbs nor redundant limbs, and he should be most righteous and truthful in speech. (21–32)
One should employ such an artisan—one endowed with knowledge of the vital points (śalya), virtuous, firm in his bonds, and unwearied—and then begin all the work. (21.33)
The characteristics of the preceptor have been declared; now hear the procedure for the ritual implements.
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, on the Characteristics of the Preceptor.
(p. 97) Now begins the chapter concerning the characteristics of the implements (*karaṇa*).
Hereafter, I shall fully explain the characteristics of the implements; since they are the requisites for sacrifice, they are known as *karaṇas*. (22.1)

The characteristics of Darbha grass, especially those of the purifiers (pavitra), as well as the characteristics of the kūrca-grass bundles, the Darbha garlands, and the ritual seats (viṣṭara). || 22-2 ||

The characteristics of the clarified butter vessel (ājyasthālī), the sacrificial porridge vessel (carusthālī), and the jars (kalaśa); the covering for the oblation vessels (havirpātra) and the characteristics of the water cistern (jaladroṇī). || 22-3 ||
The characteristics of the incense bell and the incense burner, the dimensions of the lamp-sticks, and the characteristics of the yantra. (22-4)

Likewise, I ask about the characteristics of the sacrificial vessels, the three-legged stands, and the ladles, as well as the characteristics of the canopy, the banners, and the cloths; I do not ask about the characteristics of the ritual manuals. || 22-5 ||
Likewise, [he described] the characteristics of the turban, the upper garment, the sword, the seat, the chariot, as well as the palanquin and the couch.
Of the lion-thrones, vehicles, pillars, coverings, and stages; of the sandals, mirrors, fans, and chowries.
The characteristics of white parasols and their fringes, as well as those of peacock feathers; the characteristics of auspicious amulets and the two types of archways. || 22-8 ||
The characteristics of gold bands, flowers, and globes,
as well as those of crowns, earrings, necklaces, and armlets, are indeed [described].
The characteristics of bracelets, armlets, threads, and anklets;
and the characteristics of the ornaments for women, such as those bound around the waist and abdomen. || 22-10 ||
O Gajānana, I shall now describe in due order the measurements and the characteristics of razors, scissors, and brushes. (22.11)
Darbha grass that is not dried out, which is cut, split, and likewise broken,
as well as that which is tender, dark-green, glossy, old, and white, brings auspiciousness.
Those that are soft and dark are feminine; those that are tender and firm are masculine;
and those that are neither tender nor firm are to be understood as neuter. || 22-13 ||
The characteristics of darbha grass have been declared; now hear concerning the purifiers (pavitra):
kuśa, darbha, cow-hair, and likewise kanaka grass are the purifiers.
(98) Or it may be joined with seven, five, or three [fingers]; the tip should be two fingers long.
Its stalk should be two fingers, and the knot should be one finger. || 22-15 ||
A beautiful purifier (pavitra) wound clockwise from right to left, with a width of one finger-breadth, and measuring one-eighth less than the height of the Tārā. || 22-16 ||
The sacred ring called *kanaka* should be made of refined gold,
using fifteen or eleven blades of *darbha* grass.
The length of the darbha grass, measured in finger-breadths, should be ten, nine, eight, seven, or five; for the upward-pointing [bunch], there should be nine blades of darbha.
The length of those seven or five darbha grasses should be nine finger-breadths;
they should be tied in a clockwise direction, and the knot should be one finger-breadth in size.
The tip of the *kūrca* [grass-bundle] should be four finger-breadths long; such is the manner in which the *kūrca* is prescribed.
One should place fifteen more [blades] upon the *śivakumbha*.
Having arranged twelve [units] with the remaining [units], one should arrange them upon the remaining [spaces];
indeed, one should place the upper knot and then the lower knot, just as one would place the front end.
The characteristics of the *kūrca* grass-bundles have been declared; now hear concerning the *darbha* garland.
It should consist of two, three, or five strands, twisted to the right.
One should hang two finger-breadths apart at intervals measured by the span of the hand;
one should make a beautiful cord with a thickness equal to that of the little finger.
Those darbha grasses that hang down are remembered as being most excellent;
for one performing recitation, fire-offerings, and worship, they attain the state of a central pathway.
Having carefully surrounded the sacrificial hall of the palace,
one should prepare a seat (viṣṭara) made of five darbha grass blades, with a knot measuring one finger-breadth.
A seat (viṣṭara) is prescribed with ten fingers' breadth from root to tip;
it should consist of either twenty-seven or twenty-one blades of darbha grass.
Then, a wise person should fashion a *kūrca* from fifteen blades of grass;
its knot is said to be two finger-breadths wide, while the tip should be twice that size. The stalk consists of nineteen blades of *darbha* grass for the binding of the vow.
This indeed has been declared as the sprinkling water; now hear concerning the ritual strewing.

One should bind the girdle with twenty-one blades of darbha grass; its knot should be made with a single strand, and it is desired that the root, the middle, and the tip of the girdle be of equal length.
The spreading of grass has been explained; now hear concerning the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*). They should be of the same dimensions as those prescribed for the fuel-sticks (*samidh*). (22–30)
The length is measured by the cubit (hasta), and the circumference is measured by the little finger (kaniṣṭhāṅguli); three enclosures are prescribed for the west, south, and north.
The characteristics of the enclosing sticks have been declared; now hear the characteristics of the fuel-sticks: they should not be cracked, nor hollow, but straight and free from knots. (22–32)
The sacrificial fuel (samidh) is said to be twelve finger-breadths in length and equal in girth to the little finger; the stirring-ladle (mekṣaṇa) is of the same measurement.
Thereafter, I shall describe the characteristics of the sacrificial post (sṛk); listen, O charming Vināyaka! [The wood of] khadira, śamī, bilva, palāśa, plakṣa, and candana [are suitable]. (22–34)
And likewise, fashion them from sacrificial wood as may be available;
they should be thirty finger-breadths in length and eight finger-breadths in width.
Then, half of that is declared to be the thickness, equalized by the cord;
the inner part should be six finger-breadths and seven finger-breadths in width.
Having divided that [line] into three parts at the tip, one should fashion it like a triangle;
its shape should resemble an elephant’s trunk, and it should be depressed by the measure of a barleycorn (yava).

Outside of that, one should fashion a band (paṭṭaka) measuring one yava and so forth in width; the altar (vedikā) should be well-proportioned with a width of eight aṅgulas and a length of eight aṅgulas.
In the middle of that, one should cause a pit to be made; it should be as wide as the wheel and its depth should be of the same measure, with a rim of one barleycorn's width outside of it.
A band (paṭṭikā) should be fashioned outside of that, one yava deep;
and all around the exterior of the hole, it should be half a finger-breadth [in width].
An auspicious eight-petaled lotus should be fashioned all around the pit;
it should extend from the base of the pit to its mouth, measuring one finger-breadth (kaniṣṭhāṅgula) in width.
The trench should be made for the purpose of the stream, free from depressions and elevations;
it should consist of three sections, each three finger-breadths wide, situated above the staff and below the altar.
Increasing by half a finger-breadth, it may be either circular or square;
the staff is nine fingers long, and its central nave is six fingers.
The handle (daṇḍa) should be made with its tip pointing downward, and its length should be two finger-breadths;
the bowl (nābha) is said to be eight finger-breadths; thus is the measurement prescribed.
On the lotus of the rear portion of the pedestal, one should raise the back-shaped *tulā*.
In its center, one should fashion the shape of a pericarp (*karṇikā*), and the width of the base (*pāda*) should be three finger-breadths. (22.46)
One should construct the spout with a height of one finger-breadth; its length should be one cubit, and it should be provided with an opening at its tip.
The base has a circumference of six finger-breadths, while the neck has a circumference of half that;
the opening at the base has the same circumference as the base and consists of two folds, equal in size to the nostrils.
It should be depressed by the measure of a māṣa and provided with two openings;
the staff is said to resemble a cow’s tail—this is the characteristic of the *srava* [vessel]. (22.49)
One should have it made of gold, silver, copper, or even clay;
it should be eight finger-breadths wide, deep enough to hold one *prastha* when filled.
The thickness of the vessel for the substances is declared to be one *mānāṅgula*;
now, the measurements of the substances at the time of the *homa* are described.
Among clarified butters, that which comes from a cow is the best; among liquids, a full measure of flowing [milk];
a handful of roasted grain flour, clothing, and honey—these indeed are equal to clarified butter.
A handful of parched grain should be the size of an akṣa fruit;
fuel sticks, medicinal herbs, and gifts of fruits should be according to their own natural proportions.
The measure of food for an *akṣa* should be the amount that fills [the hand], while for the *pūrṇāhuti* it is said to be the size of a horn;
for sesame and mustard seeds, however, the measure prescribed is that of a *śukti*.
Curd mixed with milk is proclaimed to be like clarified butter;
one should offer oblations of barley, bamboo-seeds, and horse-gram in the measure of a śukti.
Four handfuls of flour for the cake, and a mere fistful of other grains—such is the measure of the substances. Now hear concerning the vessel for the clarified butter.
The dimensions of the *ājyasthālī* (clarified butter vessel) and the *praṇītā* (water-vessel) are like those of the vessels for the sacrificial materials.
Its mouth should be six finger-breadths in width, and its lip should be one finger-breadth thick. || 22-57 ||
The ear is said to be one finger-breadth, and the belly is declared to be twelve finger-breadths in width; the remainder should be fashioned according to one's own intelligence.
Now hear the rule for the *carusthālī* and likewise for the jars (*kalaśa*).
The belly is declared to have a width of twelve finger-breadths.
The triple-stranded cord is wound around it; no *nāha* (encircling band) is prescribed for it. The ear-ring (*karṇa*) should have a height of two finger-breadths and a width of four finger-breadths.
The lip, however, is recorded as having a height of two finger-breadths and a projection of two finger-breadths;
indeed, the medium and inferior [sizes] should be made in the same manner, but with increased proportions.

Accordingly, the one most skilled in ritual construction should determine the covering for the shallow bowls (śarāva) according to his understanding, with a width equal to the measurement of their mouths. (22.62)
Its height should be three finger-breadths, and it should be depressed by two finger-breadths in the middle;
such is the prescribed measurement—now hear the characteristics of the water-pot (ghaṭa).
Just as it is for the Vaikalaśākara, so too is it traditionally taught;
however, by increasing the qualities fourfold, the Ghaṭa is thus prescribed.
Just as the form of the *caru*-pot and likewise the sacrificial vessel, so too is that which is called the *brahman* defined by the quantity of rice grains it contains. (22.65)
The lid should be equal to the mouth [of the vessel], and likewise there should be a ring in the middle;
a sacrificial vessel (haviḥpātra) is proclaimed to be made of either mixed copper or pure copper.
A water-vessel should be made of gold, silver, copper, or even wood; it may be either circular or square in shape.
It should be filled with ten *droṇas* of water, excluding the neck,
or filled with eight *droṇas*, or with six, or with five *droṇas*.
The task should be performed with either four or three [fingers]; now hear concerning the *vardhanī*:
its mouth should be four finger-breadths wide and provided with two lips.
That side, situated within a hollow space, should be a tube four finger-breadths long;
