it should have a large belly and a slender neck, and then one should perform the proper joining.
And likewise, there should be a water-pot (kamaṇḍalu) with its opening facing upward;
having made the lip hollow, the foot should hang down from the back.
Its hollow on the side should likewise be one finger-breadth in measure,
while the eye-like opening at the top of the mouth-tube should be the size of a *pippala* fruit.
In this manner, one should prepare a water-pot (kamaṇḍalu) endowed with all the auspicious characteristics;
[one should avoid] that which is turbid, infested with worms or moss, or situated in an impure place. (22.73)

Water that is endowed with fragrance, color, and taste, yet devoid of the rays of the sun; water that is defiled by mud or stones, or alkaline water from a salt-lake, or water from a small pond. (22.74)
Water that is free from these defects and is fit to be taken is called "unseizable" (agrāhya). A bath with eight *droṇas* of such water is declared to be the smallest (kanyasa) rite.
(102) Furthermore, consecration with water [up to] twice that amount is considered middling;
with three times that amount of water, it is supreme. Now listen to [the description of] the flower-vessel.
Its width is said to be twenty finger-breadths, and its circumference three times that; the interior circumference is likewise, and such is prescribed for the flower-vessel.
Half of that is the *arghya* vessel, which is devoid of a spout;
its tip is shaped like an arrow, and it stands upon two vessels.
The back of the shallow bowl (śarāva) and its stalk should be eight finger-breadths in length; having made it wide according to the available space, there should be a single spout at its end.
The lid is shaped like a bud and provided with many perforations;
this is described as the incense burner (dhūpapātra). Now, listen to the description of the large bell (urughaṇṭā).
The height should be twelve finger-breadths and the stalk three times that;
the tongue should be twelve finger-breadths, and the tip should be half of that.
In the middle of that, there is indeed a hollow provided with a rim;
its thickness is threefold, and that is known as the thickness of the lip at its opening.
The characteristic of the lowest [type] is that its neck has a height of three finger-breadths;
it is said that the other two are double and triple [that size]. Now listen regarding the incense bell.
One should fashion a bell from bronze; its height is said to be four finger-breadths.
Its width and its measurement should be the same, while its pinnacle shall be half of that.
The bell should be eight finger-breadths [in height], and its tongue four finger-breadths; its thickness should be one-third of that, and the thickness of its lip should be the same as that. (22.85)
This is declared to be the lowest; five finger-breadths is the middle;
six finger-breadths is said to be the highest; all others they know to be equal.
One should place the shaft (śūla) above that, with its base level and its top as the head.
One should place a vessel, or a conch and discus, or a bull upon the head.
During the time of offering incense, it should be accompanied by the sounding of a bell;
by hearing the sound of the bell, one is liberated from all sins.
One should have it made of gold, silver, copper, or bell-metal; it should be without a base, measuring one *rakti* in height, and very wide. One should not, however, have it made of bronze.
The lip should have a height of one finger-breadth;
its thickness is said to be twice that for the middle and superior types, or even two and a half times that.
The characteristics of the lamp-vessel have been declared; now hear concerning the lamp-staff.
It should begin at one cubit and extend up to nine cubits. (22.91)
The width of the staff is proclaimed to be one-eighth of the height;
at five parts of that height, the width of the base is two parts.
From the edge of the platform, its width above should likewise be measured by the span of the hand;
it should be provided with various courtesans and equipped with various jars.
Above that, the stalk is shaped like a bud and joined with knots;
this is declared by you to be the lamp-staff. Now hear about the garland of lamps.
One should have it made of copper, or of black iron, or even of wood;
having fashioned the doorway like a gateway (dvāravat), one should make it radiant in appearance at the back.
The trident should be like a trident, and the discus like a lamp with a discus;
on the head, there is a single-flamed lamp like a *dhurtūra* flower. (22.96)
These have been declared to be the bodies of the lamps; now hear concerning the mechanical parts:
a tube made of iron should indeed be fashioned with a length equal to the middle finger.
Just as the connection between the door and its bolt is properly joined here,
one should then form two faces joined together from east to west.
At its base, it should be joined with a ring and be very smooth;
such is described as the *yaṃtrikā*. Now hear about the vessel for the oblation (*balipātra*).
It is declared that the width should be made of iron, bronze, or copper, measuring four, three, or two *tālas*. (22.100)
One should place [the design] endowed with eight petals in the center of the pericarp;
the height of the two petals should be two finger-breadths, and the pericarps should be one-third of that.
The *tripādī* should be of four kinds: the *śaṅkhapādī*, the *tripādikā*, the *yavanīpāda*, and likewise the *sthalikāpāda*. (22.102)
Its height is six finger-breadths, its mouth-width is half of that, and its circumference is one *kaniṣṭhā* finger-breadth;
this is proclaimed as the *śaṅkhapāda*.
Twice the size, three-quarters, and one-quarter [of the total height] combined with the mouth;
at the base, it should have the shape of a shallow bowl (śarāva), and the remainder should be fashioned according to one's own intelligence.
The three-footed [pedestal] consists of three parts; one part is said to belong to the *vatsayavanī*.
One should know that the height of the *pīṭha* (seat-base) is equal to the height of the *sthalikā*, which is likewise one part. (22.105)

The characteristics of the three-legged stand have been declared; now hear the characteristics of the ladle: its length should be one cubit (ratni), and it should be shaped like the hood of a serpent. (22.106)
It should be eight finger-breadths wide, half of that for the foot, and half of that again for the middle part; this is declared to be the characteristic of the ladle.
Measuring five cubits in both width and length,
it should be provided with a pair of cloths, very smooth, very firm, and white.
One should likewise cause everything to be made with various colors and variegated limbs;
thus has the canopy been described, and now the characteristics of the banner are stated.
It may be made of linen, silk, fine cotton cloth, or even ordinary cotton; it should be one cubit in width and twice that in length.
Alternatively, it may have four, three, or two tails, with its head and tail being half the size of the banner;
the measurement of the flagstaff itself is twice as long as previously stated.
The rest is the same; here the characteristics of the water are stated:
[it may be] with the eyes of a silken goddess, or with cotton, or with white cloth. (22.112)
The width of the cloth is said to be half of half the height of the pedestal; its length is eight times that width, and it should be provided with a border and possess the proper characteristics.
One should discard cloth that has been bitten by mice, scorched by fire, or worn out;
thus is cloth described, for one who asks about it is not said to be asking about a *paṭa*.
The width at the entrance should be one and a half [units], and the length should be double that;
it should be avoided by those who have fallen away from sinful and cruel deeds, by nihilists, and by those who stand far from the Vedas.
Nor with those who sell dairy products, nor with outcaste twice-born men, nor even with those who sell the Vedas or those who sell the Śāstras. (22.116)

The rite for the invisible purpose (adṛṣṭārtha) must be performed; however, worship directed toward the visible [deity] is fruitless, as is the act of offering floral ornaments during the dismissal (visarjana) of the remains of the offering (nirmālya). || 22-117 ||
When the time for the offering is uncertain, one who asks is not said to have discarded the cloth;
[he should wear] a turban and an upper garment, being well-clad in fine white raiment.
The turban and the upper garment should be nine cubits in measure;
the height of the bedstead’s legs should be two *ratni*s.
Alternatively, it may be one cubit in height and twice that in width;
its length should be twice its width, and it should then be secured with cross-straps. (22.120)
The characteristics of the sword have been declared; now hear, O observer of noble vows, about the seat.
It should be joined with four lions and be one cubit in height. (22.121)
It should be made two *ratnis* wide, circular, or square;
it should be covered with trees, high, free from cruelty, and very firm in due order.
Alternatively, the base may be in the shape of a swan or even a *bhūtapāda*.
One should especially fashion the foot in the shape of an elephant or the shape of a bull.
It should be provided with a pigeon-shaped nose, adorned with various jewels,
and made either of gold, silver, or even wood.
This seat has thus been described; now hear about the lotus-seat (padmāsana).
The circular lotus-seat is known to consist of the union of the upper and lower parts. (22.125)
A pedestal (pīṭha) joined with sword-shaped [ornaments], or level and four times as long [as it is wide], and devoid of planks and feet—that is here called a chariot (ratha). || 22-126 ||
One should place two boat-shaped trees joined with four wheels;
above that, one should install the northern part provided with an altar.
Above that, one should place a lotus-band and then a small band;
one should set it upon the lintel, provided with a dove-niche.
There should be twelve minor feet, or eight, or even sixteen;
or they are declared to be twenty, and the nostrils are likewise.
A fresh bud should be fashioned, its stalk having three bends;
having placed two bulls on either side, the Grandfather (Brahmā) is situated between them.
Joined with a supporting rope and fixed at its upper end,
there should be a pavilion or indeed an archway above it, like that of a temple.
The chariot has been described in brief; now hear concerning the arena.
Having fashioned it like the base of a chariot, one should abandon the Brahmā-mukula.
Having constructed it like a performance hall (raṅgamaṇṭapa), it was built like a lower palace;
having made it with wood and two stories, the upper part was made of lacquer (raga).
Alternatively, there may be four elephants in the center, or a bull, a lion, or a tree;
above that base, one should construct three swings, or otherwise have it made as previously described.
Thus has the *raṅga* been described; now hear concerning the *śibikā*.
The *śibikā* is of three kinds: the *mauṇḍī*, the *śekharī*, and [the third]. (22.135)
The best [measurement] is seven tālas, the middling is five tālas, and the inferior is four tālas; thus the width is recorded as being of three kinds.
The length should be twice the width, or the foot may not be twice as long;
it should be adorned with ivory, heartwood, gold, or other precious materials. (22.137)
The inner part of the board and so forth should be joined with a lotus-patterned border;
the lotus petal is six finger-breadths wide, while the finger-breadth of the board is less than that.
The maximum height of the wall should be sixteen finger-breadths;
for the medium and inferior types, it should be reduced by one finger-breadth each.
The width of the band is taught as eight fingers at the best;
for the middling and inferior types, it is likewise reduced by one finger each.
In the middle, it should be provided with a wooden plank and equipped with a lattice-work of boards; resting upon the base of the wall, one should have it fixed with an iron pin.
Adorned with various forms and accompanied by various dances, it is said to be equal to a central band and elevated from the front wall. (22.142)

At the front of the wall, there is a lion's head [projection]; above that, at the level of the Makara’s head, the pedestals (pālikā) should be made, resembling [the shape of] feet, seven or eight aṅgulas in height.
Thus indeed has the *śibikā* been described; now hear concerning the *mauṇḍī* and the *śekhara*. The height of the wall is said to be equal to its width.
Just as a form shaped like a rod is fashioned with a shaven appearance, so too [the temple] is provided with peaks at the crest and joined with *kāpota* mouldings at its base. (22.145)
Thus has the *śibikā* been described; now hear concerning those born from eggs and so forth:
namely, the egg-born (*aṇḍaja*), the head-shaven-born (*muṇḍaja*), the hair-born (*romaja*), and likewise the skin-born (*carmaja*).
The left-hand bed consists of these five types specifically;
furthermore, the "egg-born" type here should be understood as originating from the feathers of birds.
That which is made from cotton is proclaimed as *muṇḍaja*; that which comes from sheep and so forth, or from the hair of wild animals, is remembered as *romaja*.
That made of leather should be from a tiger or a lion; that made of silk is said to be from a wild boar;
or it may be made of woven cloth, provided it is endowed with the appropriate colors of that region.

That which is born from an egg is white in form; that which is born from a tuft of hair is yellow in color; that which is born from body hair is black in color; and that which is born from skin is red in color. (22.150)
The left-born [hand] is white in color, and the silk cloth is of white form;
having fashioned it as is appropriate, the pillow should likewise be so. || 22-151 ||
Or with nine, twelve, or fifteen [syllables],
consisting of various colors and similar colors, endowed with diverse forms.
By these cloths, the beautiful *taraṅga* (wave-pattern) is described here;
when joined with the length of the pillar, it is not released from encircling the pillar. (22-153)
It should be made of pure bronze, with a width of one *ratni*, or else a width of sixteen *aṅgulas* or twelve *aṅgulas*. (22.154)
The height of the mirror for the deity should be half a tāla;
there, one should fashion a footstool measuring twelve finger-breadths according to its own proportions.
The length should be half the width, and the height half the width;
this pair of excellent sandals should indeed be fashioned from iron. (22.156)
The characteristics of the yak-tail fan and other such items shall now be described:
one should make a peacock-feather fan and likewise a yak-tail fan.
One should especially make the handle out of gold and jewels, or else of silver or copper; or one may make the handle from ivory or the heartwood of trees. (22.158)
I shall describe the characteristics of the white umbrella and the peacock-feather [banner]; listen! It should be seven or six tālas in height, or alternatively, five tālas. (22-159)
Having wrapped it all over with cloths, one should adorn it with pearls;
then, one should fashion a peacock-feather crest using peacock feathers.
The crown may be made of gold, silver, or even copper,
measuring nine, eight, seven, six, five, or four cubits.
The length of their staff should be three cubits, or as much as can be obtained; the wise man should make the parasol according to that same measurement.
The parasol and the peacock-feather fan are likewise declared; these are called the eight auspicious signs (aṣṭamaṅgala).
The mirror, the full water-pot, the bull, the pair of chowries, the śrīvatsa, the svastika, the conch, and the lamp constitute the eight divine auspicious signs.
Having placed auspicious objects, especially so, upon the heads of women. || 22-164 ||
Having fashioned forms such as mirrors with a height of one *ratni* and a width of twelve *aṅgulas*, one should indeed place them upon the head. (22.165)
They should all be white in color and adorned with all ornaments; they should be fashioned in the exact same proportions as those of divine women. (22-166)
The best of preceptors should have [the images] fashioned from either clay or wood, placed upon lotus-thrones with their hearts joined together. (22.167)
And having worshipped [the deity] by its own name in all auspicious rites,
[one should prepare a vessel] eight fingers wide and long, or sixteen fingers [in length].
Below that, the lotus pedestal should be made with a measurement equal to one-fourth of it;
above the lotus, one should have mirrors and other such items fashioned, or else have them drawn.

The eight auspicious emblems of the gods have been declared; now hear the characteristics of the weapons: the trident, the axe, the thunderbolt, the sword, the noose, as well as the goad, the bell, the serpent, the fire, and the razor—these are the ten weapons.
It stands at a height of one tāla above the elements.
The length for the Bhūtas is proclaimed to be twenty finger-breadths;
one should construct everything according to all the measurements, using the measurement of the Bhūtas as the standard.
The color of the name [of the deity] should be the same as the color stated for the weapon.
One should fashion the trident with one part, and the *gaṇḍikā* (the base or socket) likewise with one part.
The characteristics of the trident (śūla) have been declared; now hear the characteristics of the axe (paraśu).
A wise man [should fashion it] with the measurement of time by means of the handle-joint (gaṇḍikā) and the base of the trident.
The handle, the neck, and the knot should be joined with four faces;
thus indeed is the axe described, and its characteristics are said to be like those of a thunderbolt.
The height of the *yāma* should be one *tāla*, and its width is considered to be eight fingers;
in the middle of that, one should fashion a *gaṇḍikā* measuring four fingers.
With the remaining eight finger-breadths, it should be like a trident below and above;
on the sides there are two petals, and the wheel is situated straight in the middle. (22.177)
Thus the vajra has been fully described; now the characteristics of the khaṭvāṅga are stated: its width at the bottom should be one finger-breadth, and it should have a sheath. (22.178)
The square wooden plank shall have a width of four finger-breadths;
its corner shall be three finger-breadths, and its thickness two finger-breadths.
Above the *karṇa*, one should fashion a *pālikā* according to half the measurement prescribed for the *phalaka*;
its width above that should be one *aṅgula*, and its length half an *aṅgula*. (22.180)
Having made the blade straight and the tip [of the handle] curved in this manner is the characteristic of a sword.
A noose joined with two hoods is declared to be the serpent-marked [noose]. (22.181)

The bell should be fashioned according to the previously mentioned procedure, endowed with all its characteristic features; one should fashion the serpent with its coils complete, provided with hoods and a tongue. (22.182)
Joined with a flame of fire, this [channel] becomes half a palm in length;
its root is like a sword, being as high as the edge of a razor.
Straight, sharp, joined together, and endowed with a fine point—
thus is the ten-weaponed [trident] described, held in the hand of Sadāśiva.
In all auspicious rites, during festivals, and in sacrificial ceremonies, one should worship the weapons of the world-protectors with special care; listen [to how]. (22.185)

The vajra, the śakti, the staff (daṇḍa), the sword (khaṭvāṅga), the noose (pāśa), the goad (aṅkuśa), the mace (gadā), the trident (triśūla), the discus (cakra), and the lotus (padma)—these are known as the ten weapons. || 22-186 ||

One should have the worldly scriptures (lokaśāstra) fashioned according to the measurement previously stated for the ten weapons; as before, the characteristics of the *vajra* have been explained, and now the characteristics of the *śakti* are being described.
At the base, it should be joined with a tenon (gaṇḍikā) measuring one finger-breadth each;
the three tenons should increase in width by one finger-breadth each.
Its base is four finger-breadths [in width], and its circumference is six finger-breadths;
above that is a jointed knob (gaṇḍikā), and above that is the vase (kumbha).
Thus the staff (daṇḍa) is fully described; the sword (khaṭga) and the noose (pāśa) are as before.
The tongue, joined at its tip to the palate, is like a white crescent moon.
The one known as Aṅkuśa is said to have the characteristics of a mace (gadā);
however, for the mace, it should be fashioned as before beneath the pot.
The mace is indeed remembered as being joined with a stream of water-pots (kumbhadhārā), like a staff;
and the trident, endowed with its previously mentioned parts, is just as before, O Lord.
The measurement of the wheel is like that of the trident; it is provided with twelve spokes, possesses a hub in the center, and is joined with petals all around.
Thus the wheel has been fully described; now the characteristics of the lotus are stated:
it should be eight finger-breadths in size, in the form of a bud, and endowed with eight petals. (22.194)
One should fashion a lotus with its characteristic features having a stalk four finger-breadths long;
it may be made of gold, silver, copper, or even wood. (22.195)
Having made their height one cubit (ratni) according to the measure of a man, there is a slight distinction here: it may be according to the capacity or the form of a woman.
The remaining [deities] are in human form, adorned with all ornaments; holding weapons upon their heads, they should be saluted with palms joined in reverence. || 22-197 ||
The eastern [arches] should have the color of weapons, and their names shall indeed be those of the weapons themselves.
The characteristics of the weapons have been declared; now hear in due order regarding the arches (toraṇas), which are made of Palāśa, Khadira, Aśvattha, Śamī, Bilva, and Śirīṣa wood.
Or else, one should properly have archways constructed according to the methods of the ritualists.
It should be seven, six, or five cubits in height, with a width half of that;
in the center, it should be provided with a spike (śūla) measuring one cubit.
The procedure for archways has been declared; now the auspicious archway (bhadra-toraṇa) is described. One should install it at the gates of the gopuras during an auspicious rite.
The length should be one-quarter greater than the door, and the width should be equal to the door;
the pillar should be provided with a *kumbha* and *gaṇḍī*, its cross-beam (*viṣkaṃbha*) being as wide as a jewel;
it should be adorned with circles of *aśvattha* leaves and the eight auspicious symbols.
Having placed a trident above, measuring one cubit in length. || 22-203 ||
The auspicious archway has thus been described; now hear about the golden flower:
it should be twelve finger-breadths in width, or half of that divided by eight.
The flower is thus described as having a central pericarp and being endowed with eight petals; now hear concerning the cloth and the ball.

One should have the cloth-band made according to the measurement of the penis, with its width being one-sixth [of the circumference] and its length equal to the girth of the penis; the beads should be slightly smaller than the measurement of the penis. || 22-206 ||
The matted-hair crown of Īśa, the diadem for Śaktinandana, as well as the crown, earrings, necklace, and armlets; 22–207.
One should provide bracelets, waist-bands, anklets, and likewise waist-girdles for women; these indeed are their jewel ornaments.
Just as one perceives [the features] within a statue, so too does the wise person perceive them right there;
thus has the ornament been described. Now hear about the razor and the knife. (22.209)
The left [part] should consist of eight finger-breadths, and its width likewise half of that;
the tube for it should be made of iron and four finger-breadths long.
Measuring twelve finger-breadths and joined with the six flavors of the three steps, the razor and the knife are prescribed; one should employ them in the rite of initiation.
The cleansing with a network of ripples is done with a measure of twelve finger-breadths;
[one should use] the pith of coconut leaves combined with plenty of *sāra* [wood].
One cubit (aratni) in length at the tip and bound with a cord at the base—this is declared to be the two types of broom for the act of sweeping. (22.213)
In this context, one should discard all earthen vessels after a month has passed;
however, those made of metal, wood, and so forth, may be retained until their dissolution.
Thus has the summary of villages and so forth been declared; now hear [the rest].
This is the twenty-second chapter, concerning the characteristics of the section on the instruments [of ritual action]. 22.
Now begins the chapter on the characteristics of villages and so forth.
Hereafter, I shall fully explain the characteristics of villages and the like;
one should duly establish villages and other settlements for the purpose of worshipping the deities. (23-1)
A village, a city, a port, a market town, a hamlet, a cottage, a camp, and a royal capital. || 23-2 ||
These ten are indeed proclaimed in sequence as the divisions of the army; and for Brahmins who are truthful, it is remembered as Vāsogrāma.
That very place is remembered as the agrahāra of the foremost brahmins;
it was crowded with many castes and filled with people of various crafts. (4)
Filled with buyers and sellers and endowed with all the gods, that city is thus renowned; now hear about the port.

A place where goods from other islands are involved in buying and selling is a *pattana* (port city), while one situated on the shore of the ocean is a *kharpaṭa*; that which is a mixture of both is a *kharpaṭa*. (23.6)
Engaged in the activities of buying and selling, filled with various kinds of people, and provided with weavers—that city is thus remembered. (23.7)
That which is presided over by Śūdras is celebrated as a *kheṭaka*;
those situated at an equal distance from them are called *saṃkuṭika*. (23.8)
And the royal army, O Muni, is known as the camp (śibira), which is filled with the fourfold forces and endowed with the prosperity of the king. || 23-9 ||
That which is joined with the royal palace is called the capital city;
it is filled with all castes and endowed with the king’s residence. (23.10)
Provided with many protective measures, it is known as the "vanguard of the army" (senāmukha).
It consists of twelve thousand villages, or alternatively, ten thousand.
The three highest [levels] should be performed with eight thousand repetitions each;
indeed, the three middle [levels] are performed with seven, six, and five thousand respectively.
One should resort to the three small [mandalas] consisting of four, three, and two thousand [squares] respectively.
Thus, the ninefold [classification] has been declared; now the minor [mandalas] are being described.
One thousand, five hundred, and two hundred and fifty are said to be the best among the small [sacrifices];
and two hundred and one hundred and fifty are indeed the middling-small.
The smallest [size] is traditionally held to be forty, thirty, or twenty [finger-breadths];
among these eighteen types, one should have it made according to one's capacity. || 23-15 ||

One should invite and worship, in due order, those endowed with learning, conduct, and virtue—namely the wife, the sacred fires, and the preceptor’s son—as well as those who are poor but learned in the Vedas and Shastras. (23.16)
One should present the names of the Brahmins and so forth, along with their lineages, upon copper plates;
likewise, having determined the village boundaries, one should do so by means of the primary scribe.

One should grant the land, as determined by the authoritative measurements, preceded by the pouring of water; only when this has been done should one subsequently begin the layout of the village. (23.18)
Having leveled the ground and prepared it with trenches and furrows,
one should measure out the site for the most excellent [temple] using a five-thousand-unit staff.
A wise man should construct the middle-sized [stūpa] with a measurement of one thousand cubits,
while that of the inferior one should be made with a measurement of half that cubit.
The best of those who know the tantras should fashion it as circular, or square, or with its length facing east, or even extending toward the south. (23.21)
In the middle of that, in the south-western quarter,
having spread out a circle of stakes with a width equal to the length of a staff, he should place a marked stake in the center.
Having fashioned [the staff] from khadira, sandalwood, or wood from the śāla, aśvattha, or nyagrodha trees, twelve finger-breadths in height and half of that in circumference; || 23-23 ||
From the base, it should be sixteen [units] less at the tip, very firm, straight, and without blemishes;
it should be twice or thrice the measure of the peg for the three mandalas.
Having meditated upon Brahmā with the mind and having placed [the gnomon] in the middle of the circle,
one should observe the falling of the tip of the shadow and mark it clearly.
In the forenoon or in the afternoon, one should stretch the cord there;
having thus determined the east, the wise man should [determine] the north by means of the fish-mark.
One should fashion eighty-one squares there according to the measurement of the thread;
having visualized the deities residing therein, one should worship them in sequence with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings. (23–27)
Īśāna, Atharvan, Parjanya, Jayanta, Mahendraka, Āditya, Satya, Abhraṃśa, and Antarikṣa were those who went before. (23–28)
Agni, Pūṣan, Vitatha, Ugra, Kṣata, Yama, Gandharva, Bhṛṅgarāja, and Mṛga are likewise situated in the south. (23–29)
Niṛti, Vārika, Sugrīva, Puṣpadantaka, Varuṇa, Asura, Śoṣa, and Pāpayakṣman are in the west. (23–30)
Vāyu, Nāga, as well as Mukhya, Bhallāṭa, Soma, and likewise Ṛga, Dadhi, and Ayana— these are the thirty-two outer deities.
Marīci, Vivasvat, Mitra, Pṛthvitara, Āpa, Apavatsa, Savitṛ, and Sāvitra; || 23–32 ||
Indra-jaya and Rudra-jaya are likewise;
that [measure] is equal to two...
[omitted]. Half of that is by the minor method (*kṣudravidhi*) according to the southern and northern paths.
To the east of the commencement of the planetary hall, however, there is a separate abode for the gods.
The Śrīvatsa, the Nābhi, the Varta, the one with sides, the Padmaka, the Nandyāvarta, the Bhadra, the Svastika, and the Prakīrṇaka. (23–36)
Thus has the specific placement of villages and houses been described; the encampment of an army is threefold, known as the *kumbha*, the *vedikā*, and the *siṃha*.
One should arrange the Nāgara and other styles in what is known as the Daṇḍaka layout;
there are three streets facing east and five or seven facing north.
The arrangement with eight gates is called Śrīvatsa;
those very same rules are declared [to apply], and it is joined with a navel in the center.
The royal road on both sides and the navel-circle are described;
that which is without a navel is declared as before, and is remembered as being "joined with the sides. (23–40)
Provided with eight doors and facing east, with five types of pathways,
and having constructed the remaining parts as before, it is declared to be the Nandyāvarta.
If one sprinkles the door-frame and touches the middle of the tree, it is called by the name Bhadraka; now hear about Svastika.
The crosswise method consists of an odd number of lines facing east, forming a square;
this is called the Svastika. Now hear about the Padmaka. || 23-43 ||
The minor rites, such as the *nābhi* and *maṅgala-vīdhī*, are performed with an odd number [of repetitions];
and that enclosure around the door is called this *padmaka*.
Likewise, having formed it like a svastika with the two doorways at the center of the corners, this is the lotus with a pericarp; now hear about the *padmāvarta*.
That which extends through the middle of the road like a lotus is known as the *padmāvarta*; it is joined with a navel in its center and possesses a central pathway. (23.46)
This is declared to be *prakīrṇaka*; now hear about *kumbhaka*.
That which is surrounded by the aforementioned *ratthī* is called *kumbhaka*. (23–47)
The wise one should construct [the stūpa] for a person of middle capacity with a measurement of one thousand cubits;
however, for a person of inferior capacity, it should be made with a measurement of half that cubit.
(115) Provided with two doors, one of which may be extended as desired, this is called *daṇḍaka*; it is designated by the name of the village or other locality. (23.50)
One should not perform the cutting of the staff or the cutting of the thread as prescribed for the navel;
[the latter] with the embryo is endowed with all prosperity, while that without the embryo is the destroyer of everything. (23.51)
Therefore, first the Earth together with her embryo must be fashioned, using two hundred palas of copper, or half of that, or half of that again. (23.52)
A receptacle made of husks should be prepared, measuring one cubit in size;
it should consist of nine compartments, be provided with a lid, and be well-constructed and firm. (23.53)
Having meditated upon the seed-syllable of the jewel (ratnabīja), one should indeed place iron clods within the center of the refuse-basket and install them at an auspicious moment.
In the middle of the village, in the assembly hall, on the right side of the door, in a temple, in a cow-pen, or on the bank of a pond. (23–55)
Having thus properly laid out the womb (garbha), one should begin the series of planetary squares (grahaśreṇī),
consisting of three lines, five lines, or at least seven lines.
They know the triad of middling [sattvas] to be nine, eleven, and ten;
and the seventeen, nineteen, and twenty-one [to be the highest]. (23.57)
O wise one, among these three excellent types of lotuses, one should increase the width by two units at a time, such that each subsequent type exceeds the previous by one *daṇḍa*. (23.58)
With a width of half its length, or twice or three times as long; this is indeed called the primary residence of Puruṣa, situated to the south. (23.59)
The northern section should be thus; for women, it is the reverse.
A great seat is prescribed for Īśa, and a doorway for Māhendraka.
One should arrange the grain in the southwest; the exit for water is in the northeast.
The door facing the east is prescribed for the rites of the deities and the planets. (23.61)
Or, according to the measurement of the Mahāvīdhī, it is twenty-seven cubits;
that is declared to have two doors, indeed in the aforementioned sites of the Vāstu.
Half of that [measurement] is for the minor ritual according to the southern and northern paths;
however, to the east of the commencement of the planetary [temple], there shall be a separate abode for the gods.
In the northeast is the location of Īśvara, or else between Soma and Īśāna;
likewise, the wise one should arrange it in the middle of Indra and Īśāna. (23.64)
Above a thousand Brahmins, in the region of Vāyu,
one should indeed install Janārdana as Brahmeśa according to the rite of the five forms.
The station of Bhāskara is in the east, that of Mahāmoṭī in the southeast;
the station of Durgā is in the south, and that of Maheśī in the southwest.
The station of Viṣṇu is in the west (vāruṇī), that of Subrahmaṇya in the northwest (vāyava);
and likewise, the station of Vināyaka along with the Mothers is properly in the north.
The station of the Mothers is desired outside the ramparts and the moat;
indeed, their northern gate is for the welfare of villages and other settlements. (23.68)
The western door belongs to Sūrya, while for others it faces the east;
on the bank of the tank, however, one should install the goddess Jyeṣṭhā.
There shall be separate temples for the gods, both externally and internally;
however, the site for Śiva’s temple shall be in the exterior, in the location previously specified.
One should not pierce the joints or vital points with the tip [of the plumb line], for that is the abode of the gods;
one should demarcate the fifth part of the village boundary separately on all sides.
There, the temple known as Paiśāca is remembered;
the constant worship of Śiva there bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (23.72)
The constant worship of others will bring prosperity to the village;
however, one should not allow anyone to dwell there for even a single night at a place other than a temple. (23.73)
Indeed, when deprived of daily worship, he becomes enraged and inflicts suffering;
therefore, those who worship him should remain by his side, near his temple. (23.74)
Having duly prepared a dwelling, they should settle there free from disturbances;
however, the residence for the Śūdras should be located all around the outskirts of the villages and other settlements.
To the west of a water source, or in the southern direction, or specifically to the west of potters or in the eastern direction. || 23-76 ||
In the west [is the quarter] of those who subsist on meat; in the northwest, of those who live by fish;
in the south, of those who subsist on oil; and in the north, of those who live by flowers.
In the southeast [one should place] the barbers, and in the southwest the weavers; around that perimeter wall, outside, one should separately place the lowest castes. (23.78)
One should assign laborers either to the east or to the west;
outside of them are the artisans, and outside of those are the Caṇḍālas.
Having gone one *krośa* from the village, or half of that distance from the cities,
the cremation ground is prescribed to be located in the northeast direction of the village.
Alternatively, on the bank of a river or in the Soma region, one should construct a pond at some distance away, or arrange for a tank in one of the four directions or in a corner. || 23-81 ||
Thus has the definition of villages and other settlements been briefly declared;
now listen with your mind to the certain determination of their prosperity.
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, concerning the characteristics of villages and so forth. || 23 ||
Now follows the chapter on the determination of manifestation (*vibhava*).
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the definitive determination of manifestation;
the path is said to be twofold: that which is with form (*sāmūrta*) and that which is formless (*hāraka*). (24.1)

The *śiva* [mantra] is declared to be with the *sāman* [vowels], while others are remembered as being with the *hāraka* [consonants]. One who is unable to perform the *sāmrata* [method] should begin with the *hāraka*.
When an action previously commenced is first brought to completion, and subsequently another action reaches its conclusion, this is called the "stealing" (hāraka) path. || 24-3 ||
The wise one should respectfully prepare the nine types of sacrificial implements;
he should employ those who are devoted to the primordial Śaiva tradition, endowed with austerity, knowledgeable in the ritual rules, and possessed of the mantras.
Having invited, according to the scriptures, those foremost upholders of the Śiva-vow who are experts in the Śaiva Vedas, devotion should be generated toward that [deity]. (24.5)
This treatise, which rests upon all scriptures, is difficult to find among all forms of knowledge;
this tantra, endowed with all rites of worship, is the means for accomplishing all goals. (24.6)
This scripture is supremely divine, like the sun amidst the darkness;
therefore, this Śaiva teaching is the most excellent, like the sun among jewels. (24.7)
They possess the divine Śaivaratna doctrine and have reached the further shore of the meaning of the Śaiva scriptures;
they are, in particular, like the moving forms of Śiva himself.
Having paid homage according to the rule, he should inquire after them in accordance with the prescribed ritual;
then, having obtained their permission, he should address those who reside in his own country, who are endowed with devotion and firm in their conduct.
O Śivamukhya and others, you are my servants; therefore, from among you all, [choose one] for me, your servant and devotee, who am solely intent upon devotion to you. (24.10)
"You should grant me your permission, and let the worship be accepted;
I shall perform the initiation in those [rites] which are the supreme among sacrifices."
"May this long sacrificial session be brought to completion by you; it is most excellent.
For the sake of pacifying misfortunes, may you yourselves take up the leadership. (24.12)
Furthermore, I shall cast that great [mantra] into you utterly;
or else, having taken up one hundred and eight [recitations], it belongs to the Ādiśaivas.
This must be done by me for the completion of the sacrifice;
let us strive with special diligence according to the path of your instruction.
For the middle [grade of practitioners], there should be just enough sacrificial offerings for the enjoyment of worship;
likewise, there should be just enough for the sake of perfumes, flowers, and incense. (24.15)
Likewise, for the purpose of bathing and similarly for the purpose of festivals, there shall be this many attendants, provided with all necessary requisites. (24.16)
This much was indeed for the purpose of expiation for the Kṛttikā-lamp;
this much was for the purpose of providing refuge, consisting of abundant sacrificial offerings.
To the preceptor, as well as to all those who possess more or less [of the teachings], to the protector of the Tantra itself, and to the scribe—[to all these, one should offer]. (24.18)
For the listeners and likewise for the speaker, as well as for the astrologer and those who wish to hear, there is this much enjoyment and this much divinity. (24.19)
(119) This much was indeed for the sake of hospitality toward Śiva, as well as for the devotees, for the musicians, and likewise for Takṣaka. (24.20)
Having reflected thus, one should perform everything according to the sequence, repeatedly recollecting each task as it is appropriate. (24.21)
One should indeed designate a portion of land for their maintenance;
if it is carried away by these [animals] during that interval, the fruit of the completion [of the rite] shall be attained. || 24-22 ||
One should arrange inexhaustible food for them so that they may eat pure meals;
they live constantly with unwashed garments, yet always perfumed with fragrances and the like. (24.23)

The wise one should establish the householders, providing them with all necessary requisites, ensuring their livelihood is well-sustained, and making them firmly established in accordance with the teaching. (24.24)
He who, having provided little enjoyment for his attendants, instead torments them with hardship—
he, O Lord of Gods, being himself of unshakable nature, is indeed the one who suffers.
Whether it remains or does not remain, one should not consider it as either low or wealthy;
for it yields fruit through its own effort, yet if it is not given, it goes toward fruitlessness.

If a man should perform [this rite] with stinginess regarding wealth or with deceit regarding the Dharma, together with twenty-one previous generations of his own family as well as his descendants; || 24-27 ||
One whose mind is overcome by greed does not obtain that fruit;
therefore, one should set aside a third part of one's wealth for the sake of one's own livelihood. (24–28)
Two parts were for the sake of dharma, since life is impermanent;
and having accomplished that, he placed it entirely within a copper vessel sealed with lac.
"The certainty regarding wealth has been declared; now hear, O observer of noble vows, about its cultivation.
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, "The Certainty Regarding Wealth."
(p. 120) Now begins the chapter on plowing.
Next, I shall fully explain the plowing for the sake of the temple;
at an auspicious hour and a favorable moment, the preceptor, together with the artisans, [should perform it]. (25-1)
One should commence activities such as plowing during the period of the sun’s northern course;
likewise, there are the seasons of winter, spring, summer, and the rainy season. (25.2)
Autumn and winter are indeed proclaimed as two of the six seasons;
the cold season consists of the months of Tapas and Tapasya, namely Māgha and Phālguna.
Spring consists of the two months Caitra and Vaiśākha, known as Madhu and Mādhava; the summer season consists of the two months Jyeṣṭha and Āṣāḍha, known as Śukra and Śuci.
The two months known as Śrāvaṇa and Bhādra are called Nabhas and Nabhasya; they constitute the rainy season (prāvṛṭ).
Īṣa and Ūrja, namely Āśvayuja and Kārtika, however, constitute the autumn (śarat). 25-5.
Saha and Sahasya are known as the two months of the winter season, corresponding to Mārgaśīrṣa and Pauṣa;
the southern path is to be understood as the night of the gods, while the northern path is their superior [day]. (25–6)
It is considered that the northern course (of the sun) lasts for twelve days, while the southern course is swift;
one should avoid the months of Mārgaśīrṣa, Śrāvaṇa, Bhādrapada, and Āśvina.
All months are to be accepted as declared by Śiva;
even among all those months, spring is said to be the best. (25.8)

The best, the middling, and the inferior [times] have been declared; the southern course [of the sun], as well as the lunar mansions, fortnights, and days of the week, have already been well explained. (25.9)
Kṛttikā has Agni as its presiding deity, and Rohiṇī is Prajāpati;
Mṛgaśīrṣa has Soma as its deity, while Śiva is remembered as the deity of Ārdrā. (25.10)
Bṛhaspati is the deity of Punarvasu, Āditya of Tiṣya,
Hīnāga (the serpent) of Āśleṣā, and likewise the Pitṛs of Makha.
For Bhoga is indeed Phālguna, and Aryaman is Uttaraphālguna; Hasta is said to belong to Savitṛ, and it is honored in all undertakings. (25.12)
Tvaṣṭṛ belongs to Citrā, while Vāyu is the presiding deity of Svāti;
Indra and Agni belong to Viśākhā, and the mixed deities (the Aśvins) belong to Anurādhā.
Indra is the deity of Jyeṣṭhā, and likewise Nirṛti is the deity of Mūla;
Pūrvāṣāḍhā is said to have the Waters as its deity; all these are indeed unfavorable for the installation [of images]. (25.14)
The Viśvedevas are in Uttarāṣāḍhā, Brahmā and the Self (Ātman) are likewise in Abhijit; Hari is in Śravaṇa, and the Vasus are in Śraviṣṭhā. (25.15)
Varuṇa is the deity of Śatabhiṣaj; Aja is the deity of Proṣṭhapada; and Ahirbudhnya is proclaimed as the deity of Uttaraproṣṭhapāda. (25.16)
Pūṣan is the presiding deity of Revatī, as are Aśvinī and Āśvayuja; likewise, Yama is the presiding deity of Bharaṇī. These are the presiding deities of the days. || 25-17 ||
Tiṣya, Śravaṇa, Hasta, Ārdrā, Maitra, Āditya, Makhā, as well as Prājāpatya, Aśvayuk, Svāti, Saumya, Pauṣṇa, and the three Uttarās; || 25-18 ||
The second and the third, the fifth, the sixth, and the seventh; the tenth and the eleventh, as well as the first and the thirteenth. (25.19)

The full moon day (paurṇamāsī) and other lunar days (tithis), especially those in the bright fortnight (śuklapakṣa), as well as the zodiac signs (rāśis), are to be accepted; however, the movable signs (cararāśis) are to be avoided, with the exception of Sagittarius (dhanus). || 25-20 ||
Mercury, Venus, the Moon, and Jupiter are the best among the days; the others are not so.
The decans (drekkāṇa), navāṃśas, and horās are desired as being single in nature. (25–21)
Having abandoned the rising of the Moon and the auspicious rising of other [planets] there, this day, joined by malefic planets, causes disease and affliction here. (25-22)
The Moon, the Sun, and Mars, when situated in the third or sixth house, are auspicious;
however, those same planets, when occupying the ascendant, cause disease, grief, and fear. (25-23)
All planets situated in the eighth house cause misfortune for the doer;
all those gone to the eleventh house bestow security, health, and prosperity. (25-24)

Bhārgava (Venus) is said to cause fear when situated in the sixth, seventh, or tenth house; likewise, Guru (Jupiter) is a bringer of auspiciousness when situated in the ninth, second, seventh, or fifth house.
The day of the Moon is declared to bring happiness on the second and fifth lunar days; likewise, Sunday is auspicious when joined with the asterisms Revatī, Hasta, and the three Uttarās. (25–26)
Saturday is declared auspicious when conjoined with Svātī or Rohiṇī; the second lunar day joined with Mercury, and the sixth joined with Jupiter. (25–27)
Indeed, Indu joined with Ekādaśī causes affliction to life;
but Pauṣṇa joined with Saptamī burns the subjects like fire. (25–28)

(122) An inauspicious Monday conjoined with Uttarāṣāḍhā—one should avoid the *viṣṭi* yoga, the end of the *tithi*, the portions of the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra-khaṇḍāṃśa*), and the *gulika* periods. (25–29)
On a cloudy day, during a conflagration of the quarters, during an earthquake, a violent wind, or on a day accompanied by the sound of thunderbolts, it is remembered as inauspicious. (25–30)
At the transit of the sun, during an eclipse, at the solstices, and likewise at the equinoxes;
during a festival, at a time of pacification, or also at the commencement of the six-eighths (ṣaḍaśītimukha). || 25-31 ||
If one should act out of delusion, it will surely result in the destruction of the maker's object;
therefore, having examined this thoroughly, one should fasten [the thread] if one desires prosperity for oneself. (25–32)
On delightful mountains, or in a village or a city, or again in Indreśāna, Īśāna, or Someśāna. (25–33)
In whatever delightful location one intends to begin the construction of a palace,
one should first examine the ground and immediately thereafter perform the ritual plowing.

White, red, yellow, and black earth belongs to the Brāhmaṇas and the other castes respectively. Earth that is white bestows liberation, while that which is red likewise grants victory to the Kṣatriyas. (25–35)
Land belonging to a Vaiśya bestows wealth, while that belonging to a Śūdra grants sons;
however, one should avoid saline soil, ground infested with worms, and that situated on an anthill. (25–36)
One should dig the ground to the depth of a knee and fill the pit with that very earth; if the ground rises above [the original level], it is excellent, but if it is level, it is middling. (25–37)
One should carefully avoid what is deficient and install the deity residing therein; specifically, one should offer bali-oblations to the bhūtas, pretas, and piśācas. (25–38)

"However, having accepted the offering and worship for the purpose of establishing this abode of the God of Gods upon the surface of the earth, you should depart quickly so that it may be done with ease.
Having spoken thus to the gods, he then dismissed them and Prakarṣaṇa.
The two bulls should be tawny, well-nourished, red, and indeed free from any physical defects.
One should not make it of any other color, nor should it have the horns and hooves of a calf; having placed golden horns and hooves upon it, one should worship it with the Vṛṣamantra.
And having fastened the yoke with sacrificial wood produced from trees—
namely *śamī*, *bilva*, *khadira*, and likewise the *panasa* cluster— || 25-42 ||
p. 123) Having done so, Takṣaka bound it with iron; having fastened a plough to a yoke with a rope made of cow-hide, [he set it in motion]. (25.43)
The preceptor, being a true Śaiva, having consecrated his own body with the ritual imposition of the limbs (sakalīkṛtavigraha),
shall cause the declaration of an auspicious day to be recited and then sprinkle [the site] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
One should plow the earth, which is oriented toward the northeast and marked with the *praṇava*, while reciting the *Śiva-mantra*.
Then, having honored the preceptor, one should present him with a bull together with a cow.
One should sow sesame, mustard, mung beans, and śāli rice seeds; those that have sprouted after five nights are to be taken, while others are to be rejected. (25.46)
During those fortnights and at those times, one should report the herds of cattle;
having thus examined the earth, the best of teachers should be accepted.
When the sun has set and the day has become auspicious, this bull should be released;
one should take the measurement of the shadow of the gnomon (śaṅku) and there construct a mandala.
Having made it level there and smeared it with cow dung, its length should be twelve finger-breadths, and its width should be equal to its own length.
Having set aside one-eighth part, the upper portion of seven parts is for the *nāhaka*;
[the base] should be made of *śamī*, *bilva*, or *palāśa* wood, or especially of wood suitable for sacrifice.
Having fixed the gnomon (śaṅku) in the center of that [circle], the preceptor should rotate three circles;
then, having observed the shadow of the gnomon in either the forenoon or the afternoon,
he should cause the eastern line to fall in the middle of that [space] along the path of the cord.
And having fixed a mark there according to the measurement of the eastern thread.
Having thus conceived the water and the thread as square, it is the extent for the palaces, pavilions, and enclosures. (25.53)
Having grasped the most excellent [deity], the wise one should cause the auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be proclaimed;
having taken hold of the root-place, he should then perform the rite for the child-place.
The procedure for ploughing has been declared; now hear the procedure for the site of the child.
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, on the Procedure for Ploughing.
(p. 124) Now follows the chapter on the characteristics of the *taruṇālaya* (the young temple).
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the characteristics of the *taruṇālaya*; the *taruṇālaya* is of two kinds: the first and likewise the second. || 26-1 ||
That which was the eastern part of the original site is the Ādyantaruṇālaya;
it was made so again when the temple was being rebuilt after it had been broken and torn apart.
That which has been performed is called the second, the supreme Taruṇālaya;
all other rites are said to be the same. (26-3)

Having determined the location for the primary deity (mūlasthāna), one should prepare the location for the secondary deity (bālasthāna). After installing the secondary liṅga, one should subsequently install the primary one.
One should not construct the root site (mūlasthāna) without first establishing the site for the child (bālasthāna);
for where the site for the child is omitted, there is the destruction of sons and grandsons. (26-5)
Therefore, with every effort, one should cause the state of childhood to be performed;
at whatever time and in whatever field the appropriation of the ground has been made.
In front of it, or to the north, or in front to the left or right,
or even in the northeast, one should have the new temple (taruṇālaya) constructed with the remaining materials.
Having performed the ritual offering of sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa) on the fifth, seventh, or ninth day, or at night,
[one should install] a liṅga made of metal, stone, wood, or clay.
The preceptor, however, should especially have [the image] fashioned according to the prescribed characteristics, using *śamī*, *bilva*, *madhūka*, as well as *aśvattha* and *udumbara* wood. (26.9)
An image of Bāla should be fashioned out of well-baked clay;
twelve finger-breadths in height is proclaimed to be the best size.
The lowest of the low is indeed seven finger-breadths in height; from that, by an increase of two finger-breadths each, nine types of *bāla-liṅgas* are recorded. (26.11)
The entire movement that has become the *svadhāma-kuṇḍalinī* is described here;
one should form the head in the shape of an umbrella, even without the extraction of the *lakṣaṇa*. (26-12)
One should have the pedestal made of its own material or else of brick;
the inner sanctum (antarālaya) should be made seven, five, or three cubits in size.
Thus has the first [type] been fully described; in the second, the *taruṇālaya*, the extent of the worship-area (*pūjābhāga*) should be three-quarters or even half [of the whole]. (26.14)
(125) I have not described the measurement of the height [of the liṅga] without the application of the characteristic marks;
for Viṣṇu and Viriñca are portions [of Śiva], and thus [the liṅga] is like one whose linga has been uprooted from its base. || 26-15 ||

Having thus prepared the linga according to the measurement of the base, the womb, or half the size, it is stated here that the *bālagraha* (the head-piece) should be one-third or one-fourth [of the height]. (26.16)

Within the interior of the child’s house, there should be a pedestal equal in height to the child’s phallic emblem (liṅga), with its height being equal to its width, provided with a hollow and a water-channel. || 26-17 ||
Having divided the length of the *liṅga* into three parts, one part should be placed upon the pedestal;
it may be circular or square, joined with a sixteenth part.

One should not perform the depositing of jewels (ratnanyāsa), nor the mountain-like foot-projections (pādaśailānikāni); one should not perform [the rites] for each individual liṅga, and the same applies to the ritual cord (sūtra). || 26-19 ||
At the foremost part of that vimāna, however, one should construct a pavilion (maṇḍapa) with special care,
measuring ten, eight, nine, or even seven cubits.
It should be provided with sixteen pillars and endowed with all ornaments;
in its center, one should construct a pedestal (vedikā) consisting of one part out of nine parts.
Having smeared with cow dung a level surface one cubit in height, resembling the belly of a mirror, one should then feed the Brāhmaṇas.
On that occasion, a declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) should be performed, and especially the Vāstuhoma sacrifice;
having performed that oblation according to the rules, as well as the ritual circumambulation with fire (paryagnikaraṇa).
Having placed [the image], provided with garments, rice, darbha grass, and flowers, in the center of the pedestal, likewise in water reaching up to the neck; || 26-24 ||
Having raised the emblem (liṅga) that has been installed, one should place it upon the bathing altar, using either gold or silver, or even linen or cotton [cloth]. (26.25)
Without placing any curiosity in his heart, he should place the head of the liṅga in ghee and lay it upon the bed with its head facing east and its yoni intact.
Having worshipped the bed with perfumes, flowers,
and unbroken grains (akṣata), one should cover it with a cloth, using flowers and darbha grass held in the heart-mantra.
One should prepare a bed endowed with all auspicious characteristics,
having performed the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa) in water for either three nights or one night.
Having wrapped the jar with cloth, it should be encircled with thread; it should be joined with the five jewels and wrapped in a pair of cloths. (26–29)
Having meditated upon the formless Lord Sadāśiva as all-pervading like the sky,
one should place him within the center of the vessel while reciting the Śiva-mantra.
Having worshipped him with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings while reciting the mantra from the heart,
one should then place Gaurī upon the *vardhanī* vessel to his left, reciting the appropriate mantra.
One should worship the *vardhanī* vessel, provided with golden cloths, as before;
however, O Lord of Gods, if there is a second [vessel], one should bring it near the primary *liṅga*. (26–32)
Having informed the Lord of the Gods, the wise one [said]:
"Remain firm in the station of a child for a period from one year up to twelve years. (26-33)
Between these two sounds, one should perform the entry into the root;
however, in the second [sound], one should make the request, whereas in the first, there is no request.
In the pitchers designated as Vidyeśa, Umā, and Śiva, one should perform the placement separately for each, recollecting their respective forms and using their own specific mantras. (26–35)

The wise one, having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings those [images] provided with water-pots, endowed with garments, and possessed of all auspicious marks, using the *hṛdaya* mantra. (26–36)
One should perform the study of the Vedas according to the directions of the Ṛg, Yajur, Sāma, and Atharva [Vedas],
consisting of nine, five, three, or even a single oblation.
Then, having performed the consecration of the fire-mouth according to the previously stated procedure,
[one should offer] khadira, vaṭa, bilva, plakṣa, aśvattha, and udumbara [wood].
Then, one *śamī* and likewise one *samidh* each, starting from the east in sequence;
for the principal [deity], however, he should offer *palāśa* wood with the *hṛdaya-mantra*. (26–39)
Or he may perform it for all of them using *audumbara* fuel-sticks;
having performed the fire-oblation (*homa*) separately for each with the mantras for fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and food.
One should not offer fuel-sticks into the heart, nor ghee into the root;
having especially offered the sacrificial porridge (caru) with the Śivagāyatrī mantra.
Having offered the oblation with the limbs of Śiva through the touch [of the mantras], one should touch one's own limbs;
then, at the clear dawn, having performed the fire sacrifice, one should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with Śiva.
Having worshipped the preceptor, one should then worship the guardians of the images; having worshipped the astrologer, one should then worship the students and the attendants. (26.43)
Having raised [the deity] from the bed, one should place the very smooth liṅga in the center of the young temple; having established the liṅga in the middle of the pedestal of the seat,
one should install the Lord of the God of Gods, Śiva, who resides in the pitcher, with the Śiva-mantra.
Thereafter, one should assign the limbs of Śiva and [the goddess] Manonmanī to the pedestal (piṇḍikā).
One should place the eight Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśvaras) there on the pedestal, starting from the east;
then, with the pitchers named after the Vidyeśvaras, Umā, and Śiva, one performs the consecration with the weapon-mantra (astrābhiṣecana).
Then, having performed worship as prescribed for the ritual of adoration, one should offer the food-oblation (naivedya) in due order;
one should install [the deities] according to the rule, starting from the door and ending with the pedestal (pīṭha). (26–47)

One should perform the ceremonial bathing there according to one's ability, especially; and likewise, according to one's ability, one should hold a festival during the second consecration of the *taruṇālaya* (the young temple).
One should always worship within the *bāla* [temple], but one should not perform a festival there.
Thus the rule for the location of the *bāla* has been declared; now listen to the rules regarding the temple site (*ālayavāstuka*).
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, concerning the characteristics of the young temple (taruṇālaya).
Now begins the chapter on the characteristics of the site for a temple.
Hereafter, I shall fully explain the characteristics of the site for a temple;
having thoroughly purified the ground at the foundation, one should fashion the form of the *vāstu*.
Having caused the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited, and having sprinkled [the site] with auspicious water (*śivāmbhas*),
one should then worship the deities of the site (*vāstudeva*) with flowers and other offerings, addressing them by their respective names.
When the performer touches any limb at the conclusion of the worship, he should examine it;
therein, both in the site and in the body, he should declare the presence of a "thorn" (defect) according to the truth.
By touching the head, a bone-thorn will arise right there;
by touching the face at a distance of one cubit, it will certainly fall from the back of the neck onto a wooden surface.
If there is a sensation at the throat, there is a bone in the throat;
they know that with three cubits [of distance] from the touch of the chest, there is a chain, and if it is a thorn, it is likewise a chain. (27.5)
From the touch of the hand, one should predict the falling of a sword upon the tip of the hand;
from the touching of the arm, however, there will be embers at a distance of three cubits from the agent. (27.6)
The "horse's hoof" (aśvapāda) is specified as being the size of a foot at the ankle;
the "ring" (kaṇaka) is the size of a span (vitaști) from the touch of the foot. || 27-7 ||
From the touch of the little finger and the thumb, one *karārdha* (half-kara) is declared;
from the touch of the waist, it is a *lohaśalya*, measured by the span of both hands.
Likewise, by touching with the hand the ground or even a household utensil,
one should extract any thorn embedded in the earth and then dig up that spot.
Having excavated a pit equal to the width of the temple, or half of it, or more than half, or one and a half times that measure, according to the dimensions of the temple. || 27-10 ||
The pit should be made solid with sand equal to one-fourth or one-third of its depth, using the hooves of horses and elephants and mallets. (27.11)
Having made it level, and then having sprinkled it with the Śiva-weapon mantra,
one should drench it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) while reciting the Pavamāna hymn.
The preceptor should perform the layout of the site using ten lines;
this site-plan of eighty-one squares brings all prosperity to men. (27.13)
For the benefit of the Asuras, Śukra performed great penance;
born from that great austerity, he was of immense strength and possessed a form composed of the elements.
Then, being unprepared, he engaged in battle with the gods;
however, having realized that his weapons and other gear had been well-hidden by the gods, he was struck down. (27.15)
Then, on the ground, they are situated there facing downwards;
two bamboo poles are to be known as being situated there at the four corners.
The side-beams, the cross-beams, and the eight upper ropes are thus proclaimed;
having purified the northern-facing rope, that which is above the beam is known as the "upward beam" (ūrdhva-vaṃśa).

They say that these are the vital points (marmas) of the head; likewise, there are eight threads at the corners and sides. Here, the vessels (sirās) are to be known [by these], and the junction of those is called a joint (sandhi).
When one-sixth of a *pada* is taken, that is called a *ṣaṭka*;
when one-fourth of a *pada* is taken, that is known as a *catuṣka*. (27.19)
That which is situated at the tip of the cord is called the *marman* (vital point) alone.
In the center of the site (*vāstu*), there should be a lotus divided into one and eight parts. (27.20)
From the corner, there should be a trident, a foot, half a foot, and the hollowed palms;
many defects are proclaimed regarding the compression of these. (27–21)

The channels, the plow-like vessels, and the vital points (marmans) residing in their respective locations perish; however, in the case of the sixfold conjunction, there is the destruction of friends and, ultimately, the loss of vitality (rasa).
In the fourfold [arrangement], there is the destruction of vehicles; in the vital points (marmas), death occurs in sequence;
in the lotus-position, there is ruin; and in the trident, the destruction of the fetus.
There will be the destruction of one's wealth of cattle upon the pressing of the hollowed palms;
having installed the deities of the site (vāstudeva) starting from Īśāna and so forth, none should be omitted. (27–24)
Īśāna, Parjanya, Jayanta, Mahendraka, Āditya, Satyaka, Śāva, and Antarikṣa are the ones who go in the east. (27–25)
Agni, Pūṣan, Vitatha, Graha, Kṣata, Yama, Gandharva, Bhṛṅgarāja, and Mṛga are likewise situated in the south. (27–26)
Niṛti, Dauvārika, Sugrīva, Puṣpadantaka,
Vāruṇa, Roga, Śoṣa, and Pāpayakṣman are in the west.
Vāyu, Nāga, as well as Mukhya, Bhallāṭa, and Soma;
Ṛgu, Aditi, and Diti—these are the thirty-two outer deities. (27–28)
Having enjoyed each individual square, those beginning with the cremation grounds are well-established;
Brahmā enjoys nine squares, especially in the center of the site (vāstu).
Likewise, Samarīka is in the eastern quarter, Vivasvat in the southern, Mitra in the western part, and Pṛthivīdhara in the north. (27–30)
And situated in the four directions of Brahmā are the six-legged serpents;
Āpa and Apavatsa are stationed in the northeastern direction.
Śunāsīra and Sāvitra are situated in the southern direction (āgneyī),
while Indra and Indrajaya are situated in the southwestern direction (nairṛtī).
Rudra, Rudra, Jaya, and Uvāyu are proclaimed to be in the four corners;
these are the enjoyers of two squares each, and are recorded as occupying one and a half squares.
Carakī, Vitārī, Pūtanā, and the wicked Rākṣasī are situated outside in the corners beginning with the northeast, occupying squares that are devoid of [other] positions.
Having thus performed the ritual placement (*vinyāsa*), one should first fashion the body of the site-spirit (*vāstudeha*).
Whatever the arrangement of the site may be, all of that constitutes the form of the site-spirit. (27–35)
Having placed Īśāna alone in the pond in the region of Nairṛta, one should remain with knees and elbows resting in the direction between Agni and Vāyu. (27–36)

One should place the *liṅga* on the location of Indra; the wise man should then place the two feet on the location of Nairṛti, and having placed Marīci in the region of the belly, he should place the two breasts.
One should place [the hands] on the chest and the shoulders;
then, one should place them on the sides of the abdomen; and thereafter, one should place them on the thighs and the palms of the hands. This is the Sāvitra [mudrā]. || 27-38 ||
One should place the two feet in the middle of the thighs and forearms within Savitṛ;
and one should likewise auspiciously place Rudra and Rudrajaya as before. (27–39)

The deities beginning with Mahendra and ending with those of the intermediate space (antarikṣa) are said to be situated in the middle of the arms; having thus placed them in the well-formed knees and elbows, the wise one [should proceed] with the fire.
One should place [the deities] beginning with Pūṣan and ending with Mṛga in the shanks;
the other shanks are determined to be between Dauvārika and Pāpayakṣman. (27–41)
In the northwest wind-quarter, the deity Vāstu lies with his knees raised higher than his elbows, resting on his arms at the end of the Ṛgveda, facing downward toward the eastern ground.
Since he is fierce and most terrifying, he should therefore be worshipped by those who seek the fulfillment of their rites;
having had the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) recited, one should then sprinkle [the image] with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).
One should worship the deities of the site with perfumes, flowers, and incense;
first, one should worship Īśāna with ghee mixed with unbroken rice grains (akṣata).
One should especially offer blue lotuses and the like to Parjanya;
and specifically, one should offer a blue-colored banner to Jayanta. (27.45)
One should give the jewels of Mahendra and the canopy of Bhāskara; one should give wheat cakes to Satya, but fish to Ambhraśa.
The preceptor should offer the flesh of a bird to Antarikṣa;
he should offer a stream [of ghee] to Agni, and likewise parched grain to Pūṣan.
Milk-rice is prescribed for Vitatha, honey-rice for Graha,
meat-rice for Yama, and fragrant offerings for Gandharva.
For Bhṛṅga, [one should offer] Śākunājihvā; for Mṛga, barley and sesame;
for Pitṛ, kṛsara; and for Dauvrika, a tooth-stick.
Furthermore, [the mantra] for Sugrīva consists of as many [syllables] as there are; for Kuśa it is indeed *puṣpadantaka*;
for Varuṇa it is *davāpaddman*, and for Madhu it is *rogasya*. (27.50)
One should give rice cooked with ghee for consumption disorders (śoṣa), barley for pāpayakṣman, and specifically, one should give *maṇḍaka* soaked in ghee for fever.
Nāgapuṣpa flowers are prescribed for the principal Nāga, and a cake (pūpa) for Mukhya; Mudgānna rice is for Bhallāṭa, and milk-rice with honey (pāyasa) for Madhusomaka.
One should offer the root of the *ṛg* plant to Śālūka, and likewise red offerings to Aditi; one should also give *pūrikā* cakes to Diti. Thus is the sequence of offerings stated in order.
One should offer milk, curd, *kuśa* grass, turmeric-rice, molasses-rice,
cooked meat, pure food, and likewise cooked flesh,
as separate oblations (*bali*) to the deities beginning with Āpaḥ in the intermediate directions.
Food mixed with ghee, red-colored food, sweetmeats (laḍḍuka), and black gram (māṣa).
One should especially offer these toward the cardinal directions, starting from the southeast:
sesame seeds, unbroken rice grains, barley, as well as the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), and kuśa grass.
In that rite, a sacrificial pap (caru) should be offered, especially to Brahmā;
however, to Carakī and the others, one should present cooked meat.
For all of them, pure food mixed with molasses and clarified butter should be given; in its absence, it should be offered together with perfumes and other such items.
All mantras indeed should be joined with the name and the *praṇava* (OM);
for rites such as worship, they end with *namaḥ*, while the *bali* offering is said to end with *svāhā*.
Having thus performed the offering of the bali-oblation, one should especially recite the *puṇyāha* formula;
then, while uttering the root mantra, one should sprinkle [the area] with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).
Having then performed the Vāstu-homa in the center and in the northeast,
one should especially perform the Homa at the very beginning of the undertaking.
There, one should prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) measuring one cubit in size,
four finger-breadths in height, provided with fragrant flowers and darbha grass.
One should generate the Śiva-fire there according to the previously mentioned procedure;
one should then place Vāstu in the center of the fire, accompanied by the deities residing therein. (63)
In this manner, one should offer substances such as clarified butter (ājya) into the mouth of the Vāstu deity in sequence;
however, all substances should be offered with the Pārthiva seed-syllable.
There, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) with the names of the deities residing therein, ending each with "svāhā.
Thus, one hundred oblations for each is prescribed, or half of that, or half of that again. (27.65)
Or, in that case, one should perform the ritual with ten substances, each individually;
at the end of each substance, having offered the *vyāhṛti* oblations, one should then offer the *pūrṇāhuti* to Śiva.

Then, having dismissed the deities of the site (vāstu), he should afterwards dismiss the fire; thus the most excellent practitioner, having fully worshipped the site of the temple, [should proceed]. (27–67)
Having offered the bali-oblation and fully worshipped the fire, one should commence the work of construction (vāstukarma).
When the work of construction has begun, one should then perform the Vāstu-homa sacrifice.
If the Vāstuhoma is not performed here, the site (vāstu) is destroyed;
everything from the construction of the pond up to the fire-offering must be carried out with equanimity.
Having established the four āyapadas, one should arrange the gates according to the Māhendra [plan];
this indeed is the specific rule regarding the selection of the site for the planets.
Thus has the characteristic of the site for the temple been fully described;
now listen with a one-pointed mind to the procedure for the first brick-laying.
Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, concerning the characteristics of the site for palaces.
Now begins the chapter on the ritual for the first brick:
"Henceforth I shall fully explain; listen to me regarding the first brick. Having performed the digging and the filling, one should worship the deities of the site (vāstu)."
To the north of that, or specifically to the east, having prepared a water-shed,
one should construct a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) in its center, four finger-breadths high, made of śāli rice.
Having performed the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) at midnight, one should perform the adhivāsana for the four [deities] during the first Aṣṭakā;
if the celestial chariot (vimāna) is made of stone, one should perform the adhivāsana for the stone fragments.
In a temple made of bricks, however, the wise man should place bricks;
it should be three palm-lengths in height and twice that in width. (28.4)
One should cause it to be made with a length twice its width for the middle and superior types;
for the middle type, one should conceive of it as being one and a half *tālas* from the middle [measurement]. (28.5)
With a height of one palm (tāla), it would be the middle-lowest; thus the three middles have been stated, and now the three firsts are being described. (28.6)
One should perform the highest [type] with an elevation of eleven finger-breadths;
the middle with nine finger-breadths; and the lowest of the low with seven finger-breadths.
Thus has the elevation been described; the width should be double that, and one should cause all [the parts] to be made with lengths that are double those measurements. (28.8)
The measurement for stone has been described; now hear that for brick in due order:
its height is six finger-breadths and its width is twelve finger-breadths.
The length is indeed twice the width for the highest-of-the-high [grade];
the height of the smallest [grade] is three finger-breadths. (28.10)
When the interval between the highest and the lowest is divided into seven parts, a ninefold classification is declared; one should practice according to one's inclination.
The width at the elevated part should be double [the base], and its length should be twice that; thus, it should be made of well-baked bricks, very firm and beautiful. (28.12)
If the base is thick and the tip is thin, it is indeed female; if the tip is thick and the base is thin, it is neuter; but if both the base and the tip are equal, it is certainly male. (28.13)
With masculine mantras, it should be for men, and likewise with feminine mantras for women;
then one should take a portion of brick resembling the color of the *pāṭala* flower.

Having covered it with threads and *darbha* grass, and having carefully wrapped it with cloths, and having adorned it with perfumes and flowers, one should place it upon the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*). || 28.15 ||
To the east of that [altar], he should place water-pots wrapped in cloth and bound with thread,
joined with the lords of knowledge (vidyeśvara), upon the sacrificial mound.
One should worship the Śiva-pitcher in the center and the Vardhanī vessel to its left, with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, in due order, within the heart-mantra.
In the northern direction of that very place, the wise practitioner should perform the fire sacrifice (homa) with sacrificial fuel,
clarified butter, and cooked rice, according to the specific rules of the ritual.
One should offer a hundred oblations with sesame seeds mixed with rice, especially saturated with ghee, while reciting the Īśāna mantra.
Then, at the conclusion of the ritual substances, one should perform oblations with the limbs of Śiva and the limbs of Vidyā.
