At the auspicious hour of dawn, the laying of the bricks shall take place. (28.20)
One should first worship the Sthāpaka (the establisher) and immediately thereafter the Sthapati (the master builder).
One should perform all the rites prescribed by the mantras through the agency of the Sthāpaka. (28–21)
O Stapati, perform every rite that is devoid of mantra;
for if a rite is performed with mantras, it will lead to malevolent magic (abhicāra). || 28-22 ||
Therefore, with every effort, the wise consecrator, at an auspicious moment, should install the four bricks prescribed in the mantra in their proper sequence. (28.23)
The first sets of eight bricks (aṣṭakās) should be placed on the southern side of the door;
one should install them with four Brahmans in the four directions starting from the east.
The wise one should place the root-end toward the northeast and the tip-end toward the southeast; the root-end toward the southwest and the tip-end toward the northwest. (28.25)
With the *sadyojāta* and other Brahma-mantras, [he should worship] the Puruṣas and others in the east and other directions;
then, in the pit in their midst, he should fill it with auspicious water.
One should fill [the vessel] with water contained within the *kalaśa* while reciting the *Śiva-mantra*.
A clockwise rotation is auspicious, whereas a counter-clockwise rotation is inauspicious. (28–27)
To pacify those defects, one hundred oblations should be offered by the presiding deity Īśāna;
at that very spot, one should place the nine gems in their proper sequence.
One should place in sequence: diamond, pearl, lapis lazuli, conch-shell, crystal, topaz, moonstone, sapphire, and ruby. (28–29)
In their absence, a wise person should install one made of gold;
likewise, [one may be found] in an elephant’s tusk, in a field, in an anthill, or in a crab’s lair.
One should take earth from a bull's horn, from a lake, from a river, from a sacred ford (tīrtha), as well as from a mountain and the ocean, and fill the pit accordingly.
If clay is not obtained, however, the wise man should take clay from the bank of a river;
thereafter, the temple should be constructed according to the prescribed characteristics.
"The procedure for the first eightfold rite has been declared; now hear the procedure for the deposition of the embryo.
Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, concerning the procedure for the first eightfold rite.
(p. 135) Now begins the chapter on the procedure for the deposition of the embryo (garbhanyāsa).
Hereafter, I shall fully explain the sequential procedure for the deposition of the embryo, by which a temple becomes possessed of an embryo and brings about all prosperity for men. (29.1)
A celestial mansion (vimāna) that is without a womb (agarbha) would be for malevolent magic (abhicāra);
therefore, at the outset, one must perform the deposition of the womb (garbhanyāsa), which bestows prosperity.
Beginning with the vessel, [the materials] are gold and so forth in due order:
it may be made of gold, silver, copper, or likewise of bell-metal. (29–3)
A conch shell or even a mother-of-pearl shell is declared to be a suitable vessel for the embryo;
however, the *phelā* (receptacle) must be fashioned from metals according to the prescribed measurements. (29–4)
One should take conch-shell and mother-of-pearl according to their own measurements;
the covering should be made of non-metallic material, very smooth, very firm, and even. (29.5)
The width of the foot-protrusion (pādaviṣkaṃbha) shall consist of twenty-five padas;
its height shall be equal to its width, or it may also consist of nine compartments (navakoṣṭha).
The solid core consists of sixteen parts, and the walls of the chambers are half of that;
this is declared to be the best type, being equal in both width and height.
The height of the vessel should be three-quarters or half of its width;
the height of the wall of the compartment should be equal to, three-quarters of, or midway between [the height of] the vessel. || 29-8 ||
Having added some excess by means of a lid, and then being broken or dried out accordingly—in this way, a vessel is said to be rejected. (29.9)
Having washed the womb-vessel with cow-products and earth,
[he should place it] in a well-decorated pavilion in the northeastern direction of the house.
Having smeared [the ground] with cow dung and having had the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) recited there,
one should smear [it] with white pigment and [depict] a serpent endowed with hoods.
One should prepare a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) there, beautifully adorned with *śāli* rice; on all sides, using half that amount, one should fashion the seven continents and oceans.
Having spread it with auspicious cloths and flowers mixed with parched grain,
one should meditate upon the world within that vessel and place the womb-vessel thereon.
The central square is indeed Brahmā, and the gods are situated around it;
specifically, Marīci, Savitṛ, and Vivasvat. (29.14)

One should place Rudra, Mitra, Indra, and the Lord of the Earth (Bhūbhartṛ), as well as the Waters (Āpaḥ), in those [spaces] starting from the east; these are the presiding deities of the nine squares there. (29.15)
Īśāna, Jayanta, Āditya, Bhraja, Agnika, Vitatha, Yama, Bhṛṅga, Nirṛti, and Sukarṇaka. || 29-16 ||
Varuṇa, Śoṣa, Vāyu, Mukhya, Soma, and Ahi are recorded as the presiding deities of the sixteen external compartments; thus they are proclaimed. (29–17)
Rubies, diamonds, pearls, lapis lazuli, conch shells, crystal, topaz, sun-stones, and moon-stones. (29.18)
Having uttered the *praṇava* (the syllable Om), one should cast [the offerings] into Brahmā and the other deities:
rice, barley, wheat, black gram, mung beans, and horse gram. (29.19)
One should place sesame seeds, sinless white mustard seeds, and indeed *tāla*, as well as collyrium-dark pigment, lotus stalks, and realgar, in the eight directions on the outer circumference.
One should place the fragrant substances of Kuruṣka and Pakṣa, as well as Rocanā and Gairika,
in the chambers beginning with Jayantī, in their proper sequence.

And likewise, [one should take] earth from a mountain, a sacred ford (tīrtha), the bank of a river, or a lake; from an ant-hill inhabited by crabs, or indeed from a conch shell or an elephant’s tusk. (29–22)
And one should place [the substances] joined with water in the eight directions:
gold, silver, copper, iron, and likewise lead and tin.
And having placed the five metals in the center and in the four directions—namely, those of the blue lotus, the red lotus, and the dark-red lotus. || 29-24 ||
And one should place the roots of the *kumuda* flower in successive order;
likewise, one should cast a skull-topped staff (*khaṭvāṅga*), a deer, a trident, an axe, a bull,
a skull-cup, a tortoise, and serpents, all fashioned from gold.
Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) starting from Brahmā and ending with Īśāna by means of the Praṇava.
Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and so forth according to the prescribed rule, and having covered it with effort with a cloth, the wise man should cover it with *darbha* grass.
The wise one, intent on the instructions for the bedchamber, should arrange a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) upon the altar; having performed the fire-oblation (homa) in its southern quarter.
Having offered oblations with the thirty-eight *kalās*, the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*), and the ten syllables,
one should then offer to the deity by name both inside and outside the *vāstu*.
Having offered the *saṃpāta* oblation according to the rules, one should then perform the *pūrṇāhuti*.
Then, having sprinkled the womb-site with clarified butter from the heart-mantra, it should be well-settled. (29–30)
In the Ālaya and the Maṇḍapa, during the circumambulation of the exit;
and for all the Gopuras, during the circumambulation of the entrance. (29–31)

One should construct it at the base of a palace, or likewise on a raised platform (upāna) or within an enclosure; for those of the Śūdra caste it should be set directly upon the ground, while for Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas, O King, it should be on a raised platform.
In the southwest, the womb-place for learned brahmins is ordained; for all [other castes], it is recommended that it be situated within the enclosure or even buried in the ground. (29–33)
If one desires an eastern entrance, it should be made between the directions of Indra (East) and Agni (Southeast);
if one desires a western entrance, one should place it on the southern wall.
Or, at the junction of the door-panel and the bolt,
the wise one should place the vessel containing the embryo at the base of a pillar in the pavilion during the first enclosure.
The [image] of the Gopuras should be fashioned and installed on the right;
the wise one, having consecrated the interior of the womb-chamber with products of the cow and with earth while reciting the Hṛdaya-mantra, [should proceed]. (29–36)
Having taken the remainder and consecrated it with the Vāma mantra,
one should then enclose it with the Aghora mantra and offer the arghya with the mouth.

During the night of a nakṣatra that is not subject to waning, when there is an auspicious rising of a fixed zodiac sign (*sthira-rāśi*), the wise one should install [the image] firmly and immovably with the *Śiva-mantra*. (29–38)
Having performed firm works there with a serene mind,
the master-builder (sthapati) should first worship the architect (sthāpaka), and immediately after him, the master-builder himself.
A cow adorned with gold is the sacrificial fee for the consecrator;
now listen, my son, to the characteristics of the fingers in another manner. (29–40)
Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, the Chapter on the Ritual for Depositing the Embryo.
(p. 138) Now, the chapter on the rules for the characteristics of the fingers:
Hereafter, I shall fully explain the characteristics of the fingers;
first is the *mānāṅgula* (measuring finger), and the second is the *mātrāṅgula* (proportional finger). 30-1.
The measure obtained from the body is known as the third finger-breadth (aṅgula);
because there is nothing subtler than that, it is called the atom (paramāṇu). (30-2)
An atom (paramāṇu), and likewise a hair-tip (keśāgra), a nit (likṣā), a louse-egg (yūkā), and a louse (yava)—these are considered to increase eightfold in succession. (30.3)
This is declared to be the *mānāṅgula*; now hear concerning the *mātrāṅgula*. It is [the length] from the middle joint of the middle finger on the right hand of the preceptor. (30.4)
The *parva* (joint) measure is to be known as the *aṅgula*; now hear about the *dehalabdha-aṅgula*.
It is obtained by dividing the height of the image by the number of years [of the patron]. (30.5)
Among those, one measure belonging to the Bhāgavata tradition is known as the *dehalabdha-aṅgula*;
by this [measure], one should construct temples, pavilions, enclosures, and even gate-towers. (30.6)
In the measurement of villages, roads, fields, and groups, the rule for the finger-measure (*mānāṅgula*) applies;
however, for the measurement of sacrificial grass, fuel, and so forth, it is measured by the fingers of the preceptor’s right hand.
Regarding the *kūrca*, the *pavitraka*, the *sruva*, the *sruc*,
and other implements employed here in the sacrifice, one should follow the rule for their measurement in finger-breadths (*mātrāṅguli*).
Or one may have it made using fingers measured from one's own body;
however, a wise person should never have an image made using fingers measured from the body of another.
The designation for one finger-breadth (ekāṅgula) shall be that which is described as the "Bindu-liberation" (baindumokṣa);
however, for two finger-breadths (dvyaṅgula), they are the "Kalā," the "Kola," the "Lotus-eye" (padmākṣi), and the "Aśvinī. (30.10)
The Rudrākṣa has three qualities of fire; the Śūlavidyā is three finger-breadths;
the Yugabhāga is four finger-breadths; and the Veda is four finger-breadths, being the fourth. || 30-11 ||
The Rudra-face is the sense organ; the Bhūta is the arrow of the five-finger span.
The Karmāṅga is the vehicle, and the Rasa is six finger-spans.
The netherworld (pātāla), the ocean, and the treasures, as well as the ocean itself, belong to the seven-finger [image];
and the form of the Lord of the Vasu-world is known as the eight-finger [image]. (30–13)
The door, the thread, the planet, and the power are remembered as nine finger-breadths;
the direction, the channel, and the weapon, as well as the manifestation, are ten finger-breadths.
In the three [worlds], there are twenty-three, which is called *gatitriṃśati*;
the triple world is forty, and fifty is called *śakvarī*. (30.15)
Know that sixty is *atiśakvarī*, seventy is called *yaṣṭi*, eighty is *atyaṣṭi*, and ninety is indeed *dhṛti*. (30.16)
Atidhṛti and śatāṅguli are proclaimed as designations [of numbers]. One, ten, a hundred, a thousand, and then ten thousand (ayuta). || 30-17 ||

A niyuta, a prayuta, and a koṭi, as well as an arbuda; a vṛnda, a kharva, and a nikharva, a śaṅkha, and beyond that a padma; then a samudra, an anta, an artha, a parārdha, and another [number] likewise.
Thus, a parārdha has been described as increasing tenfold in each successive stage.
Thus, these twenty places of numerical notation have been declared:
*kāla*, *yama*, *tribhāga*, *ṣaṭkala*, and *vitasti*. (30.20)
The face with six knobs is designated as twelve finger-breadths (aṅgulas);
when joined with the thumb and the index finger, it is proclaimed as a span (prādeśa).
The span of the middle finger joined with the thumb is known as a tāla;
that which is joined by the thumb and the ring finger is called a vitasti. (30.22)
The joining of the little finger and the thumb is known by the name *gokarṇa*;
these three—the *prādeśa*, the *vitasti*, and the *gokarṇa*—are [the measures]. (30.23)
They should be employed in sacrifices and similar rites; for temples and such structures, one should cause them to be measured.
A *ratni* is a closed fist, while an *aratni* is with the fingers extended. (30.24)
The *kiṣku*, the *prājāpatya*, the *dhanurmuṣṭi*, and the *dhanugraha*—the wise declare that twenty-four *aṅgulas* constitute one *kiṣku*. (30.25)
With twenty-five [fingers] it is declared to be the *prājāpatya*;
twenty-six fingers is the *dhanurmuṣṭi*, and twenty-seven fingers is the *dhanugraha*.
The *kiṣku*, *tāla*, and so forth, up to four measures, are determined by the length of the finger;
with these measurements of the cubit (*hasta*), one should cause temples and other structures to be built. (30.27)
Fashion the bed and the seat according to the measurement of a *kiṣku*, as well as the *liṅga*, the pedestal (*piṇḍikā*), the temple (*prāsāda*), and the gate-tower (*gopura*). (30.28)
The enclosure wall and the pavilion should be made according to the *prājāpatya* measure; the bow-grasp and the quadrangle are proclaimed to have the dimension of a *daṇḍa*. (30.29)
A distance of one *krośa* is prescribed as being measured by one thousand *daṇḍas*;
a *gavyūti* should be known as twice that, and a *ghātakam* as twice that again. (30–30)
The fourfold measurement of the slayer (the pedestal) is proclaimed as being in yojanas;
one should divide the height of that image by means of the tāla-staff. (30–31)
The best [image] measures one hundred and twenty-four *daśatāla*;
the medium is one hundred and twenty, and the smallest is one hundred and sixteen. (30–32)
Thus, that which is twelve units greater becomes the best of the nine-tāla;
likewise, eight hundred and four hundred [units] constitute the middle and the smallest [nine-tāla], respectively. (30–33)
One hundred and ninety-six, and ninety-two plus two;
this is declared to be the threefold eight-tāla measurement according to the ancient tradition. (30–34)
Thus, it should be diminished by one part until it reaches the measure of a single *tāla*;
the upper lip (*mukha*) of the *jyeṣṭha* [measure] is thirteen and a half, while that of the *madhyama* is thirteen.
In the ten-tāla system, the lowest is twelve and a half [tālas] and the highest is twelve;
likewise, in the highest nine-tāla system, the face is indeed twelve aṅgulas.
The medium and inferior [proportions] are said to be less by half and half again of an aṅgula;
thus the three types for the Trimūrtis are proclaimed according to the ten-tāla measurement. (30–37)
The [height] of the women of the gods is three times nine tālas;
that of mortals is eight tālas, and that of the rākṣasas is seven tālas.
The Gandharvas should be six tālas, the Lord of the Gaṇas five tālas;
likewise, the Bhūtakas of Vāmana should be four tālas.
For the Kinnaras it is three tālas; for the fish, two tālas;
for the Aṇujas it should be one; and for the Piśācas, twenty.
The fingers have been correctly explained; now listen to the characteristics of the temple.
Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, the section on the rules for the characteristics of the fingers.
(p. 141) Now begins the chapter on the rules for the characteristics of temples.
Hereafter, I shall fully explain the characteristics of temples:
the three lowest [sizes] shall be seven, eight, and nine cubits respectively. (31.1)
Ten, twelve, and sixteen cubits are the three intermediate sizes;
twenty, thirty, and fifty are desired as the three superior sizes. (31–2)
Thus, the detailed classification of temples has been declared as ninefold;
having divided the width into twenty-five parts, the wise [architect] should proceed. (31-3)
The inner sanctum (garbhagṛha) shall consist of nine parts, while the extent of the wall shall be sixteen;
alternatively, in the case of sixteen parts, the width of the inner sanctum shall be four.
The width of the wall on all sides shall be one-twelfth [of the total];
having divided [the area] into eighty-one squares, the inner sanctum (garbha) shall indeed consist of nine parts.
The sixteenth is the outer wall; they know the inner part to be the interior wall. Beyond that is one part of water, and beyond that is one part of wall. (31.6)
On the outer wall, there should be four doors or else a single door;
the wise one should cause everything else, up to the pinnacle (sthūpī), to be made according to the prescribed uniform proportions.
As it has been stated: "The width of the wall should be equal on both the exterior and interior;
the measurement of the wall is of three kinds, whether on the outside or on the inside. (31.8)
Now hear the measurement of the width of the Liṅga-māna vimāna:
the extent of the pedestal (pīṭha) should be three times the diameter (viṣkaṃbha) of the Liṅga. || 31-9 ||
Multiplying that radius by three, one designates it as the inner sanctum (garbhageha);
one-third of the inner sanctum is prescribed as the measurement for the wall.
If one desires the width, that width is prescribed;
the pedestal (pīṭha) should be twice the portion of the worship, or specifically three times [that].
The inner sanctum (garbha) is three times the size of the pedestal, with walls constituting one-third of it.
Having inspected the level ground, one should then prepare the pedestal (upapīṭha).
The height of the upapīṭha (the pedestal-base) shall be one-eighth of its width;
that [height] may be reduced by a quarter, or by half, or divided into twelve parts. (31.13)
Two parts below the fillet (paṭṭikā), and above that, a fillet of one part;
the corner portion (karṇabhāga) shall be six parts, and the small fillet (akṣudrapaṭṭikā) one part. Above that, the neck (grīvā) shall be two parts, adorned with feet (pādas).
Just as Laṅkāra is proclaimed to be conjoined with Upapīṭha. || 31-15 ||
Then, if one should designate a site in a dry, arid land (jāṅgalabhūmi), it is specifically declared in this scripture to be of four kinds. (31.16)
The Padmabandha, Cārubandha, Pādabandha, and Pratikrama;
the height of the base (adhiṣṭhāna) shall be one-fourth of the width.
I shall now describe the Padmabandha; listen, O son of Aṅgaja.
Its height is twenty-seven [units], and the fillet (paṭṭikā) should consist of two parts.
One part is said to be the petal alone, and the base-moulding (upāna) is one part;
the jagatī should be six parts, and the half-petal (ardhadalī) is two parts in sequence.
The shoulder (skandha) should be half a part, and likewise the upper petal (ūrdhvadala) one part;
one should know the kumuda to be three parts, and the lotus (dadhobja) exactly one part.
The fillet (paṭṭikā) shall consist of one part, and the neck (grīvā) likewise two parts;
above that, there shall be one part for the lotus-band (padmabandha).
Two parts of the fillet (paṭṭikā) are joined with one part;
that single part of the true lord (tattvateśa) is known as the lotus-binding (padmabandha). || 31.22 ||
The height of the base (adhiṣṭhāna) is divided into twenty-four parts;
the fillet (apaṭṭikā) is said to be two parts, and the plinth (upāna) one part.
The jagatī is said to be six parts; the kumuda is five parts;
the paṭṭikā is said to be one part, and the grīvā is three parts. (31.24)

Know that the lower band (apaṭṭikā) is one part, the upper band (ūrdhvapaṭṭikā) is three parts, and the great band (mahāpaṭṭikā) is three parts; or it is said to be one person's height (jana). || 31-25 ||
That which is known as the "foot-binding" (pādabandha) is honored in all undertakings;
specifically, the sequence of the enclosure (vṛtikrama) should be performed like the foot-binding.
The band at the front face is said to be shaped like a water lily;
thus, in brief, the pedestal (adhiṣṭhāna) should be constructed for each face.
The foundation for the foot (pādāya) is twice as large and is approved by all;
the floor (prastara) is said to be half a foot [in thickness], and the corner (karṇa) is equal to the floor.
The *śekhara* is said to be beneficial when its length is twice that of the *prastara*; the *stūpī* should be made one part in height, adorned with all ornaments. (31.29)
On the upper portion of the *prastara*, however, it should be joined with *karṇa* and *kūṭa*;
there should be *kapotas* in the four directions, and between those two, an eight-fold lattice (*aṣṭapañjara*).
Half a part shall be the neck (kaṇṭha), and half a part shall be the pinnacle (śikhara);
thus is the single-story [temple] described—now hear concerning those with two stories and so forth.

From the top of the prastara to the base of the root-pedestal (mūlapāda), and likewise from that base upwards, each section is divided into seven parts; this is how it is proclaimed regarding the talas.
One should fashion the deity upon the ground up to twelve stories;
thus has the height been described here—now hear concerning the different types of doors.
The height of the door is said to extend from the top of the threshold (vṛti) to its upper limit; one-tenth of that height is the [thickness of the] leaf, which is reduced by two parts. (31–34)
The supreme, middle, and inferior widths have been proclaimed;
having made the door either in the east or in the west, the wise one [should proceed]. (31–35)
In the case of the *padmabandha* and other [bindings], there is an emergence above the circle (*vṛtti*),
while in the *masūra* and *pādabandhaka*, there is a cutting off below the circle.

One should perform the cutting of limbs, but one must not cause the limbs themselves to be made [of wood]. This has been declared as the "breaking of the door"; now hear the "breaking of the caste" (jātibheda). || 31-37 ||
The temple style is known to be threefold: Nāgara, Drāviḍa, and Vesara.
That which is circular starting from the neck is remembered as Vesara. (31–38)
Starting from the neck, the eight-sided vimāna is called Drāviḍa;
whereas that which is entirely square is this Nāgara type of temple.
Thus has what is known as "Jāti" been described; now hear from me its divisions:
Kailāsa, Mandhara, Meru, Himavat, and Niṣadha are recorded [as such].
Nīlaparvata, Māhendra, Nalīnaka, Pralīnaka, Nandyāvarta, Śrīvarta, and Parvatākṛti. || 31-41 ||
All such [structures] are designated as "distinct" (bheda);
indeed, the Kailāsa itself is characterized by four halls and four peaks.
That which is called *Mandhara* is said to have four halls and eight peaks; that which is known as *Meru* has eight halls and eight peaks. (31–43)
The temple known as Himavat is endowed with sixteen pavilions (*pañjara*),
possesses eight halls and eight peaks, and is possessed of all auspicious characteristics.
There was a palace named Niṣadha, which was devoid of gabled halls;
it was provided with eight halls and endowed with eight cages.
Provided with four halls and endowed with altars and stairs, it is declared to be the *nalīnaka* type; now hear about the *pralīnaka*.
The head-piece (śīrṣaka) is square, joined with compartments on both sides;
it is provided with a cage-like structure (pañjara) and a nose (nāsikā), and then there are stairs on both sides.
The *pralīnaka* has been described; now hear about the *nandyāvarta*.
It consists of four *kūṭas*, four halls, and four side-noses (*pārśvanāsikā*). || 31-48 ||
Likewise, the twelve nasalized sounds are joined with the mouth and nose;
they are specifically associated with four steps upon each successive level of the ground.
This, O child, is the Nandyāvarta diagram, which bestows prosperity; now listen to it.
Here, there are indeed four square compartments at the four corners.
Endowed with four nasal sounds and eighteen anusvāras, that which is thus possessed of these characteristics is proclaimed as "bestowing glory. (31–51)
Furthermore, that which is provided with a peaked hall (kūṭaśālā), has a lattice-like nose (pañjaranāsikā),
and is equipped with a railing and a network (vedikājālaka) is called the Parvata form.
Thus, on each successive level, one should certainly know that each part is distinct;
the different types of birth have been fully explained, and now the feet [of the verses] are being described.
They may be square, octagonal, sixteen-sided, or circular;
some are provided with pitchers, while others are devoid of pitchers.
Some are known as *pāda* because they are joined with the *vaikuṃbha* and *maṇḍi*;
their characteristics are now described, and they are called the *pādānāmā*. (31–55)
One twenty-fourth part of the width is the width of the foot;
that alone is declared to be the staff (daṇḍa) for the purpose of decorating the feet.
(145) From the width of the base (mūlapāda), one-seventh part is not for the path;
the height of the temple (maṇḍira) is two daṇḍas, and the width of the pillar-base (daṇḍapāda) is one daṇḍa. (31-57)
The height of the neck should be one-eighth [of the total], the width of the pitcher (kumbha) should be two daṇḍas,
its height should indeed be three-quarters [of that], and the plinth (aphalaka) should be one-quarter less.
The width of the triple staff (tridaṇḍa) is prescribed as [the full measure], and its projection is said to be half of that;
the width of the vīrakaṇṭha should be equal to the length of the staff.
Above that, the *potikā* (pedestal) should be one-third of its height; the triple-staff (*tridaṇḍa*) should be raised to the end of that [pedestal].
The lowest [staff] should be three *daṇḍas* in length, while the middle one should be four *daṇḍas*.
The best [measure] for the *potikā* is said to be fifteen *daṇḍas*;
one should then adorn the *potikā* with variegated leaf-patterns and ripples.
This is declared to be the *kumbhapāda*; we shall now describe the *kumbhabhinna*.
A foot joined with a *potikā*—one should not perform any other ritual action [with such a foot]. (31.62)
These are said to be devoid of a *kumbha*; that is called a *latākumbha*.
At its base it has the shape of a *kumbha*, but above that there is indeed a lotus.
Above the base (phalaka), one should fashion a creeper; the remainder of that [structure] is like the base of a water-pot (kumbhapāda). If one is unable, however, it may be omitted between the bases.
For all the lords of the quarters, that quarter shall be their exit;
it is auspicious, moon-like in its brilliance, gracious, and pleasant to behold. (31.65)
And names such as Śubhaṃkarī should especially be assigned;
for verses with sixteen syllables per quarter, the Śrīkara and Kāntaka meters are used.
Indeed, when it is octagonal with a square front, it is pleasant to behold;
however, when it is a mixture of square and octagonal, the foot-projection (pādākārya) brings about inauspiciousness.
The characteristics of the pedestals have been declared; now the arches (toraṇas) will be described.
Arches should likewise be constructed on the back and on both sides.
The height of the architrave (toraṇa) should be equal to the measurement of the door's elevation; its width is said to be half of that, when the height has been divided by six.
The *makara* [should be made] with two parts; the remainder is known as the *pāda*.
The measurement of its foot is half of that of the root-foot. || 31.70 ||
Above that, the portion marked with the letter *ma* is circular in the middle and slightly depressed;
above the circle, one should fashion four rectangular sections.
The proportions for the gateway (toraṇa) have been stated; now hear about the lintel (prastara).
As for the height of the lintel, it is divided into five parts. (31.72)
The height of the *uttara* should be three parts; the *vājana* above it should be one part. Above that, however, a *padmapaṭṭikā* (lotus-band) should be made, occupying one part.
One should arrange rows of elephants and rows of deer at the ends of the stone slabs;
thus is the *prastara* described, specifically with respect to the floor (*tala*).

Now the measurement of the *kūṭaśālā* (gabled hall) will be described; listen. Its height, up to the *kapota* (dove-cot), should be divided into six parts, and that [measurement] should be further divided [into two]. || 31-75 ||
The base should be joined with a pedestal (vedikā), and it should be provided with a neck for the base;
the base itself shall consist of two parts, and the spire (śikhara) shall likewise consist of two parts.

The wise one should indeed cause it to be constructed in this manner, joined with a pinnacle (stūpikā) at its section; having divided the width into six parts, the peak (kūṭa) should be made with one part.

The hall (śālā) should be made with two parts, and likewise the penthouse (pañjara) with two parts; thereafter, the pinnacle (kūṭa) should be square, and the hall should have the form of a gate-tower (gopura).
The nose is joined at the sides; in the middle of that is the subtle nose.
Two, three, and four are declared [as the measures], and the *kumbha* is situated above that.
A penthouse provided with a single nose is designated as a *pañjara*; this same type of penthouse, when provided with noses on all its corners, is proclaimed to be a *koṣṭha*.
The height of the neck is said to be equal to the measurement of the prastara;
having divided that into twelve parts, the paṭṭikā should consist of two parts.
The vedī is said to be two parts; the neck (kaṇṭha) is declared to be five parts;
the fillet (paṭṭikā) shall be one part, and the lotus-fillet (padmapaṭṭikā) two parts.
Above that, the pinnacle (śikhara) is prescribed; its projection should be half a part.
Dividing its height into three parts, one part is the length of the base (pāda).
One part is said to be the nose (nāsikā), and half of that is the central depression (madhyanimnaka).
Having divided the remaining portion into three parts, it is fashioned with one part for the navel.
The lattice-work (*pañjara*) is one part, and the trident (*triśūla*) is measured at one part;
the nasal ornament (*anunāsika*) is said to be four parts or half of that.
Thus the nose has been described; now the characteristics of the *sthūpī* (dome) are stated:
its height should be half that of the spire (*śikhara*), and it should be twenty-five [units]. (31.86)
The petal-base (*dalamāna*) is seven parts; that part is called its neck (*kaṇṭha*).
The pitcher (*kumbha*) consists of eight parts, while the stalk (*nālaka*) consists of four parts. (31.87)
One should make the pedestal (vedikā) two parts; the bud (mukula) shall be one part (kalā). One part below the tip of the bud is here called the sthūpipaṭṭa.
Having placed Vṛṣabha in the intermediate directions and the Mūrtis in the cardinal directions,
one should place Skanda to the east of that and Śrīkaṇṭhanāyaka to the south.
The wise preceptor, reciting the meaning of the scriptures for the sake of the sages' liberation,
should place the Nārasiṃha [mantra] in the west or in the north.
Having placed Brahmā, endowed with four faces, in the north, the seats are situated at the throat, above the palm of the bull. || 31.91 ||
The deities are said to reside in the halls (śālās), and one should lead them here into the peaks (kūṭas);
one should then appropriately assign both divine and human deities according to the proper method.
The play of Śiva, the play of Hari, and especially the play of asceticism [overwhelm] the yakṣas, rākṣasas, gandharvas, siddhas, vidyādharas, and uragas.

Having placed [the elements] in the eight directions according to the proper method, starting from the east in sequence, the characteristics of the temple (prāsāda) have been declared; now hear the rule for the pavilions (maṇḍapa). The length of the front [of the pavilion] is said to be half that of the temple, and its width is said to be equal [to that length].
Or a pavilion (maṇḍapa) is said to have three-quarters of the length of the face, plus a half. || 31-95 ||
First is the Devatā-maṇḍapa; second, the one for the purpose of bathing;
after that, the Vṛṣārdha-maṇṭapa; and fourth, the Nṛtta-maṇḍapa.
The Deva-maṇṭapa is where the deity is installed in the form of an image.
Where the installation of the water-pot (kalaśa) is prescribed, there is the bathing pavilion (snapanamaṇḍapa).
Where the bull was established, that is the Bull Pavilion (Vṛṣabha-maṇḍapa);
and where the dance was performed, that indeed is the Dance Pavilion (Nṛtta-maṇḍapa).
Likewise, in the case of a gate-tower (gopura), a non-intermediate space (athavyavāya), or an intermediate space (vyavāya),
as well as in the fourfold [arrangements], another pavilion (maṇḍapa) should be constructed outside in front.
I shall state their names; listen, my child, with a concentrated mind:
Nandavṛtta, Śriyāvṛtta, Vīrāsana, and Vṛttaka. (31.100)
The Nandyāvarta, the Māṇibhadra, and the Viśāla are thus proclaimed;
likewise the Nandavṛtta, the Catuṣpāda, the Ṣoḍaśa, and the Śrīpratiṣṭhita. (31.101)
That which is joined with twenty pillars is known as *vīrāsana*; that which is joined with thirty-two limbs is called *jayabhadrā*. (31.102)
That which is endowed with thirty-six limbs is known as the *Nadyāvarta*;
that which is joined with sixty-four pillars is the *Māṇibhadra*. (31.103)
That which is joined with a hundred pillars is designated as "Viśāla";
it is described as being like a temple (prāsāda) in its proportions up to the roof-beam (prastara).

Compared to the measurement of a temple pillar, this pillar is distinguished as being one-quarter greater, or even one-and-a-half times greater; however, it must not be double [the size]. || 31.105 ||
One-eighth of the pillar's height shall be its width;
it may be circular, square, or a combination of four and eight corners.
Or even one measuring sixteen cubits, beautifully adorned with all kinds of crafts;
it is superior to the Bodhika pillar, and even superior to the Bodhi tree itself. (31.107)
Because of the superiority of the northern [direction], one should place a seal-ring above it;
because of the superiority of the seal-ring over the scales, Jayantī is situated beyond that.
One should cover it with bricks and then pour *kalaka* over its top;
one should gradually apply sand and a fine powder mixed with *gulma* and *āṣa*.

Having crushed it with a pestle together with sugar and other ingredients, and having combined it with decoctions that are slimy and mixed with the water of the three myrobalans (triphalā), [one should proceed].
One part of *harītakī*, two parts of *vibhītaka*, and three parts of *dhātrī* are prescribed; these should be crushed together with impurities. (31.111)
Having resided there for six months, or three months, or even one month, [one should consume] curd, mung beans, water, and likewise coconut water. (31.112)
One should properly perform the ritual with milk mixed with curd,
having constructed a peaked hall and an assembly hall, especially one suitable for enjoyment.
The staircase and likewise the elephant-trunk [projection] should be constructed according to the proper method;
thus has the pavilion been described in brief, following the prescribed ritual.
One should construct a wall surrounding the temple according to its dimensions,
having firmly determined the width upon the ground according to the size of the temple.
The width of the temple is here called its *daṇḍa*;
that which is made from that *daṇḍa* is indeed like impurity within.

The single-staff inner enclosure is formed by a middle staff from the two-staff [enclosure], having constructed walls starting with the *āmaya* wall according to the measurement of four staffs. (31.117)
The wall for the Mahāmāyī and other [deities] should be seventeen *daṇḍas* in measure;
at the back and at the front, it should be half, double, or triple that amount.
The height of the walls, specifically including the parapets, should be four times the width of the gate; the thickness of the wall should be one cubit.
Whether it consists of ten thousand peak-halls or even just a single peak-hall,
it is prescribed that it be provided with a rampart and a gate-tower (gopura).

In the mandala, or at the gateway, or in the door-chamber (dvāraśālā), one should place the temple in the central bay; first, the palace (prāsāda) and then the mansion (harmya). The gate-tower (gopura) is placed in the great bay; thus is the fivefold method prescribed.
And they should be joined to the walls in each of the four directions, one by one.
Some indeed have the form of a garland, while others have the shape of a city gate;
the width of the door-decoration should be two, three, or five cubits.
The gate-hall is proclaimed to have six, seven, eight, or nine cubits; the width of the temple is eleven or thirteen cubits. (31.124)
The fourteenth and fifteenth [types] are known as the gateway-palace (*dvāra-harmya*);
the twenty-first and twenty-third are called the gateway-gatehouse (*dvāra-gopura*). (31.125)
The characteristic measurement of the door’s height is twice its width, twice that its depth,
and reaching from the ground up to the upper limit of the lintel.
Its width is declared to be half of that, and it should be adorned like a celestial chariot (*vimāna*);
one should construct an enclosed pavilion (*āvṛtamaṇḍapa*) adjacent to the wall of the enclosure.
Whether outside or even inside that, there should be a wall or indeed a pavilion;
thus there shall be five enclosures. Now hear concerning the abodes of the retinue.
One should construct the abode of the Mothers as being one-fourth, or half, or even one-eighth the size of the temple, and it should indeed have the form of a gopura.
The *hastipṛṣṭha* is declared to be excellent, especially for palaces;
it may be shaped like a kitchen (*pacana*) and consist of four halls or a single hall. (31.130)

Having constructed it with a surrounding wall, either on the outside or even on the inside, the door should be in the east; [the practitioner] faces west when [the door] is in the west, and faces east when [the door] is in the east.
The northern gate is on the south, and the southern [gate] faces north;
that which is situated between the southeast and northeast is intended as the western gate. (31.132)
The eastern gate, situated in the northwest (nīlānila), is highly praised;
there, one should construct a pavilion for the Bull (Vṛṣa) provided with four gates.
The characteristics of the temple have been declared; now hear about the eightfold [structure] on the summit.
Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, the section on the rules for the characteristics of the temple.
Now begins the chapter on the ritual for the eight bricks at the summit (mūrdhe'ṣṭakāvidhi).
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the ritual for the eight bricks at the summit; listen.
Having constructed a water-shed (prapā) according to its specifications either to the north or at the front of the temple (prāsāda), [one should proceed].
There, one should prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) with sesame, rice, and śāli grains;
having placed five bricks in sequence in its center,
one should then inscribe the syllables using flour made from śāli rice.
The letter ya is in the eastern part, and likewise the letter ra is in the south.
Having placed the letter *la* in the west, the letter *pa* in the north,
and the letter *ha* in the center, one should wrap each separately with a cloth.
On all sides, eight jars, wrapped with three threads,
provided with lids, tufts of grass, and cloths, and filled with scented water [should be placed].

The preceptor, having placed gold and gems [within the vessels] and installed the world-protectors and supreme deities, should worship them with perfumes and other offerings using their respective mantras.
It may be made of iron or wood, and should especially have three pillars;
the pinnacle should be symmetrical, long, and eight or six finger-breadths wide.
The width at the tip of the finger should be one unit, and it should likewise taper gradually;
the base should be square, and the middle part eight-sided.
Above that, the shape should be circular, situated like the foot of a peacock;
having washed it with products of the cow, one should place it upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila).

Having covered [the area] with new, unwashed cloths and having carefully spread *darbha* grass, one should then perform the *vāstu-homa* and the circumambulation of fire (*paryagni*) with that same fire. (32.10)
Then, according to the rules, one should fashion the weapons and the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) as prescribed;
they should be square or circular, and it is likewise for Śaṅkara.
Alternatively, one may prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) out of sand in due order;
all rites beginning with the placement of the fire (agnyādhāna) should be performed according to the previously stated procedure.
The five principles beginning with earth are the presiding deities of the eight bricks;
with fuel-sticks, clarified butter, sacrificial porridge, and parched grains, they are worshipped in sequence starting from the Vaiśvadeva offering.

The fuel sticks for the directions starting from the east are said to be, in order, those of the Udumbara, Vaṭa, Aśvattha, Plakṣa, and Pālāśa trees; or specifically, they may be used upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila).
Having offered one hundred or fifty oblations for each [deity], he should then offer the *pūrṇāhuti*;
then, having meditated upon the [deity] as consisting of the five elements, he should perform one more oblation in the northeast.
At dawn, when the stars and astrological configurations were auspicious, at a favorable moment and an excellent conjunction, the wise Sthāpaka and the Sthapati likewise [prepared].
Clad in white garments, adorned with white garlands and unguents,
and with their minds focused on no other thing, these two should place the bricks in sequence.
Recalling the Brahma-mantras beginning with *sadyojāta*, one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) starting from the east;
then, having placed the five elements beginning with earth, one should proceed in order from the east.
Having placed the nine jewels in the center according to the previously mentioned method,
one should install the *sthūpī* right there with the Īśāna mantra.
The master builder (sthapati) should cause the remaining works to be executed so that they are firm;
the sthāpaka is qualified for the mantras, while the sthapati is qualified for the practical work.
Having established [the pinnacle] above the spire (śikhara), consisting of five parts, three parts,
or half a part, the remainder should be joined with the stūpī;
one should construct all the components of the vimāna according to the path prescribed in the scriptures.
Whether the abode built by Śaila is described or not described. || 32-22 ||
Once the temple has been well-completed with bricks and gradually adorned with lime and other materials, the wise man should especially perform the consecration of the vimāna within it.

Having removed the mixed vessels and performed the dismissal of the artisans, one should then perform the ritual release of the site (kṣimocana), especially by means of the Vedic fire-oblation (homa). || 32.24 ||
After honoring the consecrator (sthāpaka), one should then worship the chief architect (sthapati) with garments,
gold, rings, and so forth, as well as cattle, land, wealth, and grain.
The offering of the sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa) should be properly performed according to the previously mentioned procedure on the day prior to the day of consecration, as determined by a Brahmin.
On the four sides of the temple, there should be water-stalls (prapās) measuring five cubits each in sequence;
in the center of the temple, one should construct an altar (vedī) measuring one-third of that [temple's] size.
The height should be half the width, or even just the measure of a fist;
[this applies] to the altars (vedikā) of the four directions, specifically in the east, south, west, and north.
Or, the sacrificial fire-pit (homakuṇḍa) may be described as square according to the prescribed rule;
one should perform the Vāstuhoma within the temple according to the ritual injunctions.

Having performed the circumambulation with fire (paryagnikaraṇa) with the mantra "mahāvyoma," and having caused the proclamation of an auspicious day (puṇyāha), one should then sprinkle [the site] evenly with water.
Nine jars, filled with water from the Droṇa lake, flawless, very firm,
decorated with threads, and all filled with water scented with every kind of perfume.
Having placed upon the sacrificial ground golden flowers individually wrapped in cloth and accompanied by mango blossoms.
Having drawn eight *droṇas* or half of that amount separately upon the altar,
one should draw above it a lotus with eight petals and a pericarp.
[The offerings] were made with half a grain of *śāli* rice and half a grain of sesame;
[they were placed] individually upon the altars from the center to the northeast.
Having specially established the Vardhanī vessel along with its respective mantras,
one should place the six-faced [deity] in the central pitcher situated above the eastern altar of the abode.
On its left side, one should place Sumati in the Vardhanī vessel;
in these eight jars surrounding it, one should place the world-protectors (lokeśas) along with their respective directional elephants.
One should install Śrīkaṇṭha and Śānti in the central jar on the right;
then, having installed Gaurī with her mantra in the *vardhanī* vessel on the left side. (32–37)
One should place the Vidyeśvaras, beginning with Ananta and ending with Śikhaṇḍin, all around.
To the west, however, one should place the form of Viṣṇu; this is the leftward sequence for the central pitcher. (32–38)
Having placed Śrī in the Vardhanī vessel, one should likewise place Puruṣa, Satya, Avyakta, Aniruddha, Pradyumna, and Vāsudeva.
One should properly install Saṃkarṣaṇa and Ananta around [the vessel],
and in the central jar to the north, one should install Brahmā with his own mantra.
On his left, however, in the *vardhanī* vessel, one should install Sāvitrī,
and around her the eight [sages]: Vyāsa, Agastya, Vasiṣṭha, Kauśika, Kāśyapa,
Gautama, Bharadvāja, and Parāśara.
Just as they are situated in their abodes while seated, so should one contemplate them within the jar.
One should offer oblations with the prescribed mantras, and for those not mentioned, with their respective names;
having given an offering of sacrificial food (havis) to each one, accompanied by side-dishes (upadaṃśa).

Then the wise practitioner should perform the fire oblation (homa), especially in the four directions, having performed the consecration of the mouth of the fire according to the previously mentioned procedure.
The deities residing in the central pitcher are the presiding deities (adhidevatās) of the oblations;
the Pippala, Udumbara, Plakṣa, and Vaṭa trees are situated in the directions starting from the east, respectively.

Fuel-sticks, clarified butter, cooked rice, parched grain, sesame seeds, white mustard, green gram, barley, black gram, and horse-gram, along with wild rice— these are the eleven [substances] in their respective order.

Then, they should each offer oblations one hundred and eight times, or two hundred and thirty times, or even three hundred times, using the five Brahmans and the auxiliary sciences (vidyāṅgas). || 32-47 ||
Having bathed the mountain-born gods residing on the ground above the celestial chariot (vimāna),
the preceptor, being a religious student (varṇin), should sprinkle those respective gods with their own individual mantras.
Having bound their right hands with a golden thread while reciting the *hṛdaya-mantra*,
and having covered the images with *darbha* grass, fine cloths, and the *varma-mantras*,
one should perform the recitation of the *Ṛgveda* and other scriptures, especially in the four directions.
Thus it was taught for the night; at dawn, the supreme guide [spoke as follows].
Having bathed well, performed the ritual assignment of the limbs (sakalīkṛtya), wearing a turban and an upper garment, clad in white clothes, pure, and anointed with white perfumes; || 32-51 ||

Having adorned [the officiant] with the five ornaments and golden sacrificial rings, one should worship the jars according to the rite and offer the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) with the heart-mantra. (32.52)
During the auspicious muhūrtas, having lifted the water-pots from the middle of the fire-pit,
one should carry them together with the *vardhanī* vessels onto the site of the sacrificial mound (*ṛkṣasthala*).
Having discarded the protective amulet and the garment, one should mentally arrange the clusters of syllables of one's own mantras,
beginning from the crown of the head and ending at the feet.
One should join that principle (tattva) individually into the two images from the pitcher;
however, on their left side are the deities residing within the *vardhanī* vessel.
Having joined [the vessels] with their respective mantras, one should consecrate them according to the proper method;
then, one should place those situated within the eight jars around [the central one] in their own respective directions.
Having sprinkled the deities and others within the sanctuary with water from the ritual jars,
one should sprinkle the constituent parts of the temple, beginning from the pinnacle (sthūpī) down to the base (upāna).
The wise one should worship, as before, the installer, the image-makers, the students, the attendants, and all the devotees of Śiva. (32–58)
Then one should perform the ceremonial bathing of the deity who resides within the inner sanctum;
one should offer abundant sacrificial oblations and also feed the brahmins.
Accompanied by the installation of the celestial chariot (vimāna), it bestows the fruit of worship upon the temple;
yet if the temple has not been consecrated, all that worship becomes fruitless.
Thus has the installation of the celestial chariot (vimāna) for Śiva been fully described by me;
one should perform it in this same manner according to the prescribed rule for all other deities as well.
In this case, there may be a difference in the mantras, but no difference in the ritual action is conceived;
[this applies] to the deities situated in the neck and middle of the temple with their respective mantras.
The most excellent instructor should perform everything as prescribed according to the ritual,
including the installation of the vimāna and the rite of the eight offerings (aṣṭakā) upon its summit.
Henceforth, I shall proclaim the characteristics of the *liṅga*; listen.
Thus ends the thirty-second chapter, concerning the ritual for the eight bricks (*aṣṭakā-vidhi*), on the head [of the altar]. 32.
(p. 155) Now begins the chapter on the rules for the characteristics of the *liṅga*.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the supreme characteristics of the *liṅga*, from which all beings dissolve during the period of reabsorption (*saṃhāra*). (33.1)
At the time of creation, such is the creation; therefore, the *liṅga* has been proclaimed.
The *liṅga* is said to be threefold: *sakala*, *niṣkala*, and *kala*. (33-2)
Therein, their entire threefold characteristic is stated:
it is devoid of direction, space, and time, and its sphere transcends speech and mind.
He alone, the Lord of the gods, assumes a body by his own will, having fully embraced the supreme state through qualities such as omniscience and the rest. (33–4)
For the purpose of defining the characteristics of yogins, for the emergence of the scriptures, and for the benefit of living beings, Śiva assumes a physical form. (33.5)
From that which is higher than the highest, the arising of Śiva’s power occurs;
the second is the form of Power (Śaktimūrti), and the fourth is Bindu and Nāda.
The signified and the signifier are devoid of connection with direction, place, and time;
they are free from spatial location by virtue of their power, and when accessible to the mind, they are partless.
Now hear of this partless *liṅga*, as well as that which is both with parts and without parts; for the partless is devoid of parts, while that with parts is endowed with parts.
Therefore, the Liṅga, which is both with parts and partless, is worshipped with reverence by sages, gods, and humans. (33.9)
They say that the *niṣkala* is the *liṅga*, while the *sakala* is that which has a form to be meditated upon (*bhāvyarūpaka*).
That other [aspect] which exists in a twofold state arises from *bindu* and *nāda*.
Therefore, the Mukhaliṅga is both with parts (sakala) and without parts (niṣkala) due to its two-fold nature;
one should worship Sadāśiva within the Niṣkala-liṅga as being Sakala.
Half of that is said to be Īśvara; this is called the Sakala form.
In its center, from a thousandth part, the arising of Rudra is here described.
To his left, from one part out of ten million parts, Viṣṇu arose;
and to his right, from one part out of ten million parts, Brahmā arose.
All these and likewise others are indeed so;
the Lord is remembered as the master over creation, destruction, and protection. (33.14)
Everything was produced by Brahmā; the protection of all is by Viṣṇu;
and the destruction of all worlds is by Śiva, the Supreme Lord. (33.15)
Just as that which has arisen from Śambhu, so too has it arisen from Śakti;
if this is formless, she is formless, and if it is embodied, she is embodied.
Just as heat is inseparable from fire, the power of the All-pervading Lord is likewise inseparable [from Him].
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva [are His manifestations]. (33.17)
Sāvitrī, Śrī, Umādevī, Īśvarī, and Manonmanī—
these are said to be Sadāśiva in the liṅga, while Manonmanī resides in the pedestal (piṇḍikā).
Thus, the five forms of the five primary forms are described;
therefore, having attained their emergence, the universe consists of Śakti and Śambhu.
Now hear the definition of the characteristic of the two-fold linga;
hear also the various types of linga-yonis, such as the sandy ones and so forth. (33-20)
O Lord of Obstacles, the sixfold *liṅga* is said to be made of clay, metal, gems, wood, and likewise stone, as well as that which is momentary (*kṣaṇika*). (33-21)
The twelve [types] are said to be momentary; furthermore, those made of clay are of two kinds;
those made of wood are said to be of eight kinds, and those made of metal are traditionally held to be of eight kinds. (33.22)
That which is produced from the seven precious gems is of one kind, while that produced from stone is of four kinds.
At the conclusion of the worship, the temporary ones should be discarded; as for the others, one should discard them during its dissolution.
The liṅga made of jewels and that made of metal are known as mobile;
the one made of stone is said to be both mobile and immobile, as are those made of clay and wood.
I shall describe the fruit for those seeking liberation, which is like sand for those who are momentary; it is known as rice for those desiring prosperity, and as food for the giver of food. (33.25)
River-clay brings the acquisition of land; cow-dung destroys disease; fresh butter gladdens the mind; and the rudrākṣa increases wisdom. (33-26)
Incense is prescribed for those desiring good fortune; a tuft of grass (kūrca) for those seeking liberation; flowers increase longevity; and resin (gula) grants the attainment of desired objects.
That made of flour is said to bestow nourishment; its fruit shall be momentary.
Furthermore, there is no fixed measurement nor any fixed duration for these various types of lingas.
The earthen vessel that bestows the fruit of sovereignty is distinguished by being either baked or unbaked;
one should take clay from a pure location, together with its source, for the portion of worship.
Having prepared this [mixture] and roasted it until cooked, that which remains uncooked therein is described here as follows:
with the flour of barley and wheat, and with ghee, milk, and decoctions. (33.30)
Having mixed it with the powders of sarja, guggulu, grīva, iṣṭakā, āpīttha, and nirayasa, along with clay, and having let it remain for a month while being baked, [one should proceed].
One should fashion a mature liṅga endowed with the seed of jewels,
using gold, silver, copper, bell-metal, or likewise brass.
That which is made of iron, lead, and tin is born of base metal;
that which is golden is said to bestow prosperity, while that which is silver grants the attainment of sovereignty. (33–33)
Copper bestows sons, while brass indeed causes enmity; likewise, bell-metal is used for eradication, and iron brings about destruction.
Lead removes disease, and tin increases longevity; thus have those born of metal been described. Next, that born of gems is spoken of.
Pearl, coral, lapis lazuli, crystal, topaz,
emerald, and sapphire are proclaimed to be born of gems.
A linga made of crystal is for the sake of enjoyment and liberation, while one born of gems is for the attainment of desired goals.
In the case of lingas made of metal or gems, the portion for worship includes the pedestal as well.
Just as one should have the crystal and other materials fashioned according to the measurement of the gain,
so too the pedestal (pīṭhikā) should be made upon the crystal and other materials using exactly three parts.

The pedestal (piṇḍikā), with a length and width equal to that [of the base], is said to bestow auspiciousness; it is prescribed starting from one finger-breadth up to twenty-four finger-breadths. (33–39)
They say that a linga made of metal is [defective] without the removal of its defining marks;
however, for one made of wood or stone, the Guru should remain firm and go to the forest. (33–40)
On an auspicious day, lunar date, weekday, and especially at a favorable moment,
having invited the preceptor and the artisan, [one should honor them] with garments, gold, and finger-rings.
One should worship [the deity] well with white garlands, unguents, and so forth, endowed with devotion;
and the wise person should have the implements, such as the axe and others, taken up by another.
The preceptor, together with artisans and more powerful assistants,
[proceeded] amidst the sounds of "Auspicious Day" and "Victory" conches, and the resonance of shells, kettledrums, and other instruments.

At the time of his remaining [in the womb], however, one should observe the signs—those pertaining to the heavens, the atmosphere, and the earth—which may be either inauspicious or auspicious. (33–44)
The arrival from the right is auspicious, as is the voice of the dove;
however, the *samāṃsa* and *śyenaka* birds are inauspicious when they come from the front, from the right, or from the left path. (33-45)
The sight of maidens, the mounting of a cow, curd, a full water-pot, and a Brāhmaṇa adorned with flowers; || 33-46 ||
A blazing fire, a mass of flesh, as well as the sight of a prostitute, a boar, and a horse. || 33-47 ||
Having displayed all these auspicious signs, the wise man should depart;
[but he should avoid] the falling of meteors, the burning of the quarters, and the onset of great winds.

Indeed, that which occurs in the intermediate space is inauspicious and is the opposite of what was previously stated; likewise, anointing with oil, seeing that vessel, and seeing one with disheveled hair [are inauspicious]. (33–49)
A vessel made of nine metals and one with its spout broken—these are to be known as born of the earth; thus is the examination of the auspicious and inauspicious.
Whatever [impurity] has entered into auspicious things, one should cause it to turn back from the inauspicious;
having spread fire over the inauspicious, one should offer a hundred oblations with the Śiva-mantra alone.
When an auspicious omen occurs, the wise preceptor should go forth together with the artisans;
having entered thereupon, he should proceed through forests and groves.
On Mount Mahendra, on Malaya, on Sahya, and likewise on Vindhya—
as long as there are rocks and trees, so far may the wise man travel.
The *śamī*, *madhuka*, *karaṇḍūka*, and likewise the *karṇikāra*; as well as the *tinduka* and *arjuna*, and also the *pippala* and *udumbara*.
These four classes, beginning with the Brāhmaṇas, follow their respective order; and there are many other very beautiful trees situated in the middle squares. (33–55)
Those trees which have glossy leaves, large trunks, and grow in auspicious places;
those burnt by fire, those that are forked, and those that serve as the dwellings of birds. (33-56)
The best of practitioners should avoid those situated upon creepers or anthills;
even stones are well-known through the examination of their specific characteristics.
White, red, yellow, and black—these are the four kinds [of ghee].
That which has the luster of cow’s milk or a conch shell is praised for Brahmins.
The [complexion] resembling the Japā and Bandhūka flowers is declared for kings in due order;
that which resembles turmeric or gold is praised for Vaiśyas. (33–59)
A [stone] resembling black gram (*māṣa*) or gum-guggulu brings prosperity to Śūdras;
however, a black stone for all [castes] is traditionally held to bestow all forms of wealth. (33.60)
One should carefully avoid that [ground] which is smeared with fat or saline soil, moistened, scorched by the rays of the sun, or burnt by fire. (33.61)
On its northern side, having prepared a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) with the fire facing it,
one should offer a hundred oblations with the *Śivāstra* mantra and then dwell in front of that on a bed.
Having instructed a young boy in a dream and slept at night, one should meditate upon Śiva.
If an inauspicious vision occurs in the dream, one should perform a hundred oblations at the root-mantra.
If, however, he has had an auspicious dream, then the wise man should begin the cutting;
having consecrated himself with the waters of Śiva at the clear and auspicious dawn.
Having severed it with the Aghora weapon mantra mixed with honey,
one should place its lower-end facing upward upon the back of the head.
The wise man, having conceived the two sides in this manner on both flanks, should likewise conceive the root in the south and west,
and the head in the east or the north flank.
Having marked the syllables here on the weapon, one should then begin that [rite] at that very moment.
Taking the root [mantra], the foot-stone, and whatever else is on both sides,
one should then recognize the young, the youthful, and the old woman by their characteristics.
It is smooth, with a soft surface, and possesses the sound of a young woman's voice. || 33-68 ||
That stone which is endowed with a beautiful luster and a pleasing sound is known as "youthful" (yauvanā).
A stone that is scorched by fire, worn out, rough, and lacking its natural resonance is "old" (vṛddhā).
A wise man, having abandoned those who are too young or too old, should select one in the prime of youth;
then, having examined those containing stone within, he should perform what is enjoined by the ritual rules.
Having sprinkled the liṅga with milk and ground flour mixed with *gairika*,
one should wash the liṅga with water for one night according to the true principle.
Streaks, lines, and blemishes are proclaimed to be defects of the stone;
wherever a circular mark (maṇḍala) is seen, one should designate that as the "womb" (garbha). || 33-72 ||
In the Maṇḍala site there is a snake, but in the Ratna site a chameleon; in the yellow Maṇḍala there is indeed a monitor lizard, while in the Māñjiṣṭha it would be a frog.
In a *kāpila* [complexion], a mouse is proclaimed; in one of variegated colors, a scorpion; and in one that is a mixture of white and red, there will be a *gaṇḍūka* and a *maṇḍala*. (33.74)
If it is honey-colored, there is a firefly; if pigeon-colored, a *graha* and a *gaulikā*;
if the color of molasses, a stone; and if it has the luster of a sword, there will be water. (33.75)
They should be devoid of a core (*garbha*) yet endowed with purity;
purity is known to be threefold: that called golden, that called bell-metal (*kāṃsa*), and that called iron.
Having examined them, the *liṅga* must be made free from a core and the like.
Likewise, the width of the interior of the temple should be measured with a cord.
They know that the best [measurement] for a woman is five parts of the womb's width;
having divided the womb into nine parts, the middle [measurement] is five parts. (33-78)
The lowest [type] is for the purpose of measuring the womb; it is threefold according to its dimensions.
When the womb is divided into eight parts, there are the smallest, the largest, and the middle [sizes]. (33-79)
The measurement has been declared to be ninefold; among these, the work may be performed according to one's preference.
Alternatively, in another manner, the interior (garbha) is again ninefold.
Three are declared to be superior, and three others should be designated as middling;
three are said to be inferior—thus the ninefold division has been illustrated.
The measurement in cubits (hasta) is ninefold, ranging from one cubit to nine cubits;
likewise, there is again a ninefold method ranging from three tālas to eleven tālas (rudratāla).
It should be equal [in width] and increasing [in height], and beyond that, it should be superior in auspiciousness;
its lower portion is square, and its middle portion is likewise octagonal.
Above that, it should be circular, equal on all sides with three parts; this is declared to be the "even-liṅga. Now listen to the description of the "circular" (vartamāna) type.
It should be twenty-four units in length, with seven parts forming a square;
it may be octagonal by dividing [the side] into eight parts, or circular by dividing it into nine parts.
This *liṅga* is increasing (*vardhamāna*), and beyond this it is superior to Śiva.
Having divided the height into ten parts, one should make it square from the third part. || 33-86 ||
An octagon formed by one-third [of the base] and a circle by one-fourth;
this is auspicious, preeminent among the forms of Śiva, and bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
The width of the base of the *liṅga* shall be equal to its length; the middle width shall be seven-eighths of that length.
p. 161) That circumference is proclaimed to be six parts;
for the height of the *liṅga*, the diameter is one-fourth and five parts. (33.89)
Twenty, sixteen, or nine [finger-breadths] from the base of the *vedī* and so forth is declared to be the circumference for all types of *liṅgas*. (33.90)
Listen with focused attention, O child, to the description of the Dhārā-liṅga and the Mukha-liṅga:
there are five streams, seven streams, nine streams, and twelve streams;
sixteen streams, twenty streams, twenty-four streams, and twenty-eight streams.
It is eight-cornered, extending as far as the [deity] form, and elevated by half a barleycorn toward the northwest.
Having divided the front portion into three parts, the face should be located in the uppermost part;
it shall be endowed with five heads, four faces, and a single neck.
It has eight ears and ten lips, endowed with all auspicious marks;
its lower part is shaped like a *liṅga*. Now hear the characteristics of its pedestal (*piṇḍikā*).
Three times the width of the *liṅga*, half of three times that, and four times that— these three types, beginning with the inferior, are said to be the width of the pedestal (*pīṭha*).
The height of the pedestal (pīṭha) is prescribed to be equal to the height of the Viṣṇu portion,
or else it should be provided with an eighth part of the Brahma portion.
The lotus-seat (padmapīṭha), the auspicious seat (bhadrapīṭha), the altar-circle above the pedestal, and the fourfold pedestal have been described; now hear their characteristics.
Having made the height sixteen parts, the four bands [should be] two parts each.
Above the five-fold boundary is a lotus endowed with sixteen petals. || 33-98 ||
The lotus-pit (padmakuṇḍa) described here has a height of four middle fingers;
its middle portion should be increased by two parts on all sides, being very firm and solid.
Above, there is a lotus consisting of four parts, and above that, in two parts, is the upper fillet (ūrdhvapaṭṭikā).
Above that, one should then apply one part with ghee and water.
One should make the stalk one-third of the width of the pedestal; likewise in the subsequent [sections], it should be one-fourth of that width, or half of that half, and so forth.
The root [measurement] should be double or triple that, and its tip should be reduced by half;
or else, it may be one-fourth, one-half, or even one-quarter of the width.
One should specifically make the water-channel one-third [of the width] there; thus indeed is the lotus-pedestal. Now hear about the auspicious pedestal (bhadrapiṭha). (33.103)
As before, having divided the height into sixteen parts according to the rule, the *upāna* (base-moulding) shall consist of one part,
and the *jagatī* (plinth) shall consist of four parts.
The *kumuda* should be made with three parts, but there is no *paṭṭikā* at all;
one should make the *kaṇṭha* with three parts and the *paṭṭikā* with one part.
The *bhadrapīṭha* is described as having two parts for the large band (*mahāpaṭṭikā*) and one part for the ghee-water; now the *vedipīṭha* is explained.
When the height of the pedestal (pīṭha) is divided into nine parts, the fillet (paṭṭikā) is two parts;
the neck (kaṇṭha) is four parts, and the upper fillet (ūrdhvapaṭṭikā) is indeed two parts.
A square altar-base (vedīpīṭha) surrounded on all sides by a single portion of ghee-water is prescribed; it is also said to be circular.
Indeed, this auspicious conduct is circular;
among those [elements], it may be one part, equal, three-quarters, or even half.
The entry and likewise the exit of the limbs of the pedestal, as well as the general characteristics of the pedestal for all types of *liṅgas*, [are described]. (33.110)
If, however, there is a pedestal for the *liṅga*, the wise man should cause a hollow (*avaṭa*) to be made, following the sequence of six and eight sides, in accordance with the portion of Viṣṇu.
For the purpose of entering the Brahma-portion, one should construct a square according to that measurement;
it should be provided with vessels for clarified butter and water, as well as a vessel for food, except when the deity is present in its entirety upon the seat.
I shall now describe the *nandyāvarta* stone; there are four stones beneath the pedestal (*pīṭha*), extending around it to the measure of one *tāla* or even six *aṅgulas*.
The auspicious *nandyāvarta* stones, being greater in width than the pedestal (*pīṭha*), should be square on all sides and as high as the *brahmabhāga*. || 33-114 ||

Alternatively, for a square [temple], the auspicious foundation stones for the base (pādādhāraśilā) shall be seven parts high out of eight parts of the [inner] sanctum (garbha), which is divided into nine parts; one part [of the sanctum] being used for this purpose.
Half of that, or one [unit], or likewise nine parts with one part raised;
for a square [base], one part out of eight parts should be made depressed in the center.
The measurement of the width of the excavation should be equal to the measurement of the diameter of the *liṅga*.
In the middle of that, the placement of jewels for the nine depressions is now described. || 33-117 ||
The tortoise-stone (kūrmaśilā) is established as being very firm and square, with a height equal to that of Brahmā’s stone and a width one and a half times that of the stars (tārā).
Having been addressed thus, all the limbs [of the chariot] should indeed be made slightly larger than the prescribed measure;
then, having placed them upon the chariot, the wise man should enter that village.
Having circumambulated the village clockwise accompanied by the sound of musical instruments,
the wise man should construct a work-shed on the northern side of the temple.
Having led [the image] into the center [of the hall], the wise one, placing the linga upon the pedestal with its head facing east,
should cause the fine workmanship to be executed.
The preceptor, together with the artisans and according to the prescribed characteristics, should perform the turning of the head; that is said to be of four kinds.
The first is shaped like an umbrella, the second has the form of a flower;
the third is like a hen’s egg, and the fourth is like a half-moon.
Having made the top of the liṅga one-sixth of its height,
one should then fashion a rounded section with one part, making it depressed toward the middle.
This is declared to be in the shape of an umbrella, bestowing all accomplishments;
having made the *tāra* (the syllable Om) into six parts, the circumference is made with half of two parts.
It should have the shape of a cucumber, bestowing the fruits of both enjoyment and liberation;
and upon that very [pedestal], a cock's egg should be fashioned with half the width.
Having divided the *liṅga* into three parts and wound it with two parts,
this half-moon (*ardhacandra*) is here declared in sequence for the sake of liberation.
Thus has Sadāśiva been described, the supreme bestower of all accomplishments;
one should worship the other deities of the vows with their respective meditations and mantras.
"The Sakala and Niṣkala have been declared; now hear about the Sakala, O observer of good vows.
Thus ends the thirty-third chapter, concerning the rules for the characteristics of the Liṅga.
(p. 164) Now follows the chapter on the rules for the characteristics of the *sakala* (the complete form).
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the characteristics of all [images];
because all its limbs are visible, it is called a *pratimā* (an image). || 34-1 ||
The fourfold form beginning with Īśvara is recited as being "sakala" (with parts);
these three types, beginning with sakala, are now described by me. (34-2)
That which is variegated, half-variegated, or likewise possessing a variegated appearance, and which is perceived as complete in all its parts—that is called a variegated whole (citra). || 34-3 ||
That which is visible as half a body, or likewise as half a picture,
whether painted on a cloth or on a wall, is here called a "painted image" (citrābhāsa).
Above that, the height of the image should be equal to the portion of the worship;
there, double or triple [that height] is considered the middle and the best [size] respectively in this context. (34–5)
Each one is declared to have nine measures through three variations;
having divided the *garbha* into nine parts, it is called the "ninefold illumination" (*navadhādīpya*).
When the height of the door is divided into sixteen parts,
one should discard two parts from the top and bottom for the *bhavaṅga* and the *pataṅga*.
This remaining [portion] is the pure door; it is considered excellent when measured by the mind.
That which is three parts and two parts is proclaimed as the middling.
Of those [three parts], one part is the first; each [of these] is divided by three. Thus, the measurement is said to be ninefold; now hear the measurement of the pillar (staṃbha).
The wise one should make the smallest [pillar] with half the height of the pillar;
the middle-sized is said to be three-quarters, and the largest should be equal [to the full height].
Each of these is of three types according to their proportions, as previously described for the nine measurements.
The superior [measure] is four tālas, and the middling is likewise three tālas.
Know that the lowest [measure] is two *tālas*; now hear about that which is equal to a *hasta*.
Beginning from one *hasta* and ending at nine *hastas*, listen. (34-12)
Listen now to the measurement of the nine fingers by means of the hand itself:
the eldest [measure] is equal to the sacrificer, and the middle is three-quarters of that. (34.13)
The lowest [measurement], however, is said to be half [of that], according to the suitability of the patron. These measurements have been described as divided by the *mānāṅgula*. (34.14)
Among those measurements, for the sake of a pair,
one should employ a measurement that is either increased by one finger-breadth or decreased by one finger-breadth at each successive measurement.
Beginning from one finger-breadth, one should take up to twelve finger-breadths;
beyond that one should not do it, nor below, because of the foundation.
Having divided the stated height into three parts, one should indeed construct [the structure] from the crown (uṣṇīṣa) down to the base (pāda) within two of those parts. || 34-17 ||
Now, the measurement of the pedestal (pīṭha) is one part; on one side, the lotus is threefold.
Specifically for the seat (āsana), the measurement of the pedestal should be two parts. || 34-18 ||
The height of the pedestal for a standing image should be one-fourth of the height of the image;
likewise, the standing, seated, and riding postures should be executed in accordance with their respective proportions.
One should not cause a bed to be made other than for the image of Viṣṇu;
having adopted the desired measurement for the preceptor, the artisan, and the makers. (34-20)
If one should make it out of clay, one should fashion a trident therein;
and especially one made of iron, or fashioned from lac (madhūcchiṣṭa).
Then, having performed the primary and secondary limbs (aṅga-upāṅgas), one should visualize them as being stable;
and having worshipped them with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, together with incense and lamps.
On its very right side, one should prepare the Śiva-fire;
having offered oblations eight hundred times with the Hṛdaya-mantra, using sacrificial fuel and other materials individually.
Then, having meditated upon that form within oneself, one should offer the *pūrṇāhuti*;
having uttered the heart-mantra (*hṛnmantra*), one should bind the respective limbs [of the deity]. (34–24)
Together with artisans, [one should fashion] an image complete in all its limbs;
having taken the image, it should be placed upon a high pedestal divided into nine parts.
One part is declared to be the face; the neck portion consists of three parts;
from the neck to the end of the breasts is one part, and likewise from there to the navel is one part.
The portion up to the end of the penis is two parts; the measurement of the thighs is two parts;
