the knees and shanks are three parts each; and the length of the feet is two parts.

The *guda* (the lower part) shall be one part, the [upper] portion three parts, and the length of the arms two parts; the length of the forearm (*prakoṣṭha*) is desired to be one and a half times that [of the arm].
This measure is thus renowned as the most excellent for all;
one should perform the measurement and calculation using the counting of finger-breadths (tāla). (34.29)
The face, the neck, and Yama should each be one vitasti, or twelve aṅgulas;
one should fashion the four forms beginning with Īśvara using ten tālas.
For Śakti and other deities, a height of nine tālas is prescribed;
for divine sages and humans, one should have them made at eight tālas.
For the Rākṣasas and Asuras, seven tālas are prescribed here;
for the Gandharvas, six tālas; and for the Vighnas, five tālas.
The Vāmanas are five *tālas* in height; the Bhūtakas are four *tālas*;
the Kinnaras are three *tālas*; and the Matsyas are two *tālas*.
The *ekatāla* is twenty finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) larger than the *kūśmāṇḍa*;
the distinctions between the gross and the subtle types of *tāla* are now described here. (34–34)
The measurement by that respective finger is declared to be *māna* as well as *unmāna*. *Māna* is said to be its breadth (*vistara*), while *unmāna* is its circumference (*nāha*). (34–35)
The measurement is said to be long according to the standards of measure (māna), weight (unmāna), and dimension (pramāṇa).
Then, having divided the facial portion into three parts, one determines the height of the forehead.
One part should extend to the tip of the nose, and the other should likewise be bent; the remaining parts, from the crown of the head down to the feet, should be made with finger-breadths (aṅgulas).
The uṣṇīṣa is said to be one aṅgula, while the head is three aṅgulas;
thus, in a [measurement] of thirty-six aṅgulas, the circumference of the head is declared.
The distance between the two ears there is eighteen finger-breadths;
from the crown of the head to the edge of the ear, however, it is twelve finger-breadths.
The length of the eye, including the pupil and the *māyā* (the iris), is one *kalā*; its width is half of that.
At the pupil, the line of the eyelashes is like two *yava*s of the *karavīra* seed.
The dark portion (asita) shall be one-third, and the light (jyotis) shall consist of five parts;
the length of the nose is two units, while each of the two nostril-pockets (puṭa) is half of that.
The middle of the cavity is said to be the size of a barley grain, and the tip of the nose like a sesame flower;
the height at the tip is two finger-breadths, while the height at the base is half of that.
The two eyebrows are five finger-breadths (aṅgulas) in length, and the space between them is one digit (kalā).
The lower lip is said to be one finger-breadth, and the upper lip half of that.
The mouth should be one *kalā* in length, and the chin likewise half of that in the middle.
The protrusion [of the lips] should be four finger-breadths, and the middle of the cheeks should be one finger-breadth more. (34–44)
The ear should indeed be four finger-breadths in width, with its depth being half of that;
it is said that the depression should be one finger-breadth, and the thickness of the earlobe three finger-breadths.
The thickness of the ear should be one-sixth [of the face]; its base, however, is one *kalā* more.
The distance between its two arms is the shoulders; from there, it is thirty-six *aṅgulas*.
The top [of the staff] should have a circumference of three parts, with one additional finger-breadth at the wrist;
its length is known to be two parts, measured by six finger-breadths. || 34-47 ||
Its length is seven finger-breadths, and its height is known to be two finger-breadths;
it is marked with lines, depressed in the middle like a calf, and thick on the outside.
The length of the middle finger is declared to be seven finger-breadths;
the index and ring fingers are each reduced by half a finger-breadth from the middle one.
The portion for the little finger should likewise be one finger-breadth;
similarly, the length of the thumb here should be equal to its own breadth.
Therefore, there is a reduction of half an *aṅgula* for the girths of the middle finger; however, the girths of both the index and the ring fingers should be known to be three *aṅgulas*. (34–51)
The circumference of the little finger is reduced by half an aṅgula;
the joint of the fingers shall be one-fifth part of the upper portion.
The middle [finger] is remembered as being two parts, while the forefinger is equal to that;
the thumb should have two joints, and it is considered equal from bottom to top.
The measurement of the tip of a fingernail is equal to the tip-joint of the fingers;
the height of the crown, however, should be one additional part more than the face.
Then, twice that amount plus half of it is not prescribed for me;
for Īśvara, it is four *nāhas*, and likewise for the lords of the hosts of spirits (*bhūtagaṇa*).
The specific form of all [these] is said to be identical;
however, I shall describe that of the Lord (Īśvara) in due order, as it truly is.
For the Lord is established in the reality of the Self, possessing eyes, heads, and faces on all sides;
he is the lotus arisen from the power of will, adorned with a thousand petals.
Maheśvara is the lotus, endowed with the pericarp and filaments;
he has five heads, four faces, and is joined with twelve eyes. (34–58)
Four-faced, with four nostrils, with wealth as his ears, and four throats—this body indeed has two feet, is equipped with weapons, and possesses ten arms. (34.59)
Resembling pure crystal, with a radiance equal to ten million suns,
as white as moonbeams and snow, and adorned with every ornament.
The god wears white garments and a white sacred thread;
he holds the gesture of fearlessness, a trident, an axe, a thunderbolt, and a sword in his right hands.
One should likewise represent Maheśa with a shield, a goad, a noose, a bell, and the gesture of granting boons in his left hands; now hear the characteristics of Śakti.
She has four arms and three eyes, is adorned with all ornaments, possesses broad hips, a slender waist, and elevated breasts. (34–63)
On the right [side], she holds a blue lotus; with her left hand, she bears a garland;
her hands indeed display the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and she is clothed in silken garments.
She is adorned with a crown and a basket-shaped headdress, situated on the left side of Īśvara;
she is seated upon a single throne within his circle of radiance.
One should cause this Īśvarī to be fashioned, resembling the moon, the sun, and fire, and bestowing auspiciousness upon the world; now listen to [the description] of Vāmā and the others.
One should worship the eight powers, beginning with Vāmā, and Īśvarī individually; and for the Lord (Īśvara), [the mantras] end with the jaw, the arms, and the breasts. (34–67)
The direction of Īśvarī is declared to belong to the Śaktis by virtue of its three-quarters;
likewise, the arrival of the Vrata-deities is prescribed.
The lords of knowledge (vidyeśas) and the lords of the hosts (gaṇeśvaras), who are limbs of the Brahma-knowledge, possess five limbs;
they are three-eyed, four-armed, gentle, and adorned with all ornaments. All of them offer salutations and hold rosaries and lotuses.
All are correctly described as being endowed with crowns of matted hair.
Their color has been previously described along with its characteristics;
now hear likewise of the forms of my own nature that surround the gods.
The first is seated on a comfortable throne, the second is with Umā;
the third is mounted upon a bull, and the fourth is the Enemy of Tripura.
The fifth form is named Nṛtta; the sixth is Somārdhaśekhara;
the seventh is Dhanādīśa; and the eighth is Harirardha. (34.73)
The ninth is the wandering for alms, the tenth is the destruction of desire, the eleventh is the slayer of time, and thereafter is that which belongs to the Liṅga Purāṇa. (34.74)
Thus, the characteristics of their twelve images are described;
they are likewise [to be found] on the side of Mount Meru and in the hermitages of the sages.
Seeing that naked man, those women were indeed deluded;
having recognized him, all the sages performed an incantation for his destruction.
In the center of that, one should place these in the heart: Nāga, Kṛṣṇa, Mṛga, as well as Apasmāra, Paraśu, Mukṣa, Vyāghra, and Hari.
A skull-bowl, most terrifying, and other such things have come into my possession;
likewise, a serpent, a deer, and an axe are held by me for the sake of sport. (34.77)
I struck an epileptic at the feet and a skull upon my head;
then, having slain a lion and a tiger, their skins were worn by me.
Therefore, becoming my bull-vehicle, you shall always do what is pleasing to me;
the poison of the great ocean is held at your throat, and the crescent moon is worn upon your crest.
A lotus flower was borne by me upon the mass of my matted locks while dancing;
otherwise, everything else is the same for all the images, especially.
Three-eyed, four-armed, and gentle, with the crescent moon as his crest-jewel,
adorned with a crown of matted hair and accompanied by the dhūrtūra plant and serpents.
Clad in a tiger-skin garment, adorned with necklaces and armlets,
invested with the sacred thread, and embellished by a pair of earrings.
This has been stated as the general rule for the twelve forms;
hereafter, the specific details will now be explained in due order.
Seated comfortably upon a throne, holding a deer and an axe,
his right hand displays the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya) and his left hand the gesture of granting boons (varada).
Or, with the left leg drawn up and resting comfortably upon the right thigh, and excluding Umā and Skanda—this is called the *sukhāsana*; it is said to be accompanied by Umā. (34.85)
On the seat, he [should visualize] the goddess Umā, whose face is radiant with great gentleness, having two arms, holding a lotus in her hand, and adorned with a crown and ornaments. (34.86)
Alternatively, the arm of Umā, extended from the left side of the earth known as Kaṭaka up to her breast, is indeed the measurement for Ṣaṇmukha.
Accompanied by Kaṇṭheśūla and Channavīra, [he saw] Skanda indeed in the form of a child, situated between Umā and Śaṅkara. (34.88)
Having prepared a comfortable seat, whether sitting or standing, adorned with bracelets and bearing the gesture of granting boons, one should worship the Supreme Lord as before.
Having looked at the face of the god, one should fashion Gaurī slightly [smaller];
now I shall describe the bull mounted upon the bull, standing behind him.
Having placed Umā and Rudra so that the elbow rests upon the head of the bull,
the bull-vehicled deity should be fashioned holding a deer together with an axe.
Having fashioned that body of the Destroyer of Tripura, which was equipped with a bow and arrows, held a black axe, and was accompanied by Umā; || 34-92 ||
The left foot is raised for the purpose of dance; the knee rises level with the navel, and the big toe is raised level with the knee, while the knee is raised level with the big toe.
Extending the left hand like a staff over the heart,
the right hand displays the gesture of fearlessness, while the remaining [hands] hold the skull-bowl and the ḍamaru drum.
Having raised [the cord] up to the limit of the neck, one should arrange it so as to be beautiful;
the left hand, together with the fire, is raised up to the limit of the upper arm.
Beneath his feet are apasmāra and one engaged in playing with a snake;
he holds a dhūrtūra plant, a skull, and the feathers of a crane and a peacock.
Three [braids] have five matted locks each, while seven are spread out and radiant with flowers;
likewise on the left side, they are blazing like a flaming fire.
O child, this form for dance is taught for the sake of universal peace;
it represents that god who has come straight forward as a deer, bearing an axe.
One should meditate upon the Lord who wears the sky as his garment, whose crest is the moon, and who is the one to be accomplished;
Hara occupies the right half, while Pārvatī likewise occupies the left half.
With the right foot bent and the left foot standing straight,
with the torso slightly inclined, one should thus perform the *tribhāgika* posture.
The elbow of Hara’s right hand rests upon Vṛṣaka;
his forearm is joined with Śuka, and Hara is equipped with an axe.
In her left hand she holds a bracelet, while in her right she is known to display the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*).
The goddess is dark-complexioned with a beautiful face, while Hara is red in color.
The god wears a tiger-skin garment, as does Pārvatī.
[He saw] one wearing linen garments;
Viṣṇu wearing yellow silk robes, and Hara wearing a tiger-skin garment;
Viṣṇu adorned with a crown, and Śaṅkara endowed with matted locks.
Śyāmavarṇa, Hari, and Śaṅkara, each possessing his appropriate form.
This half has been described as Hari; beyond this is the wandering for alms.
The skull belongs to the form of creation, while the body belongs to the form of maintenance.
Equipped with a hand-drum (ḍamaruka), adorned with ashes and snakes, joined with a trident at the neck, and accompanied by a hidden hero (channavīra). || 34-106 ||
The sandals and the two feet are pervaded by all beings;
thus is the wandering for alms. Now listen to the destruction of desire for offspring.
The enemy of Kāma (Śiva) should be depicted in a fierce form, having struck down Kāma at his side;
indeed, I shall now describe this form of the enemy of Kāma which destroys Time (Kāla).
In his right hand he holds a trident, and in his left, it is taught that he has fingers like needles.
Having thus placed one quarter of Time within the heart, it remains established there as a foot.
This is declared to be the destruction of time (kālanāśa), following the attainment [of the goal] through the *liṅga*.
Having fashioned the *liṅga* above, Brahmā likewise takes the form of a swan (*haṃsa*). || 34-110 ||
One should fashion Viṣṇu with the face of a boar at the base of the liṅga;
Brahmā and Viṣṇu, joined in añjali-mudrā, should be placed at the heart and on the two sides respectively.
The *liṅga* should be fashioned in the center as before, with the moon on its crest;
likewise, its lotus-feet and its crown should be invisible.
O Gajānana, the distinction between the forms of the twelve Mūrtis has been declared;
now listen as I describe the characteristics of the Goddess in brief. (34.113)
Reaching to the jaw, the ends of the arms, and the space between the breasts in height;
she has two arms, is dark-complexioned, and is adorned with all ornaments. (34.114)
One should hold an utpala lotus in the right hand and extend the left hand;
she has a crown or what is called a karaṇḍa, and possesses high, full breasts. (34.115)
One should set aside one-seventh of the previously mentioned middle circumference;
this is declared to be the middle circumference, while everything else remains the same.
Know this to be the form of Gaurī; now hear of the form of Viṣṇu—the god Hari, who bears the conch and the discus and wears yellow garments.
One should have the Lord fashioned together with Śrībhūmi, adorned with all ornaments, whether standing, seated, or even reclining. (34.118)
Having visualized the radiant Brahmā as four-faced and four-armed, bearing a water-pot and the *akṣa* rosary, and endowed with matted locks of red color. (34.119)
One should likewise fashion Sāvitrī on the left side, adorned with all ornaments; thus one should create the auspicious four-faced deity who brings about the creation of the world. (34.120)
Now, the characteristics for the ritual installation of other types of images are correctly proclaimed in their proper sequence.
This has been declared for all [the deities]; now hear the procedure for the sprout (aṅkura).
Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter, the section on the rules for the characteristics of the sakala [deities].
Now begins the chapter on the ritual for the offering of sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇavidhi). Hereafter, I shall fully explain the sequence of the ritual for the sprouts;
at the beginning of all auspicious rites, the auspicious sprout-offering must be performed.
During the installation, the sprinkling, the bathing, and likewise during the festival—whether it be for nine nights, seven nights, or again for five nights. || 35-2 ||
Beginning from the evening of that day, the sowing of the sprouts should take place in the evening;
since the Moon is the lord of seeds, one should sow them at night.
Having performed a circumambulation of the village with the sounding of conchs, kettledrums, and other instruments,
accompanied by parasols, banners, canopies, and the mounting of elephants, horses, and chariots.
And having been carried by the hosts of Piñcacāmaras, together with a trident, by the attendants of Maheśvara, they placed the *pālikā* vessels and other items upon their heads. (35–5)
The *pālikā*, the *ghaṭikā*, and the *śarāva*—these three types of vessels may be made of gold, silver, copper, or even clay. (35–6)
The width of the opening of the *pālikā* is twelve finger-breadths for the smallest;
sixteen finger-breadths in width is declared to be the medium size. (35.7)
The largest [pedestal] is twenty finger-breadths in both width and height;
half of that is the width of the base, which should be circular, very firm, and level. (35.8)
The lip here should extend all around for one-sixth of the width;
the opening is said to be well-rounded, measuring one-third of the width. (35.9)
In this manner, having fashioned the opening and the mouth, one should indeed determine the remainder as the staff;
one-third of the width is said to be the width of the staff.
Shaped like a water-clock jar (ghaṭikā-kalaśa), with a staff and a base as before;
it has four doors in the four directions and a triangle measuring three finger-breadths. || 35-11 ||
The measure of the *śarāva* should likewise be half of a *pālikā*;
[this should be done] on the bank of a river or lake, in a field, on a mountain, or in a forest. (35-12)
Having reached a pure location, one should then sweep the ground with earth;
having sprinkled it thoroughly with the heart-mantra, one should worship it with that [mantra] using perfumes and other offerings.
Then, having meditated upon Śiva with his heart, the mantra-practitioner should have a pit dug by a female artisan;
then, taking up the earth with his left hand, he should enter the temple.
Having constructed a square pavilion in front of the Ālaya,
the wise one, having caused the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be recited and having sprinkled the ground with water,
should prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) there and arrange the clay pots (pālikā) and other items.
Each one may consist of sixteen, or eight, or even four [syllables]. || 35-16 ||
Having laid out eighty-one squares, excluding twenty-four, there is a lotus with nine squares in the center; twelve [squares] are prescribed for the corners.
Having divided [the area] into twenty-five squares, one should draw a lotus with its characteristic marks in the center;
or else, having divided it into sixteen, one should place a four-square [mandala] in its center.
Having placed the pitcher upon a lotus, with Soma as its presiding deity,
it should be provided with a lid, a tuft of grass, gold, and cloth.
One should worship Soma with perfumes and other offerings, using the seed-syllable *amṛta* (am) joined with the first vowel (*a*) of the one called Anila (the letter *ya*).
One should employ a syllable here that is accompanied by an anusvāra and a gift (dāna);
having first uttered the lamp (dīpa), one should then utter the seed-syllable (bīja) at its end.
The Guru should utter the word "Soma" in the dative case while dancing;
he should then offer milk-rice with meat to Soma, the King of the Moon.

In the corner sections of the *pālikās*, one should place small water-jars (*ghaṭikā*) and ladles (*śarāvaka*), arranging them in due order starting from the east and proceeding through the four directions. (35.23)
Thus the installation is declared to be of three types—excellent, middling, and inferior.
The placement of the *pālikās* should likewise be performed according to the cardinal and intermediate directions. (35.24)

The jars (ghaṭas) are to be placed inside, while the shallow bowls (śarāvas) are prescribed for the middle [layer]. The small pots (pālikās) have Brahmā as their presiding deity, and the small vases (ghaṭikās) are said to belong to Viṣṇu.
Īśvara, however, is the presiding deity of the earthenware bowls and vessels;
one should fill them well with clay, dried cow-dung, and sand. (35–26)
Sesame, mustard, mung beans, black gram, niṣpāva, as well as śāli rice, priyaṅgu, apāmārga, barley, and śyāmāka—these indeed are the ten [grains]. (35.27)
O learned one, having washed [the object] with milk, one should purify it with the ten-syllable mantra;
the wise person should always perform the ritual sprinkling (saṃprokṣayet) using water contained within a pitcher.
One should always fill the jar with fragrant substances; having prepared it according to the prescribed rite, one should then place it in a well-concealed location.
White lines here are indeed proclaimed to be auspicious and soft;
however, those that are black, four-furrowed, or running crosswise are not.
To pacify those defects, one should offer a hundred oblations while recollecting Śiva; thus the procedure for the *aṅkura* (germinating seeds) has been declared.
Now listen to the installation of the *liṅga*.
Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter, the Chapter on the Procedure for the Offering of *Aṅkura*.
Now begins the chapter on the ritual procedure for the installation of the *liṅga*.
Hereafter, I shall fully explain the supreme installation of the *liṅga*, which bestows all accomplishments, is meritorious, and grants the fruit of all sacrifices. (36-1)
There exists no ripening of fruit other than the installation of the *liṅga*;
therefore, with every effort, the ascetic should strive for the installation of the *liṅga*. (36-2)
At the limit of the foundation of the sanctum, prior to the door-bolt,
on the top of the eightfold brickwork (aṣṭakā), or in front of it, or again at the ends of the floor-levels. || 36-3 ||
Or, upon the completion of the constituent parts of the temple, the wise one should install the *liṅga* under an auspicious asterism, lunar day, weekday, *yoga*, and *muhūrta*. (36–4)

Having first performed the rite of the sprout (*aṅkura*) on the fifth, seventh, or ninth day prior to that, one should have the rites from the commencement of the sprout until the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) performed according to the Ādiśaiva tradition.
Having fashioned the subtle lingas from the site of the Karmakuṭī by artisans,
one should then grind the linga together with its pedestal using whetstones.
One should join each individual liṅga to its corresponding pedestal according to the proper method;
having performed the removal of the marks (*lakṣaṇoddhāra*), one should then begin [the rite].
One should construct a pavilion not too far from the front of the temple, or rather on its southern side, provided with all ornaments. (36–8)
Having prepared a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) in the center, one should place a liṅga there;
having taken hold of a golden liṅga, one should draw [the design] with red ochre while reciting the heart-mantra.
Having drawn the thick lines at the end as prescribed by the rule by the artisan,
the wise one should then perform the preliminary worship and divide [the area] equally into sixteen parts.
Having abandoned four parts at the top, the bud (mukula) should be formed with one part.
The tip should be one-third of that measure; its width at the base is equal to that same measurement.
That [measurement] is declared to be the basis for its size; having discarded two parts from the bottom, the stalk (nāla) shall consist of two lines, ending at half a part of the tree.
Having drawn the two Rudras at the sides, starting from Mukula and ending with Abdhikāntaka,
one should proceed in order from their base by a third of the interval between the *tāla* measures.
Above the division, however, one should fasten the two threads all around on the back;
a depression for the thread is prescribed to be one barley-corn or half a barley-corn deep. (36-14)
The front is said to be at the tip of the thread, while the back is at the junction of the threads;
its sides are at the sides of the thread, and its base is the lotus.

The architect, having honored the master builder, should thereafter perform purification with the eight types of earth, the five products of the cow, and pure water, being wise in his conduct. (36.16)
Having circumambulated the village together with the artisans, the wise preceptor should construct a water-shed at a pure spot where the water reaches only to the knee.
One should cover the canopy, banners, garlands, and so forth with wreaths of *darbha* grass; having carefully wrapped the *liṅga* with *darbha* grass, one should then encircle it with cloths.
On a wooden plank or a seat, one should lay [the body] with the head toward the east;
then, having established the vertical thread, one should likewise do so for that seat on both sides. (36-19)
Then, for the sake of protection, he should place eight water-pots (kalaśas) all around, each containing a blade of kūrca grass,
wrapped in cloth, and presided over by the deities of the world-protectors (lokapālas).
For five nights, or three nights, or even for one night;
likewise, having fasted for one night, he should remain in the *pañcagavya* while bearing that [sacred] mark.
Alternatively, one should bathe [the deity] with an *āḍhaka* each of the products of the cow individually;
in front of the temple, there should be a square pavilion.
It should be ten or twelve cubits, or thirteen cubits;
or even ten and five cubits, or twenty cubits.
It was provided with sixteen pillars, endowed with four gates,
furnished with four archways, and encircled by garlands of *darbha* grass.
It was crowded with canopies and banners, hung with garlands of flowers,
adorned with various garments, and endowed with diverse ornaments.
In the middle of that, one should construct an altar (vedikā) with a width equal to one-third [of the area],
one cubit in height, and resembling the surface of a mirror.
Having constructed sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) around that very [site] according to the prescribed rule—
the one in the east being square and the one in the south being like a half-moon— 36-27.
In the west, there is a circular pit; in the north, a lotus-shaped one;
likewise, a yoni-shaped one in the southeast, and a triangular one in the southwest.
One should construct a hexagonal fire-pit in the direction of the wind (the northwest), an eight-cornered one in the northeast,
and a circular pit between the northeast and the east.
In an extensive [ritual], there should be nine oblations; in an abbreviated one, five oblations.
One who desires the five fires should perform the great rites; in the northeast, the fire of Śiva is the form of the Lord.
Having smeared it with cow dung and adorned it with powdered flour,
one should construct a bathing pavilion on its northern side.
Having constructed [the altar] with seven, eight, or nine cubits and having adorned it as before,
one should properly fashion a bathing-altar (snānavedi) in its center, as well as a pit (svabhra) to the north.
Having made it square and level, measuring four, three, or nine cubits,
provided with three girdles, and elevated by one tāla.
(177) With an interval of four, three, or two finger-breadths, there may be a single girdle;
and to the north, there is a water-channel exiting from the outside of the pavilion.
In the palace and likewise in the pavilion, one should feed the Brahmins in due order—those who observe the Śiva-vow, who are pure, and who are endowed with devotion to Śiva. (36–35)
Having removed the remnants of the Brahmins' meal and having applied a coating of cow dung,
one should cause the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited, accompanied by the sound of Vedic chanting.

O wise ones, let the oblation for the palace deities be performed according to the previously mentioned rule, using *darbha* grass, *palāśa* leaves, and [leaves from] the *śamī*, *pippala*, and *bilva* trees. (36–37)

Having performed the rite of circumambulation with fire (paryagnikaraṇa), one should consecrate the temple pavilion in due order by sprinkling it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and water with kuśa grass, while reciting the Śiva-mantra.
The wise man should prepare a bed together with pure *śāli* rice and barley;
it should consist of eight *droṇas* of *śāli* rice and half that amount of husked rice.
Having drawn a lotus, one should worship it with half a grain of rice and a sesame seed;
having strewn *darbha* grass over it, one should offer flowers together with parched grain (*lāja*).
One should prepare items such as those born from eggs and so forth using cloths that have not been worn for ten days;
these include what is born from an egg, what is born from a shaved head, what is born from hair, and likewise what is born from wool.
One who is most skilled in ritual procedures should prepare five types of beds:
those made of leather, and one known as "egg-born," which is produced from the feathers of birds.
That which is made from cotton and similar materials is known as *muṇḍaja* (woven from cut fibers).
That which comes from the wool of sheep and other animals, as well as from the hair of deer, is called *romaja* (hair-derived).

Silk is said to be produced from the left [side], while that produced from the skin of lions and tigers is known as "leather. A wise person should understand this distinction regarding leather when it is available. (36–44)

Having honored him with the five-fold face [mantra] upon the sacrificial ground with effort, he who is born of the Śiva-lineage, endowed with the previously mentioned characteristics, should [install] you. (36–45)
One who knows the ritual procedures of the Śaiva Tantra and observes the conduct of the covenant,
having bathed well and sipped water according to the rule, should thereafter perform the bath with sacred ash.
Adorned with all ornaments and likewise wearing fine garments, he was anointed with white garlands and unguents, wearing a white turban and fine clothes. (36–47)
One who is thus purified and white [in mind] should perform all ritual acts;
the recitation-pads (jāpa-paṭṭikā) for that are known to be either square or circular. 36–48.
The best of mantra-knowers should place [the image] upon a pedestal and railing in the center;
having purified the *liṅga* that has been soaked in the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), he should do so again and again. (36–49)

At the root of *darbha* grass, in the presence of a venerable one (*bhadanta*), at the plowing of a boar, on an anthill, at the tip of a bull's horn, by a river, and likewise on a mountain; || 36-50 ||
Furthermore, the wise one should briefly take earth from the ocean;
one should not perform a bath there using the eight types of clay in water.
Having bathed it repeatedly with water [reciting] the *vyomavyāpin* mantra a thousand times,
and having consecrated it with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), one should worship it with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
And [the vessels] filled with honey, milk, and ghee, together with gold and flowers, should be made of gold, silver, copper, or even brass. (36–53)
Having filled each one with a *prastha* measure, the wise man,
using those substances and the seed-mantra (*bījamantra*), should inscribe [the mantra] with a golden needle upon three vessels.
Having subsequently tied on the protective amulet (pratisara) amidst proclamations of auspiciousness and merit,
[one should use] a cord made of gold, silver, linen, or cotton.
Having bound her in the middle of the liṅga, one should indeed have the liṅga laid upon the bed by Śiva with a portion of the offering, with its head facing east and its face turned upwards.
One should spread an upper covering with cloths and likewise strew it with *darbha* grass;
having worshipped with the *hṛdaya-mantra* and fragrant flowers and other offerings, they should remain composed in mind. (36–57)
Having consecrated the pedestal (piṇḍikā) just as one does for the linga, starting from the base of the linga,
one should then install the arches (toraṇas) and the pitchers (kumbhas), which preside over the guardians of the directions (lokapālas).
Then, he should place there, in an even row, sacrificial grass-bundles (śakūrcas) together with their covers, wrapped in pairs of cloths and accompanied by auspicious sprouts (maṅgalāṅkura).
Taking the principal pitcher, which is filled with thirty-two [substances] and seven [others],
and which is endowed with the radiance of the image, one should likewise take the vardhanī vessel, half its size.
Having wrapped it with threads, however, using only a single thread causes a fault;
three threads are declared for rites of pacification (śāntika), and the distance between them is traditionally held to be the measure of a barley grain.
There, having wrapped another sūtra—well-filled with fragrant water, together with a tuft of hair and its lid—with a pair of cloths; || 36-62 ||
It was adorned above with a canopy of mango sprouts and flowers;
and five jewels, combined with gold, were placed in the water-pot and the *vardhanī* vessel.
For the benefit of the Brāhmaṇas, [he created] the sacrificial ladle (*sruk*), the dipping-spoon (*sruva*), and the water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*);
for the benefit of the Kṣatriyas, [he created] elephants, horses, chariots, and soldiers. (36–64)
For the Vaiśyas, the balance scale (tulā) is prescribed; for the Śūdras, the pair of ploughs (yugalāṅgalau).
The wise man should place these upon the vardhanī and the Śiva-kumbha.
The wise one should first place the deity residing in the young *liṅga* upon the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), having installed it within the water-pot (*kumbha*).
One should bring forth the Goddess seated upon her throne within the *vardhanī* vessel, together with the eight Lords of the Vidyās, accompanied by their garments, gold, and weapons. (36–67)

The wise one, having placed the ritual jars (kalaśas) around the Śiva-jar— each possessing a tuft of grass (kūrca), unbroken rice (akṣata), and a canopy (vitāna), and adorned with fruits and sprouts— [should proceed].

The knower of mantras, having invoked the lords of knowledge (vidyeśvaras), their retinues, and the deities such as the gatekeepers into their respective pitchers with their corresponding mantras, [proceeds].
At night, the fire-oblation (homa) should be performed with all the mantras individually;
having raised the young linga, the Śaivas should cast it into a flood of water.
If it is made of wood, one should burn it with fire or cast it into water;
and having severed the Śiva-śakti [connection], one should carefully wear the head [of the image]. || 36-71 ||
One should provide it with yak-tail whisks, umbrellas, banners, and canopies, and create a great sound accompanied by music, song, and dance. (36.72)
Having circumambulated the pavilion clockwise, one should hold the *vardhani* vessel;
then, one should place it upon the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) in the northeast corner of the altar.
One should worship Śiva, the limbs of Brahmā, the limbs of Vidyā, the Vidyeśvaras, and the Gaṇeśvaras,
together with the world-protectors (lokapālas) and their weapons, using the mantras themselves.
It was accompanied by song and dance, joined with the sound of musical instruments,
and likewise featured the recitation of the Ṛg, Yajur, Sāma, and Atharva Vedas, as well as the study of the primary scriptures.
Then, having performed the recitation and hymns of praise,
the wise one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) by offering oblations into these sacrificial pits according to the previously mentioned procedure.
All the ritual materials should be the same, but listen now to the specific requirements for the fuel:
one should place *śamī* wood in the eastern quarter, and likewise a *vaṭa* tree in the south-eastern quarter.
One should plant a *kaṅkata* tree in the southern direction and a *plakṣa* tree in the domain of Nirṛti;
an *aśvattha* tree in the western quarter and an *audumbara* tree in the northwestern quarter.
The *bilva* tree is indeed for the northern quarter, while the *arka* is in the direction of Īśāna;
likewise, for all fire-pits (*agnikuṇḍa*), the *palāśa* is for the fire of Śiva. (36–79)
Having offered oblations with the limbs of Vidyā and the limbs of Śiva, one should touch the Liṅga;
indeed, for each, one should perform a hundred "touch-oblations" (sparśāhuti) accompanied by clarified butter.
Having contemplated "I am Śiva" and having offered oblations effortlessly as one whose self is Śiva,
[one perceives] space, wind, fire, water, earth, and even the distant.
And there are eight forms whose nature is the Sun, bearing the forms beginning with Bhava:
Bhava, Śarva, Paśupati, Ugra, Rudra, and Bhīma. (36–82)
The renowned Mahānīśa and others are proclaimed as the bearers of the forms;
having established the fire in the sacrificial pits and protected it with fuel and other materials,
one should begin the placement of the jewels at an auspicious hour in the morning.
Having divided the width of the doorway into twenty-one parts, indeed.
Having divided the middle portion into six parts and [further] dividing it into two,
the thread that remains after setting aside one part on the left is known as the Brahma-thread (brahmasūtra).
One should install the *liṅga* in its center, and within that, one should install Śiva; for if the *liṅga* is installed otherwise, it brings harm to the king and the kingdom. (36–86)
First, having placed a firm tortoise-stone (kūrmaśilā) provided with the Brahma-sections,
one should place upon the top of the Brahma-stone (brahmaśilā) a stone marked with the Nandyāvarta design.
One should properly prepare a firm base, provided with oily substances;
likewise, one should include rubies, lapis lazuli, sapphires, and emeralds.
Pearl, gomeda, diamond, topaz, and coral— these nine gems one should place in the middle and the other positions.
Barley, millet, mung beans, sesame, mustard seeds, as well as rice, priyaṅgu, śyāmāka, and horse gram—these are the nine grains. (36-90)
Haritāla, as well as śyāma, sandalwood, realgar, saurāṣṭra, pārata, lead, red ochre, and pyrite; 36-91.

Having thus recollected, the wise one should extract the jewels known as the vital breaths, as well as the excellent seeds that are the sense faculties, from the elements and the sense organs. (36.92)
The elements (dhātu) are said to be the repositories; one should deposit them, primarily with the seed-syllables.
Having worshipped them with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, one should place the Nandyāvarta stone.

Having raised the *liṅga* from its bed and discarded those [offerings] that have become stale, he should offer the *arghya* according to the rule with the *hṛdaya-mantra*, together with a flower. (36.94)
The wise one, having turned the liṅga toward the west, should [consecrate] the preceptor, the image-guardians, the students, and the attendants with the heart-mantra. || 36-95 ||
The astrologer and those who have recited the mantras should be honored by the king with appropriate gifts;
then, from the Cāṇḍāla up to the highest caste, he should cause [the people] to perform [the rites] according to their capacity and in due order.
The chariot-borne Liṅga and the temple are circumambulated; the Preceptor touches the front [of the deity], while the guardians of the forms touch their respective directions. (36–97)
Having touched the root of the *karti* with the tip of the *vardhani*,
and having circumambulated the deity, one should stand near the entrance.
Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, and having offered the *arghya* water with the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*),
the wise ones should then cause the *liṅga* to enter the womb-chamber (*garbhagarta*) comfortably.
At an auspicious moment, during a favorable conjunction of planets, and endowed with an auspicious lunar mansion and *karana*,
he meditated upon the god Sadāśiva while recollecting the root mantra.
One should install a *liṅga* there, leaning slightly toward the northeast; having secured it with stones shaped like *nandyāvarta*, one should then join it to the pedestal.

One should firmly establish one's own source, the principal seat, and the eight [subsidiary seats] below; the consecrator (sthāpaka) should perform this through the mere intelligence of the architect (sthapati).
Then, having performed the eightfold binding (*aṣ�ṭabandha*), one should prepare *jatugulgulu* along with *siddhi*; likewise, *sarja*, *sphaṭika*, sugar, and *kuruvindaka*.
Having burned oil mixed with eight [ingredients] like a small grain of *cākkaṇa*, the wise one should then insert it firmly and evenly between the *liṅga* and the pedestal (*pīṭha*).
Then, with an extent equal to one-sixteenth part of the *pūjāṃśa*, its height is declared to be one-fourth of that; this is considered the *aṣṭabandha* [type of base]. (36–105)
The space between the *liṅga* and the pedestal should be smooth, or else joined by a vajra-bond;
then the preceptor, having bathed again, with his body armored by mantras, [should proceed]. (36.106)
Having caused the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*), one should bathe [the image] with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*);
then, having worshipped it with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, and likewise having prepared a seat.

Having invoked and worshipped the auspicious Śiva through the knower of mantras, and having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa and the satiation of the mantras, one should then perform the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti).
Having performed the special worship of the jar preceded by a formal request, one should there worship the preceptor according to one's means. (36.109)
The turban, the upper garment, and likewise the lower robe; as well as golden rings, and similarly fragrant flowers. || 36-110 ||
One should cause the crown, the earrings, the necklace, the armlets, as well as the bracelets and the waist-belt to be given to the preceptor.
The fee for the preceptor (ācāryadakṣiṇā) is ten niṣkas of gold for the lowest [grade];
for the middle, it is double that; and for the highest, it should be triple. || 36-112 ||
Having thus worshipped according to the prescribed rite, one should cause the cow along with her calf to be given away;
for the satisfaction of the preceptor’s mind is the cause of the deity’s pleasure.

The wise one should cause separate garments and a gold *niṣka* to be given to the image-guardians (*mūrtipas*). Then, the remainder of the *homa* should be led [to them] by means of the *hṛdaya* mantra.
Having informed the Lord of the Gods residing in the pitcher according to the prescribed rite,
the preceptor raises the pitcher, and the disciple raises the *vardhanī* vessel.
Then the image-makers should circumambulate the temple with the water-pots;
having rested at the doorway, the preceptor should offer the *arghya* oblation while reciting the *hṛdaya-mantra*.
Then, having entered that liṅga and standing facing north,
he should place the Śiva-kumbha upon the tripod.
Having mentally conceived the seat of the six paths (ṣaḍadhvāsana), one should display the mudrā of the liṅga;
for just as flowers, scents, sesame seeds, and oil [are offered], so does the Lord abide.
One should join the Lord of the lords of gods, who resides in the *kumbha*, within the center of the *liṅga*;
having recited the *Śiva-mantra*, one should contemplate Śiva within oneself. (36–119)
The consecration with that water which is performed upon the liṅga is said to be the vital breath (prāṇa);
having meditated upon that pervasive power (śakti), one should likewise [meditate] upon the power in the pedestal (pīṭhaka).
Having indeed visualized all the deities of the obstructions as before,
one should then invoke them into the jars and consecrate [the disciple] with that water.
Having offered incense, flowers, incense smoke, and lamps in due order,
[one should worship] all the attendants without exception, beginning with the gatekeepers and ending with those on the pedestal.

One should place each respective deity residing in its jar into its corresponding position. One should offer oblations of five colors— milk-rice (pāyasa), rice-and-pulse mixture (kṛsara), sweet rice (gaulya), mung-bean rice (maudga), and pure meat— as well as the sacrificial offering for the retinue.
One should cause a festival to be held there, preceded by the ritual procedures for the evening and other times.
The ritual procedure for consecration has been explained; now hear about the inspection.
Everything should be performed according to the rules of consecration, with proper reasoning and in the correct sequence. (36–125)
As before, one should place the jars according to the prescribed rite in the middle of the altar;
prior to the installation of the jars, one must especially perform the purification of the liṅga. (36.126)
Having smeared both the pedestal and the ground with all kinds of fragrant substances according to the sequence of the five purifications, one should then cover them with cloths.
In the rite called *saṃprokṣaṇa*, there is likewise no invocation nor the offering of the frontal vehicle;
this is the procedure for a single *liṅga*. Now hear the procedure for five *liṅgas*.
Having established Sadāśiva in the center, likewise Puruṣa in the east; having established Aghora in the south, likewise Sadyojāta in the west.
Or in the north, or in the southeast corner, or in the corners and the great directions; having thus beheld Sadāśiva, the wise one [should proceed].
The individual celestial chariots (*vimāna*) and the remaining ritual procedures are as before;
such is the rule for those with five *liṅgas*. Now hear the rule for those with nine *liṅgas*.
Their previously mentioned celestial chariot (vimāna) is prescribed for the eight directions,
having observed Sadāśiva in the cardinal and intermediate directions.
Listen to the procedure for the thousand [liṅgas] as proclaimed in the Navaliṅgavidhi:
Sadāśiva is in the center as before, and the Vidyeśas are each separately [placed];
that wise one [should know] that liṅga consists of twenty-four and is surrounded by the Vidyeśas.
For others, however, the names and forms of that which is called Sāda are proclaimed. || 36-134 ||

Having established each [deity] with its own respective name-mantra as enjoined by the ritual rules, [one should perform the rite] according to the procedure every eight days, sixteen days, or a month. (36.135)
Just as one should act in the case of the prescription for a single *liṅga*, so should one perform everything [else];
Sādākhya is accepted in the form of a *liṅga*, but the *anvaliṅga* is not desired. (36–136)
The mortal who acts in this manner shall attain union with Śiva.
The installation of the Liṅga has been declared; now hear the procedure for all [other types].
Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter, the Chapter on the Procedure for the Installation of the Liṅga.
The Svāyaṃbhuva-lingāgama,
the Kāraṇa, the Tula, the Sūkṣma, and the Suprabheda—
these are the fourfold Āgamas worshipped by Svayaṃbhū in their respective order.

The one who is most skilled in ritual procedures should worship the Daivalinga, Agama, Kamika, Vijaya, Svayambhuva, and Anala lingas of the gods, and should perform the ritual installations accordingly.
Having contemplated the *Divyaliṅgāgama*,
the *Ciṃtya*, the *Sahasra*, the *Dīpta*, and likewise the *Ayuta*,
one should perform all rites as prescribed for the worship of the *Divyaliṅga*.
The wise one should especially worship the Ṛṣiliṅga, the Āgama, the Yogaja, the Makuṭa, the Niśvāsa, the Raurava, and the Ārṣaka during the half-watch of the night.
The supreme teacher in a human land should worship Mānuṣaliṅgāgama, Vīra, Vimalodbheda, Candrajñāna, and Bimbaka, as well as the Parama.
One should sprinkle the *rākṣasa-liṅga* with the *protgīta*, *lalita*, *siddhi*, and *saṃtāna* [mantras];
and one should worship the *āsura* [liṅga] in the *rākṣasa* [manner].

One should worship the Bāṇaliṅgāgama, the Pārameśvara proclaimed with its numerical enumeration, the Aṃśumān, and likewise the Kiraṇa; and indeed, having worshipped the Bāṇaliṅga, one should perform the propitiation of the five Gaṇas.
The human [measure] is within one *yojana*; the ancient (*paurāṇa*) is ten *yojanas*;
the *ārṣa* is a hundred *yojanas*, and the divine (*daivika*) is a thousand.
(185) The Chapter on the Ritual for the Installation of All [Deities]:
Now I shall explain the installation of all [deities]; listen! [I shall describe] the general procedure for the installation of the forms of Īśvara and the others. (37–1)
This is the supreme common rule for all twelve types of images; the installation of both movable and immovable ones is identical. (37-2)
Now, listen to the procedure for the installation of a mobile [image] using stone or clay;
or, having performed the deposition of jewels in water, one should circumambulate it to the right.
In the case of a painted image, one should indeed avoid [the previous method] and perform the Ratnasetu rite;
in the case of a painted image, it should be performed with effort upon a mirror. (37-4)
Above the three-footed stand, one should pour [the water] into a wooden trough over a mirror;
one should then perform the ritual consecration in water (jalādhivāsa) and the ceremonial bath (snapana) exactly as prescribed for the ninth day.
This shall certainly be equal for all of them without exception,
provided that the offering of the ritual sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa) has been performed previously according to the procedure mentioned before.
In the front part of the palace, within a well-adorned pavilion,
one should prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) there with pure rice grains.
Having worshipped with incense, flowers, and other offerings in the center of the lotus-seat,
one should not recite [mantras] in vain, but should place the jewels according to the prescribed rule.
Māṇikya, vaiḍūrya, nīla, and likewise marataka; mauktika, gomeda, vajra, puṣya, and pravālaka. || 37-9 ||
One should not place these—the *madhyama* and the others—in the heart;
likewise, one should not place sesame, mung beans, arani flowers, or indeed mustard seeds.
Śyāma, śāli, kuluttha, priyaṅgu, and new seeds—these, when fashioned here with gold and with the mantra, [grant success]. (37-11)
Collyrium, yellow orpiment, black pigment, realgar, mercury, saurāṣṭra, siddhaka, and likewise red ochre. || 37-12 ||
Having fixed the cloth in the center of the pedestal with the Śiva-mantra,
one should join the image there and likewise cause it to be well-anointed.
Then, having prepared sand powder and strips of ox-hide,
one should rub the image with them so that it attains a state of stainless purity.
Then, for the purpose of the release [of the deity], having prepared a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) as before, one should place the image upon it, covered above by a great cloth. (37.15)
Having placed eight water-pots around [the central one], each containing a tuft of grass (kūrca), unbroken rice grains, and flowers,
he should duly worship the guardians of the directions within them according to the prescribed rite.

The preceptor, together with the artisans, while recollecting the Netra-mantra, [should perform the piercing] with a golden needle and by striking, in the case of images made of stone as well as those made of metal. (37.17)

Having delineated the colors and painted it upon a clay surface that has the appearance of a picture, one should fashion the image including the line of the eyebrows and the third [feature], the line of the eyelashes. (37.18)
Having drawn a white circle, in its center he should draw a black circle;
within the black circle, the wise man should draw a circle of light.
Having clearly instructed the artisan, the Guru should mutter the mantra over the eyes;
then, having honored the installer and the master-builder with garments and golden ornaments.
Having worshipped and gratified [the deity], and having performed the dismissal of the artisan,
one should satisfy [the deity] with honey and clarified butter, using a golden [vessel] together with dūrvā grass.
One should perform the rite for the eyes with the Netra-mantra using milk;
likewise, one should take up three vessels made either of copper or of bell-metal.
Into those [vessels], golden ones together with silver ones, they filled each one to the measure of a *prastha* with milk, clarified butter, and honey.
One should apply honey to the right eye while contemplating it as having the nature of the sun, and ghee to the left eye while remembering it as having the nature of the moon. (37.24)
Then, with milk, the Guru should show the fire-natured [form] to the eyes; recollecting the respective mantras, he should sprinkle [the disciple] with them. (37–25)
The middle, index, and ring fingers should be joined with the golden [ring];
the index finger is on the right side above, while the middle and ring fingers are on the other side.
Then, having joined [the mantras] with the heart-mantra and others, and having sprinkled her with fragrant water,
he should veil the face of the woman, whose limbs are well-nourished and who is in the prime of youth, while asking [her questions].
Having milked the cow— along with her calf— using the *godhenu-havya* mantra,
the wise man, having worshipped the cow, should show her [the vessel] while reciting the *Sāvitrī* mantra.
But afterwards, one should show it to the twice-born, especially to other twice-born ones;
thus is this entire procedure for all images declared to be equal.
By that which brings about its purification, one should purify it;
having adorned it with all ornaments, one should perform a circumambulation of the foremost village. (37.30)
One should perform the ritual immersion in water (jalādhivāsana) in auspicious water reaching up to the neck, in a place provided with four legs and equipped with a canopy and banners. (37–38ab)
In the middle of the water at the drinking station, which is provided with a garland of *darbha* grass,
it should be covered with a pair of cloths and encircled with *darbha* grass and flowers.
One should cause him to lie down comfortably on a seat or a plank with his head toward the east, for five nights, three nights, or even for a single night. (37–38)
Then, one should perform the consecration of the pavilion according to the extent of one's means, in the east, the south, the west, or the north, in a pleasing location. (37–34)
It should be ten or twelve cubits in size, joined with sixteen pillars,
provided with four doors, and adorned with four archways.
It was encircled by a garland of *darbha* grass, adorned with hanging flower garlands,
covered above by a canopy, and hung with banners in the eight directions.
Adorned with sprouts of mango and decorated with strings of pearls,
it should be placed specifically in the central part of the northern wing of the pavilion.
The secondary altar (upavedī), however, should be made with a height equal to a tāla and a width of four [tālas].
One should cause a very firm and auspicious altar to be constructed within the temple. (37–38)
One should cause sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) to be constructed according to the correct measurements in the eight directions, each one cubit (hasta) in height and resembling the surface of a mirror.
To the east, however, it should be square like a fire-flame or a pippala leaf;
in the south, it is a half-moon, and in the southwest, a triangle.
The circle is in the western quarter, the hexagon in the region of Vāyu (the northwest),
the lotus in the northern quarter, and the eight-cornered [figure] in the northeast.
One should cause a circular sacrificial pit (vṛttakuṇḍa) to be made between the directions of Īśāna and Indra;
or else, on the northern part of the pavilion, one should construct a bathing pavilion.
In the center of that [area], one should construct a bathing altar (snānavedi) measuring three, two, or one cubit [in width],
one cubit in height, perfectly level, very firm, and auspicious.
It should be provided with three girdles, measured by four, four, and three finger-breadths respectively;
or else, it may be auspicious with a single girdle measuring eight finger-breadths.
Having smeared [the ground] with cow dung, one should perform drying and purification; then, having fed the Brahmins, the Vāstuhoma sacrifice follows thereafter. (37–45)
Having performed the circumambulation with fire (paryagnikaraṇa) around the palace, that is, the sacrificial pavilion,
an auspicious day (puṇyāha) should be proclaimed there, and one should sprinkle it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
The wise man should prepare a bed upon the altar with rice;
using eight *droṇas*, or half of that, or half again, of leveled grains.
In the center of that, one should fashion an eight-petaled lotus with rice;
having carefully prepared it with eggs and other materials, layer by layer from below upwards.
In the absence of birds and other such materials, one should spread out five garments;
above that, there are the nine Śaktis, namely Icchā, Jñāna, and Kriyā.
Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, and adorned with auspicious sprouts,
one should raise the image from the water and likewise immerse it in the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
It should be performed for one night, or indeed one may perform the ritual bathing;
having then placed the image in the center of the bathing altar (snānavedi), [one should proceed]. (37–51)
The wise man, having bathed in the water of the eight nectars and worshipped with the *hṛdaya-mantra*,
should perform the offering of ghee upon the head while using gold and *dūrvā* grass as witnesses.
One should bind a protective amulet made of gold or silver upon the right hand with the heart mantra, accompanied by a protective rite.
Having worshipped with perfumes and other offerings and having led [the deity] onto the altar,
one should worship the God facing west with the heart-mantra (hṛdaya).
One should place the Lord upon the bed with his head toward the east and his face turned upward;
as for the image of Īśvara, it should be placed together with Śakti on the left side.

One who possesses excellent intelligence should perform here, simultaneously, the rites such as the placement of jewels (ratnanyāsa) and others; likewise, he should determine what is appropriate or inappropriate for other images.
Having made an upper covering with cloths, *darbha* grass, and flowers,
[he should place] the eight jars of the Lords of Knowledge (*vidyeśa*), together with the golden weapons such as the thunderbolt (*vajra*).
Covered with pairs of cloths, provided with tufts of grass and lids,
[he should place them] around the image in the eight directions with their respective mantras.
Having established a single water-pot (kumbhaka) at the northeast of the head of the image,
it should be complete with sixteen enclosures and endowed with the radiance of the image.
Having wrapped it with three threads such that the distance between one thread and the next is a barley-corn (*yava*), it should be provided with the five jewels and filled with pure water. (37–60)
Adorned with mango sprouts, provided with a beard [of grain], and accompanied by a lid,
one should wrap it in a pair of cloths and place it upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila).
For the benefit of the Brahmins, he fashioned the sacrificial thread, the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles;
and for the benefit of the Kṣatriyas, the wise one [fashioned] elephants, horses, and chariots.
Scales, measuring vessels, and bowls are indeed for the benefit of Vaiśyas;
and for the sake of the welfare of Śūdras, there is the plough joined with the bull.
Having fashioned these out of gold, one should insert them into the six limbs;
having established the image in whatever form it takes, one should meditate upon that very form.
Having established [the deity] within the pitcher while recollecting its root mantra,
one should perform the sixfold meditation, invoke [the deity], and mentally unite it with that Śiva.
One should perform the ritual placement of the mantra (mantranyāsa) by means of the very same path previously described;
the wise practitioner should worship with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings while reciting the heart-mantra (hṛdaya).
Having likewise placed the *vardhanī* vessel with the principal seed-syllable on the left,
one should place eight jars all around the edge of the small altar.
Provided with garments, tufts of grass, and unbroken grains, accompanied by threads and sprouts,
and endowed with gold, vajras, and other [implements], they are presided over by the world-protectors as their tutelary deities.
Having worshipped them with their respective mantras, one should place the pitchers at the doors;
these, in the form of the eight auspicious symbols, are to be placed outside the altar.
Having established [the deities] and worshipped them each by their own name, one should then perform the fire-oblation (homa).
Having performed the recitation of the Vedas in the various directions with the Ṛg, Yajur, Sāma, and Atharva [Vedas], [one should proceed].
Alternatively, one may employ nine, five, or three fires, or even a single fire;
one should properly perform the rite with the three sacred fires (tretāgni) in sacrificial pits (kuṇḍa) located in the east, south, and north.
Sadāśiva, Īśvara, and Rudra are traditionally known as the presiding deities of the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍa) in successive order.
In the case of three fires or a single fire, the wise man should offer oblations into the Śiva-fire from the east.
Having first offered oblations into the Śiva-fire, and thereafter the oblation to the Mūrtis,
one should meditate upon the Lord as omnipresent, from Śiva down to the earth.
Having meditated upon his own self in those respective forms, the wise one should perform the fire sacrifice:
"The Sun is the form in the east; become [the fire], O bearer of the three forms! (37–74).
In the southeast, the form of Agni is indeed the bearer [of the principle] called Śarva;
Paśupati is the bearer of the form in the south, the form of the Earth. (37.75)
In the southwest of the sky is Mūrti Rudra, who bears that form;
in the direction of Varuṇa (the west) is the one named Rudra, the excellent bearer [of the form]. || 37-76 ||
In the quarter of the wind, Vāyu indeed is the bearer of the Bhīma form;
in the north is the form of Soma, while Mahān is the bearer of another form.
Likewise, the Lord who assumes forms is himself the very form;
thus, according to this arrangement, the eight forms are the bearers of the form.
Śiva is declared to be the presiding deity, intent upon the meditation on each respective [deity];
having performed the fire-offering (agnimukha) as before, one should subsequently perform the oblation (homa) with the ritual substances.
Wood, clarified butter, fuel-sticks, food and so forth, parched grain, flour, sesame seeds, barley, white mustard, mung beans, and honey—these eleven items [should be offered]. (37-80)
Having silently prepared that fuel, one should not offer an oblation of ghee at the root;
rather, one should perform the homa with the principal seed-syllable using sacrificial wood, seeds, and caru-oblations. || 37-81 ||
One should offer parched grain with the Heart-mantra, groats with the Head-mantra,
sesame seeds with the Tuft-mantra, and barley with the Vairūpa-mantra.

For the sake of accomplishing the goal, one should indeed offer oblations with the *mudga* weapon and the *netra* mantra, using honey as the sacrificial substance; thereafter, one should recite the *vyāhṛtis*.

One should know that the fuel-sticks (samidh) for the eastern direction are of palāśa wood; for the south-eastern (āgneyī) direction, they are of kaṅkata; for the southern direction, those of vaṭa; and likewise for the south-western (nairṛtī) direction, those of aśvattha. || 37-84 ||
The Plakṣa tree is for the western quarter, the Udumbara for the north-western;
the Arka is indeed in the northern direction, and the Bilva in the region of the northeast.
Between Indra and Īśāna, there should be fuel-sticks of *palāśa*;
the sacrificial material should be one thousand, or half of that, or even half of that again. (37–86)
One should perform the offering of the substance one hundred and eight times, or fifty, or twenty-five,
or even sixteen times.
Having offered oblations with the very limbs of Brahmā, one should touch each respective part;
at the end of that, having offered the Vyāhṛtis, one should avoid sleep during the night.
At dawn, when the sky is clear, the wise man, prior to the auspicious moment for the consecration,
should first honor the preceptor with garments, rings, and other such gifts.
One should cause the preceptor to receive a golden flower-garland, as well as earrings, bracelets, female and male servants, cattle, and land. (37.90)
Ten *niṣkas* for the lowest [grade], and likewise double or triple;
such is the fee (*dakṣiṇā*) prescribed for the teacher (*deśika*) starting from the lowest grade.
Each of the image-bearers (mūrtipas) shall receive one-eighth of the portion given to the preceptor (deśika);
the astrologer (daivajña) and the Vāstu-hotṛ priest shall receive the same, while the image-bearers shall indeed receive three times that amount.
One should cause the image-maker, the reciter of the three-footed [mantra], and those who study it to each receive a golden ring and a pair of garments. (37–93)
Having caused his devotees and attendants to give according to their own capacity, he should cause food, drink, and other necessities to be given to the poor, the blind, and the wretched. (37–94)

One should offer the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) with all the mantras according to the essence of a hundred Vedas; thereafter, one should perform the concluding ritual (*upariṣṭatantra*) and everything else in the proper sequence.
Having raised Śiva from his bed a short time before the end of the muhūrta,
one should worship him with perfumes, flowers, and the like, accompanied by the sounds of conchs and drums.
Adorned with all ornaments, one should then begin the ritual placement of mantras (mantranyāsa).
Having lifted the Śiva-vessel (śivakumbha), one should place the Vardhanī vessel before Śiva.
Having arranged the *arghya* offering and performed the ritual of identifying with the deity (*sakalīkṛta-vigraha*),
one should meditate on that form situated in the fire and properly unite it with the image.
One should indeed place the Śakti on the left side with the principal seed-syllables (bījas);
likewise, having joined the principle (tattva) from the jar into the image, one should place the limbs (aṅgas).
One should perform an ablution here with jars [consecrated] by those known as Śiva and Umā, the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśas).
At the conclusion of that, having performed the ceremonial bath, there should be a great offering of sacrificial food (haviṣya).
Then, a festival should be performed there according to the previously mentioned procedure; thus has the festival for the images of Īśvara been proclaimed. (37.101)
Twelve images are prescribed, as well as for the rite of the festival; indeed, everything else—such as place, time, and form—is exactly the same in all cases. (37-102)
One should perform all the sequences of worship and so forth in due order, just as for Śiva;
for all other deities, the procedure therein is enjoined according to their respective rules. (37.103)
Likewise, the essential nature [of each deity] should be established through their respective name-mantras and so forth;
after the installation of all [the deities], perform the ceremonial bathing and the festival. (37.104)
The installation of all [the deities] has been declared; now hear the sprinkling (saṃprokṣaṇa) of them.
On the altar, the wise [practitioner] [should place] the jars for Śiva, Umā, and the Vidyeśvaras.
The wise practitioner should place the jars known as the guardians of the world (lokapāla) upon the inner altar,
and he should cast in garments and golden forms as before.
In the rite of the image, having covered that image with cloths— ranging from jewels to the bed— and with canopies, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) as previously described.
The ritual bathing (snapana) is in the northern direction; all else is the same.
One should cause the materials required for yoga to be presented to the preceptor (ācārya). || 37-108 ||
Thus is the installation of the Sakala [deity]; now hear about the establishment of Śakti.
Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter on the ritual procedure for the installation of the Sakala [deity].
Now begins the chapter on the ritual procedure for the installation of Śakti.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the supreme installation of Śakti;
like heat is inseparable from fire, so is Śakti inseparable from the All-pervading Lord.
The formless is called the "severance of form," while that which possesses form is indeed the formed.
Sadāśiva, Śiva, Rudra, Viṣṇu, and Brahmā are thus differentiated. (38–2)
Manonmanī, Īśvarī, Umā, Śrī, and Sāvitrī are thus distinguished;
this is the division of the supreme and the non-supreme, which effects grace upon the worlds. (38-3)
They know that Manonmanīśvarī is indeed established together [with the deity];
there is another threefold division of the Śaktis, and one is joined with the term "together" (saha). || 38-4 ||
But where only Śakti is to be installed, it is said that there is sin;
therefore, having first installed Śambhu, the installation of Śakti should likewise be performed according to the prescribed rule—that is declared to be proper. (38)
Then, the installation of Śakti and Śambhu together in one place, indeed simultaneously.
(193) Listen to the general [mantras] for the three types, beginning with the root mantra: the seed-syllable of Māyā together with Vyoman, along with the Bindu and the Nāda. (38–7)
The root of Ādiśakti is either the syllable *viyat* (the letter *ha*) with the bindu (*hṃ*), or it is declared to be the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) along with the pair of vowels (*au*). || 38-8 ||
The fourth and the eighth, as well as the twelfth vowel, the fourteenth vowel, and the sixteenth vowel. || 38-9 ||

Having joined together those known as the heart, head, crest, armor, eyes, and weapon, there is a specific distinction in the head-mantra (śiromantra), which is conjoined with the letter of the ocean (sa). 38-10.
Then the weapon-mantra (astra) should be with the visarga, devoid of the bindu and nāda;
it consists of the third vowel, the fifth, and the one at the end of the tenth.
And the twelve-finger space (dvādaśānta)—these five are the five Brahmans beginning with Sadyojāta.
Gaurīgāyatrī is thus declared: "We know her who is Gaṇāmbikā... (38-12).
Having uttered this, at its end one should say, "We meditate upon the Great Ascetic";
having spoken thus, at its conclusion, one should cause Gaurī to impel him.
The one known by the name Gaurī-gāyatrī consists of twenty-four syllables;
one [liṅga] is made of clay, one of stone, and the remainder is said to be made of metal.
In the case of an earthen [image], however, the consecration with water is not mentioned in that same way;
everything else is the same for all [materials] as it is prescribed according to one's capacity.

Having fashioned an image of that [deity] according to the previously mentioned procedure, the wise one should first perform the rites beginning with the consecration (pratiṣṭhā) and the offering of sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa).
Having arranged the gems as before and having had that reflected image made very smooth, one should then begin the ritual of opening the eyes.
The preceptor should begin with the two golden hammers and needles, using the Netra-mantra.
Having first drawn the line of the eyebrows, then the second line of the eyelashes,
one should draw a white circle, and after that, indeed, a black circle.
The wise artisan should fashion [the image] within the circle of light;
then, having dismissed the artisan, the preceptor should perform the subsequent rite.
The wise one should touch the ring finger and the middle finger—designated as the "Golden Claw"—at their tips with the Śakti mantra. (38–21)

Having sprinkled [the image] with honey and ghee in a bronze vessel using a golden [spoon] and *dūrvā* grass, while reciting the *Hṛdaya-mantra*, [one should offer] a milch cow together with her calf. (38.22)
The preceptor should show the cow while reciting the *gaur dhenuhavya* mantra;
having caused all the people, beginning with the Brahmins, to gaze upon it while reciting the *akṣa* mantra.
Then, having performed the purification of the image with pure waters, the wise one,
having adorned it with all ornaments, should perform a circumambulation of the village.
Thereafter, the consecration of the water should take place for three nights or for one night;
having constructed a square pavilion adorned with garlands of *darbha* grass. (38.25)
Having wrapped it with cloths, especially with flowers and *darbha* grass,
one should perform the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*) of the *śakti* there in pure water reaching up to the neck.
One should place the jars presided over by the guardians of the directions (dikpālas) all around in the water;
having constructed the consecration pavilion (pratiṣṭhāmaṇḍapa), it should be fully endowed with all ornaments.
It was provided with sixteen pillars, endowed with four gates,
furnished with four archways, and adorned with garlands of *darbha* grass.
In the middle of that, having constructed an altar (vedikā) with a width equal to one-third of it, one cubit in height, and resembling the surface of a mirror; || 38-29 ||
Having constructed a secondary platform (upavedī) with a height of one palm-tree (tāla),
one should likewise construct a bathing pavilion (snānamaṇḍapa) near its northern side.
In the center of that, one should construct a bathing altar with three, two, or even a single girdle;
and upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) above the altar, [one should spread] eight *droṇas* of *śāli* rice.
One should draw an eight-petaled lotus joined with sesame seeds and rice;
likewise, having specifically visualized the bed with the [elements] beginning with the egg-born (aṇḍaja).

In the absence of birds and other such [offerings], one who possesses the previously mentioned characteristics and is born of a noble lineage should consecrate the cloth with the five [mantras] according to the Śaiva tradition. (38–39)
Having bathed well according to the prescribed rules and being adorned with all ornaments,
one should take the image that has been kept in water and bathe it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Having placed [the image] upon the bathing altar and bathed it thoroughly according to the prescribed rite,
one should perform the ritual with water mixed with eight kinds of earth while reciting the mantra "Gaṇāmbike."

Then, the preceptor should perform the purification of the image as appropriate with ointments and other substances, and worship it with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, using the primary seed-syllable.

Then, having tied the protective amulet with a golden thread, the wise one, having offered oblations, should perform the placement upon the head with gold, *dūrvā* sprouts, and unbroken grains of rice. (38.37)
On the bed, the preceptor should cause the Śakti to lie down with her head facing east and her face upwards;
having covered her with cloths, he should [sprinkle] her with meritorious water.
On the sacrificial ground, within the altar, [he should place] auspicious, stainless, firm [liṅgas], provided with cloth and gold, along with threads, unbroken rice grains, and sprouts. (38–39)
One should place eight jars for the lords of the world-protectors in order, starting from the east, as well as covered pitchers provided with eight golden threads. (38–40)
Together with their water-pots and lids, wrapped in pairs of cloths and joined with the Śaktis beginning with Vāmā, he should install the eight [deities] while reciting the heart-mantra (hṛdaya).
The wise one, having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and so forth using the heart-mantra, [should prepare] the *vardhanī* vessels joined with threads and covered with pairs of cloths. (38–42)
Together with their water-pots and covers, they are presided over by the primordial Śakti as their presiding deity;
they are placed within golden lotuses and endowed with the nine gems.
Having established [the deity] from the seed-syllable within the presence of the image and its head,
and having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, unbroken rice, and other offerings, one should then commence the fire ritual.
Alternatively, one should duly fashion the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) in the shape of a womb, consisting of nine, five, three, or even just one fire-altar.
Having performed the sixteen rites as before, ending with the installation of the fire (agnyādhāna),
the knower of mantras should invoke that Śakti into the fire by means of the principal seed-syllable (bīja).
Having performed the fire-oblation as before with fuel-sticks and clarified butter according to his own mantra,
the knower of mantras should then perform the "touch-offering" (sparśāhuti) with the respective mantra for each.
At dawn, during an auspicious moment, one should thoroughly worship the preceptor, the image-guardians, and the astrologer, accompanied by all types of musical instruments.
Then, having offered the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with the primary seed-mantra,
one should raise up the image of the Śakti and place it upon the bathing altar.
Then, having raised the *vardhanī* vessel, the preceptor, facing north,
should place it upon the heart, the head, the navel, and the base of the image.
Having placed the Brahma-mantras and the limb-mantras, one should arrange all the *mātṛkā*s;
then, by means of the root mantra, one should unite the powers residing in the *vardhana-kumbha* with the image.
Having indeed consecrated him with that water by means of the primary seed-mantra (*bījamantra*),
and having established him with the waters from the jars of the powers (*śakti*) beginning with Vāmā using their respective mantras (38),
one should [perform] bathing, anointing, and so forth with water, specifically using their respective mantras.
One should offer water for the feet, water for sipping, and the arghya offering to the Goddess with the [mantras] beginning with the Heart;
having worshipped her with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, together with all ornaments,
one should cause milk-rice and sacrificial oblation to be offered there with the Heart mantra.
Thus it has been fully explained; I shall now state what is appropriate therein: having constructed a pavilion according to the rules, one should gradually fashion an altar in its center.
Adorned with all ornaments and decorated with canopies and banners,
one should prepare a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) in its center and worship the fire right there.
There, in the Mānuṣanāha [mandala], Umā and Rudra are in the western quarter;
having placed Umā on the left side, adorned with all ornaments. (38–57)
