The preceptor, meditating like Brahmā during the marriage ceremony and all other rites, should adorn Umā and Rudra with new garments, reciting the mantra "praśāntāya. (58)

In accordance with the previously described procedure, one should perform the rites beginning with the establishment of the sacred fires (agnyādhāna) and so forth; then, having invoked Viṣṇu at that very spot, one should likewise invoke the Goddess preceded by the offering of water.
One should cause the seed-syllable to be placed in the right hand of Rudra by means of the principal mantra;
having established Śmaśāna in the left hand, one should do so with the Gāyatrī mantra of Gaurī.

Having caused the foot of the Goddess to touch the stone by means of Rudra, the wise knower of mantras, having offered three oblations of parched grain with the Śiva-mantra, should place it there. (38–61)
Then one should offer everything endowed with power and abundant sacrificial oblations; this has been declared as the proper method. Now listen to the procedure for the simultaneous installation.
That which begins with the commencement and ends with the conclusion, encompassing all ritual actions together,
is renowned as "saha" (simultaneous), and it is the festival prescribed by the ritual injunctions.
In this very manner, it has been thus proclaimed: the hundred thousand [recitations] and likewise the Sāvitrīs;
the installation of the Śakti has been declared—now hear concerning the retinue.
Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter, the Chapter on the Ritual for the Installation of Power (Śakti-pratiṣṭhā-vidhi-paṭala).
Now follows the chapter on the ritual of the retinue.
Hereafter, I shall fully explain the sequence of the ritual for the retinue;
that which begins with the gatekeepers and ends with the pedestal is known as the retinue. (39-1)
First, one should worship the one stationed at the door; thereafter, the gatekeepers;
the bull indeed as the third; and Indra and the others as the fourth.
The fifth is the Bhadrapīṭha, likewise surrounded on the outside;
wherever there is a gateway, the teachers [should place it] with two door-panels.
In each respective case, one should specifically release [the breath] in these nine ways,
having indeed arranged the serpent and the bird above and below.
Uttara and Patākā stand on the left and right [sides];
one should place Vimala and Subāhu on the left and right [hands]. (39-5)
Having visualized Śrī and Sarasvatī above and below Skanda,
one should always place Vighneśa in the middle of him upon his own seat according to his name.
One should worship with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings using the very first letter of one's own name;
having performed this according to the rule, specifically at each door. (39–7)
The two door panels should be made of very firm heartwood and endowed with the proper auspicious marks;
if there is only one panel, it represents the void, whereas with two panels, it represents peace (śāntika).
Then, having bound the wooden pegs (daṇḍa) all around, he fixed the wooden spikes (pulaka),
including the half-moons (ardhacandra) and others, according to the method prescribed in the Śilpaśāstra.
One-eighth of the height shall be the thickness at the top and bottom respectively;
the width shall be one-fourth, and the thickness indeed from south to north.
For such is the characteristic of the door-panel; one should first worship those situated there.
The deities at the door have been described; now hear of the gatekeepers. (39–11)
At the inner gate of the enclosure, it is known as the Śakti-gate;
on the south is the Śakti who bestows knowledge, and on the north is the one who bestows dharma.
Mahākāla has one face and two hands; his waist is slender and he possesses full breasts. He is the color of saffron and likewise holds an axe as his weapon. (39.13)
Ananteśa and Paśupati are the two door-keepers on the south;
Ananta is red in color and is equipped with a garment and weapons.
Paśu is lotus-colored with the hue of a blue lotus, holding a spear in his hand and having fierce eyes;
the two guardians of the western gate are known as Daṇḍin and Muṇḍīśa. (39.15)
He has a staff, the bow of the Lord of the Gods as his weapon, and fierce fangs;
he holds a sword in his hand, is shaven-headed, and likewise wields a bhindipāla missile that possesses the luster of jasmine and the moon.
Vijaya and Bhṛṅgīśa are the guardians of the northern gate;
Bhraṃśa and Bhṛṅga are of variegated hue, holding small knives as weapons in their hands. (39–17)
Vijaya is made of indrakīla metal, holding a trident in his hand and inspiring terror;
all of them are endowed with three bends and have their feet slightly bent. || 39-18 ||
They have fierce fangs and well-rounded forms, and all hold instructional hand-gestures;
they are all endowed with four arms or two arms, and possess three eyes. (39-19)
Having two eyes and fierce fangs, with ploughs and sprouts in their hands, they were as auspicious as the height of the doorways, resplendent with crowns, armlets, and other ornaments. (39.20)
They are prescribed for the palace, the pavilion, and at every door;
they are situated on the walls of the great enclosure and on both sides of the gates and gate-towers.
One should especially cause large [structures] to be built in the four directions:
Saṃvartaka, Śriyāvarta, Kuṇḍodara, and Bṛhodara.
Having placed [the deity] with a lion's face, a horse's face, one foot, and facing downward, white in color, as well as others resembling a dark complexion. (39-23)
All [the deities] have two eyes and two arms, and likewise hold a trident and a sword as weapons;
two spirits (bhūtas) each are to be fashioned, proceeding clockwise starting from Vāsava.
Now he said: "If the seat of the retinue members is obstructed by an intermediate wall, one should seek their celestial palace (vimāna) in the second enclosure (hāraka). (39.25)
But on the right side, one should place the Mothers together with Vīra and Vighna.
Having installed Viṣṇu there, either seated or standing,
one should place Vighneśa in the southwest quarter and Subrahmaṇya in the west.
The preceptor should install Śrī in the northeast direction of Jyeṣṭhā;
he should place Durgā in the north, or alternatively, Brahmā.
Caṇḍeśa is in the northeastern quarter, Bhāskara in the eastern direction;
likewise, the location of the well is in the northeast, and the kitchen is in the southeast.
In the intermediate spaces not explicitly mentioned, according to one's particular preference, the place for the couch is described as being likewise accompanied by Pārvatī. (39–30)
The entire residence of the retinue, whether outside or inside, is declared to be the second enclosure; now hear concerning the third enclosure.
One should indeed place Indra and the other world-protectors in their respective locations in the eight directions;
the station for the Pitṛs is ordained between the positions of Śakra and Śaṅkara.
Between the directions of Nirṛti and Varuṇa is the host of Apsarases;
between the directions of Varuṇa and Vāyu, the twelve Ādityas are said to reside. (39–33)
One should especially place Bhāskara and Kṣetrapāla at Śaṅkara,
and one should install the two Aśvinīs between Cakra and Pāvaka.
One should establish the seven Rohiṇīs between the Āgneya and Dharma [squares]; the Pitṛ-sthāna (the station of the ancestors) is ordained between the Yāmya and Nairṛta [squares]. (39–40ab)
The station of the Pitṛs is ordained between Nirṛti and Varuṇa;
and between Nirṛti and Varuṇa is also the host of Apsarases. (39–36)
Between Varuṇa and Vāyu is the supreme station of the Munis;
between Vāyu and Soma, at the end, dwell the Vasus.
Indeed, between the north and the northeast are the eleven Rudras;
then, the wise one, having established the sacrificial pedestal (balipīṭha), [should do so] in the four directions.
One should arrange the two seats, the outer and the inner, at the eastern gate;
one should place all the bhūtas within, and the piśācas on the outer seat.
On the southern throne-seat is for the Yakṣas, while for the Rākṣasas it is on the west;
that [seat] is indeed inferior, and the wise one [should place them] either in front of it or within. (39–40)
The height of the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha) should be divided into five parts; four parts is said to be the best height, three parts the middling, and two parts the lowest.
The height of the door should be equal [to the height of the sanctum] for the best, while one-third of that is the middling.
Know that the lowest of the doors is equal in height and width. || 39-42 ||
Then, having divided the height into nineteen parts, the plinth (upāna) shall be one part,
and likewise the base (bhuja-gati) shall be four parts.
Having fashioned the *kumbha* with three parts, one should place a fillet (*paṭṭaka*) above it with one part;
one should make the neck (*kaṇṭha*) with three parts, and the upper fillet (*ūrdhvapaṭṭikā*) with one part.

The great fillet (*mahāpaṭṭikā*) is twenty parts; the height of the petals and the neck-base (*galoṣṭaka*) [is the same]; and the pericarp (*karṇikā*) is said to have an excellent height of one part. (39–45)
I shall describe the entrance and exit, with a width of sixteen parts;
the plinth (upāna) shall consist of all [sixteen] parts, and likewise the jagatī up to the fourteen parts.
One should know that the *kumuda* is twelve parts, the *paṭṭikā* likewise ten parts,
the width of the *kaṇṭha* eight parts, and the upper *paṭṭikā* ten parts.
The *mahāpaṭṭa* is twelve parts, and the *vedikā* is ten parts.
The width of the petals is one-eighth [of the total], while the pericarp is three parts.
One should make a square pedestal without lotus petals;
then, at the conclusion of the installation, one should worship these [deities] with special care. (39–49)
The supreme guide should perform [the rite] according to the procedure for consecration (*pratiṣṭhāvidhi*);
know that it is thus excellent and bestows all accomplishments (*sarvasiddhi*). (39–50)
The Guru should fashion the circles from the gates up to the seat of the Bhūtas in due order;
however, he should fashion the *harmya* and *aṇu* sections from the [sections] of Sūrya, Arka, and Vāruṇeya.
In the southeast, a pavilion for the students and others should be constructed;
in the southwest direction, a pavilion for hearing the Dharma should be built. (39–52)
The place renowned for all songs, especially those of Vāyu, is in the northwest; the pavilion for sacrifices, festivals, and the like is prescribed in the northeast.
Listen: it is renowned that within the middle enclosure (madhyahārā), against the boundary wall, the location for grain storage is declared to be between Gopura and Īśāna. (39–54)
One situated between the south and the southeast should construct the birth-chamber;
one should construct the armory pavilion between the south and the southwest.
One should construct the assembly pavilion (āsthānamaṇḍapa) between Varuṇa and Nairṛta;
however, the pavilion for the dance of Vyāsa should be situated between Pāśabhṛt and Vāyu. (39–56)
Between Kubera and Anila, a pavilion for the accumulation of wealth should be constructed;
between Īśāna and Soma, a pavilion for flowers (puṣpamaṇḍapa) should be made.
It is well known that [this applies] to those with walls such as the *maryādā*; now listen regarding those with the *mahāmaryādā*.
One should construct gate-towers (*gopura*) at the great gates in the four directions.
In all the intermediate spaces, he proceeded in due order by circumambulating clockwise,
[reciting] the Ṛg, Yajur, Sāma, and Atharva Vedas, as well as Chandas and Jyotiṣa.
Then [he studied] the Śikṣā, Kalpa, and Nirukta, as well as Vyākaraṇa, the Śaivasiddhānta scripture, and likewise the Pāśupata. (39–60)
Indeed, there are commentaries and practices concerning the Soma-siddhānta-tantra, as well as those of the Buddhist and Arhat [Jaina] systems, and the tantra known as Pāñcarātra. (39–61)
For the purpose of feeding the Brahmins and indeed for the feeding of the Liṅgas,
one should arrange the installation of both the Ādiśaivas and the Anuśaivas.
The arrangement of the enclosures and walls has been proclaimed;
hereafter, listen specifically to the installation of the bull (vṛṣabha). || 39-63 ||
Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter, the Chapter on the Ritual of the Retinue. 39.
Now follows the chapter on the ritual for the installation of the Bull (Vṛṣabha).
Hereafter, I shall fully explain the supreme installation of the Bull;
in the teaching of Śiva, it is distinguished [as occurring] within the inner enclosure (antarāvaraṇa) of the deities.
The gods abide within them; therefore, they remain as the retinue.
Then, the forms of the Bull [Nandin] are divided into a thousand parts.
Three kinds of pedestals have been declared: made of stone, metal, or plaster.
A pedestal made of metal should be used for a standing image, and especially for a reclining one. (40.3)
O wise one, a stone image of the Daughter of the Mountain (Pārvatī) should be fashioned for the bed;
therein, three types [of images] should be made, which bring about all prosperity for men.
O Vighneśa, if it is made of iron, it is said to be the best;
that of stone is declared to be middling, and that of lime would be the lowest.
Now hear concerning the height of the bull according to the measurement of the door.
The height of the door should be one-fourth [of the width], or likewise half, or less by one-quarter.
At that time, the length of the bull's stride is traditionally held to be seventy-two finger-breadths, whether it be equal, double, or especially triple [the standard measure]. (40-7)
There, the face shall be four parts, the nose likewise three parts,
the eye two finger-breadths, and the mantra shall have a width of one foot.
The length of the prong should be two parts, its base one part in width;
both tips should be made sharp, tapering gradually in regular succession.
The length of the ear is ten finger-breadths, its width is half of that;
the root of the ear is one kalā, and its tip is likewise the same.
The space between the two eyes is three parts; likewise, the two horns are of medium size.
The distance from the eye to the end of the ear is one part, and the distance from the ear to the end of the horn is likewise one part.

At the opening of the nose, it should be two finger-breadths wide; that curve should be made according to the measurement of its parts, and the tongue and the rows of teeth should be fashioned according to the proper method.
The thigh is eighteen finger-breadths in length, and its circumference is likewise three times that; the shank should be known as ten finger-breadths, and above that, four kalās.
From that point, the foot (pāda) shall be six aṅgulas, and the hoof (khura) is said to be half of that.

The hind part of the leg (jaṅghā-paścima-pāda) shall be one kalā higher than the top of the [fore]leg, with an additional kalā. The tail (puccha), from its tip to its base, shall be four aṅgulas in width.
The middle [part] is known to have an interval of two finger-breadths, and the tip one finger-breadth.
The two testicles should be two kalās in length and two aṅgulas in width;
thus the characteristics of the bull (vṛṣa) have been declared. Now listen indeed to its installation. || 40-16 ||
One should not perform the ritual immersion in water (*jalādhivāsa*) or the laying down on a bed (*śayana*) for an image made of metal, nor for one made of stone or plaster. (40.17)
He released the eye from the eye upon the bed;
then the eight jars of the world-protectors and the lords of the guardians of the quarters [were established].
In the center of that [space] is a bull and a jar, surrounded by cows;
it is endowed with the sound of the ringing of many bells, white in color, and of great splendor.
Or nine, five, or three, or again, a single fire.
Having prepared the Śiva-fire as before, he should invoke the Bull (Vṛṣabha) into its center;
then, having offered one hundred oblations there with the previously mentioned root-mantra, [he should proceed].
One should touch the heart and other limbs with the Śiva-mantras using the limbs of Śiva;
then, at the clear dawn, one should offer the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) there with the Astra-mantra.
The preceptor should perform the consecration with the water-pots using his own name-mantra, and with the middle jar using the Vṛṣagāyatrī mantra. (40.23)
Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, one should then cause mung-bean rice to be offered;
thereafter, having performed the bull-sacrifice (vṛṣayāga) for nine, seven, or five days.
Then, for three days or even a single day, one should perform the festival as enjoined by the rules;
first, one should perform the circumambulation of the bull, and the other rites should be performed similarly.
This is known as the Vṛṣayāga; now hear the installation of the Fire.
Thus ends the fortieth chapter, the section on the ritual procedure for the installation of the Bull.
Now begins the chapter on the ritual for the installation of the fire.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the installation of the fire; listen. When the surrounding area and the southeast chamber have been prepared as previously described: || 41-1 ||
There, the image (bera) should be fashioned according to the measurements previously mentioned;
or else, the pedestal (pīṭhaka) should be one cubit or even half a cubit in measure.
The pedestal should have three tiers, or it may be a lotus-pedestal;
whether the image is placed upon such a pedestal or is otherwise installed, one should perform the consecration (pratiṣṭhā) correctly.
That which is desired as the first seed-syllable (bīja) is endowed with the letter 'na', the vowel 'ā', and the letter 'dya';
the second shall be endowed with the letter 'ra', the eleventh [vowel], and the fire [letter 'ra']—41.4.
The third seed-syllable of Fire (Ra) is joined with the vowel at the end of the twelve;
the fourth [seed-syllable] of the Śikhās is that which is at the end of the twelve, conjoined with a vowel. (41–5)

Having extracted the seed-syllable ending with *jīva* (the letter *sa*) and joined it with the fire of time (*kālavahni*, the letter *ra*), one should then place the body of fire (*vahneḥ piṇḍa*, the letter *ha*) after that, along with *nīla* (*na*) and *māyā* (*ī*). 41–6.
All [the deities] are adorned with crowns and bestow the fruits of enjoyment and liberation;
here I shall describe the form of Vahni (Fire), which is red in color and four-armed.
With hands granting boons and fearlessness... [the deity] should have a spear in the other left hand, while holding a rosary in the right. || 41-8 ||
One-faced and three-eyed, with a red sheath rising upward, it is declared to have the form of fire; one should thus place it in the *dhāman*. (41.9)

In the sacrifice and within the fire, having touched [the offerings] according to their previously described essential forms, the wise one should perform the oblation with the five seed-syllables and the five *piṇḍas*.
In the beautiful central pavilion of the Dhāmāgra, provided with an altar,
one should duly arrange the five fires according to the sequence previously described.
One should perform [the rite] either in the three sacred fires (tretāgni) or, alternatively, in a single fire;
having arranged the placement of metals and gems, one should perform the opening of the eyes.
One should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa) of the image in water, especially in the case of one made of stone;
then, having performed the opening of the eyes and other rites outside, one should proceed to the temple.
Prior to the auspicious moment for the consecration, one should place the pedestal, gems, and other items;
likewise, nine flawless jars along with the *vardhanī* vessel and the ritual threads.
Having filled the vessels along with their wicks with fragrant substances,
they were adorned with canopies and silk bands, and endowed with gold and jewels.
Having drawn a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) upon the altar (vedī), provided with a lotus,
one should place the seat called "Principal" (pradhāna) within the pericarp (karṇikā).
Having placed the *vardhanī* vessel to his left,
and eight jars in the surrounding directions, one should install the deities Vidyeśa, Umā, and Agni.
Then, one should place the goddess Svāhā in the Vardhanī vessel, Śiva in the eastern position,
Bhāskara in the left pitcher, and the world-protectors (lokeśas) in their respective directions.
Having arranged [the deities] and worshipped them with perfumes and other offerings to the south of the jars,
and having likewise prepared a seat as before, one should cause the image to rest comfortably upon it.
Having commenced with worship and meditation, one should then perform the fire-oblation (homa);
the wise practitioner, having prepared the Śiva-fire as before in all the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas).
Having visualized the form of Agni, one should perform oblations with fuel-sticks,
clarified butter, parched grain, sesame, and the five seeds, one hundred times for each.
At dawn, during an auspicious moment, one should remove the image from its bed;
having worshipped it with perfumes and other offerings, one should perform a circumambulation of the temple.
On the bathing altar, one should not use metal; however, if it is stone, it should be placed within the sanctum, or upon a pedestal after the installation of the gems. || 41.23 ||
One should place the fifth seed-syllable in the heart, and the remaining seed-syllables in the head, the face, the navel, and the secret organ, respectively. (41.24)
Having worshipped with perfumes and other offerings, one should display the lotus mudrā;
then the knower of mantras should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) by means of the seed-syllables and the piṇḍa-mantra.

Then, having carefully lifted the jars, one should [place] the central jar with the five seed-syllables and the image with the *piṇḍa* according to the previously mentioned method of ritual placement (*nyāsa*).
One should bathe [the deity] with the seed-syllables (bīja) and the clusters (piṇḍaka) from those two jars, the Kumbha and the Vardhanī;
one should bathe [him] with the very waters contained in that Kumbha jar, using their respective mantras.
Having performed the sacrifice with substances such as incense and other offerings, one should present the great oblation;
there, one should honor the preceptor with garments, gold, and rings.
The installation of the fire has been declared; now hear the installation of the Mothers.
Thus ends the forty-first chapter, the section on the procedure for the installation of the fire. 41.
Now begins the chapter on the ritual for the installation of the Mothers (Mātṛsthāpanavidhipaṭala).
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the supreme installation of the Mothers, who were created by Brahmā for the purpose of slaying Nairṛta. (42.1)
One should represent Brahmāṇī like Brahmā, Maheśī like Īśvara, Cakrī like Kumāra, and Vaiṣṇavī likewise like Viṣṇu. (42-2)
One should fashion Vārāhī with a wrathful face, Vāminī holding a plough, Cakrāṇī like a discus, and Cāmuṇḍī of fierce form. (42–3)
Then one should have an image of Cāmuṇḍī made, with her mass of matted hair well-spread, dark-complexioned, four-armed, and holding a skull-cup and a trident in her hands. 42-4.
With hands granting boons and fearlessness, bearing their respective weapons, endowed with their respective colors, and equipped with their respective vehicles and banners. (42–5)
All of them have four arms and are seated upon lotuses;
Vīrabhadra is in the east, while Vighneśa is in the western direction.
(206) Having fashioned an image of Vīreśa and likewise of Vighneśa, seated in the vīrāsana posture, out of clay, wood, stone, or metal, the wise man [should proceed]. (42.7)

Then, having performed the deposition of the jewels, one should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) in water; afterwards, there is the opening of the eyes, or the preliminary consecration on the bed.
Having performed the rite in the fire of the crest according to the rules and having meditated, one should perform the oblation (homa);
then, at an auspicious moment, one should establish [the deity] with mantras beginning with "O you of good name" and so forth.
Having offered the oblation to the Mothers with the Mātṛ-gāyatrī mantra,
one should perform the sacrifice to the Mothers according to the sequence prescribed in the Yamala.
The installation of the Mothers has been declared; now hear the installation of Vighneśa.
Thus ends the forty-second chapter, the section on the procedure for the installation of the Mothers.
Now begins the chapter on the ritual for the installation of Vighneśa.
Hereafter, I shall fully describe the supreme installation of Vighneśa.
At first, however, I [dwelt] with Umā in the forest of Himavat for the sake of sport.
Then the female elephant had union with the lordly elephant;
having seen that by chance, I then assumed that form. (43-2)
At that time, when Umā had assumed the form of a miserable female elephant, I sported with her intensely;
she conceived a child within herself at that moment, which was the fruit of her ascetic penance.
From a thousandth part of Maheśvara, each respective form [is derived] as a tenth part;
it shines with nineteen syllables and is joined with fire (the letter Ra). 43–4.
This root mantra of the great-souled Vighneśa is known to consist of thirteen syllables, ending with the *manu* (the letter *m*) and accompanied by the *bindu* and *nāda*. (43–5)
The second [syllable] is joined with the third [syllable] and accompanied by a single-mora vowel; it is renowned as "brahmajajñān," consisting of six limbs and conjoined with lamps. 43–6.
At the end of each limb, the letter *sa* with the *visarga* is used here; the remainder, however, is joined with a vowel.
Having uttered "vidmahe" for [the mantra] "ākhudhvajāya," the preceptor then [proceeds] accordingly.
We meditate upon the one with the tusk in his hand; may that tusk inspire us.
In his right hand he holds a fruit, and in his left hand his own tusk. (43.8)
In her upper hands she holds a noose and a goad, and in her elephant-hand (trunk) she holds a sweetmeat ball;
she is said to wear a basket-shaped crown and is adorned with all ornaments. (43–9)
Having formed the radiance of the wheel on his head, he stands upon a lotus pedestal,
resembling a pomegranate flower and adorned with all ornaments.
One should have an image of Vighnanāyaka made, either seated or standing,
according to the measurement of five tālas as prescribed by this standard.
Having divided that measurement into nine parts, the measurement of the mouth is two parts;
the penis-stalk is four parts, which is known as the ulūka-taṭa.
The wise [artist] should then make the portion from the knee to the end of the shank one part,
and the foot and the ankle likewise one part each.
The length of the forearm (vāgvāya) should be two parts, extending as far as the wrist;
its forepart (prakoṣṭaka) is one tāla less than the total length of the hand.
The length of the elephant's trunk is said to be half a *hasta*;
its height at the tip of the ear is one part, while that which is well-remembered as being three-quarters of that [length] is [the circumference]. (43-15)
The length of the tusk is said here to be measured from the tip of the ear;
all of that is nine finger-breadths according to the previously mentioned measurement.
Thus has it been told and proclaimed; now listen indeed to the installation.
Having first constructed the temple as previously described, the wise man [should proceed]. (43.17)
One should construct a square pavilion in front of the temple;
in its center, there should be an altar endowed with all auspicious characteristics.
One-third of the width shall indeed be the measure of the altar's breadth;
the height [of the pits] all around, in due order, shall be knee-deep. (43.19)
Then, having performed the placement of the jewels, one should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) in the water;
one should release the eyes with the eye-mantra according to the prescribed rule.
Having spread out a bed with cloths, one should lay [the image] upon the bed;
it should be endowed with all auspicious marks and encircled by a thread.
He should place the water-filled jar, provided with a beard [of grass], a lid, cloth, and gold; he should worship it with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
Having meditated upon that form, joined limb with limb by means of the root mantra, and having projected it into the water-pot, one should display the sleep mudrā. (43.23)
One should place eight covered jars for the world-protectors and others in their respective order;
thereafter, the fire-oblation (homa) should be performed nine, five, three, or one times.

Fuel-sticks, clarified butter, sacrificial porridge, parched grain, along with a ritual grass-bundle (kūrca) and mustard seeds; likewise, sweetmeat balls, molasses, sugar-candy, fruit, and milk. (43.25)
Having meditated upon the Śivāgni as before, one should offer all the ritual substances into the fire in the center of Gaṇeśa with the Vighnagāyatrī mantra.
Then, having performed the *sparśāhuti* with that very mantra,
the preceptor should then offer the *pūrṇāhuti* while reciting the root mantra.
One should install the reality residing in the water-pot into the image;
having bathed Vighneśa with water-pots, together with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings. (43.28)
One should offer rice mixed with jaggery as an oblation, accompanied by fruit;
the festival and its ritual procedures should be performed according to one's wealth. (43.29)
That indeed has been declared as the installation [of Gaṇeśa]; now hear the installation of Skanda.
Thus ends the forty-third chapter, the section on the procedure for the installation of Gaṇeśa.
Now begins the chapter on the ritual for the installation of Skanda.
Hereafter, I shall fully explain the supreme installation of Skanda;
first, O Gajānana, hear briefly of his origin.
Having witnessed the father’s abandonment of the body, I practiced his yoga; then, having returned once more to the body of Satī, I likewise became the daughter of Himavat.
Having performed penance on the side of the mountain, his daughter shall become Pārvatī;
for it was there that our union was requested by the gods. (44-3)
Having collected his semen and cast it into a thicket of reeds (śara),
that place is therefore celebrated by the name Śaravaṇabhāva.
The installation during the six *kṛttikās* is called the "Six-faced" (*Ṣaṇmukha*). By that very [rite], one who performs it in the month of Kārttika shall indeed become free from children. (44–5)

The arising of Kumāra from a thousandth part of Ādiśakti has thus been described; it was indeed proclaimed in the past as being born from the entirety [of her power]. Now, hear about his installation.
Having constructed the temple according to the prescribed rules, one should thereafter fashion the image from stone,
clay, wood, or metal, measuring it at nine tālas.
He may have two arms, four arms, or even eight arms;
or he may have two arms with a lotus in his hand, while others hold a vajra and a śakti.
The one with four arms in the east is known as Abhayavarada;
above him are the sword and shield, the noose, and likewise the eight lotuses.
The posture may be either seated or standing, and likewise the vehicle is of three kinds;
the seated posture is said to have two arms, while the standing posture shall have four arms. (44–10)
One should fashion the vehicle upon the eight-armed [deity] and install the retinue;
[one should fashion] Skanda mounted upon a lotus and an elephant, endowed with the sacred thread.
Resembling the flower of the pomegranate tree, adorned with all ornaments, and endowed with all auspicious marks, according to the previously mentioned procedure. || 44-12 ||
Vidyā and Medhā are likewise joined together, appearing white and dark respectively;
they are adorned with all ornaments, possess two arms, and hold lotuses.
Listen now to the true nature of that remedy and its foundation:
in front of the temple, within a well-decorated pavilion.

The depositing of the jewels should be performed in water, but the consecration (adhivāsana) is not required; likewise, the opening of the eyes and the laying on the bed should be performed as the consecration.
Having placed the pitcher right there, and having again consecrated the uncovered jars as before, one should place the pitchers starting from the root in the middle of the [deity's] shoulders.

The mantra-practitioner should place the World-Protectors (Lokeśas) all around according to their respective seed-syllables; there, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) as before, consisting of nine, five, three, or one [oblations].
If there are nine fires, the guardians of the directions (dikpālas) and Skanda are known as the presiding deities of the oblation (homādhipas).
Śakti, Antaka, Jala, Soma, and Skanda are the presiding deities of the five fire-forms (pañcāgnimūrtis).

The three sacred fires (tretāgni) and Skanda, the presiding deity of the oblation, [are worshipped] with the root-mantra, the six limbs of the Brahman, and the Gāyatrī that turns back the cow. (44.19)
Having offered the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) according to the sequence starting from the root mantra,
one should then perform the touch-oblation (sparśāhuti) with the Skanda-gāyatrī mantra.
Having established [the deity] with the root-mantra of Skanda, the best of installers—
the wise one— should perform the placement on the head and in the heart, beginning with the fifth [face] and ending with Sadyojāta.
There, one should perform the festive bathing and offer sacrificial oblations;
then, the preceptor, having duly honored the guardians of the images, [should proceed].
The installation of Skanda has been declared; now hear the installation of Jyeṣṭhā.
Thus ends the forty-fourth chapter, the section on the ritual procedure for the installation of Skanda.
Now begins the chapter on the ritual for the installation of Jyeṣṭhā.
Hereafter, I shall fully explain the supreme installation of Jyeṣṭhā,
who was first born from Ādiśakti and subsequently emerged from the ocean.
While the ocean was being churned, O Gajānana, that goddess arose, resembling black collyrium and adorned with all ornaments. (45-2)
The wife is established in the heart, the daughter is the destroyer of happiness, and the son is the body;
the two sides of the knees are the jewel, or else the face of the bull, and likewise the bull itself. (45-3)
The bull should be red in color, possessing the luster of jewels and gold;
having fashioned these forms, one should duly perform the consecration.
Then, having performed the placement of jewels (ratnanyāsa) within the water,
one should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) for the bedding after performing the dismissal (kṣimocana).
Having placed the water-pots right here, one should thereafter perform the fire-oblation as before;
having established the Śiva-fire there, one should invoke Jyeṣṭhā into the fire.
On the day of Jyeṣṭhā, one should offer all the ritual substances into the fire with the root mantra;
having established [the deity] at an auspicious moment, one should then cause sacrificial food (haviṣya) to be given. (45–7)
The installation of Jyeṣṭhā has been declared; now hear the installation of Durgā.
Thus ends the forty-fifth chapter, the section on the ritual for the installation of Jyeṣṭhā.
Now begins the chapter on the ritual procedure for the installation of Durgā.
Hereafter, I shall fully describe the supreme installation of Durgā,
who is born from the Primordial Power (Ādiśakti), the auspicious younger sister of Viṣṇu’s vital breath.
The Goddess bears the conch and the discus, holds a bow and an arrow,
is equipped with a sword and a shield, and is endowed with a trident and a noose.
Or one may depict her with four arms, adorned with all ornaments, having a dark complexion and a beautiful face, standing upon the head of a buffalo. (46.3)
Or one may depict her mounted upon a lion, seated in the lotus posture; having constructed a water-shed (prapā) endowed with all auspicious characteristics in front of the temple.

One should deposit the jewels right there and cause them to be perfumed in that very water; having performed the mantra-protection and the opening of the eyes, the wise one should apply the *pratisara* cord.
One should cause the bed of intention (saṃkalpa) and the other elements to lie down with their respective mantras;
having deposited them with the jar-mantras and having meditated upon that form within oneself.

Having placed the covered jars, one should install the world-protectors (lokapālas) and perform a fire sacrifice (homa) using five, three, or one [oblation], combined with the materials previously mentioned.
Having summoned the Goddess into the midst of the fire, the wise one [should offer] clarified butter and other substances:
clarified butter, sacrificial porridge (caru), parched grain (lāja), and fuel-sticks of the udumbara tree. (46–8)
The supreme preceptor should perform the fire oblation with the root mantra of Durgā;
then, having raised the Goddess from her bed, he should place her upon the bathing altar.
Having likewise [consecrated] the seed-syllable with the status of a *kumbhāṇḍa*, one should join it with the root mantra;
thereafter, having bathed [the deity] with water-pots, one should likewise offer abundant sacrificial oblations. (46.10)
The installation of Durgā has been described; now hear the installation of Caṇḍeśa.
Thus ends the forty-sixth chapter, the section on the ritual procedure for the installation of Durgā.
Now follows the chapter on the ritual procedure for the installation of Caṇḍeśa.
Hereafter, I shall fully explain the supreme installation of Caṇḍeśa;
first is its origin, and second is the installation in due order.
All that portion of Rudra known by the name Caṇḍa, remaining within the Gaṇeśa enclosure, is indeed endowed with ten million [attendants]. || 47-2 ||
The fivefold form emerged according to the ritual injunction from Pracaṇḍa and the others:
first Pracaṇḍacaṇḍa, then Vikrāntacaṇḍaga.
The third is Bhuva-caṇḍa, and Vīra-caṇḍa is the fourth;
thus indeed are the five Caṇḍeśas, born from the five Brahmans.
This Pracaṇḍa is said to be the sovereign of the Kṛtayuga;
however, the one named Vikrāntacaṇḍa is remembered as the lord of the Tretāyuga. (47–5)
In the Dvāpara age, the Lord is indeed called Vibhu Caṇḍeśa;
but in the Kali age, Vīracaṇḍeśa is proclaimed as his own sovereign lord.
Thus, indeed, the procedure for the one named Caṇḍa is prescribed in five divisions;
in the northeastern quarter of the Ālaya, there is a celestial palace (vimāna) according to the sequence as before.
He may have three eyes or four arms, or indeed two eyes and two arms;
he is adorned with a matted lock of hair and decorated with all ornaments.

If one wishes to represent him with two arms, he should likewise hold the gesture of fearlessness (abhaya), a peaceful body, a noose, and an axe, and be endowed with the sound of the *ṭaṅka* weapon. || 47-9 ||
Then, according to the previously mentioned procedure, the white sacrificial thread, as well as white garments, the bathing, and the seat are prescribed. (47-10)
(213) Just as in the case of stabilizing the movement, one should perform everything according to the logic of the purpose;
that which is the first letter of one's own name is its root mantra. (47.11)
One should designate its short and long vowels as the limbs of Brahmā;
however, for the worship of Śiva, one should employ the ten-syllable mantra derived from that very root-seed.
The installation of Caṇḍeśa has been declared; now hear the installation of Indra and the others.
Thus ends the forty-seventh chapter, the section on the procedure for the installation of Caṇḍeśa.
Now begins the chapter on the procedure for the installation of the wheels and other [emblems].
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the supreme installation of the wheels and so forth.
The wise one [should place] Indra in the eastern quarter; Indra is [established] from the thunderbolt and the goad.
Having visualized Śyāmāṅga mounted upon an elephant and accompanied by hosts of Apsarases,
one should likewise visualize Agni mounted upon a goat, red in appearance with red eyes.
With upward-pointing crests of hair, he holds the stream of the power of reasoning;
Yama, however, has a formidable staff in his hand and is seated upon a buffalo throne. (48.3)
Terrible and black in color, with fruits and sprouts in his hands, he is joined with a sword and a shield; Nṛti is dark blue in color.
Terrible, with a deformed appearance, mounted upon a lion, possessing two eyes, Varuṇa has a noose in his hand and possesses a luster equal to the color white. (48–5)
With one hand granting boons, adorned with all ornaments,
smoke-colored like a smokeless fire, and mounted upon a deer— this is the banner of Yama.
One should visualize oneself according to the prescribed rite as dark-complexioned and holding a goad in the right hand;
and [one should likewise visualize] Takṣakeśa, who has a mace in his hand, is dark-hued, and inspires fear.
[One should meditate on] Īśāna as having two arms, adorned with red garments, with red eyes, and holding a lotus in his hand;
[and Īśāna] as having four arms, three eyes, and wearing matted hair. (48–8)
Having visualized the trident-bearing god mounted upon a bull, with hands granting boons and fearlessness,
and having likewise visualized the lute-bearing god as well as Brahmā and Viṣṇu as before.
Āryamā, Indra, Varuṇa, Pūṣan, Viṣṇu, and Bhaga, as well as Ajaghnya, Jaghanya, Mitra, and Dhātṛ—these are remembered [as the Ādityas]. (48.10)
Vivasvān and the others, including Parjanya, are known as the twelve Ādityas;
they have two arms, hold lotuses in their hands, and are seated upon red lotus-thrones. || 48-11 ||
Endowed with a circle of rays, these leaders of the world are deep red;
Nāsatya and Dasra—these two are celebrated as the Aśvins. (48-12)
Wearing white garments and turbans, with books and the gesture of fearlessness in their hands,
they possess upper robes and their own natural forms, resembling white gold.
Kumbhinī, Granthinī, Kūrcakuṭṭinī, Vikāriṇī, Rudrāṇī, and Vikārī are proclaimed as the seven [attendants] of Rohiṇī. (48.14)
Adorned with serpent ornaments and graced by the weight of their hair,
they have the forms of serpents, yet grant boons and fearlessness with their hands.
The father, the grandfather, and the great-grandfather—listen now to the characteristics of those ancestors as they are being praised. (48.16)
The three ancestors are described as being very firm, with yellow ears, holding parasol-staffs, and clothed in white garments. (48.17)
Rambhā, Vipulā, Urvaśī, and Tilottamā were endowed with slender waists and possessed full thighs, hips, and breasts. (48.18)
Bhṛgu, Vasiṣṭha, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kṛtu, Kāśyapa, Kauśika, and Āṅgiras—these are the sages. (48-19)
Adorned with beautiful bark-garments and matted locks, possessing handsome faces, fangs, and hands, their forms graced by ornaments at the waist, they were auspicious and clad in white garments.
Piṅgalā, Caṣa, Netrā, and the others are proclaimed as his seven wives;
likewise Dharodhṛva, Soma, Sāvitra, Anila, and Anala. (48.21)
Pratyuṣa and Prabhāva, possessing formidable forms with excellent tusks, held swords and shields in their hands, with knitted brows and beautiful eyes. (48.22)
Adorned with all ornaments and likewise wearing variegated garments, they are said here to be clothed in red garments; indeed, such is their attire.
Gīriśātoga, Girīśa, Keśanāśa, likewise Bhūtakāsa, Tadeka, Buddhi, and Bhavana. (48.24)
Kapālīśa, Aja, and Buddhyacchadramauli are proclaimed [as the lords];
their bodies are smeared with ashes, and they likewise hold tridents and nooses. (48.25)
Or, in the thirty-three-fold division, it is joined with the Lokapālas; hear now the installation of all of them, together with their prescribed colors and names. (48.26)
Just as in the case of establishing movement, everything is to be performed individually and specifically;
or else, the installation is prescribed by another method. (48.27)
For them, indeed, the rites for the pavilions and so forth should be performed together;
likewise, there should be a separate water-pot for each, and especially a separate fire for each.
One should have [the images] fashioned with their respective mantras and install them individually.
The installation of Indra and the others has been declared; now listen to the installation of Āditya. (48–29)
Thus ends the forty-eighth chapter, the section on the ritual procedure for the installation of the wheels and other [mandalas]. || 48 ||
Now begins the chapter on the ritual for the installation of Āditya.
Hereafter, I shall fully explain the supreme installation of Āditya;
he is called Āditya because he possesses the nature of being a son of Aditi. (49-1)
In the half-portion of Īśvara, he is remembered as the Eye of the World;
having described him as two-armed and gentle (saumya), one should therefore worship that gentle one. 49-2.
One should seek all accomplishments, especially in the midst of a village; however, for the sake of worldly prosperity, the preceptor [should establish it] in a residence on the left side. (49.3)

Having constructed the temple according to the prescribed rite, one should place images in the four directions, endowed with the splendor of twelve eyes (the sun) and accompanied by horses and elephants.
Red, white, yellow, and dark blue, with colors such as those of the sun and other luminaries,
it is endowed with artistic ornaments and possesses the characteristics of a temple.
The door facing the village should be at the western side of the temple;
then, having fashioned an image out of wood, metal, or stone, one should proceed.
Two-armed, with a lotus in his hand, red in color, and possessing his natural form;
he is endowed with a basket-shaped crown and adorned with all ornaments. (49.7)
The halo in the center is twice the width of the crown;
the goddesses Uṣā and Pratyuṣā are stationed on the right and left sides respectively.
Placing a lotus of that same nature before him,
one should meditate upon Bhāskara, the destroyer of sins, seated in the midst of his chariot drawn by seven horses.
One should indeed arrange the seat there, situated upon a red lotus throne;
one should visualize everything as the Sun according to the previously mentioned procedure. (49-10)

If one should fashion an image for a rite dedicated to the gods out of clay, it should likewise be made by a skilled artisan using materials such as wood, rope, or earth, with the appropriate distinctions of color.

Having established the ritual action in the middle, now listen briefly to the procedure for the installation of [an image] made of stone or metal, as well as that of gems and so forth, up until the final consecration. (49-12)

Having constructed a pavilion according to the prescribed ritual in front of the Ālaya, one should fashion an altar in its center with a width equal to one-third [of the pavilion's dimensions]. (49-13)
Having constructed fire-pits around [the central area], measuring one cubit in size and resembling the surface of a mirror, using either clay or sand. (49–14)
Having prepared a leveled altar with śāli rice, the preceptor should deposit the jewels;
however, if even jewels are unavailable, he should instead place pearls there.
Having provided an upper covering with *darbha* grass and cloths on all sides,
and having wrapped it with a cloth, the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*) should take place in the water.
Having brought the image and kept it in water, and having bathed it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya),
one should now release the eye [of the image] by means of a golden needle through the eye-opening.
Having tied the protective amulet (pratisara), the master of mantras should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) upon the bed;
having made an upper covering with darbha grass and cloths on all sides.
In the direction of the head of the bed, one should wrap a water-pot with cloth;
one should worship the pots, together with their brushes and lids, according to the ritual procedure using perfumes and other offerings.
Having meditated upon each of their respective forms,
[one should place] the eight jars, presided over by the world-protectors (lokapālas), in their proper order.
Having placed [the items] separately with a cloth, a tuft of grass, a cover, and so forth, the fire-oblation (homa) should then be performed nine, five, or three times. (49.21)
Having meditated upon the Śiva-fire as before and having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) with the first [mantra] in the central [fire],
one should offer sacrificial fuel (samidh), clarified butter (ājya), cooked rice (caru), parched grain (lāja), groats (saktu), and mustard seeds (sarṣapa).
The preceptor should offer all the substances into the fire with the Sūryagāyatrī mantra; then, having performed the sparśāhuti, he should do so with its root mantra.
At dawn, during an auspicious moment, having offered the full oblation with his own mantra,
he should worship the preceptor there with garments, gold, and rings.
Having raised the image from its bed, one should then lead it to the bathing altar;
having performed the offering of clarified butter to the head, one should lead the water-pot into its presence.
One should place the deity who resides in the pitcher into the heart of the image;
having thus established him, one should worship with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings using the very pitchers.
Having offered abundant sacrificial oblations with the root mantra, the preceptor should commence the festival there according to the means available to the patron. (49.27)
In the ritual procedure for that festival, everything prescribed in the Āgama scriptures has been stated;
the installation of Āditya has been explained—now hear the rite for Kṣetrapāla.
Thus ends the forty-ninth chapter, the section on the ritual procedure for the installation of the Sun-god. 49.
Now follows the chapter on the ritual for the installation of the Lord of the Field (Kṣetrapati).
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the sequence of the ritual for the Lord of the Field;
likewise, the origin of the Kṣetrapāla is from a ten-thousandth part of Īśvara.
In the northeast direction from the village, for the purpose of protecting the world,
one should likewise construct a temple and an image there according to the previously mentioned procedure.
The western door is the principal one; the southern is remembered as the middle;
and the eastern door is the inferior. Thereafter follows the description of the images.
He has four arms or three eyes, or six arms and eight hands;
he possesses fine tusks, has a terrifying form, is black in color, and is naked. (50.4)
He wears a sacrificial thread made of serpents, a garland of skulls upon his head,
has hair standing erect and large, round eyes, and is adorned with ornaments of snakes.
In the right hand a trident and in the left hand a skull-cup;
in the right hand a sword and in the left hand a shield. (50–6)
Know him thus as four-armed; now hear of the six-armed form:
a serpent in the right hand and a lance in the left hand.
He is proclaimed as having six arms, equipped with the previously mentioned weapons;
the trident, the hand-drum (ḍamaru), and the skull-topped staff (khaṭvāṅga) are in his right and left hands. (50.8)
Thus the eight-armed form has been described, resembling the weapons of the six-armed one;
having performed the installation in water as before, preceded by the placement of jewels and other rites.
One should properly perform the consecration of the Kṣetrapāla with his own mantra.
The procedure for the Kṣetrapāla has been declared; now listen to the installation of the Śūla. (50-10)
Thus ends the fiftieth chapter, the ritual procedure for the installation of the Lord of the Field (Kṣetreśa). || 50 ||
Now begins the chapter on the ritual procedure for the installation of the *śūla* (trident).
Hereafter, I shall fully explain the supreme installation of the *śūla*, which is said to be the conscious essence (*cetanāṃśa*) of the Lord Sadāśiva. (51.1)
Now hear the characteristics of the trident (śūla) which embodies all the gods;
it should be as high as the temple (prāsāda), or even equal in measure to its pillar (stambha).
One-fourth more than a quarter, or half a quarter, or even just a quarter;
this is called "excessive space" (vyoma), while that which is specifically devoid of it is [the opposite]. (51-3)
The width of the petal is said to be one-tenth of its height;
half of that is the width of the stalk, and a quarter of that is remembered as its thickness.
The tips of the two side-petals are fashioned like the tips of mango leaves;
the thickness of the petals is remembered as being one-third of their width. (51.5)
The thickness of the petals should be stated as half the thickness of the [main] slab;
above that, the intermediate space should be double, and the plank should be square.

Then, one-eighth of that is declared to be the thickness; below that, a pitcher (kuṃbha) is desired, shaped like a plank, with a height equal to half its width, and its elevation being half of that [width].
The neck-thickness at both the bottom and the top of the pitcher (kumbha) is nine parts;
it is traditionally taught that the neck-thickness is one-eighth of the pitcher's circumference.
Below that is a half-kumbha, and below that, a staff-lattice (daṇḍapañjara) of half its size;
it should be made of wood, or else of metal, provided there is no other [material].

The height of the pedestal (pīṭha) is one-fifth of the length of the blade, plus one-third of the thickness of the hilt; this measurement extends from the base down to the end of the sword's tang. 51–10.
The width of the pedestal (pīṭha) should be three-fifths of its height;
it is traditionally taught that the pedestal may be shaped like a lotus, square, or [otherwise] according to the form of the base.
Having divided [the area] into eight parts, the pericarp (karṇikā) is made with one part;
the height of the petals is four parts, and the tip of each petal is one part.
The pedestal (pīṭha) shall be five parts square, with its height starting from one part;
its thickness is declared to be half the thickness of the plinth (phalaka).
Then, with wooden rods, one should construct a lattice-work of rods above the seat;
in the middle of the wooden rod, however, one should fasten it firmly with a yoga-band.
Then, one should draw a lotus on the middle petal with the mark of a trident-point at its tip;
having thus fashioned the trident-weapon, one should then begin its installation.
Having performed the ritual immersion in water and the ceremonial bath, and having prepared the pavilion,
one should cover the trident with cloths upon the sacrificial bed on the altar.
Having placed the deities who are the lords of the tridents and having worshipped them in due order,
one should arrange the ritual jars there, together with the lords of the trident-weapons.
Then the wise man, having offered into the fire the weapons along with their sheaths and the seed-mantras, each with its respective mantra.
At an auspicious moment and a favorable conjunction, while recollecting the respective mantras:
Rudra is the presiding deity of the central petal, and Pitāmaha is in the south. (51.19)
Likewise, Viṣṇu is on the left petal;
the deities of the three petals are Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Raudrī, who are the deities at the base of the trident.
The blade has Skanda as its presiding deity; Varuṇa resides in the hilt;
half of that has Agni as its deity; and Sarasvatī is present in the shafts.
Likewise, on the pedestal, the wise one should gradually install Goddess Umā and Vasundharā upon the ground portion, accompanied by perfumes, flowers, and unbroken grains of rice.
One should consecrate [the disciple] with water-pots using the seed-syllable beginning with one's own name;
having worshipped him in the heart, one should indeed offer sacrificial food (havis).
The installation of the trident has been declared; now hear the procedure for the King of Weapons (Astrarāja).
Thus ends the fifty-first chapter, the Chapter on the Procedure for the Installation of the Trident.
Now follows the chapter on the ritual procedure for the King of Weapons (Astrarāja).
Hereafter, I shall fully explain the worship of the King of Weapons:
[one should meditate upon him] as four-armed and three-eyed, blazing with a crest of flames.
With a trident in his left and right hands, and displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, he is indeed the fierce Pāśupata; thus is the form of Bali described.
Having prepared either a standing posture or a seated one endowed with majesty,
one should fashion the image there according to the previously mentioned proportions.
Just as with the installation of water, everything up to the installation of the jewels and so forth should be performed using that very mantra; all else shall be the same. (52–4)
The ritual for the King of Weapons has been declared; now hear the establishment of the scripture.
Thus ends the fifty-second chapter, the Chapter on the Ritual for the King of Weapons.
Now begins the chapter on the procedure for establishing the Teacher.
Hereafter, I shall fully explain the supreme establishment of the Teacher; he is called the "Teacher" (śāstṛ) because he is the instructor of the entire world. (53.1)
Listen indeed to its described nature and its installation;
likewise, it was taken up during the churning of the ocean for the sake of the nectar of immortality.
Hari assumed a female form known by the name Mohinī;
having seen that Mohinī once, I became attached to her. (53-3)
Then the Great Teacher was born, O lords of Medhyāhva and Āmravatī;
having manifested with two eyes and two arms, he was adorned with all ornaments. (53–4)

One should visualize him as possessing a dark complexion, wearing a white sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), playing with dogs, cocks, rams, and other animals, and bestowing all spiritual accomplishments (*siddhi*). (53–5)
Then, one should place on both sides the two deities Madana and Avarṇinī, endowed with yellow garments and adorned with all ornaments. (53–56)
Having placed Damanaka on the left, he is remembered as having a deformed appearance due to his hatred;
the Lord has two arms, with a discus and a staff in his right hand.
With hands holding fruit and sprouts, and two feet drawn up, he has the form of a spirit with a large belly and is adorned with dark locks of hair. (53-8)
The characteristics of the Teacher have been declared; now hear the true procedure for his installation.
It should be performed in the south-western part of the temple, and likewise in the south-western part of villages and other such places. (53-9)
In the eight directions, starting from the east, a wise man should have a temple built facing away from that village; specifically, one shaped like the back of an elephant.
Alternatively, a maṇḍala should be made, and then an image [should be placed] seated upon a bhadrāsana or likewise upon a vīrāsana. (53.11)
The one most learned in the scriptures should have [the image] fashioned from clay, wood, stone, or metal;
the remaining rites, such as the mantra-recitation and meditation, are to be performed as previously described for the installation of a stone [image].
Therefore, just as in the application of the root mantra,
the knower of mantras should meditate on that form in the midst of the fire using only the first syllable and perform the oblation.
Pervaded by the meditation on that form, one should perform the installation and other rites;
that image, the *kautuka*, should be placed in front of the primary *mūlabera* statue. (53.14)
Likewise, one should have images made of iron and other metals, or of clay, stone, and so forth;
having worshipped them according to the prescribed rite, one should then offer sacrificial food (haviṣya). || 53-15 ||
"Thus indeed is the establishment of the Teacher; now hear the procedure for the restoration of what is decayed.
Thus ends the fifty-third chapter, the Chapter on the Procedure for the Establishment of the Teacher.
Now follows the chapter on the procedure for the restoration of the decayed (jīrṇoddhāra).
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the sequence of the procedure for the restoration of the decayed;
just as one whose body is worn out casts off that body and attains another.
Likewise, when an image becomes worn out or moves, the deity abandons it;
indeed, all such occurrences are caused by the possession of Rākṣasas and other malevolent beings. (54.2)
Rākṣasas, asuras, piśācas, and brahmarākṣasas [also cause harm];
therefore, with every effort, one should carry out the restoration of what has fallen into decay.
At the time of decay, one should then restore the temple, the primary linga, the pedestal, the enclosure wall, the pavilion, the gate-tower, and the retinue of deities. (54–4)
One should avoid that which has a pinnacle, a hall, a pigeon-cot, a gabled cage, or is joined with a foot-rest. (54.5)
Having fashioned the celestial chariot (*vimāna*) as before, perform the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) according to the rules;
if any one of its parts is missing, the wise man should restore it as previously described. (54–56)
This has been declared regarding the ālayas; now hear concerning the pratimās:
the brow-line, the hairline, and the nose should not be diminished. (54–7)
In the case of a *liṅga* with its *sūtra*, one should observe the lines on the corners; for other parts, having observed their decay, one should do so specifically on the pedestal (*pīṭha*). (54–8)
Now listen to the procedure for the removal of a worn-out linga situated to the north:
the wise man should draw a mandala to the south of the Shiva-linga. (54–9)
Having mentally conceived the seat and performed worship, one should commence the external ritual of worship;
once the mouth of the fire has been prepared, one should offer oblations purified by mantra into its presence. (54.10)
Or with *dūrvā* grass, *ghṛta*, milk, sesame seeds, and rice;
with the ten-fold self, the limbs of Śiva, the five *brahmans*, and the six *aṅgas*. (54.11)
One should offer one hundred, or fifty, or twenty-five oblations for each [deity];
for the sake of ensuring the immobility of the *liṅga*, one hundred oblations should be made with the root mantra alone.
There, one should offer the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with the thousand-syllable mantra,
mixed with its bark and a rope made of cow-hair.
And one should adorn with worthy ornaments a bull that corresponds to the caste of the performer, which is endowed with auspicious marks, young, and strong. (54.14)
One should tie that *liṅga* to the tip of the hump of the bull with a rope;
then, having bound the vital breaths (*asus*) with that rope while recollecting the one of manifold forms, [one should proceed]. (54.15)
The practitioner of mantras should extract that linga along with the bull and Śiva;
there, he should worship the preceptor with garments and golden ornaments.
Having placed the worn-out linga upon a palanquin or even a chariot, one should create a great sound with conchs, trumpets, and other loud musical instruments. (54.17)
Surrounded by devotees of Śiva accompanied by hymns and praises,
one should immerse the liṅga along with the ocean using mantras ending in salutations.
In the case of reservoirs and the like that cannot be dried up, one should either bury it in the ground or cast it away;
however, if the linga is made of wood, one should discard it in fire or water.
Having fashioned both the image and the pedestal according to the previously described characteristics,
the wise one should install them by the prescribed rite for the welfare of the king and the kingdom.

Having performed everything for the restoration of the ruined [shrine], one should first prostrate before Śambhu, who resides within the maṇḍala, make a formal request, and utter: "May there be Śiva! (śivam astu). || 54-21 ||
Having worshipped Śiva as before, the knower of mantras should dismiss the Śivāstra with the Aghorāstra mantra for the purpose of removing any defects in that [rite]. (54.22)
Having offered one hundred and eight oblations of clarified butter, one should perform the oblation with the *vyāhṛtis*.
Having dismissed Śiva who resides in the fire, one should complete the remainder of the *homa*.
One should indeed restore all dilapidated [images] of the deity;
however, for those that are movable, one should restore them in this manner, excluding the bull, according to the sequence. (54.24)
Having quickly removed images made of clay or wood, one should discard them; but when an image of metal has been removed, one should fashion a new one from that same material.
One should perform it in this manner as a general rule; now hear the specific detail:
it should be made with superior materials and likewise exceeding that [standard] measure.
Otherwise, it must not be performed; if it were performed, it would bring destruction upon the performer.
Regarding the walls, pavilions, and so forth, that which is dilapidated should be removed from there. (54.27)
Having made that firm and beautiful as before, the wise one should proceed;
for if he were to act otherwise, it would bring harm to men. (54.28)
In this case, there will be total ruin; indeed, everything becomes utterly fruitless when, during the months or their halves, both inauspicious and auspicious [planets] [are positioned thus].
Without investigation, one should then perform the restoration and re-installation;
this is declared to be the *jīrṇoddhāra* (restoration of the decayed). Now listen to the expiation (*prāyaścitta*).
Thus ends the fifty-fourth chapter, the procedure for the restoration of dilapidated [shrines].
Now begins the chapter on the rules for expiation (prāyaścitta).
Hereafter, I shall fully explain the sequence of the rules for expiation;
"prāya" is said to mean destruction, and "citta" means restoration—thus is expiation (prāyaścitta) defined. (55.1)
I shall now declare the expiation beginning with worship and ending with the fire-oblation.
If the time for worship is missed, one should recite the Śiva-mantra one hundred times. (55–2)
If the time for worship is missed during the twilight (sandhyā), the rite must likewise be performed twice;
if there is a break in the ancillary rites (aṅga) for even a single day, one hundred oblations (āhuti) should be offered with the heart-mantra (hṛnmantra).
If the recitation of the Ṛgveda is deficient for one day, the ceremonial bathing (snapana) should be performed with nine jars;
if it is deficient for two or three days, it should be performed with twenty-five jars.
If the fourth cause occurs within five days, yet a deficiency in worship arises,
then after ten days have passed, a ceremonial bath with a hundred jars [of water] should be performed.
If the worship is deficient for one month, it must be performed again with three hundred jars;
if it is deficient for three months, it must be performed in due order with a thousand jars. (55–56)
If worship is omitted for more than six months, one should perform a ritual sprinkling (saṃprokṣaṇa).
However, if the bali offering is omitted during the twilight (sandhyā) rites, one should recite the Rudra mantra one hundred times.
If the bali offering is omitted at the two twilights, the preceptor should perform one hundred and fifty recitations;
if it is omitted at the three twilights, he should then cause a ritual bathing (snapana) to be performed.
In the rite for the cessation of offerings (*baliviccheda*), [the procedure] from two days up to one month is as follows:
having meditated upon the Śiva-fire as before, the bathing should be performed one hundred and eight times.
If, however, it is deficient by more than one month, the wise preceptor should perform a thousand oblations of clarified butter with the [mantras of the] limbs for Śiva, but not for Śivā. (55–10)
The wise one should cause the ceremonial bath to be performed with one hundred and eight jars;
furthermore, he should conduct the daily festival as before, with special care. (55–11)
Furthermore, during the time of the Bali procession, the Liṅga may indeed become fallen, cracked, displaced, broken, severed, or split. (55-12)
In that very place, or else in the middle of the temple, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa);
having first offered the bali-offering to the liṅga there, one should then circumambulate it clockwise.
Alternatively, having performed as before, the wise one should offer oblations in sequence at the end of the circumambulation and there recite the eight-syllable root mantra one hundred times.
Whether it is forbidden or permitted, one should mutter the root mantra a hundred times;
at that time, having remained there even if devoid of a lamp, one should then offer the bali.
Having again brought forth the lamp and performed the remaining circumambulation,
one should offer double the quantity of cooked rice in the food offering.
But when the sacrificial substance is lacking, a wise man should perform the rite with double the effort;
likewise, when the constant [daily] offering lacks the substance, he should then perform it with double the effort.
If the daily fire-ritual (agnikārya) is omitted, one hundred oblations should be offered with the heart-mantra;
now hear the specific expiation for that omission during a festival.
In the event that the banner, the flagpole, or especially the bell is cut, broken, or fallen, or if they are seized by thieves and the like; || 55-19 ||
Having performed all that as before, perform the rite of re-awakening;
having offered a hundred oblations with the heart-mantra, one should bathe [the image] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
If the time for the sacrifice has been lost, one should perform the oblation with the root mantra;
if the sacrificial materials are lacking, however, one should offer a hundred oblations with the heart mantra. (55.21)
At the time of offering the oblation, if a dog arrives while the vessel is empty,
one should perform a hundred oblations with the *hṛdayamantra* for the purpose of universal pacification.
Whether the trident-weapon has fallen or any other of the eight auspicious weapons, there shall be a ceremonial bath for the trident and a hundred oblations for the others. (55.23)
If an image, or even a single image, has been touched by those belonging to the lowest castes or outcasts,
one should perform a ritual bathing there and offer oblations with the root mantra.
If, through negligence, a break or a cut occurs, perform the rite as before;
if any limb is deficient among all the limbs, one should apply the limb again.
If the image is deficient above the neck, a wise person should have it restored; this may be done regardless of the lunar day, the weekday, or the auspicious hour.
One should perform the duties beginning with the formal acceptance (adhivāsana) immediately;
having especially established [the deity], now hear the expiation (prāyaścitta). || 55-27 ||
If the time for the ceremonial bath (snapana) has passed, one hundred oblations should be offered with the head-mantra;
if the substances for the bath are deficient, half of that number should be offered with the crest-mantra (śikhā).
If the vessel is cracked, fallen, broken, or has been pierced or cut, the wise one should remove it and fashion another as before. || 55-29 ||
Or even upon touching something untouchable, or being touched by a dog, a crow, or the like,
one should take another jar and fill it with water while reciting the mantra.
Having offered a hundred oblations with the *hṛdaya-mantra*, the bathing ceremony should be performed there as before;
if [the practitioner] lacks compassion, the wise one should perform that as previously described. (55.31)
If a fresh linga is found upon a pedestal or associated with broken or split fragments,
one should discard that linga in water and install a new linga as before.
One should restore a fallen or displaced *liṅga* in due order, as previously described.
Now listen, O Vighneśa, as I shall explain the procedure regarding the primary *liṅga*. (55.33)
A *liṅga* that is cracked, split, decayed, or likewise broken—having abandoned such a *liṅga*, one should install one that is not deformed. (55.34)
Whether it has been moved, or fallen, or swept away by the current of a river; or even if it has been overturned by an elephant, or stolen by thieves or madmen. (55.35)
Having installed that liṅga there, one should perform the remaining rites as before. This applies even when a great liṅga situated in deep water is moved by the current. (55.36)
Or, in the case of another image, one should employ [the rite] with a hundred-fold staff;
if the root-liṅga is invisible, however, a new liṅga should be used as before. (55.37)
In this same way, for a pedestal as well as for other images,
if the primary image is located in a place lacking consecration, one should certainly not perform even a hundred oblations.

Just as one should not perform the root rite according to the scripture if the ritual action is deficient, so too, when the ritual action is devoid of mantra, there shall be a hundred oblations with the *śikhā* [mantra]. (55.39)
O Vighneśa, if there is a deficiency in materials, one should perform a thousand oblations with the *varman* mantra;
in all cases where there is an excess or a deficiency in the ritual actions, one should recite the root mantra one hundred times.
One should avoid defilement by crows, dogs, donkeys, camels, and those who are intoxicated or insane;
one should perform the *sparśāhuti* offering, and especially the *puṇyāha* rite. || 55-41 ||
Having offered oblations with the Śiva-mantra either a thousand or a hundred times,
[one should purify] that which has been touched by outcasts (caṇḍāla) and others, or that which is situated nearby.
One should perform sprinkling, re-consecration, and again the ritual bathing,
when the temple has fallen, been broken, shattered, or likewise destroyed.
Having led Śiva to the temple of the child and having prepared a celestial chariot as before,
one should perform the ritual sprinkling according to the rules and thereafter commence the festival.
In the womb-chamber (garbhageha), having filled the hollow with liquid using a ladle and other implements,
one should then perform the Vāstuhoma at its conclusion and have the Puṇyāha recited there.
If the sacrificial pedestal (balipīṭha) is destroyed, one should install a new sacrificial pedestal; if the temple of the retinue deities is deficient, one should arrange it as before. || 55-46 ||
If that image falls, breaks, or is cut, one should avoid [the ritual];
however, having offered oblations with the Śiva-mantra, one should fashion images as before.
One should perform the consecration as before, according to one's own ritual procedure.
Now, I shall describe the pacification of portents, which destroys all defects.
Everything becomes discolored when the image weeps, and likewise when fever and pestilence arise, or when diseases such as boils and the like occur. (55.49)
When a new palace collapses, when a sacred tree (caityavṛkṣa) falls, and when such other calamities arise that bring harm to villages and the like; 55–50.

To pacify those defects, one should perform a rite of propitiation (*śāntika*) for three weeks in cases of earthquakes, conflagrations in the cardinal directions, or the appearance of mock suns (*pratisūrya*). (55–51)
If a star appears during the day, or if a rainbow appears at night, there will be famine; and when the Śatruvardhanī [appears], it brings fear to the king and the kingdom.
Likewise, for one month, one should perform a propitiatory rite (śānti) for the removal of defects, wherever an anthill is seen upon a temple, a pavilion, or similar structures. (55–53)
When the palace produced from the Jewel-Maiden was occupied by Madhu,
and likewise when the anthill and the termite mound had entered within the interior of that palace.
Having dug up that spot, one should fill it with pure soil;
having sprinkled it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one should perform the rite of pacification once again.
I shall briefly describe the rite of pacification; listen to the truth, O Gajānana!
Having doubled the sacrificial oblation, one should especially provide lamps and flowers. (55–56)
One should cause the cool-water jar (śītakumbha) to be placed above Śiva according to the prescribed rite;
then, having performed the oblation for the directions (diśāhoma), one should especially perform the oblation for the deities of the forms (mūrtihoma).
In the four directions, the teaching of the four Vedas was likewise performed by them in the past; and the daily ritual bathing was conducted properly according to their means. (55–58)
One should perform the consecration daily with clarified butter and milk according to one's ability;
one should also perform the consecration with the waters of a coconut.
At the end of that [period], one should rub the linga with night-powder and purify it;
it is taught that at the end of that, the oblation of clarified butter should always be double the usual amount.
Thus is peace proclaimed, which destroys all misfortunes;
where peace is thus established, there is an increase of wealth and grain.
But for all those [offenses] not mentioned, having understood their relative gravity or lightness, one should cause penances to be performed according to the types already described. || 55–62 ||
The preceptor should perform the pacifying oblation (śānti-homa) for the remaining [deities] according to the prescribed rules.
This expiation has been declared; now hear regarding the intermixture of those [castes]. || 55-63 ||
Thus ends the fifty-fifth chapter, on the rules for expiation.
(p. 229) Now follows the chapter on the procedure for the blending of tantras (*tantrasaṃkaravidhipaṭala*).
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the supreme blending of the tantras:
the Śaiva, the Pāśupata, the Soma, and the Lākula—thus they are fourfold. (56–1)
A wise person should practice according to their respective scriptures, following the various divisions and sub-divisions within the four types of tantras as they desire. (56-2)
The wise one should perform the rites beginning with plowing and ending with the installation;
he should have everything from the plowing to the installation performed according to a single ritual manual.
It is the foremost bestower of enjoyment and liberation; one shall attain all perfections.
Having performed it first by one person, it was indeed performed afterwards by another.
But this confusion caused by him brought harm to the king and the kingdom;
both the preceptor and the performer [of the sacrifice] were thus utterly destroyed. (56–5)
Whatever has been commenced according to a particular scripture, perform that very thing according to that same scripture;
if it is performed according to another scripture, it will lead to a defect in the ritual system.
The Śaiva [tradition] is remembered as being twofold: the gentle (saumya) and the fierce (raudra). Of these, the former is known as the gentle;
the other is proclaimed there as being exclusively fierce.
When I am worshipped with fierce [rites], I bestow fierce fruits;
likewise, when I am worshipped with gentle [rites], O child, I bestow gentle fruits.
The fierce should be worshipped with the gentle, and the gentle should not be worshipped with the fierce;
