because of its connection with Vedic conduct, the gentle is remembered as superior. (56–9)
Because it stands outside the conduct prescribed by the Vedas, it is called the "other" (apara) and is said to be fierce (raudra).
One should establish [the deity] in a village with gentle (saumya) rites, but one should not cause it to be performed with fierce rites.
If [the image] is installed with a wrathful [mudrā] out of delusion, the destruction of the village will certainly occur;
for everything in this world, both moving and unmoving, consists of both gentle and wrathful aspects. (56.11)
Therefore, with every effort, one should worship the fierce [deity] with gentle means;
for this brings about all accomplishments—this has been declared by the one whose self is Śiva.
Having first established [the deity] with a gentle rite, one should subsequently worship with a fierce rite;
if this is done out of delusion, the king and his kingdom shall perish. (56.13)
(230) What is the use of saying more here, O gentle one? One should certainly not worship [it].
The twenty-eight tantras beginning with the Kāmika are remembered as Śaiva. (56–14)
That alone is declared to be the gentle (saumya) Siddhānta; indeed, that alone is it.
Any other than that is declared to be the fierce (raudra), such as the Pāśupata and other systems.
In the Śaiva Siddhānta Tantras, one should perform [the rite] according to a single tantra;
if this is not stated, one may use another, for there is no fault in such a combination.
Likewise, there is indeed no fault in various other tantras;
thus, the commingling of tantras has been briefly proclaimed.
The Kriyāpāda has been well-proclaimed through fifty-six chapters.
This is the Kriyāpāda, O child; now listen to the Caryāpāda.
The introduction of the tantras and all else has been briefly explained by me; however,
their final synthesis within the Śaiva Siddhāntas exists as fifty-six chapters in number.
But his feet, beginning with all [the scriptures], were not worshipped by wicked people, even though they were accompanied by the Śaivas.
Thus ends the fifty-sixth chapter, the Chapter on the Rules for the Interfusion of Tantras.
Thus ends the Kriyāpāda in the Suprabheda; Oṃ, consisting of Śiva.
Now, from the *Suprabheda*, in the section on Conduct (*caryāpāda*), the chapter on the Ritual of Generation (*utpattividhipaṭala*):
"Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the sequence of the ritual for the section on Conduct."
Now, listen to the origin of the Śaivas from that very foot. 1-1.
The Śaiva, Pāśupata, Soma, and Lākula—this fourfold scripture is remembered as being without internal division (bhedābhāva). || 1–2 ||
He who has been consecrated through devotion to the fourfold scriptures in their proper sequence is called "Sakalāvadhi" by the name of the [third] scripture. 1-3.
But for those established in the fourth [state], which is partless (niṣkala) and devoid of parts (kalā), Śiva abides within men; thus they are proclaimed as "Śaivas. || 1-4 ||
In the Pāśupata and other scriptures, names are likewise proclaimed;
in these three systems of doctrine, the divisions differ according to their respective paths.
Now, the divisions of Śaivism shall be described in brief:
the scripture is to be known as fourfold—Vāma, Dakṣiṇa, Miśra, and [the fourth]. (1.6)
Thus, the fourth [initiation] is proclaimed as being endowed with the Siddhānta;
those who undergo initiation sequentially according to the various divisions of the Vāmā and other scriptures [receive it].
They are celebrated as the Vāma, the Dakṣiṇa, and the Miśra Siddhānta.
For the Vāma belongs to Śambhu, while the Dakṣiṇa has Bhairava as its essence. (1-8)
The *Miśra* is said to be the *Yāmala*, which has the seven Mothers as its primary focus;
the *Siddhānta* is the pure Śaiva, and likewise the *Kevala* is the *Śāmbhava*.
The Siddhānta is indeed the essence of all, pure in its reality, and remembered as auspicious;
then there is the Vāma and the Dakṣiṇa, and also that which is a mixture of these two.
Those who are outside the Śaiva fold are declared to be unworthy of worship even within the Śaiva tradition;
furthermore, there are twenty-eight compendia (saṃhitās) according to the divisions beginning with the Kāmika.
The pure Siddhānta of the Śaivas, along with their various divisions and subdivisions, is called the "Mixed Siddhānta," known as the Nine Yāmalas. (1.12)
The left-hand practice (vāmācāra) indeed [is taught] in the fifth [chapter], and likewise the right-hand practice (dakṣiṇa) as well;
the teachers have prescribed five each for these two combined.
Listen to the established doctrine and the characteristics of the five mixed Śaiva classes:
the Ācārya, the Sādhaka, the Samayin, and likewise the Putraka.
Known as Citrakeṭaka, he was honored in the Mātṛyajñas;
he was initiated in due order into the Siddhānta known as Śuddhaśaiva.
The Ācārya is traditionally held to be the presiding lord over the fourfold group beginning with the Sādhaka;
[his duties include] the installation and worship of the Mothers, and the libation for the Fire.
The master alone should perform the bathing festival, the rites for pacification, and so forth;
the other rituals mentioned therein should be performed by those [disciples], such as the practitioners (sādhakas) and others.
Having belonged to the lineage of the elder brother of Śiva, [there were] the four beginning with the Ācārya;
Pāraśiva was also mentioned by the name Citrakeṭaka.
Listen now to the true origin of the Śaivas who are mixed with those of other traditions:
first are the Anādi-Śaivas, and second are the Mahā-Śaivas.
The first are the Śaivas, the third are the Anuśaivas, and the fourth are the Antaraśaivas;
thus, the Śaivas are remembered as being of five kinds.
Śakti, Mūrti, Viśakti, Nāda, and Bindu are traditionally taught; likewise, Sadāśiva and Īśvara are established in these six locations. (1–21)
These are declared to be the Anādiśaivas; now hear about the Mahāśaivas.
Likewise, those beginning with Ananta and ending with Śikhaṇḍin are the Mantramaheśvaras. (1.22)
From Māyā down to the earth, those Rudras of great power,
as well as the Daityas and the sages, are all disciples of Ananteśvara.
The gods, beginning with Brahmā and Viṣṇu, together with the hosts of Yakṣas and Rākṣasas, are renowned as Mahāśaivas; now indeed hear about the Ādiśaivas.
Indeed, these are remembered as followers of Śiva, together with the Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Uragas;
they consist of the four castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇas, originating from Kaśyapa and others. (1–25)
(233) By the grace of the Supreme Lord, they were appointed to their office for the purpose of illuminating the Śiva-dharma and for the awakening of all beings. 1-26.
The installation of the forms of the sages was performed by Śiva, the Supreme Self, according to the ritual procedure of consecration and sprinkling for the purpose of accomplishing his task. (1.27)
And all those who are to be favored, known as the various sub-sects of the Śaivas,
are all endowed with the knowledge of Śiva and are devoted solely to the dharma of Śiva.
The teachers who know the Śiva scriptures and the knowledge of liberation are like Śiva on this earth;
one should regard them all as Śiva—this is the certain conclusion of the scripture. (1–29)
I shall briefly describe the sphere of activity (gocara), the lineage (gotra), and the sūtras.
Indeed, the sphere of activity is the sign of Śiva, while the lineage consists of one's own group of sages. (1.30)
Thus, the Sūtra regarding the conduct of the Śaivas is declared in sequence:
Śiva, the Topknot (śikhā), likewise Light (jyotis), and the Sāvitrī residing in the ether. (1.31)
These five names belong to the Śaivas in the teaching of Śiva; they are called the *gocara* and the *kula*, and they are the insignia for those of the four castes. (1.32)
Kāśyapa, Kauśika, Bhāradvāja, Gautama, and Ātreya—these five are to be known as the sages (ṛṣis) proclaimed here. (1.33)
The domain of Śiva is said to belong to the sages beginning with Kāśyapa;
namely, Kāśyapa, Namuci, Manuja, and Manubha. (1.34)
Viśvāmitra, Vālmīki, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, Sanatkumāra, Medhāvī, Savyaṛkṣa, and Parāśara. || 1.35 ||
Sanandana, Sadiirgha, Sanaka, and Sanātana—
the sphere of Śiva is the sphere of these groups of sages.
The range of the crest is said to belong to the sages beginning with Kauśika:
Kauśika, Kuśika, and Prājāpati as the fifth. (1.37)
Śaddhyāyantam, as well as Bhūmi, Sananta, Khadyapūraṇa, Śāṇḍilya, Ujanaka, and Suvarṇasthāṇḍila. || 1.38 ||
Śaṅkhasthūla, Ṛtu, Vīraju, and Romaharṣaṇa—
all of these are said to be within the range of vision of those sages.
The range of light for the sages, beginning with Bhāradvāja, is now declared:
Bhāradvāja, Vasiṣṭha, Mārkaṇḍa, Sthaṇḍila, and Guru. (1.40)
(234, 235 missing;

page 236) The installation, the sprinkling, and the initiation were performed according to the ritual procedure for the sake of the rite. Those who were fashioned by Śiva, the Supreme Self, have been created by Śiva. (1.41)
Together with Śaivī, they shall gradually proceed from the mouth of Brahmā to the mortal world;
they are celebrated under names such as Kāśyapa and others, appearing in the forms of sages.
In the beginning, you existed as Śiva; thus you are declared an Ādiśaiva. Those who have been initiated by Śiva are remembered as Śivabrāhmaṇas. (1.43)

They are the most excellent of all, supreme teachers, the best among Brahmins, and the highest among Śivas; they are the most eminent of the twice-born, manifestations of Śiva, whose very essence is Śiva.
These synonyms have been told to you in brief:
from *krimi*, *kīṭa*, and *pada* come *parśapaḥ*, *prājñāḥ*, and *ājñakāḥ*. (1.45)

Men are superior even to animals; among them, the twice-born (dvijas) are likewise superior. Among the twice-born, the Brahmins are superior; and among the Brahmins, those of sharp intellect are superior. (1.46)
Among those who possess ritual action and wisdom, those who possess renunciation are superior;
among those who possess renunciation, those worshipped by Śaṅkara are the most excellent. (1.47)
Thus ends the first chapter, the Chapter on the Procedure for Generation, within the Section on Conduct. || 1 ||
Now begins the chapter on the rules for the classification of castes.
Hereafter, I shall duly explain the procedure for the classification of castes:
first the creation by Śiva, and subsequently the creation by Brahmā proceeds. (2-1)
The spheres of activity are the divisions arising from that; the Śiva-divisions are remembered as being twofold.
From his mouths were born the Brāhmaṇas, and likewise from his arms the Kṣatriyas. (2-2)
The Vaiśyas are to be known from the thighs, and those of the Śūdra caste from the feet;
[these distinctions arise] from the union of the four castes, whether in the direct or inverse order.
At the time of their conjunction, however, intermediate beings are born;
from that, through their activity, they are further produced—listen now to their origin.
(237) O Mother, just as in each and every caste [the deities] consist of both Śakti and Śambhu, it is said that Śakti is of the form of the woman, while Puruṣa is called Śambhu. (2.5)
They declare this entire world of moving and non-moving beings to consist of Śakti and Śambhu;
likewise, the four castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇas have indeed performed their ablutions in due order.
I shall now describe their livelihood, conduct, and essential nature, according to how they are born solely from the mouth through the creation of Śiva. (2.7)
One should lead the four castes, who are pure in their conduct, to Śiva through initiation.
Now hear how the conduct of all should proceed according to the path of worldly custom. (2.8)
Studying and teaching, sacrificing for oneself and officiating at sacrifices for others, as well as giving gifts and receiving them—these are said to be their duties. (2.9)
O high-minded one, from the arms of Brahmā were born the Kṣatriyas;
likewise, the Nṛpas, Kṣatriya kings, Rājās, Bhūpas, and Bhūpakas.
These six have their own names, which are synonyms for them;
the protection of the world consists in their preservation of their own respective duties. (2.11)
The birth of Brahmins is ordained from the thighs, while that of Vaiśyas is ordained from the yellow [portion];
indeed, the Vaṇijas born from the yellow [portion] are granters of desires throughout all worlds. (2-12)
These five, which I have declared, are synonyms for the Vaiśya; they are engaged in the three occupations of cattle-rearing, agriculture, and trade. (2-13)
From his feet, create the Śūdras as attendants of the [other] three castes;
service to the twice-born is declared to be the livelihood of the Śūdras. (2.14)
*Kṛṣṇa*, *kārṣaka*, *śūdra*, *vṛṣala*, and *preṣyakāraka*—these five names are synonyms for the Śūdra. (2.15)
Furthermore, a Śūdra who is devoted and virtuous should indeed be regarded as a Vaiśya;
those Śūdras who do not drink liquor and are of noble birth are proclaimed to be "true Śūdras. (2.16)

In those respective castes, they are born in due order according to the rule; thus arise the four castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇas, as well as the specific sub-castes (jāti) within each caste. (2.17)
These four castes have been declared; now hear from me about those born in the natural order (anuloma): one should know the first to be the Sūta, and the second the Ambaṣṭha. (2.18)
The third is the Pāraśava, born from Brāhmaṇa progenitors;
these two, named Matgu and Ugra, shall be born as attendants to the king.
The *cūcuka* is to be known as the [offspring] of a Vaiśya; however, there are exactly six types of *anuloma* [progeny].
Having lawfully obtained a red-complexioned maiden with the recitation of mantras, a Brāhmaṇa [begets these]. (2.20)
One born there is of the same caste (savarṇa), yet among those born in the anuloma order he is honored;
though designated as a Brāhmaṇa, he has indeed forgotten his duty and unrighteousness.

One born when Jupiter is conjoined [with a planet] may ride a chariot drawn by horses or elephants, or may serve at the command of a king, or may even hold the office of commander-in-chief of armies throughout his life. (2-22)
From the union of a yellow woman and a Brahmin, one named Daṃbaṣṭha is born;
his livelihood shall be the management of elephant trappings as well as dancing with flaming torches.
One born from the union of a Śūdra woman and a Brāhmaṇa is known as a Pāraśava;
his livelihood consists of carrying a palanquin, playing small musical instruments, and acting as a messenger. (2.24)
Dancing and instrumental music should be performed, as well as the maddala drum and the vṛttikā.
One born from a red man and a yellow woman is known as a mataguru. (2-25)
But the great merchant, by name Vaiśyapratyupajīvana, has his livelihood right here;
he should perform his work under this lunar mansion. (2.26)
Born from the union of Kṛṣṇā and Rakta, he is known as Śrotra;
being intensely red in his ritual function, one should have him perform the act of punishment right there.
Born from the union of the black and the yellow, he is indeed the nipple;
his livelihood consists of wood, grass, and other forest-born products. (2.28)
Those who live by trade through the fruits and leaves of the betel-nut tree are called *anuloma*.
Now hear about those who are *pratiloma*. (2.29)
The Vaideha, the Pulkasa, the Caṇḍāla, as well as the Āyogava and the Māgadha—these five are born from desire. (2–30)
And thus the Sūta is said to be born from the reverse order of the king;
indeed, one born from the union with a Vaiśya woman is known as the Dehaka. (2.31)
One should properly carry out the protection of cows, buffaloes, and sheep;
likewise, one may subsist by tending them and engage in their purchase and sale. (2–32)
One born from the union of a Raktā woman and a Kṛṣṇa man is called a Pulasa;
his livelihood is recorded as being the collection and sale of liquor. (2-33)
239) One born from the union of a Śūdra with a Śvetā woman is called a Caṇḍāla;
having an ox-hide fastened to his ear and likewise iron ornaments [on his body]. (2.34)
Having shaken off all impurity from his body with the *jhallarī* gourd,
he may enter a village in the forenoon or enter it in the afternoon.
From the union with a yellow woman by one who is red, a person known as Āyogava is born;
he indeed subsists by weaving cloth and becomes a weaver. (2.36)
One born from the union of a Brahmin woman and a Pīta is called a Māgadha;
he should perform salutations to all and especially offer praise. (2.37)
If one touches the ground while eating black food, that food must not be consumed;
having sent away everyone, one should subsist on water produced from that [act]. (2-38)
If a son is born from a Brahmin woman by a king according to the prescribed rule, he is honored among those born in the inverse order (pratiloma) and is known by the name Sūta. (2.39)
However, for those born outside the pale of the Śvetas, this very [Veda] is prescribed;
their study is declared to be that which brings about the awakening to the dharmas. (2.40)

These have been declared as those born in the inverse order; now hear concerning those born in secret. A son born in secret to a Brāhmaṇa woman from a Brāhmaṇa through negligence is likewise to be known as a Brāhmaṇa, though he is excluded from performing sacrifices and teaching.
In the wife of a Brāhmaṇa, he is born as a thief for the king alone. || 2-42 ||
Astrology, mathematics, the definitive meaning of the *bhūtatantra*, and the eight-limbed science of medicine (*āyurveda*) are said to belong to the courtesan. (2.43)
From a Brāhmaṇa with a Vaiśya woman are born the Cauras and the Kumbhakārakas; those who live by the occupation of a potter (kulāla) and the Nāpitās are likewise of that same [mixed] origin. (2.44)
In cases of birth-impurity (sūtaka) or death-impurity (pretaka), one should offer [the water] above the navel;
however, a Niṣāda born from a Śūdra woman and a twice-born man [is treated] like a twice-born man when it comes to theft.

One who lives by gathering wild beasts, snakes, and other such creatures is a Śvapāka; one born from a Śūdra woman and a Kṣatriya man is an Āyogava; and one born from a Vaiśya woman and a Kṣatriya man is a Rathakāra. || 2.46 ||
He should always behave like a Śūdra, avoiding the white [garment]; he should relinquish his vehicles as well as their attendants. (2.47)
p. 240) Because he steals the red [fluid] from the one who is red, he is known as "the Red-thief" (Raktasañcāraka).
Even without formal consecration, his instruction consists of the binding of the turban. (2-48)
One who always follows the conduct of a Raktavarna is called a Bhoja;
one born from a Punarbhū through a Raktā is known by the name Rakta. (2.49)
One should know that from a Vaiśya woman [a son] is born who is a thief of blood and is said to be engaged in the business of horses; he is a king-like leader of a host of thieves. (2.50)
One who steals blood from a low-caste woman is called a Cūlika;
furthermore, he is appointed by the king's command to perform tasks involving impalement on a stake. (2.51)
Born from a Brāhmaṇī woman by a Pītasa thief, he is known as a Kāla;
his livelihood consists of sprinkling clothes with water and washing them. (2.52)
In the red [line], one who steals yellow objects is a forest-dweller who lives by the livelihood of a hunter;
in the yellow [line], one who steals yellow objects is said to be a maker of jewels. (2.53)
By selling gems, one performs the work of a *śambā* artisan; by stealing yellow cloth from a low-caste woman (*vṛṣalī*), one is said to engage in the occupation of a weaver. (2.54)
From the theft of a black [bull] from a white [cow], a Vedakāraka is said to be born; from the theft of a black [bull] from a red [cow], one born is called a Vaiṇaka. (2.55)
One who is untouchable by the three castes should perform the recitation of the *vaiṇava* mantra;
one born from the theft of black salt when [the moon is in] Pīta performs the sale of salt.
He alone is to be known as Kṛkī, subsisting on oil-cakes;
born from a thief in the city of Kṛṣṇā, he is called Mālava. (2.57)
The livelihood of cows, elephants, and horses, or perhaps the carrying of loads of grass—these are declared to be the intermediate occupations; now hear of the [other] occupations. (2.58)
The cause for the [distinctions] among the four castes, whether by direct order or inverse order, is indeed the livelihood and reputation of the humans born therein. (2.59)
From an Abhiṣṭha father and a Brāhmaṇa mother is born the Vāpakavṛttika;
from a Raktā mother, one who follows the practice of a Pītava is born; and from a Yogā mother, he is called a Dadhna or a Nāpita. (2.60)
One should perform the shaving of the body hairs, but not below the navel;
from the nipple of a brahmin woman, Takṣaka was born. (2.61)
When it was red, he became a garland-maker for that very same man;
when it was yellow, he became Sāmudra Paśyajīvaka. (2.62)
From the *majjā* [caste], however, the status of a *śravaṇa* is prescribed for one born of a *viprā* woman;
one born of a *raktā* woman alone is known as a *karmakāra*. (2.63)
One born from an Agrastrī woman and a Puṣkala man is called a Rajaka; one born from a Caṇḍāla man and a Brāhmaṇa woman is called a Śvapaca. (2.64)
One should cause them to eat dog-flesh and dwell in cremation grounds; one should employ such various stratagems as are consistent with reason. (2.65)
Therefore, it is not possible to describe the distinctions here even in hundreds of years;
however, the distinctions have been stated by way of summary—now listen to [the description of] the initiates (dīkṣārbhaka).
The Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras have indeed been proclaimed;
one should appoint these four castes to the office of teacher. (2.67)
The supreme teacher should perform the ritual for others;
six [types] are declared to be in direct order (anuloma), and three are recorded as being in reverse order (pratiloma). || 2-68 ||
The Sūta, the Māgadha, the Āyogava, the Sūta, the Antarāla, and all others were engaged in the rites of initiation. || 2.69 ||
All Vrātyas, however, are to be excluded from all ritual acts;
thus I have declared the distinctions of caste. Now hear concerning the Maṇḍala.
Thus ends the second chapter, on the rules for the distinctions of castes. || 2 ||
Now begins the chapter on the ritual procedure for the mandala.
Hereafter, I shall fully explain the mandala that fulfills all desires;
it is called the essence of the mandala, for it is made the abode of all the deities. (3.1)
This mandala was proclaimed by Śiva, the Supreme Self;
by the mere sight of this mandala, one is liberated from all sins. (3.2)
Prior to the time of initiation, the wise one should prepare the mandala according to the rules; having first examined the ground, he should then perform the ritual appropriation of the site.
On Mount Mahendra, Malaya, Vindhya, Himavat, or Pāriyātraka; on the bank of the Gaṅgā, at any holy river, or even in a coastal region. (3–4)
Always in a flower garden, or near a milk-exuding tree, in a pure and delightful place, or in a house or even a temple. (3–5)
On a site sloping toward the northeast, the wise man should draw a mandala on the seventh,
the ninth, or even the eleventh lunar day.
The rite of initiation (dīkṣā) is praised on the thirteenth lunar day or the new moon;
they declare the auspicious constellations to be those occurring on Sundays or Mondays.
Jupiter, Venus, the Moon, and Mercury are auspicious for the rite of initiation (dīkṣā).
Prior to the year of the disciple's birth, one should examine here the disciple's virtues and faults.
One should accept those endowed with good qualities and avoid those devoid of qualities;
having offered the sprouts according to the previously mentioned procedure, one should proceed. (3.9)
One should know that the first is the mandala; the second is the rite of initiation (dīkṣā);
and the third is the consecration (abhiṣeka), which is prescribed in this very sequence. || 3.10 ||
Now, O observer of good vows, hear briefly concerning that maṇḍala:
one should dig the ground to the depth of one cubit and fill the pit with that very earth.

Likewise, that which is superior is considered excellent; that which is middling is considered mediocre; and land that is deficient is considered inferior. Such is the fruit corresponding to the quality of the land.
The best [site] is for the sake of all accomplishments; the middling grants one's own desired objects;
and that which is devoid [of these qualities] is the lowest. Among those that are auspicious, the middling and the best are preferred.
Having made it square and level, and having sprinkled it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya),
one should prepare either a pavilion or a water-shed, fully endowed with all ornaments.
It should be twenty, sixteen, or twelve cubits [in length], or twenty-one, nine, or eight cubits; its center should be devoid of pillars.
Equipped with four gates and adorned with four archways,
the wise man should construct an altar in its center, and within that, a mandala.
One should feed the devotees of Śiva and sprinkle them with water consecrated by the Astra-mantra;
one should then perform the Vāstu-homa according to the prescribed rite for the worship of Vāstu.
There, a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) named after Śiva should be prepared, and one should place a water-pot (kalaśa);
on the left side, however, one should place a vardhanī vessel filled with gold, jewels, and water.
Provided with a pair of garments, equipped with a beard, and furnished with a cover, [the linga] called Śiva is consecrated with the Śiva-mantra, and that called Umā by the name of Gaurī. (3-19)
Having thus performed the worship according to the prescribed rite with auspicious waters from those two jars,
he should sprinkle the ground, the ritual materials, and the disciples with water consecrated by mantras.
Having performed this sacrifice of the sages (ṛṣiyajña) during the first part of the night, the preceptor should then perform the consecration (adhivāsa) together with the collection of Śiva-mantras.
Then, one should place the entire Śiva-sacrifice, conjoined with the Śiva-substance,
in the center upon the Yoga-pīṭha, which is endowed with the three principles (tattvas).
Having worshipped Śiva according to the prescribed rule, either in a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) or upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila),
one should then generate the Śiva-fire according to the ritual procedure as previously described.

Having worshipped the fire according to the prescribed rite, he should cause the disciples— and indeed the members of the castes beginning with the Brahmins, whether women, men, or eunuchs— to undergo the preparatory consecration (adhivāsana).
The knower of mantras should always initiate those who have been urged and are devoted to Śiva;
having given them sacrificial food (caru) consecrated by the mantras of Śiva. (3.25)
Then, having brought that vessel and washed it with auspicious water,
he should honor it with perfumes and flowers and fill it with one āḍhaka measure of rice.
The wise one should surround it with flowers and darbha grass while reciting the armor-mantra (kavaca),
and then fill it with the milk of a tawny cow mixed with ghee.
Having placed the vessel in the middle of the fire, one should cook it slowly with a mild flame; when the food therein is cooked, then one should remove it from the fire.
Having consecrated the sacrificial porridge (caru) there with cow-ghee while reciting the heart-mantra,
and having prepared it according to the rite, one should offer oblations with all the mantras, each one once.
Having offered that oblation into the fire, he should then place the remainder of the clarified butter into his own stomach,
having presented to the Lord one-fourth of that portion.
One should cause one-third of the disciples who have observed the fast to consume it according to the rule,
without touching it with their teeth, while recollecting the five Brahmans.
Having consumed [the offering] according to the prescribed rule, the wise one should perform the rite of the funeral cakes (piṇḍa);
then, having used a tooth-stick, he should cause [the deity] to drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Having recited the ten-syllable mantra together with the limbs of the Vidyā and the Brahma-mantras, one should then recite the principal seed-syllable, and especially the Kṣurikā. (3.33)

Then, having tied the *pratisara* (protective cord) on each disciple individually, the preceptor, having honored them with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings, should sleep for the night by the side of Śiva.
Reclining upon a bed of ashes, devoted to the meditation on Śiva, [he recited]:
"Oṃ! To Śambhu, the three-eyed, the tawny-hued, the Great Soul... (3.35)
"Salutation to Vāma, who possesses all forms, the lord of dreams.
Having recited this mantra, one should likewise place the disciple upon the bed.

The practitioner of mantra should dwell at the site of sacrifice together with his disciples in the presence of Śiva. Then, in the morning, whatever dream was seen by the guru during the night [should be reported].
Having related the dream as it truly is, whether auspicious or inauspicious, one obtains happiness regarding auspicious dreams; this is the worldly fruit for the disciples.
If it is inauspicious, then liberation is not attained;
in that case, the entire initiation sacrifice must be performed using the disciple's own wealth, devoid of any worldly success.
Having abandoned the boundary-tie and performed the ritual bath according to the rules at night,
one should subsequently draw the maṇḍala at dawn.
Having seen that, the embodied soul is liberated from the bondage of all fetters—
whether it be one cubit, two cubits, four cubits, or eight cubits.

The twelfth and the sixteenth cubit are considered the limits; one should not construct [the image] beyond that. Having tied the intervals of the measuring lines, one should mark off two or three parts. || 3-42 ||
One should cause the laying of the thread to be performed with the Vāmadeva mantra;
having fixed the thread in the eastern and western directions, one should remain composed. (3.43)
Then, having stretched out the auspicious *tatvasūtra* extending from south to north,
one should then take up its thread as it is fashioned by the hermitage.
One should stretch a thread there from east to north,
and having cast a thread originating in the southeast, one should extend it to the northwest.
One should extend the originating thread from the northeast to the southwest;
having made it a perfect square, let it be divided into nine parts.
One should draw it upon the pericarp (*karṇikā*) of the lotus using its middle portion;
that lotus, adorned with eight petals, should consist of four parts. (3–47)
The first part is the pericarp; the second is indeed the filaments; the third is at the junctions of the petals; and the fourth is the tips of the petals. (3.48)
The wise one should draw a line outside the lotus in the enclosure of the image;
such is the measurement of the lotus, because Śiva is infinite.
In a small [temple], it should be made small; in a large one, it should be extensive.
Furthermore, the procedure may be according to half the measurement of a lotus or according to the full measurement of a lotus.
The *vīdhyāsa* becomes the *padma*; the *śobhā* rests upon the *padma*.
On the cheeks equal to those [of the *padma*], there are the *śobhā* and the *upaśobhā* which are equal to it. (3.51)
The fifth [type] has equal doors specifically on all four sides; it should be two cubits or one cubit [in width], and one should avoid making it larger than that. (3.52)

Having constructed the temple of the God so that it is neither too thick nor too thin, not deficient, and free from crookedness or flaws, it is said that such a structure bestows the attainment of liberation.
A thick [line] is said to portend all manner of fear; one should indicate quarrels in the mouth.
A deficient [line], however, indicates a lack of success, while at the bindu it is a source of fear from enemies.
When the [figure] is emaciated, disease arises; when there is a mixture of colors, famine occurs.
There will be no prosperity, and there will be no splendor from the king when the thread is thin. (3.55)
Therefore, with every effort, one should perform [the rite] endowed with the proper characteristics;
white, red, and black thread—silver is likewise remembered as being of three kinds. (3.56)
On the left are Jyeṣṭhā and Raudrī, the presiding deities of the letters;
for the sake of illuminating the moment, there is the descent of the white color. (3.57)
For the purpose of generating passion for that [object], one should cast down a red-colored [image];
however, for one who is dominated by tamas, having turned away from it, one should cast down a black-colored [image]. (3.58)
To ensure their attainment of the fruit of the sacrifice, one should cause a yellow-colored [mark] to fall, having drawn it with white and other colors, struck by the little finger. (3.59)
Another sūtra has declared that [the movement] is like a barley grain; it is remembered as being shorter than short.
One seeking liberation should perform it with the left hand, while one seeking worldly enjoyment should do so with the right.
One should write with the supreme "Fist of Śrīkāma," which grants all accomplishments, especially using white-colored substances mixed with powdered pearls. (3.61)
A red color is praised when made with the powder of ruby;
a black color is proclaimed when made with the powder of sapphire. (3.62)
The color of Umā is described as being from powdered gold;
in its absence, it may be made with powdered conch-shell or with powders of the *jāti* flower.
With powders of black collyrium and powders of realgar;
or, in the absence of those powders, with powders of rice grains. (3.64)
Then, with powders of baked bricks and powders of burnt rice,
one should indeed fashion a lotus here using powders of turmeric.
With a pericarp of yellow color and filaments resembling gold,
there are twenty-five filaments upon it, each raised by the measure of a barley grain.
The filaments are like the thread of saffron, while those above and below are white in color;
the eight petals of the lotus are white, and indeed black within the intervening lines.
On both sides of the lines, the edges should likewise be red;
then, the path surrounding the lotus should be of red color.
The doors should be made yellow in color, and on both sides of the doors,
one should have the *śobhās* and *upaśobhās* fashioned using all colors.
Thus, when the lines have been completed, the wise one should invoke Śiva;
having worshipped Sadāśiva in the center with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
Having fully worshipped the enclosure of the womb (garbhāvaraṇa), one should then worship the enclosure of the Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśāvaraṇa),
followed by the enclosure of Gaṇeśa, and thereafter the enclosure of the World-Guardians (lokeśāvaraṇa).
In this manner, one should worship the armor of weapons according to the prescribed rule;
having worshipped Īśvara on the right, one should worship Gaurī on his left.
The procedure for the mandala has been declared; now hear the procedure for initiation.
Thus ends the third chapter, on the procedure for the mandala.
(p. 247) Now follows the chapter on the procedure for initiation (dīkṣā).
Hereafter I shall explain specifically the path of initiation:
for [through it] that state of Śiva is bestowed, and the cage of sins is destroyed. (4.1)
Because it possesses the specific quality of destroying [impurities], it is called *dīkṣā*.
Having worshipped the mandala, one should then perform the worship of the fire in front of it.
Having offered oblations into the Śiva-fire according to the rules, as previously prescribed by the ritual procedure,
he should then initiate the disciples in the proper order, beginning with the Brāhmaṇas.
One who possesses the characteristics of a teacher, is wise, knows the Śaiva Siddhānta, is a lifelong celibate (naiṣṭhika), and is a knower of Śiva-yoga, is the supreme guru for all. (4-4)
Having bathed well, the knower of Śiva-mantras, with his body consecrated through the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa,
should first perform the sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) and then administer the initiation on another day.
Having worshipped according to the prescribed rules, he should perform the second initiation for his disciples;
then, after those disciples—beginning with the Brahmins—have bathed cleanly and have their senses subdued.
Having strewn flowers and *kuśa* grass upon the mandala facing north,
one should sprinkle it with auspicious water, using the *astra-mantra* on the fingers and with sacred ash.
One should burn the entire body with the fire of time (*kālāgni*), like dry wood;
then, one should perform the rite of immolation for him using the seed-syllable of Śiva and the mudrā. (4–8)
Having touched the heart with the *hṛdaya* mantra, the head with the *śiras*,
the crest-lock (*śikhā*) with the *śikhā*, and the space between the breasts with the *kavaca*.
Having touched eye with eye and having remembered [the deity] in all the limbs,
the Hand of Śiva (śivahasta) should be bestowed, consecrated by the Īśāna mantra.
The wise one should cause their hands to rest upon his head three times;
having honored them with perfumes and other offerings, this is called *prokṣaṇa*.
Having constructed a square mandala before him,
adorned it with flour-dust, and strewn it with darbha grass and flowers.
The wise one, having placed Īśāna in the central position, Aindra (Vaktra) in the east, Aghora in the south, and Sadyojāta in the west, [should proceed]. (4.13)
In the north is Vāmadeva, and then the Heart in the southeast;
the Brahma-head is in the southwest, and the Tuft-mantra (Śikhā) in the region of the northwest. (4-14)
One should perform the rite of armor (kavaca) in the direction of the Lord (Īśa), using the respective names;
then, facing the deity, one should address the disciples whose bodies have been smeared with holy ashes.

Having wrapped the eyes with new cloths while reciting the Netra-mantra, one should provide flowers of the corresponding color for the disciples, beginning with the Brahmins, according to their respective castes.

Having cast [the flower] into the center of the maṇḍala while reciting the Śiva-mantra, [one should determine] upon which [deity] the king's flower falls; that [deity] is then of the nature of his name and lineage.
The faces of Īśāna, Vidyeśāna, Ghora, Brahmā, Sadyojāta, Rudra, and Vāma, along with the syllable Huṃ—these are said to be the nine names. (4.18)

For the four castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇa, the initiation name is prescribed to end with a word signifying a group (gaṇa) and beginning with Śiva; for women, it is prescribed to end with the name of a Śakti.
For those who have reached the final goal, there is a distinction regarding their sphere of activity (*gocara*) and the lineage succession (*gotrasantati*).
Śiva, the topknot (*śikhā*), as well as light (*jyotis*) and Sāvitrī—these are the spheres of activity. (4.20)
The lineage (gotra) for the four beginning with Dūrvāsas is said to be of that same color;
as for what is proclaimed in the Caryāpāda, that is the Sūtra spoken by Śiva.
The teacher, the sphere of activity, the lineage, and the sūtra are prescribed for those initiates as previously described; the Guru stands facing them. (4.22)
Having first performed the ritual placement on the hands (*karanyāsa*), one should carry out the burning and flooding;
then, having performed the placement of the thirty-eight energies (*kalānyāsa*) as previously described.

One should perform the placement (nyāsa) of the heart, the six limbs, and the five Brahmans; thereafter, one should perform the placement of the Rudra-mantra consisting of ten parts and the Prāsāda mantra.
Having thus conceived the six paths as the face of Śiva, how could it not be so? [One should assign] from the hand up to the water-vessel (pāna) in sequence, starting from one's own head.
Then, one should place each [of these] individually within the bodies of his disciples;
having thus performed the purification of the six paths (ṣaḍadhva), one should subsequently carry out the fire sacrifice (homa).
The path of reality (tattvādhvan), the path of words (padādhvan), the path of phonemes (varṇādhvan) consisting of the worlds,
the path of mantras (mantrādhvan), and the path of kalās (kalādhvan)— one should offer one hundred oblations for each of these.

With the respective mantras of the Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśas), with the respective mantras of the Lords of the Gaṇas (gaṇeśas), with the respective mantras of the World-Guardians (lokeśas), and with the mantras of the ten weapons (daśāstras). || 4-28 ||
The wise one should offer oblations with clarified butter, one hundred for each [deity].
If one is unable to do so, one should instead perform the initiation (dīkṣā) therein.
Having caused them to hear the pledges in the presence of the God of gods,
one should always cause those who have been initiated to enter the irreproachable Śiva-scripture.
One must not transgress against the teacher or those who are senior; likewise, one should avoid sexual union with a woman who has not been initiated. (4.31)
One should not consume the remains of offerings (nirmālya), nor should one revile that which is associated with sacred ash;
these eight observances (samayas) are proclaimed for those who have been initiated.
For these must likewise be observed; listen to the words of those who have been initiated:
one should possess good character and excellent conduct, as well as devotion to Śiva and [reverence for] the guru. (4.33)
When one has devotion to the Śiva scriptures, as well as patience and mastery over the senses—if these eight qualities exist in a man, he attains the supreme goal. (4.34)
Those who, out of delusion, do not protect [the precepts] go deeply into hell;
however, having performed the offering to the guardians of the directions (dikpāla) there, provided with perfumes, flowers, and other such items— || 4-35 ||
Then, together with their wives and disciples, and joined by their own labor,
having thus performed according to the rules, the fire-oblation (homa) is thereafter proclaimed.

Having prepared the Śiva-fire as before, the knower of mantras, having summoned the disciples, should worship them while they are seated facing him with water for the guest-offering (arghya), water for the feet (pādya), and other honors. || 4.37 ||
I shall now explain this as it truly is; listen presently to its fivefold nature.
Among all those who have spoken, she alone is declared to be the most excellent. (4.38)
Earth, water, fire, air, and space are said to be the five principles (tattvas) by which Śiva is established, beginning from time (kāla). (4.39)
The Pārthiva [kalā] is indeed situated in Nivṛtti; Śatarudra is established in Āpatti; Vidyā extends as far as Prakṛti within the human [body]. (4-40)
The principle of fire (tejas) is indeed to be known through knowledge (vidyā), extending as far as Vidyēśvara;
but the principle of air (vāyu) is to be understood through command (śāsti), extending from there up to Sadāśiva.
The wise one should know that up to the end of the *śakti* is called the *nābhi* (navel) by the *śāntyatītā*; *nivṛtti* extends to the knees, and *pratiṣṭhā* ends at the navel. (4-42)
Vidyā indeed extends thus to the edge of the ears, while Śānti extends to the edge of the mouth;
beyond Śānti, however, above that, is the state ending with Parāparaśiva.

One should perform the rite of cessation (nivṛtti) with the Sadyojāta mantra, consecration (pratiṣṭhā) with the Vāmadeva mantra, the oblation for knowledge (vidyā) with the Aghora mantra, and peace (śānti) with the Tatpuruṣa mantra.
Then, for the sake of pacification and transcendence, the wise one should offer oblations with the Īśāna mantra;
having offered one hundred for each [deity], or half of that, or even half of that again.
In this very way, having offered oblations with the five principles, the wise one should offer a hundred oblations with the heart-mantra for the destruction of other births.
Therefore, the state of being a bound animal (paśutva) is destroyed, and indeed the state of Śiva is attained.
Then, having offered the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with the five Brahmans themselves— || 4.47 ||
Having thus completed that initiation, hear now about the consecration (abhiṣeka),
which is performed in a well-decorated pavilion, [the candidate] being adorned with all ornaments.
Having prepared the Śiva-fire as before, one should perform the consecration (abhiṣeka),
[constructing the altar] from one cubit up to five cubits, according to one's means.
Having established the kula-vessels according to the procedure for the ritual bath,
one should place the disciple’s seat, firmly secured, upon the auspicious throne (bhadrapīṭha).
Having worshipped according to the rule and performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) according to the prescribed method,
the teacher is always formless (niṣkala), while the practitioner is always with form (sakala).
Then the best of preceptors should perform his consecration in this manner,
using the ten-syllable mantra and the eight peak syllables in their proper sequence.
Then, according to his means, having bathed [the image] with auspicious rites for a fortunate day (*puṇyāha*), the mantra-practitioner, adorned in white garments, should proceed. (4–53)
Having worshipped with perfumes and flowers, and remaining upon the yoga-seat,
one should bind on a fine turban made of pure white cloth.
The forehead-plate should be given as prescribed for a king,
along with a crown, earrings, and all other types of ornaments.
One who knows the ritual procedure should hold an umbrella over [the head] and wave a fly-whisk;
however, if even these materials are unavailable, one should fashion them out of *darbha* grass.
Alternatively, one should mentally contemplate everything with the Śiva-mantra:
the rudrākṣa beads, the sacred thread, the turban, and the upper garment. (4-57)
A book, a sacrificial ladle (sruk) and spoon (sruva), a small knife (karaṇī), and likewise scissors;
as well as the worship of Śiva, the fire-ritual (agnikārya), and recitation and meditation according to one's ability.
The teacher, having bestowed upon the disciple the state of full authority, should always perform the favor of providing this explanation. (4.59)
Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras born of pure lineages are to be known as those who may receive the preceptor’s [initiation], but never others. (4.60)
The knowledge of the recitation and meditation of all mantras, cultivated through true being,
is to be understood as equal for all, just as it is for those initiated at a sacrifice through the *hotr* and other rites.
In this manner, by the power of the mantra, one should perform the rites of consecration;
furthermore, one should initiate members of the four castes and others into the Śiva sacrifice.

Having thoroughly understood both the direct and reverse orders, the Guru should initiate [the disciple], having given a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the Guru while avoiding any stinginess regarding wealth. (4.63)
Clothing and ornaments, as well as a crown and earrings, a golden sacred thread, and an offering of golden flowers. || 4.64 ||
One should cause the hand gestures (mudrās), beds, seats, and so forth to be offered to the Ācārya.
O Vināyaka, listen to the sixteen rites pertaining to them according to their true nature. 4-65.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, the Chapter on the Ritual of Initiation.
Now begins the sixteenth chapter on the ritual procedures.
Hereafter, I shall fully explain the sixteen rites for the Śaivas—
those mortals who, through their fitness for initiation, are established in the sacrifice of Śiva.
Of these, sixteen have been proclaimed by Śiva, the Supreme Self:
the first is the union during the fertile period (ṛtusaṅgamana), and the second is the impregnation (garbhādhāna).
The Puṃsavana rite is the third, while the Sīmanta is indeed the fourth;
the Jātakarman is the fifth, and the Utthāna is the sixth.
(252) The naming ceremony is the seventh [rite], the first feeding of solid food is the eighth;
the tonsure may take place in the ninth month, and the rite of increasing the funeral cakes is in the tenth. (5.4)
After that comes the return home (samāvartana), and marriage shall be the sixteenth.
These sixteen [rites], indeed, I shall describe individually and concisely.
In the first period following menstruation, sexual union is likewise permitted;
however, after three nights have passed during that fertile period, she becomes pure on the fourth day.
If the menses occur during the first part of the night, one should accept that night;
however, if they occur during the latter part of the night, one should avoid that night.
On the first day she is a Caṇḍālī; on the second, a slayer of a Brahmin;
on the third, she is called a washerwoman; on the fourth day, she becomes pure.
For three nights, she who has been defiled by impurity must avoid bathing and other such rites;
eating but one meal a day, she shall not drink water from a broken vessel nor from her cupped hands.
On the day of the planetary inspection, one should not sleep during the day nor eat with a small piece of wood;
then, on the fourth [day], having bathed with myrobalan and other substances, one should use a tooth-stick and so forth.
One should not speak to women or Śūdras who are adorned with clean garments, ointments, and the like; however, one may look at a woman who has bathed, for by doing so one obtains such a son.
If she should not see another [object] than that, she should instead show it to him;
and in the case of a maiden, she should do so for the first time while adorned with all her ornaments. (5.12)
Having performed the auspicious rites as instructed by the scriptures, especially that [rite],
one should prepare the Śiva-fire as before, according to the previously stated procedure.
Having established Śiva in the center and worshipped him in due order as before,
one should perform the fire oblation (homa) in this manner with the Brahma-mantras, which are the limbs of Śiva.
Having performed the ritual interval after her bath at the end of her season, she stood there on the left;
having bathed well and sipped water according to the rules, her body was smeared with sacred ashes.
Standing in the western direction of the fire, facing the east,
the fire that has been worshipped by the preceptor is then offered oblations with the mantra.
Then, one should perform the ritual sprinkling (pariṣeka) after consecrating it with the limbs of the Vidyā;
or indeed, having offered oblations (homa) one thousand or one hundred and eight times with the five Brahmans.
One should mark the edge of the cloth and place the sacrificial oblation there;
on the right side of the nose for a son, and on the other side for a daughter. (5.18)
One should not practice celibacy (nirvīvana) [in this context], and one should avoid both desiccation and anger;
having made the resolve solely for the sake of a son, never for the sake of sensual enjoyment. (5.19)
They declare that [the period] lasts until the end of the twelfth or the sixteenth day from the onset of menstruation;
having omitted the first three days as primary, it begins on the arrival of the fourth day. (5.20)
Know that in the case of an even [number of days] there is a male, and likewise in the case of an uneven [number] there is female offspring;
through an increase of semen a male is born, while through an increase of blood female offspring is produced. (5.21)
If the blood and semen are equal, however, a eunuch is produced there;
it is like a male pine bud, so too is that which has entered the womb. (5.22)
The drop (bindu) located within the womb is split in two by the wind;
having taken up the embryo in two parts, the body clearly becomes twofold. (5.23)
Lifespan, karma, wealth, and so forth indeed proceed according to the Lord;
the union during the fertile period has been declared—now hear concerning the rite of conception (garbhādhāna).
Learn from me the symptoms of a woman who has recently conceived:
she experiences bodily distension and distress, and she feels aversion toward her husband. (5.25)
Here, at the source of Ciṅkhara, endowed with a throbbing vibration, he beheld her whose womb was visible, surrounded by auspicious stars. || 5-26 ||
Having worshipped Agni as before, one should offer one hundred and eight oblations with the *sadyas* mantra, having offered barley,
milk, curd, and ghee in equal proportions.
This, however, has been declared as the well-known [rite]: one should cause [the victim] to swallow [it] with the mantra of Īśa;
having performed the sakalīkaraṇa of his wife, one should touch her belly with the Puruṣa-mantra.
This is declared to be the rite of conception (garbhādhāna); now hear concerning the rite for ensuring a male child (puṃsavana).
It should be performed in the second month, or in the first, or again in the fourth month of pregnancy. (5.29)
When there is a conjunction with an auspicious lunar mansion, having propitiated the fire as before,
one should offer oblations a thousand times or eight hundred times with the Vāmadeva mantra.
There, one should cause beans and grain to enter both separately and together,
having indeed thoroughly ground them with sacrificial tree buds mixed with milk.
The wise man, having meditated upon Śiva, should cause that substance to be placed by his wife into her nostril using a new cloth, while reciting the Vāmadeva mantra. (5.32)
Having fed the Śaivas, one should then worship the preceptor (ācārya).
Thus the *puṃsavana* rite is declared; now hear concerning the *sīmantonnayana*.
In the fourth, sixth, or eighth month, one should perform the *sīmantonnayana* rite;
or, under an auspicious constellation, one should perform the fire ritual as previously described.
Having offered one hundred and eight oblations with the Aghora mantra, the Vyāhṛtis are then offered there;
having tied darbha grass, udumbara wood, garlands, and so forth [to the head], this is performed during the Simantonnayana rite.
Having drawn [the design] from the forehead to the middle and the end of the head, one should complete it;
that rite should be performed with a limb of the Vidyā, and one should cause a new cloth to be given.
Having worshipped with golden garlands and perfumes, one should then perform the *sīmantonnayana* (parting of the hair) in front, facing east, while reciting the Īśa mantra, as previously prescribed.
After a man has touched water and recited the Śiva-mantra, the *sīmanta* rite is thus declared; now hear concerning the *jātakarman* (birth ceremony).
Having inspected the maternity room and performed the purification according to ancient tradition,
one should fumigate the interior of the house with the powder of sesame and mustard seeds.
Then, one should cause the woman who has recently given birth to enter with eight young women,
having worshipped the essence of the planets while remaining unaware of their specific positions.
If the prince is being born,
one should offer a hundred oblations with the weapon-mantra (astra) for the sake of protection from others and for his complete safeguarding.
Once the son is born, having meditated upon Śiva, one should show his face with the left hand;
then, having cut the umbilical cord with the Astra-mantra and purified the limbs, indeed.
Having recited the five Brahmans, one should sprinkle [the water] upon the head of the son;
then, having muttered the Tatpuruṣa mantra into his right ear.

Having given [the offering] mixed with honey, clarified butter, and molasses, as well as the Brahma-vessel, and having bound it with golden darbha grass, they [should offer] that very clarified butter along with the heart-mantra.
Having given [the offering] with the mantra "hiraṇyarūpā," the best of practitioners should give it;
having placed it in the hand of the Mother, he should wash her breasts with the *sadyojāta* mantra. (5.45)
The right breast should be offered with the mantra "praśāntāya";
having worshipped the jar right there with the Aghora weapon mantra.
A wise person should place a vessel full of water at the site of the arrow for the sake of protection;
one should offer oblations there, untiringly, both morning and evening for ten nights.
This task must indeed be performed for one's master day after day;
every three, five, or seven days, one should clean the beds and other such items. (5.48)
This birth-rite (jātakarman) has been declared; now hear, O one of good conduct, about the rite of rising (utthāna).
When ten nights have passed, having performed the rite of rising... (5.49)
One should diligently avoid all such substances and vessels made of clay, wood, iron, and so forth; this is called impurity of mind. (5.50)
Having purified the cloth with compassion and purified the gold with ashes,
one should take hold of it and smear it with water mixed with clay and cow dung.
Having performed the rite of shaving for the couple while they are still in their soiled state,
the wise man should then perform the ritual bath followed by the circumambulation with fire (paryagnikaraṇa).
Having cast away the old vessels, one should cause [the practitioner] to consume the five products of the cow (pañcagavya);
then, having caused the proclamation of an auspicious day (puṇyāha), one should sprinkle the people in due order.
Having placed Kuśa-grass water in a shallow bowl along with the groups of Śiva-mantras,
he should have that water, which has become Śiva himself, drunk by the couple in succession.
This is declared to be the rite of awakening; now hear the instruction regarding the names.
The instruction on the names is performed sequentially on either the eleventh or the twelfth lunar day.
Having duly established the Śiva-fire, the knower of mantras, having touched his son,
should perform the naming ceremony for the son, dedicating it to the deity.
The first is Mahādeva, the second is Maheśvara,
the third is declared to be Śaṅkara, and the fourth is Vṛṣabhadhvaja.
The fifth is Kṛttivāsas, while the sixth is indeed Kāmanāśana;
the seventh is Devadeveśa, and Śrīkaṇṭha is remembered as the eighth.
The ninth is declared to be Īśvara, the tenth is Pārvatī’s beloved;
Rudra is the eleventh, and likewise Śiva is the twelfth.
p. 256) A wise person should recite these twelve names, ending with Śiva, which are the names of liberation, in the presence of the fire, starting from Kṛttikā. (5–60)

With *dūrvā* sprouts mixed with unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), one should cause [the disciple] to apply [the ashes] from the feet up to the head upon the right or left hand, identifying them with the limbs of Śiva.
Having uttered the Śiva-mantra according to the name of the girl's Śakti—
Ambikā, Pārvatī, Gaurī, and Bhavānī, who is worshipped by the gods— 5-62.
Dākṣāyaṇī, Haimavatī, Mahādevī, Haripriyā, Umā, and Śivakarī— these are indeed the twelve forms of Girijā.
One should apply the name Śakti to those beginning with Kṛttikā;
having performed the worship of the Ācārya, one should fully honor those devotees of Śiva.

The declaration of the name has been explained; now hear concerning the rite of first feeding with solid food (annaprāśana). This rite of annaprāśana should be performed in the sixth month under an auspicious lunar mansion.
On an auspicious day and at a favorable moment, one should not touch a child with food remnants;
rather, having worshipped the fire as before with cooked food, milk, and clarified butter, [one should proceed].
The wise one, using the seed mantra, should especially feed all people with milk-rice (pāyasa) served in a vessel of bell-metal.
A wise man should have the food for the *homa* prepared, but not the food for the act of eating.
Such is the procedure for the first feeding of solid food; now hear concerning the departure on a journey. (5–68)
On that day, at an auspicious moment, during a delightful gathering,
one should first perform the establishment of the sacred fire (agnyādhāna) and then offer oblations one hundred and eight times with the Sadyojāta mantra.
Having adorned both father and son, especially with auspicious sounds,
the father should smell the crown of his son's head while reciting the Tatpuruṣa mantra.
Then, having recited the Śiva-mantra, he should go slowly to the temple;
and having prostrated before the one containing the bull with the Vṛṣagāyatrī mantra, [he should proceed]. (5.71)
Having paid homage to the God of gods together with his son and kinsmen,
he then went to the cave-dwelling and bowed down before the imperishable Guha.
Having led the planet very slowly and performed protection with ashes, I shall describe the Piṇḍavardhana rite; the installation of the fire is as before.
Having offered oblations one hundred and eight times according to the rule with the *brahmaśiras* mantra, one should proceed from the right thumb in due order up to the *īśāna* [face]. (5.74)
Having performed the recitation, the wise man should likewise perform the rite with the ten-syllable mantra,
diligently feeding the devotees of Śiva with sweet substances and liquids.
Thus indeed is the Piṇḍavardhana; now hear about the rite of shaving (kṣurakarma):
in the third year, under an auspicious lunar mansion, on a favorable lunar day, and during the northern course of the sun.
On the day prior to that [rite], one should again perform the *dīkṣāmukha* for the *caula*,
the *upanayana*, and likewise for the *samāvartana*.
At their marriage ceremony, the Nāndīmukha rite is prescribed first;
having invoked the ancestors and the deities, one should worship them with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
Having thus mentally resolved [the offerings] for the fathers, grandfathers, and great-grandfathers by means of these names, following the sequence according to the disposition toward Śiva.
Having thus performed the *nāndīmukha* rite and given a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) according to one's ability,
one should sprinkle [the site] with water while reciting the *astra-mantra*, bind it, and fasten the *pratisara* at night.
At dawn, for the purpose of the tonsure ceremony, the most excellent of men should prepare a sacrificial mound there;
having duly offered oblations into the Śiva-fire, he should perform eight hundred oblations to Rudrāṇī.
Having placed that child to the east of the fire, one should worship it with cow products and the like;
then, with cries of "Hara, Hara" and auspicious utterances.
Having performed the offering of ghee upon the head with *dūrvā* grass, unbroken rice, and other items, along with hymns of praise,
and having touched the razor with the *astra-mantra*, the father should have both the son and himself shaved.
One should likewise place the [substances] beginning with Īśa and Aja on the knees, and those beginning with Śiva and Brahmā on the [other] knees;
then, one should cast the respective hair-roots into the middle of the vessel containing the cow's urine and semen.
Know that the crest-lock (śikhā) in the middle of the head consists of twenty-five parts;
having made the crest-lock perfectly circular, one leaves the remainder and has it bound upward.
Also during travel abroad, at the Piṇḍavardhana rite, at the tonsure ceremony (caulakarma), at auspicious occasions, and when one possesses faith and wealth. || 5.86 ||
Then, for the virgins, one should perform the fire sacrifice (homa) with the mantra;
likewise, the ritual bath should be performed there, excluding the protective cord (pratisara).

Having adorned him with garments and other items, such as turmeric, perfumes, and flowers, one should worship him, seated comfortably to the east of the fire, with unbroken rice and other offerings. || 5.88 ||
Having offered [the oblations] with the Śiva-mantra a thousand or a hundred times, the wise one should then perform the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with the same mantra as previously mentioned. (5.89)
Thereafter, one should honor the preceptor and cause him to receive a cow along with its calf.
Having collected cow dung together with its blood and hair, mixed with grain,
one should place it in the middle of the mud while facing the cows.
Or, having performed [the rite] at the root of a *darbha* or *udumbara* tree, one should rinse the mouth and enter again.
This rite of the *caula* has been declared; now hear concerning the *upānayana*.
It should take place from the time one year has passed until the fifth, sixth, or seventh year. (5.92)
In the eighth or ninth year, respectively, one attains knowledge of one's true nature,
as well as spiritual luster, longevity, and especially the bestowal of prosperity.
Alternatively, one should perform the initiation ceremony (upanayana) up until the end of the sixteenth year;
however, once the sixteenth year has passed, one should perform it at the end of the period of study (uddālānta).
Having eaten barley gruel for two months, one should cause milk to be given for one month;
one should consume half of the curdled milk daily.
When the milk has been curdled, it is known as *sāmīkṣikā*.
One should let it ferment on the ground for eight nights, using either black or tawny cow's milk. (5.96)
In the Dvāpara Yuga, when [the age] has passed, one should remain standing for six nights, likewise subsist on water for three nights, and observe a fast for one day and night.
O Vināyaka, one should perform the single-vṛtta rite according to the sequence of Uddālaka;
the bath at the conclusion of the Vācāśvamedha is performed with these words for the two of us.
One should perform this rite of conception (garbhādhāna) in due order as previously described;
it should be carried out during the spring or during the northern course of the sun.
On an auspicious lunar mansion, especially at a favorable moment (muhūrta),
the rite of sowing the germinating seeds (aṅkurārpaṇa) should be performed here either within seven days or on the fifth day.
One should likewise prepare the sacrificial cord (upavīta), the deerskin (ajina), the girdle of muñja grass (mauñjī), and the staff (daṇḍa).
I shall now describe the procedure for the sacrificial cord, as well as the turban and the upper garment.
And when there is an auspicious conjunction of the lunar mansions, one should diligently cause those [images] to be bathed by a Brāhmaṇa woman, a princess, or again, a Vaiśya maiden. (5.102)
The thread should be spun by three [virgins], or else by a Śūdra girl;
a thread spun by any other woman must be avoided with great care.
Alternatively, the supreme practitioner should collect the thread for the ritual activities;
at the time of collecting the thread, he should purify it with water and ashes. (5.104)
The wise one, having commenced in the forenoon, [should prepare] the thread with the *sadyojāta* mantra;
it should be ninety-six threads, each measuring four finger-breadths.
That triple-stranded thread which has been smeared with the [sacred] substances is here called the *sūtra*;
standing facing east and west, one [draws it] toward the south and north. (5.106)
First, the right hand is indeed placed above the back;
subsequently, the left hand is likewise placed above, specifically at the end of the three-fold [sequence].
Having cast it on the ground or elsewhere, and having placed a leaf, flower, or blade of grass with its tip pointing east and its base pointing north, it is rendered subject to one's will.
Having sprinkled it with the Vāmadeva mantra, one should take up the rope as an implement;
[measuring] from the neck and the hands across, from the thumb to the end of the arm.
That cord is equal in length to one sūtra and consists of three strands; it serves as the sacred thread (upavītaka).
Vāgdevī is well-established within that knot of the rope.
Sāvitrī and Gāyatrī shall dwell at the top and the root [of the thread];
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra are the deities of the three threads.
Having bound it with the Aghora weapon-mantra, one should hold it with the Bahurūpa mantra;
it should be wound clockwise around the navel and above the navel according to the rule.
That thread for celibate students (*brahmacārin*) consists of six strands, while for householders (*gṛhastha*) it is likewise six.
For forest-dwellers (*vānaprastha*), nine [folds] are prescribed, and for ascetics (*yati*), twelve are traditionally taught.
The rule for the sacred thread (*upavīta*) has been declared; now hear about the upper garment (*uttarīya*).
It should be made from a cloth of three white stripes, and it should be worn like the sacred thread.
This is declared to be the upper garment (uttarīya), while the turban (uṣṇīṣa) shall be described here:
having extended it from below up to the head, one should effortlessly cover both ears with it. (5.115)
The head-wrapping with a soft white cloth is declared to have the characteristics of a turban; now listen to [the description of] the black antelope skin.
The hide of a black antelope is for the purpose of a leather garment and not for any other use; however, one who is free from disease may certainly die naturally of his own accord. (5.117)
The black antelope skin is prescribed as being three finger-breadths long, or equally [in length], and likewise one finger-breadth in width; its length is equal to that of the sacred thread. (5.118)
Having recited the *sadyo* mantra, one should bind it with a leather cord or even a cotton cord; listen now to the truth regarding the girdle (*mekhalā*). (5.119)
Having taken a muñja-grass cord situated in a pure place, one should then dry it;
having pierced it with the point of a needle, it becomes a threefold rope wound three times.
The girdle has been described in brief; now hear the characteristics of the staff (daṇḍa):
it may be made of Palāśa, Bilva, Khadira, Śamī, or Vaikaṅkata wood. || 5.121 ||
It should be straight and smooth, joined with leather, neither too short nor too long, and equal in length to his own white arm. || 5.122 ||
Having first performed the *nāndīmukha* rite, and at its conclusion the initiation (*upanayana*),
one should then establish the *śivāgni* as before and have the hair shaved according to the rules for the tonsure ceremony (*caula*).
Having removed the hairs that have fallen face-downward, leaving behind only the topknot and the eyebrows,
one should perform the bath right there while adorned with all ornaments.
Having fed the wise [disciples] with the sacrificial porridge (caru) for the sake of purifying the body,
the learned one should then place the ritual marks, such as the sacred thread (upavīta), upon them in the proper sequence.
The supreme preceptor, having sprinkled the pure vessels with mantras,
then summons the disciple and positions him to the south of the fire.
Having sprinkled [the disciple] with the five Brahmamantras while reciting the *śucī vo havyam* mantra,
he should worship the disciple facing north with unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*) and other offerings.
I shall begin the primary rite preceded by the sprinkling (pariṣecana).
For each limb of Brahmā and for the Goddess, there are five oblations (āhuti) performed with the fire-drills (tapanī).
The sprinkling must be performed; one should worship Śivā with perfumes and other offerings.
Having indeed tied that new rope as a girdle with the mantra "iyaṃ raktā," || 5.129 ||
Having fashioned the cloth like a loincloth with the remainder hanging down the back,
he himself should recite that mantra and cause the sacred thread (upavīta) to be given.
Having donned the black antelope skin, the wise one should offer it as an upper garment with the mantra: "To the Tranquil One. (5.131)
p. 261) His crown-protrusion (uṣṇīṣa) is without tantra; however, for those in other stages of life (āśrama), that [protrusion] exists.
Having applied the staff with the weapon-mantra, it is purified on the ring finger. (5.132)
Having circumambulated the fire and paid special obeisance to it,
he should wash his feet according to the rules and perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) twice with particular care.

One who knows the mantras should drink the *brahmakūrca*—the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) combined with *kuśa* grass—while reciting the *Śiva-mantra*. This is what is traditionally known as *brahmakūrca*. (5.134)
Having sipped water again according to the rule, [one performs] the binding of the girdle with the Sāvitrī;
indeed, one circumambulates the head while the five Brahmans are offered as oblations.
Having offered an oblation with the mantra "sāvitrī kāṇḍarṣayaḥ," and having then recited the Sāvitrī and Gāyatrī mantras eight times, he should thereafter [release] this binding of the hair.
Having circumambulated the fire and paid homage according to the rule,
and having performed the sprinkling around it, one should offer a hundred oblations with the Śiva-weapon mantra.
Having indeed broken the vessel into a hundred pieces with [the mantra] consecrated a hundred times, one should perform the sprinkling; thereafter, [one should recite] the Gāyatrī and the Vyāhṛtis.
Having prostrated before the God of gods and the gurus in due order as is fitting, one should perform the oblation correctly with the limbs of Brahmā, seven times for each.
Therefore, one should honor the teacher according to one's means; indeed, a person should give an alms-bowl adorned with gold and other precious materials. (5.140)
The staff is in his left hand, while the alms-bowl is in his right;
having spoken the words "Give alms" separately to each person, he proceeds. (5.141)
One may accept rice for one's own sake when receiving it from a donor;
however, during a journey, one may strike cattle and other animals with a staff.
Having bathed well according to the rule and sipped water (ācamana), one who knows the procedure should always perform the daily rite at the three times of day with the previously mentioned mantra.
In accordance with the Śaiva scriptures and following the lineage of gurus, the wise man, having become disciplined through self-restraint, should drink purified water.
Having offered arghya, accompanied by kuśa grass, flowers, and unbroken grains (akṣata), to Śivasūrya,
one should then recite the Gāyatrī mantra separately at each of the three junctions of the day.
The wise person should meditate on Śiva and recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times;
he should perform this day after day for the purification of all sins. (5.146)
One who knows the mantras of the fire should worship it well according to the prescribed rule in the evening and in the morning,
performing the rite with the spirit of the mantra, beginning with the *vyāhṛtis* and using clarified butter.
The oblation is offered with the aforementioned mantra and with sacrificial fuel-sticks (*samidh*);
thus it is prescribed for three days, and on the fourth day comes the release from the staff (*daṇḍamocana*).
Having offered eight hundred oblations with the *sadyojāta* mantra according to the previously stated procedure,
one should perform the dismissal in the morning using the aforementioned mantra.
Having removed the worn-out sacred thread and placed it to the south, O wise one,
he should arrange new sacrificial threads and other items as before.
Then, having sprinkled water according to the rule, one should offer one hundred and eight oblations with the *vyomavyāpin* mantra for Śiva, using the *śiva-mantra* and the word "svāhā. (5.151)
Having thus offered an oblation of clarified butter, which is remembered as an accessory of Śiva,
the most excellent practitioner should then request the state of celibacy at the proper time.
In that regard, within the teaching of Śiva, there are two types of celibates (brahmacārins) for the sake of peace:
the temporary (bhautika) and the lifelong (naiṣṭhika); these two are declared to be the celibates. (5.153)

The practice of lifelong celibacy (brahmacarya) is prescribed specifically for the perpetual student (naiṣṭhika), even more so than for the householder who has entered the stage of life of one still subject to worldly elements. || 5.154 ||
Having decided upon one of those two, he should again offer a hundred oblations of clarified butter;
then, having offered the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti), he should worship that [deity] every day.
Whether at a river or a lake, one should discard the sacred thread and other such items;
having bathed and sipped water according to the rule, and having bowed to the God of gods.
Then, having understood the procedure for worship and having fully worshipped the Supreme Lord,
one should thereafter worship the Lord of the gods residing in the fire according to the prescribed rite.

Having prostrated before the Guru according to the prescribed rite, one who truly honors the Guru [should know that] therein the Sadyojāta face consists of the Ṛgveda and Vāmadeva consists of the Yajurveda.
The Sāmaveda is known as the non-terrible (Aghora) face, and the Atharvaveda is remembered as [the fourth];
likewise, Śiva is composed of all the gods, is the Lord (Īśāna), and is endowed with his limbs.
(263) Here, the Kāmika and other Āgamas are declared to be directly identical with Śiva; these very studies are remembered as that very study itself. (5.160)
For him, teaching these very subjects here is indeed his act of teaching;
likewise, for Śiva, worship consists of performing sacrifices and officiating at them.
Whatever substance is given for the sake of Śiva, as well as that very act of giving, or the acceptance [of it]—that is called his sixfold duty (ṣaṭkarma). || 5.162 ||
For the wise and pure Śaiva who is endowed with the true nature of Śiva, one should not practice any other sūtra, even those beginning with the purificatory rites (saṃskāra). || 5.163 ||
One who performs other [unauthorized] fire-offerings is excluded from all rites; knowing himself to be "fried in a pan," he should undergo initiation once again. (5.164)
Having prepared the materials for the arrow and performed the ritual for the commencement of the hunt,
and once the hunt was completed, he performed the rite of releasing the arrow.
Having first performed the rites beginning with the *samāvartana*,
and having offered the *nandīmukha* oblation into the fire, one should commence the ritual during the night.
At the end of the first watch of the night, having bound the protective amulet (pratisara) in due order with the mantra for Puruṣa itself, [one should use] one made of gold or indeed of linen.
Having sprinkled [the disciple] with the Astra-mantra, one should perform the veiling with garments;
then, having recited the Vyomavyāpin mantra, there is no dream nor any speaker.
And at dawn, having performed the subsequent rites there in that very manner, beginning with the fire as before, one should offer a hundred oblations at the root. (5.169)
A celibate student (brahmacārī), having understood his duty, should take refuge in the tranquility of a householder;
having performed a shaving of the head like that of a tonsure ceremony (caula), excluding only the topknot and the wrist-hair.
There, having bathed the tooth to be cleansed with *rajanī*,
and having offered a hundred oblations with the mantras beginning with Īśāna, he should then release the girdle of muñja grass and the other items.
Having given him that sacred thread consisting of six strands according to the previous mantra,
and having adorned him with earrings and other ornaments using the heart mantra.
Then, having offered perfumes and other items with the mantra "Vāmadeva," the wise one should apply collyrium to the eyes and show him a mirror.
