The honey-mixture (madhuparka) should be offered with the mantra "vāme veti";
then, having circumambulated the fire clockwise, one should pay homage before it. (5.174)
Having taken up his umbrella, sandals, staff, and other items, he proceeded toward the northern direction;
having turned back, he remained well-seated there on his seat together with his kinsmen.
The father, brothers, paternal uncles, and kinsmen should eat together;
that is declared to be the *samāvartana*. Now hear about the taking of the hand (*pāṇigrahaṇa*). || 5.176 ||
Marriage may take place at any time, excluding the months of Māgha and Proṣṭhapada.
Marriage has been declared to be of eight kinds by Śiva, the Supreme Self. (5.177)
The Brāhma, the Daiva, the Prājāpatya, and the Ārṣa;
the fifth is declared to be the Āsura, as well as the Gāndharva and the Rākṣasa;
the eighth should be known as the Paiśāca—these indeed are what are spoken of again.
Age, conduct, and accomplishments are perfected in one who possesses both proper behavior and noble birth. || 5.179 ||
Having invited [the groom] and given him a maiden along with cattle, land, and gold, that is designated as the Brāhma form; among marriages, it is the most excellent choice. (5.180)
In sacrifices, the giving of a daughter to the officiating priest is the divine (daivika) form of marriage;
it is for a well-behaved Brahmin who is in need of a wife. (5.181)

Having personally performed the fire-offering (homa) rites, and having intentionally given away a garment, an ornament, or a maiden, that which is thus bestowed is remembered as the Prājāpatya form of marriage. (5.182)
Having given a beautiful maiden along with a pair of cattle, or even a single pair of cattle, this is remembered as the Ārṣa form of marriage. (5.183)

When a maiden is being repeatedly asked for in marriage, the act of taking her away after having given wealth, which is the formal acceptance of the bride at that time, is known as *āropya-āharaṇa*. (5.184)
But that which is performed by the ignorant is demonic and should be recognized as such;
even when there is a union of both, if it has come about through passion between a woman and a man. (5.185)
The giving away of that very maiden by him is declared to be the Gāndharva [form of marriage], after having waged a most terrible battle involving killing, binding, and beating. (5.186)
This [is the rule] regarding the forcible abduction of a weeping maiden from among Rākṣasas;
or when a maiden is abducted by stealth while she is asleep or intoxicated. (5.187)
That which is known as Paiśāca is preceded by five libations of water;
however, among those, the first four belong to the high-souled Brāhmaṇa.
One should perform either the *āsura* rite or [the *brāhma* and *gāndharva* rites], while avoiding the other three;
[one should marry] a woman of good character, endowed with beauty, born of a noble family, and possessed of wealth. (5.189)
For a wise man, having taken a virtuous bride from a different lineage, should adorn her with perfumes and the like, and cause garments and gold to be given to her. (5.190)
Having first uttered the names and the bodies of those two, the wise father, brother, or maternal uncle, having offered water into his hand, [should perform the rite]. (5.191)
This is declared to be the gift; however, in the event of a breach of agreement, it is as previously stated:
having propitiated the fire upon the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), [the penalty applies] indeed to the one who receives, in the absence of such receipt.
Furthermore, water should be offered for the husband, or even for all four [ancestors].
Thus is the ritual offering of water; now hear about marriage, O one of good conduct. (5.193)
Having prepared a seat in the western part of the fire-altar, he should summon the husband and wife, adorned with all their ornaments. (5.194)
With the mantra "śivātmaka," one should cause the garment and flower to be offered;
having indeed placed the husband on the right and the wife on the left.
Then, having performed the sprinkling, the oblation is offered with the very limbs of Brahmā;
having uttered "mama hṛdaya," one should touch the heart of the husband.
Having meditated upon oneself as Śiva and one's wife as being of the nature of Śakti,
one should offer a hundred oblations with the root mantra, preceded by the syllable Om and ending with Svāhā.
Having consumed the madhuparka according to the previously mentioned procedure,
he should likewise display the chosen [bridegroom] with the Gāyatrī mantra, as well as the wealth.
Having sipped water again according to the rule, one should offer a hundred oblations with the Vyāhṛtis;
then, on the southern side of the fire, one should duly sacrifice to the Prāṇāgni in sequence.
One should show a calf there with the *gorddhenu-havya* mantra;
then, one should again perform one hundred and eight oblations with the *śiva-mantra*, ending with *svāhā*.
Then, having gone seven steps to the left side of the fire,
one should place the funeral pyre in the west and worship it with unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*) and other offerings.
The husband, having lifted the wife's right foot with his own hand,
should place that foot upon a stone while reciting the Śivagāyatrī mantra.
Having walked seven steps in succession, the wise man, using the Vāma mantra,
should take hold of her hand with his own right hand.
Having offered three handfuls of parched grain (lāja) with the Umāmaheśa mantra, and having paid homage to the God of gods, one should request the ornaments for the limbs. (5.204)
The offerings for the planetary deities are made with the *vyomavyāpin* mantra;
having offered the *vyāhṛtis* at the beginning and end, one performs them everywhere as an expiation.

Having offered oblations into the *aupāsana* fire with the *brahmāṅga* mantras every day, and having grasped the hand as before, one should proceed when the planetary positions are auspicious. (5.206)
Adorned with all ornaments and decorated with strings of pearls,
having performed the purification with *sadyas* [powder], one should provide cushions made of *kataira* wool.
Having remembered the *upala* as being like a spear, one should cast it between the husband and wife;
having made the lord of the day the presiding deity for the night, and previously [making] Soma the presiding deity.
On the second day, the Gāndharva rite, and on the third, the Agnidaivata rite;
the wise man should recite the respective mantra ending with "namaḥ" thirty times.
If, however, there is contact with those two during the night in a dream,
one should bathe well and perform the *aupāsana* rite every day according to the rules after sipping water (*ācamana*).
In the fourth [day], having performed an oil massage before midday,
and having bathed [the image] together with that, one should indeed prepare the fire at night.
There, having shown her Arundhatī, one should offer oblations with the limbs of Brahmā;
having addressed her with the mantra "Arundhatī" and indeed having prostrated before her.
Having prepared a stone as before, or else the sanctuary itself,
one should raise the bed with the *hṛdaya* mantra and sprinkle it thoroughly with the *Śiva* mantra.
Having scattered the sword, the mat, or the pillow, and having prepared the bed as before, he should then perform [the ritual] upon it.
Having meditated upon himself as Śiva and his wife as Śakti, the wise one,
having performed everything according to the mantra with the left hand, [proceeds] by means of union during the fertile period.
Having gone together with the afflicted person to their home, he should again offer oblations to the Gaṇas and honor guests who have arrived day after day.
O Vināyaka, listen now to the truth regarding the conduct and the customary practices of those born of the pure Śaiva lineage, for whom sixteen rites have been prescribed. (5.217)
Thus ends the fifth chapter, concerning the ritual procedure for the sixteen actions.
(p. 267) Now begins the chapter on the rules of conduct (*vṛtācāravidhipaṭala*).
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the supreme conduct in brief.
For conduct is said to be of two kinds: the general and the particular. (6-1)
The student, the householder, the forest-dweller, and the mendicant—
thus indeed is the fourfold stage of life (caturāśrama) commonly ordained by the sacred law.
In the Śiva-āgama, this [practice] regarding the four spheres of activity is equal [for all];
the religious student (brahmacārī) is to be known as twofold: the temporary (bhautika) and likewise the lifelong (naiṣṭhika).
Having reached the remaining stages in due order, one becomes a *bhautika* celibate student;
however, for the *naiṣṭhika*, the observance of celibacy lasts until death.
Wearing a topknot, or shaven-headed, or with matted hair, equipped with a loincloth, a girdle, a staff, and a sacred thread, and provided with ashes and rudrākṣa beads. || 6-5 ||
Free from craving, having conquered anger, well-restrained, and speaking the truth,
he should always dwell in the teacher's house, eating almsfood only once a day.
One should avoid perfumes, garlands, and the like, as well as mirrors, sandals, turmeric, collyrium, betel, and salt.
Having performed the sacrifice to Vṛteśvara at the topknot during the initiation of a student, he becomes a celibate; thus indeed is the rule for the initiated. Now hear the rule for householders.
Having performed the gathering of the household and the marriage according to the prescribed rite,
she likewise honored guests and visitors to the best of her ability.

One should constantly increase the worship of the gods, fire, and gurus, as well as the dharma pertaining to the planets, by means of faith and devotion through the sixfold ritual (ṣaṭkarma) taught in the Śiva Āgamas. || 6-10 ||
Or one should adorn the bound crest with a white sacrificial thread made of gold, silver, copper, or even crystal. (6.11)

One should always maintain harmony with one's wife, especially during her fertile period; and having adorned oneself with sandalwood paste, garlands, and other ornaments when the planets are auspicious.

This stage of the householder has indeed been described; now hear about the forest-dweller’s stage (vānaprasthāśrama), which, according to the speech of Śiva, is of two kinds: that of one without a wife and that of one with a wife. (6.13)
Dwelling constantly in the forest, he should subsist on vegetables, roots, and the like; just as the conduct of a householder is defined by his wife, so too is it for him.
p. 268) Having described the mode of life for one with a wife, listen now to that for one without a wife:
he should constantly practice celibacy and remain free from accepting gifts. (6.15)
Whether on level ground, on a stone, or even on a bed of kusha grass, or indeed upon any objects of the senses—one should avoid pride in all circumstances. (6.16)
Having performed his bath at the three times of day and worshipped the gods, the fire, and the guru,
he should dwell constantly in the forests, subsisting on fruits, roots, and other such foods.
Listen now to this way of life for ascetics who are without wives:
having perceived the Self as being like Śiva and having offered all actions [to Him]. (6.18)
Having personally bestowed his own authority upon a worthy disciple, he himself is devoid of formal initiation;
for all other forms are indeed thoroughly permeated by the sense of "mine-ness."

Equanimity toward pleasure and pain, free from all undertakings, arises when one remembers that gold remains the same whether it is in a mine or [refined], and thus becomes equal toward the pleasant and the unpleasant. (6.20)
He should maintain internal and external purity and dwell at the outskirts of villages;
this is declared to be the conduct of renunciation—now hear indeed the remaining duties.
Likewise, from the Śivaliṅga, light and Sāvitrī became perceptible;
that which emerged from the body of Śiva is called the perceptible Tulā.
The one named Śivagocara was [established] by the sage Kāśyapa and others, while the one named Jyotirgocara was [established] by the sage Bhāradvāja. || 6-23 ||
The sphere of Sāvitra was proclaimed by the sages beginning with Gautama,
while the sphere of Vyoma was proclaimed by the sages beginning with Ātreya.
Listen now to the specific modes of livelihood for those pure Śaivas, which consist of four spheres of activity arising from their duties toward Prajāpati and others. (6.25)
The first is the *prājāpatya* and so forth; the second is the *mahiṣāla*;
the third is indeed the *kapota*, and the fourth is recorded as the *granthika*.

From the student’s life (brahmacarya) up to mendicancy (bhikṣā), and from the Prājāpatya stage onwards, these are proclaimed here as the different modes of livelihood for those whose sphere of activity is Śiva. (6.27)
Dhṛtarāṣṭravṛtta was the first, followed by Balavṛttidvitīyaka;
then Aṃsagopālaka and Jyotirgocaravṛttika.
The first is declared to be *tudikā*, the second likewise my *aṅkurā*, and the third is declared to be *kulitā* within the scope of the name Sāvitrī. (6.29)
The fourfold sphere of conduct has been declared; hear from me its divisions:
study of one's own [Vedic] texts, service, self-restraint, and speaking the truth. (6.30)
A student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārin) should always observe the vow pertaining to Prajāpati;
those skilled in rites such as pacification (śānti) and others should be well-disposed toward [the performance of] rites such as killing (māraṇa).
But the protector of all the buffaloes, having been surrounded by the buffalo-herds,
fell to the ground and was devoured like a pigeon by the falling fragments [of their hooves].
They are called "pigeons" (kapota) because they desire the life of a pigeon; for they constantly bind themselves with the very bond of the sixfold group [of sense objects]. (6.33)
For even those known as granthikas abandon their deities; they have been cited as examples. Having constructed a hut on the ocean or at the bank of a river, one should dwell there.
For these are considered to have chosen the life of a celibate student (brahmacārin) until the end of their hut; they live together with their wives in secure groves or at sacred fords (tīrtha).
They indeed become Vetālas endowed with constant enthusiasm;
they subsist on divine pilgrimage sites and sun-leaves, and are devoted to the fire-oblation of lotuses.
Having entered the stage of the forest-dweller (vānaprastha), they are proclaimed as Padmas and Caṇḍas,
endowed with Vedic conduct, discernment, and the yoga of knowledge.
Having eaten with eight pills, and having indeed moved through the regions, the seats are the size of a pill; at the end of the pill, they are greatly protected.
Having undergone corporal punishment, one should always remain intent on the heroic posture (vīrāsana);
because of this punishment by the chosen [discipline], no further punishment is prescribed for you.
One should reside with the Guru, bathe at the three times of day, and consume only what is permitted;
one must maintain celibacy—this is declared to be the vow of Brahmodya.
Because they move about in small huts, possessing their own wives as their light, with pure minds, and endowed with wealth obtained through begging, they are called *kuṭīcārakas* here.
Those who move within the impure world yet take refuge in the stainless vessel,
dwelling eternally in the forest, are proclaimed as the swans.
Is it intended that they should move from dwelling to dwelling according to the rule of spending one night in a village?
Indeed, those who remain are said to be chosen; this is the chosen range for those on their rounds.
Having performed the sacrifice to Vṛteśvara before the enclosure, there is the release of that enclosure.
Listen now to the sacrifice to Vṛteśvara within the enclosure according to its essential nature and in brief. (6.44)
Having fashioned a square mandala and smeared it with cow dung, one should draw five lotuses there; in the center, a white lotus is prescribed.
The eastern lotus is yellow in color, while the one in the south is black;
in the western part it is white, and in the north it is the color of the sun.
One should place Īśāna on the middle petal, Puruṣa likewise on the eastern lotus,
Aghora on the southern lotus, and Sadyojāta on the western lotus.
Having worshipped Vāmadeva in the gentle lotus [petal] starting from the northeast (īśāna),
one should worship him with perfumes and other offerings using their respective mantras, being well-composed.
Having performed the recitation of that respective mantra one hundred times, or even fifty times, and having again paid homage to Vrateśvara with the desire for the completion of the vow; || 6.49 ||
Having informed the Lord of his vow, one should perform the dismissal ceremony in the forenoon;
thereafter, one should especially perform the ritual bathing of the God of gods.
Having prostrated before the Lord of the Vow, one should cause the purification of the vow to be proclaimed;
for the worship of the Lord of Vows is indeed for the sake of accomplishing the vow.
In the absence of that, listen to the rule for casting [the image] into water:
whether in a river, or in a pond, on a level and auspicious bank. (6.52)
Having specifically fashioned a liṅga out of food, clay, cow dung, or other such materials,
and having worshipped it, one should then duly take it up after purifying oneself with clarified butter.
O Śivā, that liṅga which pervades the sky should not be cast into water;
however, with the exception of the ritual bathing, everything else is the same.
The Vṛteśvara sacrifice has been proclaimed; now hear the rule for its performance.
[One should worship] Śiva, the all-pervading Lord, who consists of everything and is known as the Praṇava, the name of all phonemes.
The seer is Sanatkumāra, the syllable is Oṃ, its color is white, and Gāyatrī is said to be its meter; it indeed arises from the principle of Śiva.
"All yogins declare that the single syllable 'Om' is Brahman; it is called the Praṇava because it expresses [the Absolute] in brief. Now, listen to the five-syllabled [mantra]. (6.57)
The designator (vācaka) is to be understood as the *sat* (Being), while that which is designated (*vācya*) is remembered as Śiva.
Recitation (*japa*) is praised as bestowing enjoyment (*bhukti*), whereas absorption (*laya*) in that is desired by the sage.
Listen now, in due order, to the seers, meters, phonemes, principles, and deities:
Kāśyapa, Kauśika, Bhāradvāja, and Gautama. (6.59)
The sages beginning with Nārada are traditionally remembered as belonging to the lineages of Ātreya and so forth, [and their meters are] Anuṣṭubh, Triṣṭubh, Jagatī, and so on. (6.60)
The Vedas have described everything; now hear from me about the colors alone:
red, black, as well as dark-blue, yellow, and resembling crystal.
These are proclaimed to be the principles (tattvas) beginning with earth, and their essential nature has been declared.
Sadyojāta and the other five Brahmās are proclaimed as their presiding deities.
One should likewise practice at the time of recitation joined with the *praṇava*;
thus the six-syllabled mantra is proclaimed, for even the tridents are not equal to it. (6.63)
Japa is said to be fourfold for all those who desire to perform it:
mental, that which is in the throat (kaṇṭha), the whispered (upāṃśu), and the clearly articulated (vyakta).

The audible (vyakta) is ten times [the merit of] the whispered (upāṃśu); from that, the recitation with the throat and lips (kaṇṭhoṣṭhaka) is a hundredfold; the mental (mānasa) is a thousandfold; now hear about the recitation with the fingers and so forth.
Counting with a finger yields a result equal to [the merit of] recitation;
counting with lines is said to be eightfold, and with living beings (seeds), it is endowed with tenfold merit.
At the time of twilight, a knot of *kuśa* grass yields a thousand-fold merit;
with coral beads it is ten thousand-fold; with jewels it is one hundred thousand-fold; and with pearls it is said to be one million-fold.
The merit gained from lotus seeds is multiplied ten millionfold by the use of rudrākṣas; yet, compared to rudrākṣas, it does not exist at all.
Therefore, listen now as I describe the origin of the rudrākṣa.
For a thousand divine years my eyes remained open;
tears flowed from my two eyes, and that is called Rudrākṣa.
By meditating upon Śiva, who has one face and is manifest as infinite, one obtains the fruit [of liberation];
he who dies while maintaining this meditation attains the supreme goal.
The two-faced is said to be Śakti; the three-faced is called Nāda;
the four-faced is Bindu, and the five-faced is Sadāśiva. (6–71)
Īśvara is said to have six faces; Rudra is remembered as having seven mouths;
likewise Viṣṇu has eight faces, and Caturmukha has nine faces.
The fruit [of wearing these] increases tenfold from nine faces up to one face.
They should be worn on the hand, the neck, the crest-lock, and the ear, together with sacred ash. (6.73)
They are liberated from all sins and shall attain union with Śiva;
its sight destroys evil, while its touch bestows all perfections.
It has been stated previously that the merit derived from wearing [rudrākṣa] bestows the fruit of all spiritual accomplishments;
one should always wear rudrākṣa, for the merit gained from wearing rudrākṣa is [immeasurable]. (6-75)
Those who, at the time of death, have consumed a rudrākṣa and then pass away, attain the state of Rudra; for them, there is no further rebirth.
Therefore, with every effort, one should always perform the recitation (*japa*) using *rudrākṣa* beads.
Now, the time for recitation and the remaining matters will be explained in brief.
In the forenoon, at midday, in the afternoon, and at midnight—whether four times or three times a day—hear now concerning that place as well. (6.78)
One should perform the sacrifice on the bank of a river or a pond, in a cow-pen, or even in a temple; or in a forest, or on a mountain, in a sacred place, or at a planetary shrine. (6-79)
When the measure is seen even from afar, one should pay homage with devotion;
when the celestial chariot is seen on the path, one should pay homage once one has become weary.
One should first perform the circumambulation clockwise for half [the distance] while remaining calm;
however, at the time of beholding the Liṅga, one should offer flowers and prostrate.
One should not approach the presence of the God of gods with empty hands;
likewise, one's head should not be empty of leaves, flowers, or fruits.
When one who is smeared with ashes is seen, one should display the *liṅga-mudrā*;
likewise, those who bear the marks of Śiva and are endowed with devotion should follow after him.
Seeing an animal mired in mud, he raises it up and then departs;
having abandoned slander, he is supremely compassionate toward all living beings. (6.84)
Having touched a person who has not received initiation, one should avoid those joined with sin.
Japa has been briefly explained; now hear about the Pavitrārohaṇa.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, on the rules for conduct and behavior.
(p. 273) Now begins the chapter on the ritual procedure for the offering of the *pavitra* (sacred thread/filtration).
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the offering of the *pavitra*; listen!
It is for the sake of the complete success of all worship and for the fulfillment of all desired aims. (7-1)
The wise one should perform the rite for the fulfillment of all purposes for those whose every action has failed;
beginning with the deity in the temple, it brings about all prosperity. (7-2)
The performer of Śiva-pūjā should carry out the rite of Pavitrārohaṇa either in the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha or especially in Śrāvaṇa.
In the month of Proṣṭhapada, or in the month of Svayuja, during the dark fortnight—
specifically on the second, fourth, or sixth lunar days.
The wise one should perform the purificatory rite (*pavitra*) that bestows all accomplishments, beginning on the eighth day, or on the tenth, or even on the twelfth. (7.5)
On the fourteenth day, the concluding rite of the Pavitrārohaṇa ceremony should be performed;
one may carry it out for seven days, five days, or even three days.
On the seventh or the thirteenth lunar day, under the asterisms of Revatī,
Kṛttikā, Ārdrā, or Rohiṇī, one should have that sacred thread (pavitraka) prepared.
Having first performed the offering of the sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa), the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) should be carried out;
then the ritual bathing (snapana) according to one's capacity, and especially the fire of Śiva (śivāgni).
Having performed a special worship and having paid particular homage,
I have here offered various gifts and chosen materials.
"By this worship, may all [your desires] be fulfilled; be gracious! Having thus made this request to Śambhu, one should pay obeisance with devotion. (7–10)
One should bring together those ashes, tooth-sticks, water, and a thread;
or one may take possession of them on a riverbank, in a cremation ground, or in a vessel filled with ashes.
As before, he should take for him a tooth-stick made of *pālāśa* wood, or else from sacrificial trees, nine or seven in number. (7.12)
I shall fill a new earthen jar, twelve finger-breadths in length and measured by the span of the little finger,
with water purified by a cloth.
Whether it be thirty-two *prasthas* full, or half of that, or even half of that again;
having wrapped it with threads and carefully enveloped it with cloths.
Having deposited the five jewels— or, if the jewels are not obtained, gold—
and having first secured the thread prepared by the daughter of a twice-born man (7.15).
Just as one would purify the *saṃbhava-sūtra* with ashes and water, that sūtra is said to be doubled; it should indeed become double that [length]. (7.16)
The sacred thread, which consists of nine strands and bestows the accomplishment of gold,
has the Śaktis beginning with Vāmā as its presiding deities upon those nine threads.
In the case of a temple, the sacred thread (*pavitraka*) should have a length equal to the height of the phallus (*liṅga*);
however, a sacred thread with a length of one cubit (*hasta*) is also auspicious here.
The wise one should increase the pavitraka by means of threads in nine ways:
with nine, sixteen, or twenty [threads], which constitute the three lowest grades.
Twenty-five, thirty-two, and thirty-six constitute the three middling [types];
fifty, seventy, and ninety constitute the three superior [types]. (7.20)
Then, according to one's ability, having tied the purifier (pavitraka) endowed with the proper characteristics using the mantra "praśāntāya," [one should offer it]. (7.21)
Having tied ten knots in its center, the preceptor should apply the thread;
or, being wise, having made a knot with nine, seven, or eight threads. (7.22)
And Indra and the other world-protectors are the presiding deities of the knots;
thus has the collection of threads been described in sequence, even for one's own sake.
The height for all the images has thus been proclaimed;
the consecration by night is prescribed, especially for the purificatory threads (pavitra).
On the appointed day, having purified the sacred materials for the presiding deities,
[one should perform the rites] in a beautiful pavilion facing east, adorned with canopies and other ornaments.
One should fashion the mandala in its center according to the previously mentioned method; then, by means of the path prescribed for the ritual of worship, one should install Sadāśiva within it.
Having presented the sacrificial offerings and various kinds of fruits and edible foods,
one should consecrate the purificatory items (pavitra) before him during that night.

Likewise, at the very beginning of the purificatory rites, having prepared the Śiva-fire as before— either in a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) or on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila)— one should offer oblations of fuel-sticks and clarified butter.
For the sake of purifying that pavitra, one should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) at night;
meanwhile, a square sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) should be prepared with rice grains, flowers, and other offerings.
Having spread a cloth on top and provided it with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, the wise one should place the sacred threads upon the cloth and worship them. (7.30)
Having covered [the head] with garments, one should fumigate it with the *hṛdaya* mantra;
pure ashes are placed to the south, and clay powder in the western direction.
Having established these tooth-sticks in the eastern direction,
one should worship them with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, using the *hṛdaya-mantra*.
Having spread an upper covering and placed darbha grass above it,
one should there worship the Lord of Gods with perfumes, flowers, garlands, and other offerings.
Having covered it according to rule with perfumes, having diligently covered it with flowers,
and having subsequently covered it with *darbha* grass, the wise man should then encircle it with threads.
At night, having worshipped it with the Heart-mantra, one should install the auspicious *pavitra* together with the pedestal (*piṇḍikā*), accompanied by incense and lamps. (7.35)
Having offered oblations into the fire and worshipped the purifying linga,
one should present abundant food offerings, especially those of five colors.
Having offered a hundred oblations into the Śiva-fire with the root mantra, the wise practitioner should then offer the ritual substances into the heart-fire, and subsequently offer the Vyāhṛtis.
One should avoid sleep at night while engaged in dance and song;
having bathed according to the rules at dawn, one should consecrate one's body with the ritual gestures (sakalīkṛtavigraha).
One should discard the withered flowers that served as purifiers,
having performed the worship as before, especially at the conclusion of the ritual bathing.
First, the application of powdered clay, then the application of ash;
the best of teachers should then clean his teeth with tooth-sticks. (7.40)
Having performed the ritual bath with water from full jars, the preceptor [should worship] again with perfumes and other offerings,
as well as with garments and ornaments, using the root mantra.
Having worshipped the Lord of the gods of gods with dance and song,
and having recollected Sadāśiva, one should recite the root mantra.

Having performed the rite of ascending the purifier (pavitrārohaṇa), one should worship Śiva— the Lord of Gods together with his pedestal— seated within the mandala, with perfumes and other offerings in due order.
Having offered oblations with the thousand-syllable mantra (sahasrākṣara-mantra) and having indeed entrusted the fire [to the disciple],
one should consign the sacred fire (pavitra-vahni) and then perform the final circumambulation (pariṣeka).
One should offer the *pavitraka* to the five guardian deities with the Heart Mantra, and one should likewise cause the *pavitraka* to be given to all other deities. (7-45)
The preceptor, having indeed bestowed that pavitraka upon the patron, the preceptor himself, their wife, the disciples, and the attendants— || 7.46 ||
Having worshipped with perfumes and flowers, and especially with incense and lamps, one should afterwards cause abundant sacrificial offerings, such as milk-rice and the like, to be presented.
In that same manner, the meal for the sages should be performed from beginning to end,
after having given all appropriate gifts to the people there according to their merit.
Then, one should worship the preceptor with garments, ornaments, and other offerings,
as well as the ascetics who are pure Śaivas and other devotees of Maheśvara.
Having given a gift of special food there according to one's own capacity,
one should afterwards cause the assembly to hear [the teachings] in the presence of the God of Gods.
"These gifts of clarified butter are complete; may you be gracious.
Thus one should address the deity, as well as for the conclusion and the dismissal.
Having prostrated like a staff upon the ground and having paid special homage, you ought to grant liberation from the bonds of the net of worldly existence.
From that time until the end of the year, for six months, four months,
or even for that month or that day, he who is disciplined should conduct himself according to the rule.
The wise one should worship within the observances (niyamas) and extract [the deity] as described for the linga;
then, having discarded the remains of the offering (nirmālya), he should bathe and perform the worship.
One should insert that very *pavitra* every day without breaking it; when the thread is completed according to the rules, then follows the descent of the thread (*sūtrāvarohaṇa*).
One should offer flowers sacred to Rohiṇī;
then, having performed worship as before, one should present abundant sacrificial oblations.
One should indeed cause the materials for the sacrifice and its accessories to be presented to the preceptor;
this is declared to be the "Pavitrārohaṇa," which is the sacrificial thread of Hiraṇyagarbha.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, the procedure for the offering of the purifier (pavitrārohaṇa).
(p. 277) Now follows the chapter on the procedure for the weighing ceremony of Hiraṇyagarbha.
Hereafter, I shall fully explain the golden Hiraṇyagarbha-weighing;
these two [ceremonies] are proclaimed as those which must be performed by kings who have received initiation. 8-1.
It is praised at the time of an eclipse, at the equinox, and at the solstice; likewise during the full moon and new moon, and during ancient divine festivals. (8.2)
The Liṅga established by the Pau-ṛṣis is proclaimed as Pau-ṛṣa;
that which was spoken by the Ṛṣis is called Ārṣa, and that by the gods is Daivika. (8-3)
A self-manifested liṅga is certainly ancient;
from the Pauṣa month up to the ancient Pauṣa, the increase of fruit is progressively greater. (8.4)
Therefore, the most wealthy person should have it constructed at an ancient site;
it is known as middling when done at a site for the gods, and otherwise it is recorded as inferior.
In the northeastern part of the temple, or in the east, or even in the south,
or in the west, or in the north, or in any other delightful intermediate space.
Having constructed a square pavilion provided with four doors,
measuring ten or twelve cubits [in extent], and furnished with sixteen pillars.
It was provided with four gateways, adorned with every kind of ornament,
encircled by garlands of *darbha* grass, and beautified by strings of pearl necklaces.
In the middle of that, one should construct an altar (vedikā) with an extent of one part out of nine;
its height should be equal to the thickness of the sacrificial rice-offering (caru), and it should be as beautiful as the surface of a mirror.
One should indicate the fire-pits (agni-kuṇḍas) together with the previously mentioned procedure;
or indeed, they may be square or circular in the intermediate directions.
Between Cakra and Śaṅkara, one should fashion a circular sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
Having offered oblations into the fire as before, one should perform the limb-offering of the Vidyā with the Heart-mantra.
On the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) at the altar, one should likewise draw an eight-petalled lotus with its pericarp using pure rice grains.
Having worshipped [it] thoroughly with perfumes and flowers, and especially with incense and lamps;
having placed beneath a golden vessel a lotus-petal together with its pericarp,
and having fashioned the upper portion provided with four doors.
Likewise, the practitioner of mantra should place [the seed-syllable] on both sides with the primary mantra.

Having washed [the image] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and having worshipped it thoroughly, the wise one, having first performed the cleansing of the teeth, should then perform the ritual bath with water. (8.15)
Then, having performed the ash-bath, he should be anointed with white sandalwood paste,
wearing white garments and a sacred thread, and adorned with white garlands.
Wearing a turban and an upper garment, adorned with all ornaments,
he should enter the interior of the vessel while standing facing the east.
Having recited the Śiva-mantra, being entirely devoted to the meditation on Śiva,
the wise one should cover [the head] with the upper part [of the hand] while [touching] the heart with the [middle of the] palm.
Having carefully wrapped it with threads and adorned it with flower garlands,
and having contemplated, "I am Śiva," as long as one's own welfare is secured— 8.19.
Therefore, having emerged from there and paid homage to Sadāśiva,
one shall not undergo rebirth again from the abode of Hiraṇyagarbha.
Having become the Ordainer (Vidhātṛ) among all living beings by means of Hiraṇyagarbha,
he there prostrated before his teacher and honored him especially.
Having honored the officiating priests according to the rules with garments, gold, and rings,
one obtains the fruit of all sacrifices and gains the merit of every kind of gift.
This must be performed with great effort for kings who have been initiated,
as well as for those established in the Śaiva path, including both householders and those bearing the sectarian marks (liṅgins).
There, the king should cause a golden vessel to be given to the devotees; this is called the Hiraṇyagarbha. Now hear about the Tulābhāra. || 8-24 ||
That which was previously described regarding place and time must be performed by the king;
[using] khadira, candana, as well as tāla, campaka, and vilva.
Then, having fashioned those two supports from other strong woods,
one should place them above that [base] and join them to the middle of the staff.
Having made a hole at both ends of a staff measuring seven, six, or five cubits, or thirty-two finger-breadths in circumference, one should bind it firmly with a chain.
It should be three cubits in circumference and consist of two copper vessels;
they should be slightly concave with a hollow at their center, and these two should be bound together with cords.
The wise man should have it made very smooth in the middle with iron;
having wrapped it with garlands of *darbha* grass, it should be adorned with flower garlands.
Having wrapped the pillar with cloths and adorned it with all ornaments, the king, himself decorated with every kind of jewelry, shall mount the scale. (8.30)
The wise one, having joined it with the heart-mantra and the balance-mantra, should place it in the remaining vessel; the cavity of the golden essence is equal to that.
Having recited the Śiva-mantra while being intent on meditation upon Śiva,
he should descend from the scale and [give away] that gold as before.
One should cause gifts to be given as is appropriate to the Daivas, the Śaivas, the Brāhmaṇas, the Gurus, and likewise to the Ādiśaivas and Anuśaivas. (8.33)
Or if one were to recite it thousands of times, even by means of hundreds of Rājasūya sacrifices or thousands of Aśvamedha sacrifices, one would obtain a fruit equal to those.
The weighing against gold for the sake of Hiraṇyagarbha has been declared; now listen to the procedure for the fire-offering.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, the section on the rules for the weighing of the Hiraṇyagarbha.
Now follows the chapter on the procedure for cremation.
Hereafter I shall explain the sequence of the rite of cremation,
when one should commence the act of cremation for one who is devoid of consciousness.
The burning, the fashioning, the auspicious rite, and that of the fire in the pit—listen briefly, O virtuous one, to all the rituals beginning with the pit. (9.2)

Those who have suffered miscarriage, those who have had stillbirths, those mortals for whom the rites of tonsure and so forth were not performed, and those who died in pits—[these are the ones to be offered]. (9.3)
Burning, plowing, and similar labors must be diligently avoided by those whose death occurs daily for a year, rising upward with the wind.
These rites, beginning with the offering of the bali-oblation, have been described together.
Once ten years have passed, one should cause the bali-offering to be presented for ten days.
Now, the procedure for the fire in the pit is briefly described:
having performed the purification of the body, one should adorn it with *rajanī* flowers. (9.6)
Having carefully wrapped [the body] with *darbha* grass, the wise man, surrounded by his kinsmen, should have it covered even with a garment of cotton. (9.7)
Having become pure through devotion to Śiva, with his body smeared with ashes, wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya), and having made a garment of darbha grass; || 9-8 ||
Having gone to a cremation ground, or to a pure and beautiful place,
one should dig the earth to that same measurement in depth and to that same measurement in width.
Having placed [the corpse] in a pit one cubit deep, strewn with *darbha* grass, unhusked rice, and other such items,
one should likewise lay the deceased with its head toward the southern direction.
Having silently worshipped [the corpse] with perfumes and other offerings, one should cover that corpse with *darbha* grass;
having filled it with earth right there, it should be well-smeared with gold.
At that time, a bath must be performed together with the sapiṇḍas;
however, where there is no cremation rite, one should not perform the bali offering.
The pit-fire has thus been described; now hear about its form.
Muṣṭikā is indeed death by weapon for one who speaks [inappropriately].
Killing oneself by means of diseases such as vasūri, consumption, or leprosy, or by water, or with a horned animal, or especially by fire; 9.14.
By these [omens], the death of those [beings] is indicated; their specific forms are described when one has traveled from one region to another by means of a snake, a beast, or a nāga. (9.15)
When twelve years have passed, the cremation of the body is prescribed;
if his wife is present there, she shall undergo widowhood in due order.
Having performed the other propitiatory rites (balikarma) accompanied by mantras,
and subsequently, whether [the obstacle] has departed or not, one should likewise don auspicious ornaments.
One should fasten an auspicious upper garment around the neck of the wife;
one should honor the preceptor with great respect until the end of life.
Where there has been a birth following a previous rite, one should not perform the funeral rites;
however, where death occurred by weapons or other such means, the rite should be performed after one year has passed.
One should burn the body without mantras after digging it into the earth;
having fashioned a figure with well-prepared [materials] and having wrapped that figure with threads.
Having wrapped all his limbs with palāśa leaves and prepared him accordingly,
the wise practitioner should indeed cause all the rites to be performed as if he were dead.
The cremation of the physical form has been explained; now hear the procedure for the cremation itself.
Having first performed the purification of the corpse, one should thereafter perform the ash-bath (*bhasmasnāna*). (9-22)
Having prepared a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) on the sand according to his own proportions, the instructor,
having spread darbha grass over it, should place the deceased (preta) there.
Having bound his feet and hands, and having adorned the stage with garlands, he—
whose body takes the form of the limbs of Brahmā— first meditates upon the form of Śiva’s body.
Having performed the whispered recitation (*japa*) of the ear-mantra and the principal seed-syllable according to the mantra,
one should bathe and perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*) according to the rules, placing the sacred thread (*upavīta*) on the left side.
Having thus bathed [the deceased] with his sapindas or kinsmen in the auspicious fire-pit,
and having decorated it as a square, he should dig three stakes [into the ground].
The wise one, having placed the vessel above them and the fuel below,
should kindle the fire beneath it according to the ritual procedure in the fire of the syllable *ṣa*.
One should meditate upon the Śiva-fire there and perform the worship of the fire with perfumes and other offerings;
having placed it in a pure location, one should perform the examination of the breath.
The wise knower of mantras, having touched the regions of the heart, nose, and ears in succession, should purify the breath with the *hṛdaya* mantra. (9.29)
Having raised it up with the Aghora mantra, he is then deposited in the cremation ground;
one should cause the earth to be dug to a depth equal to the height of the deceased.

Having sprinkled [the site] with water containing sesame seeds, unbroken rice, and *kuśa* grass— either to the extent of a handspan or half of that— while reciting the *Vāmadeva* mantra, one should bathe and then drive stakes into the corners.
Having wrapped the wood all around with threads, the wise man should place it right there;
on the southern side of the deceased, he should establish the Śiva-fire as before.
Having offered one hundred oblations with the *hṛdaya-mantra*, one should offer one hundred oblations with the [deity’s] name;
the remainder of the *homa* should be performed with clarified butter, *caru*, milk, unbroken rice (*akṣata*), and so forth.
One should place [the mantra] with the heart-mantra at the navel, the heart, and the region of the face;
then, having placed it upon the fuel, one should subsequently place the head on the right.
Having offered pieces of gold at the nine gates, the wise man [should offer them] there to his two eyes, his two ears, and likewise to the two openings of the nose and the private parts.
And one should place the nine-gated *liṅga* within the heart;
having offered [it] mixed with milk and rice, one should hold it in the mouth with the left hand.
Then, having cut the noose with the Aghora weapon, the knower of mantras should likewise provide a garland and clothing along with the sapindas and brothers. (9.37)
Having performed three circumambulations along the edge of the water's rim, the wise one [should place] a jar of fresh clay situated upon the fire, joined with a stream of water.
Following the rule of circumambulation, the preceptor,
having performed three circumambulations with the weapon-mantra (astra-mantra), should indeed place [the vessel] on his left side.
Then, one should apply the waters from the skull-cup to the vital points (prāṇasthāna),
beginning from the head down to the feet, as a beautifully adorned anointing with clarified butter.
Having touched both feet and remembered the cow as if it were sacrificial oblation,
one should cast [the remains] into the fire with the Aghora mantra and meditate on Śiva in the place of the head.
Having bathed well in a river or a pond together with the disciples,
and having drunk the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and clarified butter, one should recite the root mantra one hundred times.
Just as by giving a gift of power to impoverished Brahmins, or by going to a sacred ford and performing the ritual bath according to rule together with the sapindas; 9.43.
Water with sesame seeds should be offered to him, preceded by his name;
thus the procedure for cremation has been declared in due order for those in the stages of celibacy and so forth.
One should not perform cremation for ascetics using a pit-fire;
rather, they should be carried on palanquins and the like, accompanied by the great sounds of musical instruments.
The wise man should perform all auspicious rites there as before, having dug a pit measuring one *daṇḍa* in depth and facing the east.
One should not perform a ritual bath there, nor is there any need for purification for the minister;
however, the bali-offering should be performed, with the exception of the rites specific to the ekoddiṣṭa ceremony.
The cremation has been briefly explained; now hear the procedure for the ancestral sacrifice (pitṛyajña). Thus ends the ninth chapter on the procedure for cremation.
(p. 283) Now begins the chapter on the ritual procedure for the ancestral sacrifice (pitṛyajña).
Hereafter, I shall fully explain the sequence of the ritual for the ancestral sacrifice:
having performed the offering (bali) at the conclusion of the cremation, one should perform the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite in its proximity.
The rites of offerings, funeral cakes, and water-libations for the three stages of life (āśramas) should be performed at the left of the door, having placed one's own alms-bowl there. 10-2.
One should place a broom of kuśa grass, a span in length, in the midst of the stones;
having invoked the ancestors and the deities, one should worship them with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.
On the first day, the wise man, having offered a bali-oblation with his heart for that [deity] by means of its clan-name, should likewise cause it to be given on the other days.
When one performs the worship of the ancestors after having diligently caused that which is pleasing to him to be given, it shall always grant him satisfaction.
On the second day, the self, consisting of the subtle body (tanmātra), joined with the burner,
goes together with the sapindas to the cremation ground and then again to the fire.
One should perform the cremation of the remaining limbs combined with ghee and sugar-cane juice;
likewise, on the seventh day, there is the collection of the bones and the preparation of the new vessel.
One should cause parched grain, fried rice, boiled rice, and cakes to be offered in the four directions;
having placed the limbs and so forth upon the body, one should deposit them with that very mantra.
But the wise one named Puṇya, for the welfare of embodied beings,
[should perform the rite] on the ninth day or in the afternoon, using earthenware bowls and stones as previously described.
Having passed ten nights, one should dismiss all those stationed within;
having removed all the waters and indeed smeared [the ground] with cow-dung.
On that occasion of the planetary rite, one should perform the *puṇyāha* ceremony in its entirety;
on the eleventh day, one should perform the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite and then conclude it.

Starting from the time of the Kṛttikās, a wise man should cause a water-station (prapā) to be established, whether on a mountain pass or in front of a city, providing good food for travelers without expecting anything in return.
In a square, level, and bright [area] adorned with all ornaments,
he should cause all those who are knowers of the Śaiva Tantras to enter into its center.
Having offered water for the feet, water for sipping, and the arghya offering, and having remembered [the deity] "Namaḥ" before him, one should say:
"May this sacrifice to the ancestors of mine indeed be in accordance with the meaning of all the scriptures. (10.14)
One should say, "May you accept [this]," while turning twice around a pair of *vaṭa* trees;
having commenced the *śrāddha* rite, one should do so on the right side for those seeking that goal.

Those who seek the meaning of the sacred texts, those for whom the Viśvedevas are the foremost cause, those whose conduct is governed by the Śaiva tradition, and those learned in the Vedas who are pleasant to behold. || 10-16 ||
Having gathered these [materials] and paid homage, perform the purification of the feet;
then, having first caused the two [feet] to be washed, one should spread darbha grass around them.
Then, having cast sesame seeds into the center and anointed [the image] with oil,
one should perform the anointing of all [the deities] and then carry out the bathing of all of them.
For the sake of the sacrifice to the gods, the fire, and the ancestors, there are indeed three sacrificial mounds (sthaṇḍila) here;
one should establish the Lord of the Gods in the northern mound and the fires in the middle one.
To the south, the preceptor should devoutly fashion a funeral rice-ball (piṇḍa) for the ancestors in the shape of a winnowing basket, and likewise a fan for Śiva according to the prescribed rite.
Having offered oblations into the fire in the center according to the rules, one should circumambulate the Dakṣiṇāgni fire;
likewise, there [should be] enclosing sticks, as well as fuel-sticks, clarified butter, boiled rice, and sesame seeds.
Having performed the fire-oblation according to one's ability with the thousand-syllable mantra, one hundred oblations for each [deity] should be offered at the root of the *hutāyana*.
Having offered one hundred oblations with the Aghora mantra, one should offer one hundred oblations with one's own name;
then, having partaken of the three-fold food as a sign, one should worship Viśvau Devau.
Having worshipped with perfumes and other offerings, one should present a *vardhanī* vessel filled with rice,
as well as a garment, a bronze vessel, gold, a bed, and sandals.
And one should cause a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to be given according to one's ability, endowed with devotion;
having especially offered betel leaf and having bowed down single-mindedly.
Having thoroughly wiped [the vessel] with the tips of darbha grass, the preceptor should thereafter place the rice-ball (piṇḍa) in a winnowing basket (śūrpa);
he should then mix it with cooked rice and grind it with side-dishes (padaṃśaka).
The ritual ball (piṇḍa) should be shaped like a plantain flower and especially have its tip pointing toward the south;
this mantra is declared to end either with "svāhā" or with the syllable "oṃ. (10.27)
In the middle of the thread, ending in the dative case, one should place the name [of the deity] together with it;
likewise, the thread, along with perfumes, flowers, incense, and especially lamps. (10.28)
Having offered sesame seeds, water, and even betel leaf, the wise attendants, meditating upon Śiva as the supreme reality and the oneness of truth, [should proceed]. (10.29)
Having lifted the funeral ball (piṇḍa) into the vessel, one should then join it with the syllable *haṃsa*.
Having diligently fed the devotees of Śiva, one should cast the ball into the water at night.
The ritual procedure for the ancestral sacrifice (pitṛyajña) has been declared; now hear the rite of Sapindikarana. Thus ends the tenth chapter on the ritual procedure for the ancestral sacrifice.
Now begins the chapter on the procedure for the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the supreme Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa,
which is performed on the twelfth day, or in the third month, or in the sixth month, or even after a year.
One should arrange the items such as the oil for anointing and so forth as previously described;
one should place the Lord of the Gods in the center and the fire-sickle in the south.
Having performed all the worship as before, one should then feed the symbolic offerings (nimitta),
which are earth, water, fire, air, and space.

Having thus conceptualized all the principles (*tattvas*) within those [elements], one should specifically place the five [principles] into each of the five aggregates (*piṇḍa*), beginning with the earth element.
Therefore, one should worship Sadāśiva, who is known as the "Supreme Bestower," having specially fashioned a liṅga twelve finger-breadths in length. || 11-5 ||
One should worship Śiva within that [liṅga] according to the procedure prescribed for worship;
having prepared that piṇḍa as before, one should then unite it with each respective Tattva.
Having first united them with *sālokya*, secondly with *sāmīpya*,
and thirdly with *sārūpya*, may she be joined with the fourth [state].
Having meditated thus, that which is the proper *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite shall take place.
Now listen, O one of good conduct, to the summary of the performance of the *aṣṭakā-homa*. (11.8)
Especially on both the full moon days of the months of Māgha and Proṣṭhapada, as well as when the Sun, Saturn, and Mars [are in conjunction]. (11.9)
If a learned man performs the *aṣṭakā* rite at his door,
he should offer oblations into the Śiva-fire as before and perform a hundred oblations with the five Brahmans;
furthermore, he should especially feed five or six Śaiva ascetics.
And he should give a sacrificial fee according to his ability, preceded by garments and gold.
Perform it according to your ability on each preceding afternoon;
having thus described the Aṣṭakā-homa, now hear the rule for expiation.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, the section on the procedure for the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite. || 11 ||
Now begins the chapter on the rules for expiation (prāyaścitta).
Hereafter, I shall fully explain the sequence of the rules for expiation;
however, the expiation for kinsmen and those of the same lineage (sagotra) is not stated here.
Likewise, one should not transgress the worldly custom of those bound by society;
for failing to provide a guarantee to one who has awakened [from ignorance], an expiation is prescribed. (12-2)
Having touched one initiated into his own caste, especially one who is smeared with ashes, he should perform a bath;
upon touching a Śūdra, he should perform a bath with his clothes on.
For all intermediate periods, there are two baths upon touching [an impure object].
If a learned man touches [such a thing] through negligence, a bath in water is prescribed. (12.4)
Then, having performed the ash-bath (bhasmasnāna), one should recite the Śiva-mantra a hundred times;
the acts of touching with the intellect and so forth constitute the ritual of bathing as previously described.
When that meal has been seen [as forbidden], the wise man should discard the remainder of that food;
then, having performed the two ablutions and having recited the root mantra eight hundred times.
If a foul odor should reach the tip of the nose due to the wind, one should likewise smell cow dung and immediately recite the five-syllable mantra. (12.7)

Having eaten the food of those initiated into his own caste, the wise man should indeed recite the *vyomavyāpin* mantra without desire; however, if he eats out of desire, he should recite it one hundred times.
If one eats the food of a king, the physician should mutter a hundred times the terrible mantra;
if he has eaten the food of a Vaiśya, he should likewise mutter it up to a thousand times in due order.
If one eats the food of a *rudra* unintentionally, one should perform the *kṛcchra* penance and the *cāndrāyaṇa*.

If one eats it intentionally, one should indeed perform the *cāndrāyaṇa* and the *kṛcchra-kūṣmaka*. Furthermore, if one eats it for more than one day, one should perform the *kṛcchra* and the *cāndrāyaṇa*.
If one eats continuously for a month, the state of a Śūdra arises.
If he is joined with a Śūdra woman, he should always behave like a Śūdra;
having had sexual union with a Śūdra woman, he should then perform seven Kṛcchra penances.
For those who commit [the offense] once every month or every half-month, one should perform the Saptakṛcchra and other Kṛcchra penances;
for those who do so every six months or annually, one should perform the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa penances.
Beyond a year of such association, no expiation is prescribed.
And likewise his conduct, especially at the end of life. || 12-14 ||
Upon touching a menstruating woman or eating from leaves of the heramba, kavaṭa, or aśvattha trees, one should bathe and chant the Śiva-mantra. (12–15)
Whether out of desire or even without desire, one should recite the Śiva-mantra one hundred times when [the tongue] is smeared with food remnants, or mixed with ghee, milk, and salt. (12-16)
Having recited the Heart mantra there, which destroys all defects,
and having seen the food, one should discard it upon seeing hair and purify it with ashes.
Having reached water, one should remember the Lord of the gods and becomes purified;
one should discard garlic, fish, meat, and the remains of offerings (nirmālya).
But having consumed [forbidden food] through negligence, one should recite the Śiva-mantra while pure;
if it has been eaten out of desire, one should recite the Śiva-mantra one hundred times.
(288) And hear now, O Suvrata, briefly about all the mortal sins (*pātaka*):
the killing of a Brahmin, the drinking of liquor, and likewise the theft of gold. (12.20)
Approaching the wife of one's guru is likewise remembered as the fifth;
these three—violating the teacher’s bed, drinking liquor, and killing a Brahmin—are [the great sins]. (12.21)
Listen now to the death of those who are facing their end:
when the seed, joined with its husk, is violently severed at the root. (12.22)
Likewise, one who has violated the Guru’s bed shall die by holding a palm leaf with its stalk;
a drinker of liquor shall meet death by grasping heated objects in his hand. (12.23)
"Listen to my words: because of negligence, a crack occurred through which fire arose; having abandoned that mark of misfortune, you have attained your own true state."
Or he may go to a village of those who have killed a Brahmin and perform the rite of departure;
having entered that village once, he must not enter it a second time. (12.25)

A woman who meets her husband at the edge of the village while he is leading [the cattle] at night should be understood as having done so unintentionally; hear now, O virtuous one, regarding what is done intentionally.
Having performed the preliminary rites as before, up until the end of twelve years,
when the time for ascending above has arrived, one should enter water, fire, or the void.
Even after entering [the fire], he should lead [the disciple] to death; he will become pure.
Through that yoga, there is also the piercing of gold (*svarṇastobha*); listen to the summaries, O you of good conduct! (12.28)
Having performed acts of charity everywhere and having bathed at all sacred fords for a year,
an embodied being should mutter the Śiva-mantra and thereafter perform the Uddālaka rite.
This expiation for the theft of gold is prescribed; it consists of four [stages] and applies whether the act was committed intentionally or unintentionally. (12.30)
Having recited the five Brahmans at dawn for three years, whether in a temple, in the abode of Śiva, or even in the forest, the wise man [attains his goal]. (12.31)
Likewise, O seeker of merit, one who desires [results] should bathe in the water every day;
having explained the specific sins, O one of good conduct, now hear about the general ones. (12.32)
For the killing of a deer species, one should recite the *Sadyomantra* one hundred times;
for the killing of a domestic animal species, one should perform the previously mentioned rite.
If one desires to increase the species of birds, one should recite that terrible mantra a hundred times;
if there is injury caused by reptiles and the like, one should recite it for a man a hundred times. (12.34)
For the injury of stationary beings, one should mutter the Īśa-mantra a hundred times;
and for the sake of a teacher’s fee, one incurs no fault for the injury.
General sins have been declared; now hear about general secretions (semen emissions):
they may occur through desire or without desire, involving earth, wood, stone, or metal. (12.36)
Having recited the mantra of Īśa one hundred times, or indeed one hundred thousand times with longing, the wise man [attains his goal].
Theft has thus been briefly explained; now hear concerning birth-impurity (sūtaka). || 12.37 ||
Due to the conjunction of a planet with a lunar mansion, there are two types of impurity: that arising from birth and that arising from death.
For a Brahmin, purification occurs after ten days; for a Kṣatriya, however, it is after twelve days.
Purification for a Vaiśya is said to take half a month, and for a Śūdra, one month;
therefore, a person of perfect knowledge who abides by his own duty should not abandon a kinsman.
At that very moment, the knower is purified, while the ignorant one shall become a partaker of what has been declared;
otherwise, there would be a loss of the lineage, even if an expiation were performed. (12.40)
If one is deficient in the worship of the gods, the fire, and the guru, it becomes twofold;
if there is an excess, one should likewise recite the Aghora mantra a hundred times while fulfilling one's own dharma.
Having eaten food at dawn or at the end of the day, one should perform the *kṛcchra* penance right there;
likewise, if one eats milk-rice (*pāyasa*) and similar foods during the three junctions of the day, even for the sake of a deceased ancestor (*pretaka*).
When one birth-impurity (sūtaka) occurs upon another birth-impurity, one becomes pure by the duration of the first birth-impurity;
likewise, when one death-impurity (pretaka) occurs upon another death-impurity, or even a birth-impurity upon a death-impurity, it is the same.
The day on which the period of impurity has arrived becomes pure and is extinguished by the preceding impurity, provided a person of lower caste is always residing in the house. (12.44)
Having renounced all possessions, purification through *kṛcchra* penance is prescribed;
namely, *kṛcchra*, *atikṛcchra*, and likewise *taptakṛcchra*. (12.45)
Listen now to the performance of the Parāka, Cāndrāyaṇa, and Uddālaka penances:
eating once a day for three days, followed by three days of eating only what is unasked for. (12.46)
One should eat only at night for three days and remain without food for three days;
this is declared to be the *kṛcchra* penance. Now hear about the *atikṛcchra* from me.
One should drink one *kuḍuba* of milk for twenty-one days, accompanied by ritual bathing and meditative recitation; this is remembered as the *atikṛcchra* penance. (12.48)
Having drunk hot water for three days, one should drink milk for three days;
having drunk hot ghee for three days, one should subsist on air for three days.
The *taptakṛcchra* has been fully described; now hear about the *parāka*.
By not eating for twelve days, while performing ablutions at the three junctions of the day, [one performs the *parāka*]. (12.50)
That which is known as *parākama* is the foremost of all types of interest;
for half a month there shall be an increase like that of a crocodile (*grāha*), and for the other half-month, there shall indeed be a decrease.
This is declared to be the Cāndrāyaṇa; now hear about the Uddālaka.
It is traditionally taught that one should drink curd-whey (āmikṣā) for a fortnight, and ghee for eight nights.
One should subsist on unasked-for food for six nights and drink water for three nights;
with a fast for one day and night, this is known as the Uddālaka vow.
Having bathed repeatedly during these expiations, one should mutter the Śiva-mantra.
Then one should recite [the mantra] eight hundred times, or even a thousand times according to one's capacity.
These four types of Śivaśvetā have been fully described; listen now.

The *uditodita* is said to be [a verse] exceeding by one quarter (*pāda*); the *adhikamodita* exceeds by half; and the *adhikānta* exceeds by more than that—in brief, these are the two-fold [increases]. (12.56)
Whatever has not been stated here in this treatise, one should perform as a general rule;
thus has this expiation been briefly declared in the section on Conduct.
The Caryāpāda is thus completed; now hear the Yogapāda.
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, the Prāyaścittavidhipaṭala.
Thus ends the Caryāpāda in the Suprabheda;
Oṃ,
it is composed of the nature of Śiva.
The Suprabheda: Now, in the *Yogapāda*, the chapter on the procedure for the channels and wheels (p.
291). Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the *Yogapāda* in brief.
Now, listen to the sequence of the network of channels (nāḍīcakra) in that eastern foot.
Seventy-two thousand channels (nāḍīs) are proclaimed;
by these channels the body is pervaded, like the leaves of a withered aśvattha tree.
With eighty-four hundred thousand variations,
the gods sport within the body at will, O Supreme Lord.
And by the four classes of living beings arising from all wombs:
those born from eggs, those born from sweat, those born from sprouts, and those born from a womb. || 1-4 ||
Those entities that are born from eggs are proclaimed as egg-born;
those entities that are born from sweat are proclaimed as sweat-born. || 1-5 ||
Those born from the earth through water and seed are proclaimed as *mudbhid* (earth-sprouts).
Those that are born joined with a membrane (*ilva*) are proclaimed as *jarāyuja* (viviparous).
And by means of the four classes of beings, humans and the others become sixfold:
namely, humans, wild animals, domestic animals, and birds; || 1.7 ||
Those who speak with their speech, saying "these are men," regarding the sixfold origin of birth—namely, the crawling and the stationary—are thus celebrated as human beings. (1.8)
O Vināyaka, one should know that a deer is characterized by an upward-pointing tail and its increase [in size];
those with long tails pointing downward are declared to be of the animal species.
Those with two wings are called birds; those that move are called reptiles; and that which is established is called stationary. Thus, the living being is indeed sixfold.
The various types of wombs have been explained; now hear concerning the field (kṣetra) which consists of the earth and other elements, wherein the principles (tattvas) abide during their dissolution.
That place of rest was declared to be beyond the principles (tattva), higher than the highest;
from that, the severed [state] arose, and from that, Śakti was born.
Therefore, that which has arisen from Ādi, and from that, that which is born from Bindu;
from that, Sadāśiva is proclaimed, who becomes fivefold for the sake of creation.
From that, the Self (Ātman) has arisen, innate and joined with impurity.
One should know him as the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), and he is likewise said to abide in power (śakti).
Therefore, the pure states of the upper realm have been proclaimed;
upon attaining the excellent [state] of the auspicious or inauspicious, they go there and are born. (1-15)
From the realm of Māyā down to the earth, that which is bound to a body is seen here;
birth occurs upon the arising of karma, while death is known to occur at the end of karma. (1.16)
The assumption of a body was made for the sake of experiencing pleasure and pain.
The body is said to be of two kinds: namely, masculinity and femininity. (1-17)
Masculinity is marked by the male organ (liṅga), and femininity is marked by the womb (yoni).
The liṅga is said to consist of Īśa (the Lord), while the yoni is remembered as consisting of Śakti (Power).
Therefore, indeed, this entire world of the moving and the unmoving is Śiva’s power;
his body is said to be twofold: the gross and the subtle.
Earth, water, fire, air, and space—these are said to be the seed;
semen is declared to be the portion of the field, while blood is remembered as the portion of the womb.
Bone, sinew, and marrow—these three indeed are born from the father;
skin, flesh, and blood—this triad alone is born from the mother.
Thus the six sheaths have been described; from them, the ends of the body arise:
the nails, teeth, body hair, head hair, and likewise the channels.
Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell—these fivefold elements; joined with these groups of elements, the gross body comes into being. (1.23)
Know that the subtle sphere (golaka) is the means for both the auspicious and the inauspicious;
from it, birth and death arise through the power of karma.
Thus, the gross body has been described by me in brief.
They know the ear, skin, eye, tongue, and nose to be the organs of perception (buddhīndriya).
Speech, feet, hands, anus, and the generative organ are recorded as the organs of action (karmendriya).
Prāṇa, samāna, udāna, and vyāna. || 1-26 ||
The serpent, the tortoise, the discus-bearer, Devadatta, and Dhananjaya;
as well as mind, intellect, ego, and consciousness—these are known as the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa). (1.27)
Arrogance, envy, pride, and so forth constitute the subtle body (*sūkṣmaśārīraka*).
This body is indeed the *liṅga* (the mark or vehicle); now hear of their birth from that [subtle body]. (1.28)
Having been conceived by the father with the semen and remaining in the womb of the mother, all [the elements] beginning with karma are grasped, and the hollow interior is attained. (1.29)
Through the portions of the field and the portions of the seed, one enters the body;
due to an excess of blood, a female offspring is born, and due to an excess of semen, a male is produced. (1.30)
If it is born with semen and blood in equal measure, it becomes a neuter;
like a seed placed in a vessel, it grows very gradually. (1.31)
Likewise, that which has entered the womb is shaped like the bud of a *punnāga* tree;
furthermore, by means of the supreme [knowledge], one perceives the signs of death and other such karmic events. (1.32)
Having obtained there this hexad— longevity, power, ritual action, knowledge, death, and happiness— he then enters the womb.
The qualities (guṇas) and the three defects (doṣas) arise therein for living beings;
sattva, rajas, and tamas are said here to be the triad of qualities.
Truth, knowledge, austerity, silence, memory, intelligence, fortitude, forgiveness, enthusiasm, resolve, and steadfastness—these indeed are the qualities of the sattvic nature. (1.35)
Arrogance, great egoism, despondency, speaking of what is dear, exertion, and envy are said to be declared as the qualities of rajas. (1.36)
Laziness, the sleep of delusion, fickleness, lack of modesty, wickedness, and reviling others—these are the characteristics of the quality of darkness (tamas). 1.37.

The state of equilibrium among the qualities (guṇas) is called the root-nature (mūlaprakṛti). In brief, it is declared to consist of the three qualities; now hear from me about the three defects (tridoṣas) as well. 1.38.
Wind (vāta), bile (pitta), and phlegm (kapha) are known as the presiding deities of diseases; they exist commonly in all living beings, either in equal measure or in excess. (1.39)
One should enter other such hollow cavities as these;
just as [the embryo] is split by the wind when it has reached the time of being situated in the womb. 1.40
Then, having attained a twofold form, it increases very gradually;
in five days or ten days, like water resting upon a lotus leaf. (1.41)

At the end of one month, it resembles the fruit of the Aksha; at two months, it has the appearance of a Mṛdvīkā fruit; at three months, it is eight finger-breadths long; and at four months, the head is formed. (1.42)
In the fifth month, the two hands and the two feet are said to be formed;
likewise, the nails, the fingers, the toes, the ankles, and the shanks. (1.43)
The calves, knees, thighs, hips, buttocks, and the pelvic region;
then beginning from the breasts, sides, and abdomen, up to the armpits, the chest, and both arms. (1.44)
Indeed, [one should examine] the lines on the feet and hands, the nails and joints of the thumbs, the throat, the ears, the tongue, the lips, the teeth, and the nose. (1-45)
The eyes, the eyebrows, the forehead, the head, the hair, and so forth—all these limbs are produced during the sixth month. (1.46)
In the seventh month, food and drink are consumed through the umbilical cord;
or else, in that month, she gives birth, or she does not give birth due to the wind (vāyu).
Having arisen in the eighth month and taken hold of the neck of a lute,
he indeed attains here the eightfold sovereign powers, beginning with the power of becoming minute (aṇimā).
He understands the three times, and through his knowledge, everything is revealed;
he is born in the eighth month, and once born, he lives a long life.
He is born in the ninth month or again in the tenth;
thereafter, in the eleventh month, people are impelled by Māyā.
One who possesses power must recognize that certain [afflictions] such as fatigue, fever, hunger, and so forth, increase gradually and ever more slowly. (1.51)
Having been produced there, the seven constituent elements (dhātus) increase by means of vigor through food.
Indeed, it is taught that blood arises from the essence (rasa) produced from the liquid portion of food. (1.52)
From the blood, flesh is produced; from flesh, fat arises; from fat, bone is produced; and from that, marrow comes into being. (1.53)
Marrow and semen have arisen; these are the seven constituents (dhātus). The body is composed of constituents, and the aggregates of sound are composed of constituents. (1.54)
Knowledge of objects such as sound arises when two months have fully elapsed;
furthermore, the twenty-five principles will now be explained in brief. (1.55)
The elements, the subtle elements, and from them the organs of perception, the organs of action, O Lord of Obstacles, as well as the internal organs; || 1.56 ||
The twenty-fifth principle is declared to be conjoined with the Unmanifest;
it attains the entire body, beginning with the elements such as earth and ending with the Unmanifest.
Earth, water, fire, air, and space—these are declared to be the great elements (mahābhūtas). Now hear indeed their classification. (1.58)
That which is solid is earth; that substance which is indeed called water; that which is hot is fire; and here, it is air that moves. (1.59)
When there is space and openness for these groups of great elements, they are here proclaimed as the bones, skin, flesh, hair, and the channels. (1.60)
The portions belonging to earth should be known as such, and from that, hear the watery portions: phlegm, blood, urine, marrow, and likewise semen. (1–61)
It should be known as the constituent part of substance (dravyāṃśaka), residing within all living beings:
hunger, sleep, darkness, laziness, and likewise sexual desire. (1.62)
These five qualities are declared to be established as the portions of fire (tejas):
sitting, lying down, moving, stretching, and contracting. (1.63)
These five qualities are declared to be the well-proclaimed constituents of wind:
desire, anger, greed, fear, and likewise delusion. (1.64)
These five qualities have been declared; they are proclaimed to be the constituents of space (vyomāṃśa).
Thus the quality of the elements has been stated, and their specific functions will now be described.
Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell are the fivefold [objects].
Sound is the quality of space; touch is the quality of wind. (1.66)

One should assign form as the quality of fire, taste as the quality of water, and smell as the quality of earth; one should then place the elements beginning with the earth [in their respective positions].
But that which is known as the "object" (viṣaya) is said to be the quality of living beings;
the meritorious object, such as sound and so forth, increases on the earth. (1.68)
The four qualities increase [in earth], while in fire there are three;
for wind it is said to be two, and for space, only one.
Likewise, the objects have been described; now hear of the organs of perception:
the ear, skin, eye, tongue, and nose are the organs of perception. (1.70)
The means for perceiving objects such as sound have been proclaimed;
now hear of these sense organs, which consist of divine beings. (1.71)

The ear is said to be the internal (adhyātma); that which is to be heard is the elemental (adhibhūta); and Śivahasta is the divine (adhidaiva). They know the skin alone to be the internal (adhyātmaka). (1.72)
Touch is the elemental [aspect], and Vāyu is the presiding deity therein;
the eye is said to be the internal [aspect], and that which is to be seen is its elemental state. (1.73)
The sun is the presiding deity there, and they know the tongue to be the internal self (adhyātma);
the sense of taste is the elemental principle (adhibhūta), while Varuṇa is the presiding deity.
