The nose is said to be the internal [self], that which is to be smelled is the elemental [nature], Bṛhaspati is the presiding deity, and it is traditionally remembered as the power of the morning. (1.75)

The organs of cognition have been described; now hear of the organs of action. Speech is said to be the internal organ (adhyātma), while that which is to be spoken is its external objective correlate (adhibhūta). || 1.76 ||
Sarasvatī is the presiding deity (adhidaivata), Vāṇī is the internal self (adhyātmika), and that which is to be given is the elemental sphere (adhibhūta); Śakra is the presiding deity therein. (1.77)
The feet are declared to be the internal self (adhyātma), and movement is the presiding element (adhibhūta);
Śakra is declared to be the presiding deity (adhidaivata), while the wise know air to be the internal self.
The generative organ is said to be the internal self (adhyātma), and bliss is its objective correlate (adhibhūta). 1.79
The presiding deity of Prajāpati is known as the power of action (kriyāśakti);
the organs of action have been described, so now hear about the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa).
The wise know that the mind (manas), the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra), the intellect (buddhi), and the heart (citta) constitute the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa).
The mind is declared to be the "internal self" (adhyātma), while that which is to be thought upon is its "objective correlate" (adhibhūta).

Soma is said to be the presiding deity (adhideva) of the intellect; they know Ahaṃkāra to be the presiding deity of the self (adhyātma); and Rudra is the presiding deity (adhidaivata) of the Ahaṃkāra as the elemental principle (adhibhūta).

The intellect (buddhi) is said to be the internal self (adhyātma), that which is to be known (boddhavya) is the elemental principle (adhibhūta), and the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) is the divine principle (adhidaiva); the mind (citta) is recorded as the internal self. (1.83)

For consciousness is the presiding element (adhibhūta), while the Lord is the presiding deity (adhidaivata); having known that, one regards the mind as the ego-maker and the ego as the act of egoizing. (1.84)
Because it is to be awakened, it is called *buddhi*; because it thinks, it is called *citta*.
And the mind (*manas*) is said to be of two kinds, known as the moving and the unmoving. (1.85)

Egoity (ahaṅkāra) is to be known as threefold: that which modifies the elements (bhūta-vaikārika), that which is fiery (taijasa), and that which arises from the essence of the elements (bhūta-sāra-samudbhava); this shall be explained in brief. (1.86)

First, however, is the subtle element of sound (śabdatanmātra), and then the subtle element of smell (gandhatanmātra) and so forth; these five subtle elements are said to be the creation of the gross elements. (1.87)
The sense organs may arise from the taijasa ego;
the sense organs may also arise from the vaikārika ego. (1.88)
The presiding deities arise from the vaikārika-ahaṃkāra.
Intellect (buddhi) is to be known as eightfold, consisting of the eight qualities beginning with dharma and adharma. (1.89)
The mind (citta) is to be known as one; the wise know it as the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa).
With the four internal organs, the [principles] are said to be twenty-four.
Indeed, their substrate (upādāna) is the unmanifest (avyakta), which is censured;
the property of the unmanifest is proclaimed to be the three qualities (triguṇa). (1.91)

There is that which is characterized by darkness (tāmasa), that by passion (rājasa), and the third is that by goodness (sāttvika). Those of a dark nature go to hell; those of a passionate nature are said to go to heaven.
In the *sāttvika* [state], liberation is said to occur; therefore, it is called *sāttvika*.
In the *sāttvika*, all actions are performed with a single-pointed mind; thus, it is *sāttvika*. (1.93)
Therefore, with every effort, one should take refuge in the quality of goodness (sāttvika-guṇa).
Thus, the twenty-five principles have been proclaimed in brief. (1.94)
Now hear from them a summary of the eleventh principle:
Puruṣa, Rāga, Niyati, Vidyā, Kalā, and likewise Kala. (1.95)

Pure Knowledge (Śuddhavidyā), Pure Power (Śuddhakalā), and likewise Pure Māyā; then the principle of Self (Ātmatattva), the principle of Knowledge (Vidyātattva), and beyond that, the principle of Śiva (Śivatattva). (1.96)
Indeed, the eleven principles are situated within the body; having gradually entered the three coverings over time, O most wise one. (1.97)
He who causes the existence of the self is embraced by destiny; since primordial nature (prakṛti) exists for the sake of the person (puruṣa), he is therefore called "puruṣa. (1.98)
They know that a single part of a hundred thousand rising suns exists therein;
it is celebrated as *sañjīva* and is also called *saṃsārī*. (1.99)
Pervading everything from Pradhāna down to the Viśeṣas by means of its pervasive power, it is known as the Kalā-śakti; and by those who are not yet liberated, it is called the Cause.
"Due to the connection with merit and demerit, the innate [nature] is known as *dāṇava*.
Because of such connections, [the qualities] are established within bodies. (1-101)
In connection with that individual soul (jīva), the threefold suffering is here described as being internal (ādhyātmika), external (adhibhautika), and celestial (adhidaivika). (1.102)
One encounters three kinds of suffering; hear now concerning that which is internal (ādhyātmika). Internal suffering is said to be twofold: namely, physical and mental. (1.103)
It manifests in many ways as gulma, agniśoṣa, sāra, fever, colic, and so forth;
and it is caused by men, wild animals, piśācas, cowherds, birds, thieves, and rākṣasas.
The bodily suffering has been described; now hear, O observer of noble vows, about mental suffering, which arises from grief, malice, humiliation, envy, hunger, thirst, and so forth.
Thus has the mental [suffering] been described; now that which is caused by external beings (ādhibhautika) is being spoken of:
[it arises] from cold, heat, wind, rain, lightning, thunderbolts, and storms. (1.106)

Through these elements, the suffering of living beings is said to be of three kinds: that caused by the divine (ādhibhautika), that caused by the self (ādhyātmika), and that caused by fate (ādhidaivika).
Furthermore, there is the suffering of the womb, birth, old age, ignorance, death, and likewise that born of hell.
Thus, indeed, the threefold suffering is experienced in these states;
thereafter, one is tormented by the fire of the womb through the mother's own nature.
The suffering within the womb is ten million times greater than that of birth;
thus, the embodied being experiences such sufferings in succession as it is pressed through the mechanism of the birth canal. (1.109)
Waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and then hear of the fourth state (turya): having withdrawn the senses and the intellect, and having performed all actions without exception. (1-110)
All the functions that are seen indeed occur while one is awake;
having bound the instruments—the sense organs—one should surely abide in the support. (1.111)
The intellect resorts to sleep and perceives the results of past actions;
one should understand dream to be thus. Now hear about deep sleep (suṣupti) thereafter. 1-112.
Having taken up the instruments of action, the intellect attains consciousness;
then, at that very time and depending upon that [intellect], it becomes aware of its actions.

That which is renowned as Suṣupti (deep sleep) is the fourth state, occurring without the instruments [of perception]. The living being (jīva), having entered the mouth of waking, takes recourse in the ear during the dream state. (1-114)
In deep sleep, [the Self] rests in the heart; in the fourth state (turya), it is said to be all-pervading.
Thus established within the body, listen now to the description of the channels (nāḍīs). (1.115)
The root of the navel is the heart-lotus stalk, and the channels are like a wheel;
thus, O dear one, they pervade everywhere—sideways, upwards, and downwards.
For these are arranged like a wheel, and twenty-eight are the primary ones;
among them, the ten channels beginning with Iḍā are indeed the most important.
Iḍā, Vimā, Śoṣā, Pṛthivī, Āpanī, as well as Tejovatī, Vāyu, Gamanī, and Mardanī. || 1-118 ||
Rodanī, Raktavāk, Mṛdaṅgī, Śṛṅgiṇī,
as well as Śabdā, Sparśā, Pūrṇā, Sadrūpā, and Rasadhāriṇī.
For these twenty-eight principal channels reside in all the limbs;
and within those channels abide the ten vital winds, beginning with prāṇa.
Prāṇa, apāna, as well as vyāna, udāna, and samāna;
nāga, kūrma, cakraka, devadatta, and dhanañjaya. || 1-121 ||
The ten vital breaths (prāṇas) have been declared and fully enumerated as the winds;
among these nine winds, that which is proclaimed as prāṇa is their sovereign.
Abiding within the bellies of living beings, they manifest as inhalations, exhalations, and coughs;
they are celebrated as having the form of the vital breath (prāṇa), resembling the color of a sapphire.
Joined with the *nāda*, it constantly relies upon the individual soul (*jīva*) until the end of life;
it takes its place in the heart, the navel, the tip of the nose, and extends as far as the big toe.
The *apāna* wind relies upon the back and exits through the left and right [nostrils].
The characteristic of prāṇa has been declared; now hear that of apāna.
The apāna wind, having taken refuge in the vital breath (jīva), possesses its color like that of a rainbow;
its location is at the base of the penis, while its exit is at the base of the anus.
The location below the navel is at the base of the penis;
it is the exit for the discharge of feces and the like, as well as the exit for the prāṇa and apāna breaths. (1.127)
Constantly mounting the great chariot called the body, which is sustained by the prāṇa and apāna breaths, the Lord,
like a lamp situated within, made the Great Mantra his protector.
Pervading the entire vyāna-vāyu and awakening touch and the other sensations, its color is like cow’s milk; its location is in all the joints of the limbs. (1.129)
There, one should cause the diseases of the *udāna* power to arise;
its color is proclaimed to be like lightning and fire. (1.130)
The location, the two sides, the two ears, as well as the eyes and the two nostrils [of the deity]; the color of the Samāna wind is like the luster of an *atasī* flower.

Having brought the tongue to the shoulders, the head, the shanks, and likewise the ankles, and having conveyed the essence of food and drink from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head. (1.132)
One should cause all food, drink, and so forth, combined with the fire of Viśvanara,
to be offered as an oblation right there in that pit known as Āśaya.
In that regard, the "Nāga-gold" is like the rising sun; one should cause it to be fashioned with gold, kancana, and hair-raising [ornaments], and with divisions for singing. (1-134)
The rising [point], the forehead, the location beginning with the nose, and the seat—these are proclaimed as the abodes of the tortoise-wind (kūrmavāyu), having a form like a kunda flower. (1.135)
Having reached the eyelids of the eyes, perform their closing and opening;
the color of the *kṛkara* [vital breath] should be like the luster of crushed collyrium.
Established at the tip of the nose, it constantly produces hunger and other sensations;
the color of Devadatta would be like the luster of pure crystal.
Having specifically raised the face, the back, the feet, and the sides, as well as the one who is standing, lying down, or sitting; thereafter, the act of yawning. (1.138)
In the form of Dhanañjaya, possessing a luster like blue collyrium,
he stands within Dhanañjaya’s body and even releases the immortal nectar.
But afterwards, having made [the body] a Brahmin, the body is broken and [the self] departs.
Thus these ten winds, beginning with prāṇa, are described. 1-140.
The channels, beginning with the *iḍā*, are likewise pervaded throughout the body;
therefore, the vital air (*vāyu*) shall circulate through the midst of those channels in due order. (1.141)
The great channel called Kuṇḍalī is proclaimed to be in the center of the navel;
it is thus eight-fold in its coils, like the sleeping Kuṇḍalī.
Above the navel there is a lotus like a pond-lotus in bloom;
situated in its center is the living soul (jīva), possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns.
Within that, it is declared, resides the circle of the Sun, Moon, and Fire;
situated in their midst is the God, possessing a radiance equal to ten thousand suns. (1.144)
On the left side is the iḍā nāḍī, and on the right side is the piṅgalā nāḍī;
the suṣumnā is in the middle, extending as far as the tips of the big toes.
Gāndhārī is in the right eye and Hastijihvā in the left;
Pūṣan is indeed in the right ear and Yaśasvinī in the left ear.
Alampuṣpa and Meḍuṇḍu are situated in the anus, while Kuhū resides in the rectum; Śaṅkhinī is located in the middle of the penis, and indeed ten channels (nāḍīs) are established there.

Because all the channels without exception revolve within the body like a wheel, or because it is surrounded by them like a wheel, it is therefore called here the "wheel of channels" (nāḍīcakra). || 1-148 ||
This wheel of channels has been explained; now listen to the Wheel of Time (Kālacakra).
Thus ends the first chapter, the section on the procedure for the wheel of channels. || 1 ||
Now follows the chapter on the ritual procedure of Kālacakra.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the characteristics of Kālacakra;
because he brings about time (*kāla*), he is thus called Kāla. (2-1)
Time, which is formless, is declared to be the cause of the destruction and birth of both living beings and gods; its characteristic is observed through its effects. (2.2)
Time is declared to be threefold as defined by Śiva;
it is celebrated as the time of creation, the time of maintenance, and dissolution. (2–3)
Thus has the creation from Śiva down to the earth been described;
as for the maintenance of all beings, it remains established from Śiva down to Ananta.
When [the elements] from earth up to Śiva dissolve into the higher and lower [principles], that is declared to be the threefold determination of time known as withdrawal (saṃhāra). || 2-5 ||
They exist in three times; from that, the passage of the past occurs, and the time called the present is indeed spoken of separately for each.
When that which remains has been completed, it is known as "past"; and when [the remainder] is still dependent upon time, it is called "future. (2-7)
When that which has been commenced but not yet completed is mentioned, it should be understood as referring to the present time; this is what has been stated regarding gods and other beings. (2-8)
Creation and dissolution occur simultaneously; during the period of maintenance, they cease.
Some indeed create by means of time, and some wander about by means of time. (2.9)
Now hear from me the calculation of time for humans, ancestors, and gods;
time is said to be of two kinds: gross and likewise subtle. (2.10)
The pearl is said by the Yogins to be both gross and subtle.
O child, the gross [pearl] is of two kinds: that which moves with the moon and that which moves with the sun. (2-11)
The period of the moon’s movement is proclaimed as that of human beings,
while the period of the sun’s movement is proclaimed as that of the gods.
In the Kālacakra, however, the planets beginning with the Sun revolve; likewise, on the wheel endowed with twelve spokes, the signs beginning with Aries are the spokes for the Sun. (2.13)
The wind is proclaimed to be located on the strip [of skin], at the navel, and in the center;
the wheel situated on the summit of Meru is established within the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa). || 2-14 ||
Like the wheel of a potter's loom, O deities, the constellations and the planets perpetually revolve right there, circumambulating Mount Meru. (2-15)
The wise know that the day begins at sunrise and ends at sunset;
likewise, the night is said to begin at sunset and end at sunrise. (2.16)
A day and night is traditionally defined as being composed of two [periods] of day and night;
"day," "morning," and "daytime" are declared to be synonymous terms. (2.17)

The terms *śarvarī*, *rajanī*, *sāyam*, *niśi*, and *nakta* refer to night; *rātrika* refers to that which belongs to the night. For the deities, [the offering] begins with the afternoon (*hāyādi*), while for the ancestors, it begins with the morning (*prātarādikam*).
It is established in the scriptures that this is the day and night of human beings;
it is for the benefit of humanity and for the sake of bringing about all prosperity. (2-19)
In the forenoon, at midday, and in the afternoon during the fourth watch; therefore, one should worship with every effort during the four junctions of the day.
One should worship especially during each watch at the eight junctions;
since half a watch is called a junction, one should worship throughout the day and night.
p. 303) A day of humans is said to consist of fifteen days; likewise, there are two fortnights: the bright fortnight and the dark fortnight. (2.22)
Where the moon and the sun are together in a single zodiacal sign, that is called the new moon (amāvāsyā); that fortnight is said to be the bright one (śukla). || 2-23 ||

When the moon has entered the seventh zodiac sign, it is there that the full digit (kalā) occurs; therefore, that is declared to be the full-moon day (paurṇamāsī), and from then follows the fifteen-day dark fortnight (kṛṣṇa).
A fortnight, likewise a month, twelve months, a year, and a *varṣa*—these are proclaimed as synonyms for a year (*abda*). (2.25)
The lifespan of human beings is declared to be one hundred years;
for all species of wild animals, a lifespan of one hundred years is proclaimed. (2.26)
The lifespan of human beings is proclaimed to be one hundred years;
having thus spoken regarding humans, now hear the duration of time for the ancestors (pitṛs). || 2-27 ||
One day and night of humans becomes one ghaṭikā for the ancestors;
thirty ghaṭikās constitute a day and night, and the bright fortnight (śuklapakṣa) is their day.
One should know that the night is dark; that is the day and night of the ancestors. The new moon (amāvāsyā) is the morning twilight, and the eighth lunar day (aṣṭamī) would be midday.
The afternoon of the full moon day and the half-watch of the eighth day [constitute the period];
twelve days make a month, and twelve months make a year. (2–30)
The worship performed on the new moon day (amāvāsyā) which bestows grace upon the ancestors—this is declared to be the proper time for the ancestors, indeed for the benefit of human beings. (2-31)
The time of the gods will now be described, beginning with the *tuṭi* and ending with the dissolution (*pralaya*):
the *tuṭi*, *lava*, *nimeṣa*, *kāṣṭhā*, and likewise the *kalā*. (2.32)
A moment (kṣaṇa), a muhūrta, a ghaṭikā, the junctions, and a watch (yāma) constitute the day and night; likewise, the day, fortnight, month, season, solstice, and year [are divisions of time]. (2.33)
Now hear the definitions of the yuga, the manvantara, the kalpa, as well as the dissolution of the mahākalpa, and everything from the *tuṭi* up to the final dissolution. (2–34)
The opening and closing of the eyelashes of one who is at ease constitute a *nimeṣa*.
A fourth part of a *nimeṣa* is declared to be a *tuṭi*. (2.35)
Know that two *tuṭis* are a *lava*, and two *lavas* are a *nimeṣa*.
Fifteen *nimiṣas* are a *kāṣṭhā*, and thirty of those are a *kalā*. (2.36)
Half a *kalā* is declared to be a *kṣaṇa*, and two *kṣaṇas* constitute a *muhūrta*. Half of that is declared to be a *ghaṭikā*, which is established as the end of all activities. (2.37)
The wise call three quarters and three ghaṭikās a "junction" (sandhi). Likewise, two such junctions constitute one "extension" (yāma), and four extensions are known as a day. (2–38)
That day alone should be known as a great day-and-night; fifteen such days are remembered as a fortnight, and two fortnights likewise as a month. (2–39)
The two fortnights, the bright and the dark, are called the two pakṣas; two months are declared to be a season (ṛtu), and three seasons indeed constitute an ayana.
For two solstices constitute a year, which is indeed one day and night of the gods;
the period beginning with Capricorn and lasting for three seasons is declared to be the daytime of the gods.
The three seasons beginning with Cancer are likewise declared for the night;
these are proclaimed as the transits (saṃkrānti), the equinoxes (viṣuva), and the solstices (ayana).
When the sun has entered another zodiac sign, its transition occurs within that sign;
when the sun is situated in Libra or Aries, those two are proclaimed as the equinoxes.
When Cancer and Capricorn are reached, there is the southern and northern solstice respectively;
the transit at the northern solstice is proclaimed to occur during the forenoon.
In the month of Caitra, at the equinox, it is midday; but at the southern solstice, in the month of Āśvayuja, it is declared to be the equinox, which for the gods is midnight.
Therefore, one should worship the Lord of Gods at the four junctions:
the daily junction for humans, and the junction of the fortnight for the ancestors.
And at the junctions of the years, one should worship the gods according to the prescribed rule;
thus is the day and night of the gods proclaimed. (2.47)
Thus has the sequence of years been declared; now the duration of the ages (yugas) will be explained.
Some are proclaimed in the scripture as beginning with the age of the egg-born (aṇḍaja).
In the scripture, the four yugas have been defined by Śiva:
the third yuga is Tretā, and likewise Dvāpara and Kali.

The Kṛta age lasts for four thousand years; the Sandhyā period shall be eight hundred years, and likewise the Sandhyāṃśa is to be known as one hundred years. Tretā is half [of that], and Dvāpara is less by a quarter.
The periods known as Catuḥśata, Sahasra, and Dvāpara, as well as the Kaliyuga, stand above and increase again and again. (2.51)
By twelve thousand such years, four yugas are completed;
seventy-one such cycles are said here to constitute an *manvantara*.
An *manvantara* is likewise to be known as consisting of eighty thousand years plus fifty-two thousand, according to the divine year (*divyasaṃvatsara*). (2.53)
First was Svāyambhuva Manu, and after him Svārociṣa;
then likewise Auttami, Tāpasa, and Cākṣuṣa.
She is indeed Vasvata and she is Varṇameru;
she is Varṇa and she is Dakṣa; she is indeed Varṇa and she is indeed Brahma. || 2-55 ||
"O Rudra, that which is called 'of the same color' (savarṇa) refers to the fourteenth [Manu], Raucya Bhautya; thus, in brief, the Manus have been fully described. (2.56)
If one should contemplate that very moment as the navel of Brahmā, then five such moments would constitute a single Kalpa, beginning with the creation of Brahmā. (2.57)
Thus has the *kalpa* been fully described; now hear of the *mahākalpa*.
It consists of thirty-three [deities] and so forth, three hundred, and three thousand.
The dissolution of the gods is said to occur at night; that constitutes one day and night of Brahmā, and at that time, the dissolution of Indra takes place. (2.59)
Three hundred and sixty days are declared to be one year of Brahmā;
therein, the dissolution of the wheels occurs again and again thirty-six times.
By that measure of years, the dissolution of Brahmā occurs at the end of his hundred-year lifespan;
for as long as that duration of Brahmā’s dissolution lasts, it constitutes a single day and night for Viṣṇu.
Three hundred and sixty such [days] constitute a dissolution (laya) there again and again;
by that measure, one should understand the lifespan of Īśvara to be one hundred years.
The dissolution of Īśvara, however, lasts for one *nimeṣa* of Sadāśiva;
by increasing [the duration] from there by a hundredfold, the dissolution of Sadāśiva is recorded as lasting for a hundred years.
The dissolution of the bindu and the nāda is said to occur right there through that lineage;
likewise, the dissolution of the form of the nāda occurs from Śakti into Śakti for the duration of a day.
O Beloved, as long as the hundredfold increase of the days persists, Śakti remains constant;
know that the dissolution of Śakti occurs when the next day arrives. (2.65)
The dissolution of the Supreme alone occurs for a period of one hundred times that number of years.
First is the Śaktika [dissolution], which is peaceful; Śiva is the synonym for this. (2.66)

That which is known as the cause of the destruction and arising of both the higher and the lower is called "Time" (kāla) for the gods; it is also called "Time" with respect to the principles (tattvas). (2.67)
That which begins with earth and ends with Śiva is proclaimed as the duration of existence;
it lasts until the dissolution of Īśvara, at which point the dissolution of the Self occurs. (2.68)
From the periphery of Sadāśiva up to the end of Nāda, there is indeed dissolution;
from there, up to the dissolution of Śakti, one should proceed toward the ultimate end of Śiva.
The dissolution of the principles (tattvas) has thus been described; now hear from me concerning subtle time:
the vital breath (prāṇa) consists of *truṭis*, and six such breaths constitute one *ghaṭikā*.
Then, specifically, one should increase the day-and-night (ahorātra), the sixty ghaṭikās, and so forth,
as well as the fortnights and other units, by means of the daily increment as previously described.
O Lord, through the yoga of subtle time, one reaches the abode of Brahmā and the other deities;
indeed, this is proclaimed as the subtle time for the wise and the yogis. (2.72)
This Kālacakra has been proclaimed as the relationship between the support and the supported; listen.
Thus ends the second chapter, the section on the ritual of Kālacakra. 2.
Now begins the chapter on the method of the support and the supported.
Hereafter, I shall fully explain the characteristics of the support and the supported.
The support is said to be the site (sthāna), and the supported is the presiding deity (adhidevatā).
"O child, because of the multiplicity of bases (*ādhāra*), yoga is said to be manifold due to the relationship between the basis and that which is based upon it (*ādhārādheya-sambandha*). (3.2)
What has been called "yoga" for yogis and "knowledge" for the wise,
that yoga I shall now describe in brief, and not in detail.
O practitioner, first listen to me regarding that which is to be accomplished by yogins.
First is the seat, and second is the yoga-band. (3–4)
One should know that the third is the rosary, the fourth is the bamboo staff,
and the fifth, in particular, is the water-pot.
I shall now describe their characteristics: the seat should be fashioned like a tortoise, made of *khādira*, *devadāru*, *madhuka*, or *bilva* wood. (3–6)
Alternatively, having fashioned the tortoise posture (kūrmāsana) from trees suitable for sacrifice, the seat is likewise of three kinds: being one-quarter less than that, or half of it. (3-7)
O Vināyaka, the seat for the practice of yoga is described as being like the surface of a mirror and likewise level at the bottom. (3.8)
The first [type] is made from a tiger skin, while the second is made from a black antelope skin;
alternatively, the threefold yogapaṭṭikā may be made from woven thread.
The width is said to be three finger-breadths, and its measurement is like that of the sacred thread (upavīta).
There are the rosary of recitation (japamālā), the crown garland (śiromālā), the garland of *hṛṃ* syllables (hṛṃmālā), and the armlet garland (bāhumālakā).
The series [of beads] starting from behind the ear and ending at the navel is known as the "chest-garland" (uro-mālā);
the "head-garland" (śiro-mālā) has that same circumference, while the "arm-garland" (bhuja-mālā) is equal to the length of the arms.
Listen now to the mere enumeration of the rosary beads in their respective proportions:
for those seeking liberation, the recitation is prescribed with twenty-five Rudrākṣa beads. (3.12)
Twenty-six for the sake of Śiva and for the sake of knowledge; twenty-seven for the destruction of enemies; twenty-eight for the sake of prosperity. (3-13)
Thirty beads are for those seeking victory; fifteen are for malevolent rites (*abhicāra*).
This is what is called a rosary (*japamālā*); now hear the procedure for the rosary.
Since the Praṇava is uttered in all mantras,
I shall explain the Praṇava in brief, but not in detail.
The letter *a*, the letter *u*, and the letter *m* in the form of a *bindu*:
the letter *a* has Brahmā as its presiding deity, and the letter *u* has Viṣṇu as its presiding deity.
The letter *ma* has Rudra as its presiding deity, while the *bindu* indeed has Īśvara;
the *nāda* is said to be Sadāśiva—these are the presiding deities. (3.17)
The syllable *a* is located in the heart; the syllable *u* is in the region of the ears;
the syllable *m* should be in the middle of the palate; and the nasal dot (*bindu*) is in the forehead. (3.18)
And above that, the location of the *nāda* is indeed proclaimed as follows:
the three letters beginning with *a*, along with the *anusvāra* and the *visarga*. (3.19)

The five colors are praised as being born from the syllable *a*; those beginning with *ka* up to *ma* are like the color of bees, while the letter *ya* is placed upon the bindu. These fifty [letters] are traditionally taught as having arisen from the letter *a*.
They know the Praṇava to be the name of all phonemes and to consist of all the gods;
its seer is Sanatkumāra, and the syllable Oṃ is white in color.
It is said that its meter is Gāyatrī; its essence is indeed Śiva-tattva, and its name is the single syllable "Oṃ. || 3.23 ||
The Praṇava has been explained in summary; now hear the five-syllabled mantra remembered [by the sages].
"Namaḥ śivāya" is this five-syllabled mantra, known as the Pañcākṣara. (3.24)
The verbal [mantra] is to be understood as that which expresses Him; Śiva is remembered as its denoted meaning.
Recitation (japa) is praised as bestowing power, and liberation is desired through the "malla" [mantra]. (3-25)
Now hear, in order, the sages, meters, phonemes, principles, and deities:
Kāśyapa, Kauśika, Bhāradvāja, and Gautama. (3.26)
Ātreya, however, [taught] *na*, *kārā*, and so forth; likewise, O sages, [the meters are] in sequence:
*anuṣṭubh*, *triṣṭubh*, *bṛhatī*, *jagatī*, and *ati-jagatī*. (3.27)
Indeed, the Vedas are fully described by their syllables and so forth; listen now to them in order:
red, black, dark-blue, yellow, and resembling crystal. (3.28)
The principles (tattvas) beginning with earth have been proclaimed; their true nature has been declared.
The five faces, beginning with Sadyojāta, are proclaimed as their presiding deities. (3.29)
When joined with the *praṇava* at the time of recitation, it is likewise said to be the six-syllabled mantra; however, this is prohibited for women, *śūdras*, and others. (3.30)
Japa is said to be fourfold for all who desire to perform japa: mental, that which is at the throat, whispered, and clearly articulated. (3.31)

(309) A whispered recitation (*upāṃśu*) is ten times more effective than a manifest one; that which is performed with the throat (*kaṇṭha*) is a hundred times more effective than the whispered; and that which is mental (*mānasa*) is a thousand times more effective than that. Now hear concerning the recitation performed with the fingers and so forth. (3-32)
The merit of counting with a finger is equal to a single fruit;
that with the joints is said to be eightfold, and with a rosary (*dīpa*) it is a hundred times greater. (3.33)
A rosary made of kuśa-grass knots is worth one hundred; one made of coral is worth one thousand;
one made of jewels is worth ten thousand; and one made of pearls is said to be worth one hundred thousand.
The merit gained from lotus seeds is multiplied ten millionfold by those made of rudrākṣas; yet even with rudrākṣas, it is not [merely] that. Now listen as I describe their origin. 3-35.
For a thousand divine years my eyes have been opened; they shed tears, and it is said that one who has taken refuge in the rudrākṣa is liberated.
Śiva himself is the single-faced [form]; the fruit of this infinite concentration is that he who dies while maintaining it attains the supreme goal. (3.37)
The two-faced is said to be Śakti, the three-faced is Nāda, the four-faced is Bindu, and the five-faced is Sadāśiva. (3.38)
Īśvara is declared to have six faces; Rudra is remembered as having seven mouths;
Viṣṇu is remembered as having eight faces; and the Four-faced One has nine mouths. (3.39)
The fruit [of wearing it] on the hand, ear, crest, or neck—up to nine faces or one face—is a hundredfold greater than the previous; it should be worn together with sacred ash.
They are liberated from all evil and shall attain union with Śiva;
its sight destroys sin, and its touch bestows all supernatural powers (siddhis).
One should always wear the rudrākṣa, for it bestows merit upon all limbs;
those who die after consuming a rudrākṣa at the time of departure [from this world] attain liberation.
One attains the state of Rudra, and for such a person, rebirth no longer exists.
Therefore, with every effort, one should always perform recitation using rudrākṣa beads. (3–43)
The time for recitation and the place shall now be stated in brief:
during the forenoon, midday, afternoon, and at midnight. (3–44)
Listen now to that place, which should be visited four times or three times a day:
on the bank of a river or a pond, in a cow-pen, or even in a temple. (3.45)
One should perform the recitation (japa) in a forest, on a mountain, in a sacred region, or within one's own home;
thus has the location been described. Now hear the number of recitations. || 3-46 ||

A constant practitioner of yoga should always recite it one thousand times, or half of that, or half of that again, or one hundred and eight times; this brings about the destruction of all sins. (3-47)
Merely by reciting [this], one goes to the imperishable world of Śiva.
The number of recitations has been declared according to the rule; now hear the rule for the bamboo staff.
The elevation [of the mark] should be on the head for Brahmins, on the forehead for Kṣatriyas,
on the nose for Vaiśyas, but one should avoid it for Śūdras and others.
A bamboo staff that is straight, smooth, and free from curves or hollows—this is declared to be the rule for the staff; now hear the rule for the water-pot.
Filled with three *āḍhakas*, it is the best; filled with three *prasthas*, it is the middling; and filled with two *prasthas*, it is the lowest—such is the measurement of the water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*).
Whether it be made of gold, silver, copper, or even clay—one should have it fashioned exactly as described in the treatises on craftsmanship (śilpaśāstra). (3.52)
The practice of the Śaivas has been declared and described as fivefold;
I shall now speak of the eight limbs of yoga—listen with a one-pointed mind. (3.53)

Restraints (yama), observances (niyama), and posture (āsana), followed by breath control (prāṇāyāma), withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra), meditation (dhyāna), concentration (dhāraṇā), and absorption (samādhi). || 3-54 ||
The eightfold means for achieving yoga by practitioners of yoga should be known as: non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, and non-possession. (3.55)
Yama has been declared to be fivefold; now hear about Niyama: purity, contentment, austerity, self-study, and meditation. (3.56)
And the observance of devotion to the Lord (īśvarapraṇidhāna) is remembered as the fivefold restraint (niyama):
Gomukha, Svastika, Padma, and Ardhacandraka. (3.57)
The Vīra posture and [the Svastika]—these are known as the sixfold postures. Placing the right kneecap upon the left knee... (3.58)
One should place [the hands] on the two soles of the feet and on the two sides of the back;
having done this, it becomes very smooth and possesses the characteristics of the *gomukhī* [mudrā]. (3.59)
Placing the soles of the feet on the sides of the thighs is the *svastika*;
placing them on the surface of the thighs is here called *padmāsana*. (3.60)
Having made the three ankles even, one should place them upon the palms and the secret parts;
this is declared to be the Ardhacandra posture. Now hear about Vīrāsana.
With two arms, the left foot fallen and the right placed upon it, this firm posture is called Vīrāsana; now hear of Yogāsana from me. (3.62)
The body is joined together and covered by a yogic band (yogapaṭṭikā), with the two elbows placed [on the knees]; this is called here the yogic posture (yogāsana). || 3-63 ||
Having performed even one of these, one should then practice yoga;
however, prior to the practice of yoga, perform three breath-controls (prāṇāyāmas).
One should practice the yoga of exhalation (recaka), inhalation (pūraka), and retention (kuṃbhaka);
prior to the practice of yoga, however, perform three rounds of prāṇāyāma.
Exhalation (recaka), inhalation (pūraka), and the second, retention (kuṃbhaka):
exhalation is the solar disc, and inhalation is the lunar orb.
The *kuṃbhaka* is to be known as pertaining to Agni; one should worship it with meditation upon the body.
From exhaling (*recana*) it is called *recaka*, and from filling (*pūraṇa*) it is then called *pūraka*.
One should practice the three [breaths]—exhalation, inhalation, and retention—with the syllable *praṇava* through restraint.
Twelve *mātrās* are prescribed for exhalation (*recaka*), and that same number of *mātrās* is traditionally taught for inhalation (*pūraka*).
In this scripture, retention (*kuṃbhaka*) is definitively established as twelve *mātrās*.
Exhalation (recaka) has Brahmā as its deity; inhalation (pūraka) has Viṣṇu as its deity.
Kumbhaka has Rudra as its presiding deity; thus, these three deities are traditionally taught for the yogi during day and night—namely, recaka and pūraka as well.
Having released the *sūtaka* and *protaka*, one should fill [the breath] by means of *kuṃbhaka*;
this is declared to be the sequence of *prāṇāyāma*. Now hear about *pratyāhāra*.
As long as the senses remain established in their respective objects, for that long it is said that withdrawal (pratyāhāra) has become stabilized. (3.72)
Having conceived the essential forms upon their respective seats according to their positions, one should understand that meditation in this manner is the remover of all suffering. (3.73)
I shall describe the characteristics of the support in brief, but not in detail:
four finger-breadths below the navel is the circle of fire.
The first [center] is said to be the Mūlādhāra, located below and adorned like a Kadamba flower; the second is at the root of the navel and is triangular in shape.
The great channel called Kuṇḍalā, which has the form of a serpent’s coil and consists of eight circles, is said to be the solar orb.
The lotus above the navel is called the lunar orb;
it is located in the heart, at the base of the ears, at the base of the palate, and on the forehead.
Having formed a mental resolve at the location of the crown of the head, one should meditate [on it] like a lotus flower.
I shall now describe, in due order, the characteristics of the heart-lotus.
At the navel, the root of that stalk has its stalk pointing upward and its opening downward;
there is an eight-petaled lotus with a pericarp, like a plantain flower. (3.79)
In this treatise, the characteristic of the support (ādhāra) has been declared as the sustaining channel joined with the heart-lotus; now hear about that which is supported (ādheya). 3.80
That which is to be supported and that which is employed by it are thus combined in meditative concentration;
likewise, the *iḍā* and *piṅgalā* are on both sides of the neck of the lute.

The Suṣumnā is situated there in the middle, and likewise, there is a hollow in its center; joined with the individual soul (jīva) and the vital breath (prāṇa), it moves through those central channels.
Moving about at that time, established within its supports, the yogi should resort to the "bird" (khaga) yoga which is declared to be joined [with the breath]. || 3-83 ||
Then, when the fire is joined at the *mūlādhāra*, one should practice yoga;
through the practice of yoga, that yogi shall touch the world of fire.
Having meditated upon the Sun above that, one attains the world of the Sun;
having meditated thus, he goes to the world of the Moon above that.
Having remembered Brahmā in the heart, one attains the world of Brahmā;
but having meditated upon Viṣṇu situated at the root of the throat above that, [one attains his realm]. (3.86)
The yogi should pervade the person with the qualities [of Rudra] through the practice of yoga;
desiring the state of the world of Rudra, he should meditate on Rudra at the root of the palate. (3.87)
Having meditated upon Īśvara on the forehead—pervading up to the limit of the upper region of Puruṣa by means of his own splendor—one shall attain that world. (3.88)
Having meditated upon Sadāśiva at the crown of the head, one enjoys [the fruit] right there;
then, having gone to the center of the heart-lotus, one [perceives] the Bindu, the Nāda, and the Śakti.
One should visualize the form of a lamp measuring four finger-breadths;
having worshipped it in the four locations with their respective forms in those very places. (3.90)
One should place upon the head the imperishable Brahman, endowed with the partless [state].
Therefore, the yogi who is fully engaged in yoga shall obtain the fruit of yoga.
Because one obtains [the power] even in the measure of an atom (aṇu), it is designated as "aṇimā" (atomization); or, having traveled by the thousands to the region of the root-syllable. (3.92)
Because one obtains [this power] by one's own will, it is known as *laghimā* (levity).
Having performed mental recitation upon the earth, one is honored by those who discourse on the scriptures.
Because it is honored everywhere, therefore that shall be its greatness;
the attainment of all substances is declared to be their "acquisition" (prāpti). (3.94)
Having entered into bodies that are subject to their will, they shine forth;
because they have not attained [such power] in relation to the sun and other [luminaries], their lordship is proclaimed [only in those cases]. (3-95)
If lordship exists there, that very lordship is prescribed;
by virtue of attaining union with Śiva (śivasāyujya), it is traditionally known as "Śiva-hood" (śivatva). || 3.96 ||

The yogi especially attains the eightfold supernatural powers, beginning with atomization (aṇimā), and the yogi also attains the fourfold characteristics, such as residence in the same world (sālokya) and so forth. || 3.97 ||
Sālokya, Sāmīpya, Sārūpya, and likewise Sāyujya— having attained the world of meditation (dhyānaloka), one is established in that world (sālokya). (3.98)
Because of its proximity to that deity, it is called "sāmīpya" (nearness);
and having attained those respective forms, it is remembered as "sārūpya" (conformity). (3.99)
The form united with Śiva is called "union" (yujyam). Yoga has thus been briefly explained; now hear the section on knowledge (jñānapāda). || 3.100 ||

That *yogapāda* which was explained here in brief according to the [various] authorities has been presented in due order; it consists of the channels (*nāḍī*), the wheels (*cakra*), and the wheel of time (*kālacakra*) together with the foundation (*ādhāra*),
contained within three chapters.
Thus ends the third chapter, concerning the procedure for the support and the supported.
Thus ends the Yogapāda of the Suprabheda;
Oṃ,
all is Śiva.
Now, from the *Suprabheda*, in the *Jñānapāda*, the chapter on the procedure for Śiva’s creation (p.
315): Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the *Jñānapāda* in brief.
First, listen with a one-pointed mind to the creation of Śiva.
Knowledge arises for the sake of destroying the delusion regarding the calf, for the destruction of the series of paths, and for the manifestation of Śiva. (1–2)
Knowledge is said to be like darkness, while knowledge is also said to be like a lamp;
the object of knowledge is declared to be like the sun, and afterwards the knowledge itself perishes. (1.3)

Having severed the nets of bonds, that which is called the knowledge of the piercing [of the knots] and so forth is attained; by means of this knowledge, the wise one transcends the state of being a bound soul, the bonds, and the Lord. (1.4)
In knowledge alone, however, there is the attainment of liberation; of this there is no doubt.
Now hear the characteristics [of the levels] from Śiva down to the earth. 1–5.

For the benefit of yogins, for the sake of liberation, and likewise for enjoyment, as well as for the purpose of the creation of all living beings, that twofold creation is traditionally taught. (1.6)
The first is the creation of Śiva, and the second is the creation of the bound souls (apaśu).
That which is conjoined with the pure deities is declared to be the creation of Śiva. (1.7)
Having veiled the pure Self with impurities, the creation of bound souls (paśu) is proclaimed;
through the distinctions of the moving and the unmoving, the Supreme Lord sports. 1-8.
O Gajānana, listen briefly to the creation of Śiva;
Śiva, who is higher than the highest, is remembered as the object of knowledge (*prameya*), like Brahman. (1.9)
That which possesses impurity is to be known as censurable; that which is free from impurity is uncensurable.
It is incomparable and peerless, possessing rightness (dakṣiṇatva) that is immutable. || 1-10 ||
Beyond the ether, it is supremely subtle, eternal, and the cause of emptiness;
because it is all-pervasive, it is said to be omnipresent; and because of its state as the master, it is the sovereign over all. (1.11)
(316) Because it is distinct from speech and mind, its domain transcends the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
O son, listen with a concentrated mind to [the nature of] direct perception and the other means of valid cognition. 1-12.
Perception, inference, and verbal testimony, along with comparison, presumptive testimony, and non-existence—these are remembered as the six means of valid cognition. (1.13)
That which is perceived through the sense organs, such as the eyes, is here called direct perception (pratyakṣa).
The cognition of the indicative mark (liṅga) and that which is not an indicative mark (aliṅga), and so forth, is traditionally known as inference (anumāna). (1.14)
Thus, the verbal testimony (śabda) has been illustrated as that which is to be understood through the words of a reliable person (āpta);
and because of its similarity to that, the simile (upamā) is likewise proclaimed as that which is to be understood. 1-15.

From the statement "there is eating during the day," it is understood that "there is none at night. Presumption (*arthāpatti*) is traditionally defined as the cognition of a fact through the very force of another fact. (1.16)
For when there is an absence in erroneous cognition, self-cognition itself is apprehended;
when there is a presence through error, self-cognition is proclaimed to be "absence. (1.17)
By such means of valid cognition as these, that Śiva is remembered as difficult to perceive;
this is declared to be the reality of Śiva (śivatattva), the essence of all principles (tattvas) and of all selves. 1.18
For the sake of creation, for the protection of the world, as the cause of the world's emergence, and for the benefit of practitioners, he assumes a body by his own will. (1.19)
That body should be known as threefold: partless (niṣkala), both-with-and-partless (sakalaniṣkala), and with-parts (sakala);
thus it should be specifically understood as being of three kinds.
The Niṣkala is fourfold, and the Sakala is likewise;
both the Sakala and the Niṣkala are proclaimed in succession as being ninefold. (1-21)
From the thousandth part of the Śiva-tattva, she who is nameless arose as Śānti;
they call her "Śānti" (Peace), which is a synonym for the Supreme (Parā). || 1-22 ||
And from that very thousandth part, she who is named Śakti emerged;
indeed, "Śakti" and "Vidyā" are stated to be synonyms for her.
And from that very thousandth part, the manifestation of the form of Nāda arises;
Nāda and its Pratiṣṭhā are proclaimed to be synonyms.
Therefore, by means of one-tenth of that, the emergence of the reality of the *bindu* occurs;
both *bindu* and *nivṛtti* are synonymous terms denoting it. (1.25)
Starting from the supreme state, [he perceives] the qualities such as omniscience, as well as unmanifest forms and likewise actions that are beyond the reach of defining marks. (1-26)
Thus, the fourth is indeed called the partless Śivatattva;
however, the second [form] of partlessness is devoid of meditation and worship.
Thus, that which is partless is declared; it is remembered as the supreme state (para-bhāva).
From that, by a tenfold and single division, arises the principle of Sādākhya.
According to the manner of the Liṅga-pīṭha, Sadāśiva is the characteristic of the Tattva;
from the Liṅga, Śambhu has arisen under the name Sadāśiva.
On the pedestal (pīṭha), Śakti has arisen, known by the name Manonmanī;
and in the liṅga and on the base (pīṭhikā), both Śakti and Śambhu have arisen.
The *liṅga* is thus masculinity (*puṃstva*), and its pedestal (*pīṭha*) is femininity (*strītva*).
The *liṅga* and the pedestal are partless (*niṣkala*), while Śakti and Śambhu are with parts (*sakala*).
The *niṣkala* is devoid of parts (*kalā*), while the *sakala* is endowed with parts;
[this applies] to ascetics, practitioners of mantra, men of knowledge, and yogis.

For the purpose of meditative worship, one should always worship the Lord of Gods by means of the manifest (sakala) and unmanifest (niṣkala) forms, according to the method of the liṅga and the pedestal.
That which is endowed with the thirty-eight *kalās* is indeed known as *sakala*;
one should then contemplate Sadāśiva, beginning from Īśa and ending with Sadyojāta. (1.34)
One should fashion the five heads with the Īśāna mantra;
one should fashion the four faces with the Puruṣa mantra alone.
One should perform the placement of the heart and other limbs using the Aghora mantra itself;
one should arrange the secret parts and so forth using the Vāmadeva mantra.
One should assign the limbs, beginning with the feet, using the Sadyojāta mantra, according to the sequence of eight, thirteen, eight, four, and five [syllables]. (1.37)
Sadyojāta, Vāmadeva, Aghora, Tatpuruṣa, and Īśāna are known as the Sakalas (the manifest).
Thus, the Sakala has been declared; this is indeed the certain conclusion regarding the Sakala.
The wise know the "entire" (sakala) as consisting of hands, feet, and limbs through conceptualization;
it is the Lord of Gods, the principle called Sādākhya, manifest and facing in all directions.
The lotus, born from the power of will (icchā-śakti), adorned with a thousand petals and joined with filaments and pericarp—therein indeed resides Sadāśiva. (1.40)
He has five heads, four faces, and is endowed with twelve eyes;
he has four mouths, four nostrils, eight ears, and four necks.
Having ten arms and one face, with two feet standing upon a lotus,
resembling pure crystal and possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns.
[He saw] the god, cool as the rays of the moon, gentle, adorned with all ornaments,
wearing white garments, and having a white sacred thread.

In the right hands, he holds the gesture of fearlessness, the trident, the axe, and the thunderbolt, as well as the shield, the goad, and the noose; and in the left hands, the bell and the gesture of granting boons. (1.44)
Endowed with these characteristics, he is remembered as Sadāśiva.
On his very left side is the primordial power, Manonmanī.
Just as heat is inseparable from fire, the power of the All-pervading Lord is likewise invariable.
Without Śakti there is no Śiva, and without Śiva there is no Śakti. (1.46)
All these gods are remembered by me as being composed of Śakti and Śambhu;
therefore, this entire universe, consisting of the moving and the unmoving, is declared to be composed of Śiva.
She has one face and four arms, adorned with all ornaments;
she has broad hips, a slender waist, and elevated breasts.

Having meditated upon Manonmanī, who possesses the characteristics [of the goddess] and is endowed with the powers (śaktis) such as Vāmā and the rest, the wise one should worship her indeed for the sake of bringing joy to the world. (1.49)
They arose in succession from the limbs of Brahmā, from the limbs of Vidyā, from the Vidyās themselves, from the lords of the Gaṇas, and from thousands of world-protectors.
All of them were endowed with their respective qualities and marked with their respective insignia;
they possessed all limbs in their entirety and shone with the splendor of infinite suns.
Four-armed and three-eyed, wearing crowns of matted hair,
they bowed to Sadāśiva while bearing their respective weapons.
Endowed with various colors, adorned with various ornaments, possessed of various fragrances, and beautified by various flowers. || 1.53 ||
When one's own self is always Śiva, and likewise the deities are enveloped therein, then the formless one, being himself formless, should perform worship with particular distinction. (1.54)
Whatever type of linga is to be fashioned, it should be prepared individually within the inner sanctum;
likewise, one should contemplate the forms and other features upon the pedestal of the linga. (1.55)
Now hear about all the gods with their veils (sarvāvaraṇa) and all [their aspects]; the forms beginning with Īśvara are proclaimed as the Sakala [category]. (1.56)
That which is called Sadāśiva is likewise said to be Īśvara;
and that which is Manonmanī is likewise said to be the reality (tattva) of Īśvarī.
One should likewise arrange the enclosures beginning with the mouth as before;
one should fashion images from wood, metal, stone, or clay. (1.58)

The wise one should understand that Śambhu, established in the principle of Vidyā and adorned with all ornaments, is the "festoon" (kautuka) of the Liṅga, and thus he is the "possessor of parts" (sakala). || 1.59 ||
At the conclusion of the worship of the Liṅga, one should worship Īśvara in due order;
it is said that the manifestation of Rudra arises from a thousandth part of Īśvara.
The four-armed, three-eyed god, whose crest is adorned with the crescent moon,
resembles a mass of lightning and holds an axe and a deer.
With all his limbs complete and adorned with every ornament,
he was on the left side of Goddess Umā, who was endowed with all auspicious marks.
Viṣṇu is proclaimed in that very same place as being a ten-millionth part of Īśvara;
Hari is dark-complexioned with reddish eyes, bearing the conch and the discus. (1.63)
Then the God, wearing yellow garments and accompanied by Śrī and Bhūmi,
was born from Brahmā, who himself was but a ten-millionth part of Īśvara.
He has four arms and four faces, wears a crown of matted hair, holds a water-pot and a rosary, is yellow in color, and possesses beautiful eyes. (1.65)
Accompanied by Sāvitrī, he is there remembered as the form of creation;
Viṣṇu is the form of preservation, and Rudra is the agent of dissolution.
Furthermore, the three forms are renowned as being established within the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa);
however, the partless (niṣkala) is the place of dissolution, and that [state] is without office (niṣkalām adhikāram).
320) Thus, the entire [universe] constitutes enjoyment (*bhoga*), consisting of dissolution, enjoyment, and authority;
the supreme is said to be partless (*niṣkala*), while the highest is remembered as having parts (*sakala*).
Thus, the supreme and the non-supreme have been declared; likewise, there is the manifest and the unmanifest.
Having understood the supreme and the non-supreme as they truly are, one becomes liberated and a destroyer of bonds. || 1-69 ||
Thereafter, three deities arose, from whom the thirty-three were born;
these were preceded by the eleven Rudras and joined by the twelve Ādityas.
The Vasus, the Aśvins, and the thirty-three presiding deities, as well as three thousand and thirty-three deities, are present there within those forms. (1.71)
Indeed, they weave garlands for the gods from the very essence of their bodies;
however, consciousness, when maintained through its connection with the stainless sovereignty, shall destroy [that impurity].
This has been declared as the emanation of Śiva; now hear the emanation of the bound souls (paśu).
Thus ends the first chapter, the section on the procedure for the emanation of Śiva. || 1 ||
Now follows the chapter on the ritual procedure for the release of the bound soul (paśu). Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the sequence of the ritual for the release of the bound soul;
in the teaching of Śiva, the state of being a bound soul is said to be beginningless.
The Self exists from Śiva, indeed for the very purpose of creating the universe;
through its connection with the principles of Vidya and the rest, it is proclaimed as the "Self-principle" (Ātma-tattva). (2-2)
Now, the Self is eternally stainless and pure, yet it is bound by *māyā*;
due to its connection with innate impurity, it is called "the bound soul" (*paśu*) by the wise. (2–3)
The individual soul (paśu), however, is formless, eternal, devoid of qualities, inactive, and sovereign;
yet, having entered the belly of Māyā, it is all-pervasive and remains engaged in the means of experience. (2–4)
"But 'exclusive' (sakevala) is said [to refer to the soul] due to its bondage by the impurity of the individual nature (āṇavamala).
The individual (āṇava) is said to be innate (sahaja), like a conch-shell [spiral], in successive order. (2.5)
Delusion, pride, passion, dejection, and envy, as well as exhilaration and hypocrisy—these seven are the innate impurities. (2.6)
That which is innate (sahaja) is described as being solely associated with impurity (mala).
It is called "innate impurity" (sahaja-mala); now hear about adventitious impurity (āgantuka-mala).
In the practice for attaining Śiva, this [impurity] is twofold: that which consists of illusion (māyā) and that which is born of karma.
The former is characterized by bondage through power (śakti), while the latter is marked by the principles beginning with kalā and ending with earth.
One should understand that [bondage] is dependent on *māyā* and born of merit and demerit through karma;
furthermore, within *māyā*, it becomes threefold: that which is atomic (*āṇava*), that which is born of desire (*kāma*), and that which is born of *māyā*. || 2-9 ||
Impurity, ignorance, darkness, and likewise that which causes obscuration—these are synonyms for my term "avidyā" (nescience). (2-10)
The self, when bound by the three impurities and accompanied by the *sakala* [state], is called *sakala*. Thus, the bound self is a transmigrator as well as one who possesses sense objects. (2-11)
The field, the knower of the field, the enjoyer, as well as the one possessing knowledge, the experiencer, and the embodied one—these are synonyms for the self (ātman). || 2-12 ||
Indeed, there are eighty-four thousand divisions of the womb,
which are attained there under the name of "living beings."
The state of being possessed of all [impurities] has been declared; now hear about the pure state from me.
For the purpose of destroying the impurities, there is another [means], namely, the descent of power (śaktinipāta). || 2.14 ||
As long as the descent of power (śaktipāta) lasts, so long does the experience of ignorance persist;
all previous karmas [are exhausted] when the descent of power is equal. (2.15)
Just as devotion toward Śiva arises by depending upon the state of Sadāśiva, so too, having entered initiation, one should perform worship with devotion. (2-16)
Then, having practiced yoga, one should practice the system of knowledge (jñānatantra);
then, one should destroy the darkness of ignorance with the lamp of knowledge. (2.17)
That gnosis is pure by its very nature, and its essence is likewise stainless;
for it is just like a crystal in relation to dark blue and other colors. (2.18)
Through such reality and great effort, it becomes like a pure crystal;
just as a lamp hidden within a jar shines forth when the jar is destroyed. (2-19)
Just as the sun is said to be covered by a jar, so too it may be [said to be] released;
in that same way, bondage and liberation are proclaimed to belong to the self. (2-20)
The wise say that one who perceives the self as enveloped by impurities is "impure," whereas the wise say that one who perceives the self as freed from impurities is "pure. (2-21)
At that time, having attained the state of being stainless through the recollection of the Lord,
I then recollected the Lord and subsequently became absorbed in Him.
Just as a man who, wandering at night with the notion that it is a snake, stands upon a rope, does not see the snake when his delusion has vanished in the course of time; || 2-23 ||
Now, because it is pure by its very nature, the self is liberated from bondage;
liberation through the knowledge of that nature is indeed what constitutes one who is liberated while living (jīvanmukta). (2-24)

Upon the destruction of the body, there is the attainment of the Supreme, just as space remains when a jar is destroyed; once this knowledge of "I am That" has arisen, one should indeed avoid the path of ritual worship.
For all principles and all beings are seen as indeed the Self alone;
it is equal toward both pleasure and pain, and thus the same toward the pleasant and the unpleasant. (2.26)
However, the karmas initiated by the body are experienced by oneself alone;
just as when asafoetida is removed from its vessel, its fragrance does not vanish from there. (2-27)
Just as the potter’s wheel continues to spin even after the work is finished, so too,
O Knower of Reality, do all actions persist until their destruction within the bodies.
Seeds scorched by fire do not sprout upon the earth;
likewise, for one who knows the one abiding in the three castes, rebirth does not exist. (2-29)
This is declared to be the pure state, characterized by all the qualities such as the principles (tattvas) and so forth.
The Puruṣa is said to possess three states; now, listen to the paths (adhvan) from him. 2-30.
Thus ends the second chapter, the section on the ritual for the emission of the sacrificial animal (paśu).
Now, the chapter on the method of the paths (adhvavidhipaṭala). (p.
323) Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the paths in brief. O Vināyaka, the path is said to be sixfold, beginning with the path of reality (tattvādhvan). 3-1.

Know that the path of reality (tattvādhvan) is the first, the path of worlds (bhuvanādhvan) is the second, the path of mantras (mantrādhvan) is indeed the third, and the path of phonemes (varṇādhvan) is indeed the fourth. || 3-2 ||
The path of words (padādhvan) is to be known as the fifth, and the path of kalās (kalādhvan) is remembered as the sixth.
Through these sixfold paths, one should enter the one Lord.

Listen now to a brief account of the path of reality (tattvādhvan), beginning with the terrestrial shell (bhūkaṭāha) and so forth; the path starting from earth and ending with Māyā is described in sequence. (3–4)
From the fire of time (Kālāgni) up to the end of the hundred Rudras is known as the Brahmāṇḍa;
now, the height of the shell of that egg is said to be ten million yojanas.
Above that, they know the world of the god Kālāgnirudra;
it stands surrounded by many tens of millions of Rudras.
The lion-throne was a great island, adorned with various jewels,
three thousand yojanas in extent and one thousand yojanas in height.
By heating the earth, six crores [of years] are ordained. || 3-8 ||
The great mass of the fire of time (Kālāgni) consists of seventeen crores;
above that, one should know there is a hell extending for four thousand [yojanas].
By their power, thirty-two principal [hells] arise among them; of those, three are situated one above the other.
Now hear of the thirty-two hells.
Raurava is declared the first, Mahāraurava the second;
Śītoṣṇa is indeed the third, and Santāpana the fourth.
The fifth is likewise the *padma*; the sixth is the *mahāpadma*;
the seventh is the *kamala*, and the eighth is the *sūcimukha*.
The ninth is the black thread, while the tenth is remembered as the glorious face (śrīmukha). The eleventh is the razor-base (kṣurādhāra), and the twelfth is the sword-edge (asidhāra).
(324) The eleventh among the hells is remembered as the unblazing Raurava;
Kumbhīpāka is the first, and Huṃkāra is the second. (3-14)
The three [mudrās] known as Reśī, Nokaha, and Tuṇḍa have been proclaimed;
blood and pus are the fourth, while Gajapāda is the fifth.
Kṛkaraccheda is the sixth, while Taptamoha is the seventh;
Trapuloma is declared the eighth, and Taptavāluka is the ninth.
The tenth is Astibhaṅga, primarily characterized by the Kuṃbhīpāka hell;
know that Avīci is the first, while Jalūka is the Sadānadī (the River of Ever-flowing Water).
The third is indeed Haimavarṇa, and the fourth is Śālmalī; Anadhvāsa, Nirucchvāsa, Pūtimāṃsa, and Anudaka. (3.18)
Jatupaṅka, Cakraloha,
and Yugmaparvata are the foremost among the nine hells, specifically within the Avīci group.
Raurava, Kumbhīpāka, and Avīci—these three are indeed known as the hells belonging to the lords of kings of kings. (3-20)
One should contemplate Raurava as impure, Kumbhīpāka as Tāpana, and Avīci as being filled with a mass of worms. (3.21)
Surrounded by seven secondary hells for each of the three,
there are twenty-nine hells, each further encircled by three.
Thus the hells have been described, beginning with the forty;
these most terrible hells are triangular in shape and so arranged. (3.23)
Hell is declared for sinners, while heaven is said to be for the righteous;
those who misappropriate the property of the gods and those who revile the scriptures of Śiva [fall into hell]. (3-24)
Having committed the murder of a father, the killing of a Brahmin, and other such acts many times over,
he fell into the ocean of hell, taking refuge in a place of torment.
Endowed with freedom from anger, purity, right conduct, patience, and skillful means, whatever merit arises from devotion to Śiva is accompanied by compassion for all living beings. (3-26)
All such base men indeed go to hell;
now, my dear son, listen with a concentrated mind to the dimensions of those hells.
They know that each [of the nine mountains] has a height of ninety million [yojanas];
the interval between them is known to be only one wing-span (pakṣa), and is recorded as being one hundred million [yojanas]. (3-28)
Thus, three hundred thousand hells have been proclaimed;
the one called Adhaḥraurava is said to be the lowest, while Kumbhīpāka is the middlemost.
Above Avīci, three locations for them are said to be known;
however, below and above the hells, there are twenty thousand [yojanas]. (3.30)
He is the lord of hell, this Kūśmāṇḍa who resides there;
his city is proclaimed to have ninety-nine thousand [enclosures].
One hundred thousand is to be known as a *lakṣa*;
he is also called the lord of the *kuśmāṇḍas* and is remembered as the master of the hells.
Above that, I shall describe Pātāla in brief:
Mahātala, Sutala, Rasātala, and Talātala. (3.33)
Pātāla, Śaṅkara, Ābhāsa, and Sapaka—
these are known as the seven Mahātalas, collectively designated as Pātāla.
The Nāgas, Cāraṇas, Rākṣasas, Devas, and likewise Apsarases,
dwelling happily in Mahātala, were sporting with joyful hearts.
The height is nine hundred thousand [yojanas], and the interval is said to be one hundred thousand;
the distance between the netherworlds (pātālas) is likewise measured at exactly one hundred thousand [yojanas].
Beyond that is the golden Pātāla, measuring ten lakhs [yojanas];
above it dwells the divine Vasu, Hāṭaka, the Supreme Lord.
Because all that— adorned with various ornaments and surrounded by ten million cities—
is made of gold (hāṭaka), he is therefore called Hāṭakeśvara.
Above that, nine lakṣas are proclaimed to be in the intermediate space (antarikṣa);
the shell of the earth (bhūkaṭa) is ordained to have a thickness of ten lakṣas of clay.
The station presided over by Kūṣmā is known as śatalakṣa;
śatalakṣa is to be understood as koṭi, and fifty koṭis is what is remembered [as the next stage]. (3–40)
The characteristics of the earth have been declared up to its limits; now hear concerning the worlds of the earth (bhūloka).
It is renowned as the world of the earth, endowed with seven oceans. (3-41)

The world of the earth (bhūrloka), the world of the atmosphere (bhuvarloka), the world of the sun (svarloka), as well as the world of radiance (maharloka), the world of birth (janaloka), the world of austerity (tapoloka), and the world of truth (satyaloka) is the seventh. (3.42)
I shall declare the measurement and the characteristics of the seven worlds;
first, I will speak of Bhūrloka—listen indeed to this in brief. (3.43)
It is filled with various inhabited lands and endowed with diverse objects;
it comprises Jambūdvīpa and the other continents, and is joined with the milk-ocean and the Bodhi tree.
In its center stands Mount Mahāmeru in the form of gold,
measuring one hundred thousand yojanas, arranged sequentially in the shape of a lotus seed-vessel (karṇikā).
It has entered sixteen thousand [yojanas] beneath the earth,
and it is ordained to extend eighty-four thousand yojanas above.
The upper portion has its base level, with a width at the summit twice that of the base;
it is endowed with various peaks and adorned with various terraces, jewels, and creepers.
Above that, one should know the assembly halls of the high-souled Brahmā;
they are named Ānava-tī and consist of a collection of all kinds of jewels.
It measures fourteen thousand yojanas in extent;
it is adorned with various ornaments and filled with hosts of ṛṣis and siddhas.
Above that, in the northern direction, is what is called Jyotiḥśikhara;
its width and height are both twenty thousand [yojanas]. (3.50)
Adorned with various ornaments and composed of various colors,
it was joined with golden palaces and featured golden ramparts and gateways.
Accompanied by Gandharvas, surrounded by hosts of all the gods,
joined by all the Gaṇas, and adorned by thirty thousand [attendants].
Indeed, I shall dwell there eternally together with the goddess Umā;
to the western side of that place, there shall be the peak known as Kuṇṭha.
Adorned with every ornament and surrounded by hosts of sages and perfected beings,
it measures fourteen thousand [yojanas] in both width and height.
Resplendent and composed of all kinds of jewels, with golden walls and arched gateways,
Viṣṇu dwells right there, surrounded by hosts of all the gods.
For the sake of protecting the world of beings, they dwell there with joyful hearts;
likewise, they perform the acts of creation, preservation, and destruction in due order.
One thousand yojanas below the summit, to the east, lies the city of Indra known by the name Amarāvatī. (3.57)
The city of Agni, renowned by the name Tejovatī, is proclaimed as being in the eastern quarter; and in the southern region of Yama is the city named Saṃyamanī.
To the west is the city named Kṛṣṇāṅganā, the abode of the Rākṣasas belonging to Nirṛti;
and indeed, to the west of Varuṇa is the city named Śuddhavatī.
In the wind-quarter of Vāyu is the city named Gandhavatī;
and in the northern quarter of Soma is the city named Mahodayā.
In the northeastern quarter of Īśāna flows the river named Dhāvatī;
it is adorned by all thousands of millions of cities.
Having bathed well in the waters of the Gaṅgā, they sport with joyful hearts;
Bhagiratha [bestowed] four niṣkas, starting from the east, in due order.
Mandara is in the eastern quarter, Gandhamādana in the south;
Piṅgala is in the western part, and Supārśva likewise in the north.
White, green, blue, and the color of a pomegranate flower;
they are fifty thousand yojanas in height.
The Lord desired eight thousand and forty-two for the extensive [foundation];
the width at their base is double the width at the top.
Situated above Mount Mandara is a tree named Kadamba;
it is one thousand yojanas in height and is adorned with thousands of trunks.
That flower is like a potter's wheel and resembles a conch shell; there are a thousand of them, and upon the summit of Mount Gandhamādana stands the tree known as Jambū.
Its trunk and branches are twice as high as the kadamba tree;
moreover, its jambu fruits are the size of great elephants.
From those fallen fruits, the river Jāmbūnadī was produced;
there, by the name Vegavatī, she performed a circumambulation of Mount Meru.
O King, everything brought in by him was gold for ornaments;
likewise, all those who dwelt there were made of Jāmbūnada gold.
The *aśvattha* tree, indeed known by the name Ketu, stands upon the summit of Vipula;
it rises a thousand *yojanas* high and is adorned with thousands of trunks. (3.71)
It should be known as resembling the fruit of the aśvattha tree, adorned with the names of its circular forms;
by its side stands a nyagrodha tree, situated directly above it.
It is joined with seven groups, diverse, manifold, and auspicious; and the four castes are said to be situated from the east to the north.
To the east is a forest named Caitraratha, adorned with flowers;
in its midst there is a lake named Vāruṇodaya.
Adorned with crocodiles, many fish, and lotus flowers,
there is especially a forest there named Nandana to the south.
In its center is celebrated the lake named Mānasa;
indeed, on its western side is the lake Vaiśrāja, which possesses abundant water.
To the north is a most enchanting lake named Patravana;
Meru is proclaimed to be situated there, endowed with such characteristics.
On the slopes of Meru lie the regions known briefly as the Pāruṣas;
Jambūdvīpa is proclaimed to extend as far as the salt ocean.
Jambū, Śāka, Kuśa, Krauñca, Śālmalika, Gomeda, and Puṣkara are declared to be the seven islands; now hear about the oceans.
The salt-water ocean, the milk-ocean, the ghee-ocean, the sugarcane-juice ocean, the honey-ocean, the wine-ocean, and the fresh-water ocean— these are celebrated as the seven great oceans.
O Leader, one should know that Jambūdvīpa, which is one hundred thousand yojanas in extent, is surrounded by the Salt Ocean beyond it, as described by Kamalākṣa.
Surrounded on the outside by a double [the size], it is named Śākadvīpa;
indeed, in this manner, each island and ocean is double the size of the preceding island.
The measurement from the edge of the sweet-water ocean to Mount Meru and so forth is said to be fifty million five hundred and seven lakhs; now hear [the rest] up to the end of the lordship.
The gods and the rākṣasas were likewise well-impelled by the Lord;
formerly, Svayambhū Manu protected the seven continents.
His son was Mahāvīrya, Priyavrata, and Surakṣaka; ten sons of great strength were born to him through his power. (3.85)
Agnidhṛt, Agnibāhu, Medhā, Medhātithi, Vibhu, Jyotiṣmat, Dhṛtimat, Bhavya, Avasāna, and Putra. || 3.86 ||
Agnibāhu and Medhāvī—these three sons went forth as renunciants;
the remaining seven sons became the sharers of the portions of the seven continents.
Agnidhṛt protected Jambūdvīpa by the strength of his arms; Nābhi and Puruṣa likewise, as well as Hari, were surrounded by water. || 3.88 ||
Bhadrāśva, Ketumāla, Puṣkara, and Hiraṇmaya;
then the ninth, named after his son—these are proclaimed as the nine sons. (3.89)
Jambūdvīpa was indeed divided into nine parts for them:
three were designated as the southern [division], and likewise three in the north.
Three mountains are renowned as being in the middle region, separated by other ranges;
likewise, Himavat is in the south and Makūṭa is to its north.
It is declared to be to the north of Niṣadha and Hemakūṭa;
and Nīla and Triśṛṅga extend out from the north.
Situated to the east, extending toward the west, and more auspicious than the ocean,
these six mountains were then endowed with all sovereign powers.
To the east and west of Mount Meru are the Mālyavat and Gandhamādana mountains;
the Niṣadha and Nīla mountains form their boundaries, situated respectively to the south and north.
The Himavat mountain is eighty yojanas in width and two thousand yojanas in height;
it is white as snow, while Hemakūṭa is golden.
Niṣadha has the luster of a ruby; Gandhamādana has the appearance of sapphire; Mālyavat is yellow in color, and [Nila] is likewise composed of lapis lazuli.
Śveta, however, is white in color, three-peaked like a moonstone;
these are said to be the boundary mountains. Now hear of the countries and the lords of those countries. (3.97)
On the northern side of Triśṛṅga and on the southern side of the salt ocean lies the region known as Kmaradeśa; its sovereign shall be Guru. (3.98)
It should be known as being shaped like a bow, measuring nine thousand yojanas; the sands there are to be understood as being like gold, remaining so situated. (3-99)
People dwell everywhere, eating the fruits of the trees of desire;
they indeed live for three hundred thousand years.
Likewise, women give birth to twins;
they have complexions resembling dark flowers and are free from fear and suffering. (3.101)
And there, on that very same Kulaparvata, is the lovely Sūryakānta;
know that it is named after Ruru, and from that indeed comes Kuruvinde.
Having entered the salt ocean, that which is called Candradīpa is situated;
in its northwestern direction, the island Bhadrākara is recorded.
The people there have a lifespan of a thousand years and subsist on the fruits of divine mango trees;
between Triśṛṅga and Śveta, there is the region of Hiraṇmaya.
Nine thousand yojanas in width and extending as far as the ocean in length,
all the people there have moon-like faces and subsist on the fruit of the *vakula* tree.
Thus, their lifespan is proclaimed to be a thousand years while they live;
between Sunīla and Śveta, there is remembered a delightful region called Varṣa.
Having consumed the fruit of a banyan tree, which is nine thousand yojanas in width and ten thousand yojanas in height, they attained a radiance equal to that of a blue lotus.
They live for twelve thousand years, free from fear,
[visiting] the region of Merupradakṣiṇa as well as Avadhūtana.
Extending nine thousand yojanas all around,
it is illuminated by the rays of the moon and by the brilliance of the fire of Meru.
Having drunk the juice of the jambu fruit, people were freed from disease;
their lifespan is proclaimed to be thirteen thousand years. (3.110)
To the east of the ocean and to the west of Gandhamādana, however, is the region named Ketumāla; its people are likewise dark-complexioned.
Having eaten the fruit of the *panasa* tree, the rivers flow for ten thousand leagues;
they extend thirty-four thousand *yojanas* from south to north. (3.112)
Its east-west extent is thirty-two thousand [yojanas],
from the western part of the ocean to the eastern part of the Vāhyavat mountain.
The region named Bhadrāśva is indeed inhabited by people who resemble the moon;
by eating the fruit of the black mango, they attain a lifespan of ten thousand years. (3.114)
Its length and breadth extend from the Ketumāla mountain range to the south of Niṣadha and to the north of Hemakūṭa.
Know that Harivarṣa extends to the edge of the ocean,
being recorded as ten thousand [yojanas] in length and nine thousand yojanas in width according to measurement.
The inhabitants there, who have the luster of silver, drink from the Ikṣu river;
their lifespan is proclaimed to be exactly twelve thousand years.
To the south of Hemakūṭa and likewise to the north of Himavat,
