in the middle lies the region of Kiṃpuruṣa, with the same dimensions in width and length as previously described.
The people there are golden-hued and subsist on the fruit of the *plakṣa* tree;
their lifespan is said to be twelve thousand years until the end of their lives.
O Bharata, on the southern side of the Himavat and to the north of the salt ocean, there was the Nābhi-vṛkṣodbhava; he is remembered as his son.
That region is called Bhārata-varṣa after his name; it is described as being shaped like a bow, nine thousand [yojanas] in extent, and stretching as far as the ocean.
Crowded with various settlements and beset by the fear of disease among the people,
their happiness lasts for a single *kalpa*, yet they endure great suffering, subsisting on food produced through agriculture;
their lifespan is one hundred years, according to the cycle of the four ages.
In this way, one should understand that virtue alone brings about the acquisition of auspicious and inauspicious fruits. || 3-123 ||
Know this to be the land of action (*karmabhūmi*), and likewise another is the land of heaven (*svargabhūmi*).
Having attained the fruit of liberation and enjoyment, one then attains auspiciousness (*śiva*). Thereafter, Bhārata-varṣa is divided into nine regions.
Nine sons were born to Bharata, preceded by Indrapūrva.
Indra, Kaśeru, Tāmravarṇa, Gabhastimān, the Nāga Saumya, the Gandharva, and Varuṇa are the Kumārikās. (3.126)
Their respective islands should be understood by their very names, in order:
Indradvīpa, Kaśerumān, Tāmravarṇa, and Gabhastimān. (3.127)
Nāgadvīpa, Saumya, Gāndharva, and likewise Varuṇa;
the ninth is called Kumāra—these are proclaimed to be their divisions. (3.128)
Separated by the ocean, there shall be five hundred [leagues] of land;
the islands other than Kumāradvīpa are proclaimed to be the islands of the Mlecchas. (3-129)
It is endowed with the four castes and joined with the four stages of life;
furthermore, five hundred [sacred sites] of the nine [rivers], beginning with the Gaṅgā, are to be known.
Tens of millions of sacred fords have been described as yielding the fruit of great merit;
on the slopes within the Himalayas lies the great peak of Kailāsa.
The great Śeṣa, silver-colored and frequented by sages and Siddhas, was adorned with every ornament and beautified everywhere by trees. (3.132)
Dwelling there eternally, accompanied by the goddess Umā,
he presides over the sixty-eight great sacred fields (mahākṣetra) established from the beginning of the Purāṇa.
The six continents, beginning with Jambūdvīpa, are situated within the oceans;
[they are bounded by] Mahendra, Mandhara, Sṛṅgavān, Śuktimat, and the Ṛkṣa mountain. (3.134)
The Vindhya and the Pāripātra—these are the principal mountain ranges;
Malaya, Dvīpa, Gālaṅkā, and Cāmīkara are auspicious and golden.
Endowed with various wonders, they take delight with the lords of the Rākṣasas.
Jambūdvīpa has been fully described; now hear about the Salt Ocean (Lavaṇoda).
The salt ocean, which surrounds it, has an extent of two hundred thousand [yojanas];
and twelve mountain ranges indeed enter into the salt ocean.
Prabhāva, Dhūmra, and Dundubhi are situated in the eastern quarter;
likewise, Cakra, Maināka, and Valāha are in the south.
Situated between Maināka and Cakra is the submarine fire (vaḍabānala);
Varāha is in Somaka, and Śvanandana is in the western direction.
Kaṅka, Candra, and Droṇa are likewise situated in Uttara;
it is said that the salt ocean [surrounds it]. Now hear about Śākadvīpa.
Puṣpavān is the lord of Śākadvīpa, as is Kuśavān in Kuśadvīpa;
Jyotiṣmān is in Krauñcadvīpa, and likewise Dyutimān in Śālmalidvīpa.
These nine, who dwell in Gomedadvīpa, are said to be possessed of great strength.
The two sons are declared to be equal, and they are said to have two shares each there. || 3-142 ||
The mountain named Mānasottara is ring-shaped;
the duration of time for the inhabitants of the islands beginning with Śāka is like that of the Kṛta and other yugas.
p. 333) But the extent of Meru and the other [mountains] is five crores and seven hundred thousand; this has been proclaimed there in brief. (3-144)
Beyond that, the ground made of gold extends for ten koṭis;
it is said by me to be there for the sake of the play of the gods. (3.145)
The mountain named Lokāloka, which is circular in shape,
is one thousand yojanas in width and one hundred thousand yojanas in height.
The world-protectors stand there, attended by perfected beings and gods;
within it shines the sun, and beyond that, moreover, is darkness.
The Lokāloka mountain, having surrounded the oceans of the interior of the world (garbhodadhi), surrounds those [oceans];
and the Pārthiva mountain, having surrounded the garbhodadhi oceans, is known as the enclosure (varaṇa).
Surrounding the terrestrial shell, which extends for one hundred million [yojanas], the shell is said to extend for fifty million [yojanas] up to the center of Mount Meru. (3.149)
This Bhūrloka is known to extend equally in the ten directions for a measure of one billion [yojanas]. Now hear concerning Bhuvarloka. (3.150)
The world of the Sun is ordained to measure one hundred thousand yojanas;
likewise, there are twelve Ādityas, eight Vasus, and eleven Rudras.
The two Aśvins and thirty-three [deities] move about by the will of Śiva; it is traditionally taught that they do not perform a circumambulation of Meru within the Bhuvarloka. (3-152)
Above that, at a distance of one lakh [yojanas], the world of the Moon (Candraloka) is situated;
and one lakh above the Moon, the circle of the constellations (Nakṣatramaṇḍala) is located. (3.153)
One should know Mercury at two hundred thousand [yojanas]; Bhārgava is recorded at two hundred thousand;
Aṅgāra likewise at two hundred thousand, and Bṛhaspati at two hundred thousand. (3.154)
O sages, it is said that at two hundred thousand yojanas [from the sun],
Atri, Vasiṣṭha, Pulastya, Pulaha, and Kratu reside at one hundred thousand yojanas.
Bhṛgu, Aṅgiras, and Marīci are proclaimed as the seven sages;
above them, Dhruva is said to be situated at a distance of one hundred thousand [yojanas].

From the world of the moon up to the pole star (dhruva) is proclaimed as the heavenly world (svargaloka). From the surface of the earth to the end of the pole star is fifteen hundred thousand [yojanas]. (3.157)
Beyond that, the Maharloka is recorded as being twenty million yojanas;
and the Janaloka is recorded as being eighty-five hundred thousand [yojanas]. (3.158)
Eighty million [yojanas] high, the world is situated layer upon layer;
likewise, Satyaloka is established at a height of twelve million [yojanas]. (3-159)
From the Maharloka up to Satyaloka, the Rudras are the inhabitants there;
Brahma-loka is ordained to measure sixteen crores [of yojanas].
The world of Viṣṇu is proclaimed to measure one koṭi yojanas;
the world of Rudra is said here to measure nine koṭis.
The thickness of the shell of the cauldron is recorded as fifty crores;
thus, with one hundred crores of yojanas, the Brahmāṇḍa is indeed situated there.
Hear now, indeed, the hundred names of the sustainers of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) therein:
Kapālīśa, Aja, Buddha, Vajradeha, and Pramardana. || 3.163 ||
Vibhūti, Avyaya, Śāstṛ, Pinākī, and Tridaśādhipa—endowed with sovereign power, they have overtaken the strength of Indra. || 3.164 ||
The great Rudras, honored by Śakra, the king of gods, roam about:
Agnirudra, Hutāśa, Piṅgala, Kādaka, and Hara. (3.165)
Jvalanodahana, Babhru, Bhasmāntaka, Kṣayāntaka—having overcome the power of Agni, they were endowed with sovereign might. || 3.166 ||
The great Rudras, worshipped by Vahnirāja, roam about;
in the southern direction are Amṛtyuhara, Dhātṛ, Vidhātṛ, Karty, and Kālaka. (3.167)
They are the uniter and the disuniter, as well as the abiding nature of dharma and adharma;
having overcome the power of dharma, they are endowed with sovereign might.
Wandering about, honored by Yamarāja, the great god Nairṛta is a slayer of Māras, cruel of gaze, and terrifying. (3-169)
With hair standing erect, with deformed eyes, and possessing smoke-colored and red fangs,
they have overcome the power of Nirṛti and are endowed with sovereign might.
The great gods, well-honored by the Rākṣasa and endowed with sovereign power,
moved about after having overcome the host of Varuṇa.
The great gods, well-honored by Varuṇa, move about;
[the wind] is swift, light, possessing the speed of the wind, subtle, sharp, and the bringer of destruction at the end.
Pañcāntaka, Pañcaśikha, Kapardin, and Meṣavāhana,
having overcome the strength of Vāyu, were endowed with sovereign power.
The great gods wander about, honored by Soma as their king;
and there is the omniscient Vidyādhara, the bearer of knowledge who has reached the further shore of the Vedas. (3.174)
Sureśvara, Sarveśa, Bhūtapāla, Balipriya, Sukhakṛt, and Duḥkhakṛt—these are [the forms] of Śiva in brief. (3.175)
Having overcome the power of Īśāna and being endowed with sovereign might,
the great gods wander about, honored by Īśāna himself.
Vṛṣa, Vṛṣadhara, Kānta, Krodheśa, Anilāśana,
Grāsana, Udumbara, Phaṇīndra, and Vajradaṃṣṭravat.
Having overcome the power of Viṣṇu,
the great gods, endowed with sovereign might and highly honored by the name of Viṣṇu, move about.
This earth has been described; now hear concerning its ending in water.
Having established [the earth] all around the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), one should provide it with a tenfold enclosure. (3.179)
Amareśa and Prabhāva, Naimiśa and likewise Puṣkara;
Āṣāḍhīśa, Piṇḍīśa, Hārabhūta, and Vākula.
Thus, the Proṣṭha and the Guhyāṣṭaka are situated within the covering of water;
above that, by a factor of ten, is the great covering of fire.
[They] praised Hariścandra, Suśaila, Amrātikeśvara,
Mahākāla, Madhyama, Kedāra, and likewise Bhairava.
Thus, the eight most secret [mantras] are based on the enclosure of fire;
however, the enclosure of wind above the deity is ten times greater.
Gaya and Kurukṣetra, Nakhala and likewise Nākhala,
Vimala and Aṭṭahāsa, Mahendra and Bhīma as well.
Thus, the eightfold secret of secrets indeed exists, surrounded by the layers of wind;
above that, however, there is the ether (vyoma), situated and surrounded tenfold.
Vastrāpada, Rudrakoṭi, Ravimukta, Mahālaya, Gokarṇa, Bhadrakarṇa, Suvarṇākṣa, and Sthāṇuka. || 3.186 ||
Thus, the eight purifiers (pavitrās) are indeed situated within the enclosure of space (vyomāvaraṇa).
Above that, however, stands the ego-principle (ahaṃkāra), which is ten times [the size] of the former.
Khagalenduka, Karaṇḍa, Umākoṭi, Maṇḍaleśvara, Kauñjara, Śaṅkhukarṇa, Sthūleśvara, and Sthaleśvara—
one should know this to be the group of eight sacred sites (sthānāṣṭaka), situated in the east and other directions, bringing about peace.
The eightfold white secret has been proclaimed, as well as the red which is indeed not to be loathed.
The eightfold secret-most, the yellow and the black, the purifier,
and the eightfold station resembling crystal— thus the five groups of eight are remembered. Having sprinkled [the area] shaped like a wing, one should indeed take up residence there.
These are proclaimed to be the abodes of enjoyment for the Lord Śrīkaṇṭha.
Furthermore, when the intellect (buddhi) exists in the upward direction, enveloped by ten qualities, it is known as the eightfold divine womb (devayoni):
that of the Piśācas, Rākṣasas, Yakṣas, Gandharvas, and Indras;
as well as that of the Soma, Prajāpati, and Brahmā.
Know this to be the city of eight, which relies upon the veil of the intellect.
The divine abodes have been described, endowed with all sovereign powers;
however, above the veil of the qualities (guṇāvaraṇa), that of the intellect (buddhi) is remembered as being tenfold [superior].
The Akṛta, the Kṛta, the Bhairava, and the Brāhma;
the Vaiṣṇava, the Kaumāra, the Kaumīśra, and the Ekarṇa. (3.195)
Thus, the eightfold yoga has been declared, which rests upon the veil of qualities;
among the lords of yoga, he who is the enjoyer is worshipped with devotion by those intent on yoga.
Their abodes are divine and endowed with the power of yoga;
above that, however, stands the Unmanifest (avyakta), enveloped tenfold.
Krodha, Caṇḍa, Saṃvarta, Jyotis, Piṅgala, Sūraka, Pañcāntaka, Eka-vīra, and Īśvara accompanied by Śivā. || 3-198 ||
Thus, the eightfold Mahādeva resides within the veil of the manifest; moreover, the unmanifest is called both *prakṛti* and *pradhāna*. (3.199)
Beyond this, there is another which the wise know as the veil called rāga;
from that, the supreme principle of puruṣa is a hundred times greater. (3-200)
Therein are Rudra of great splendor, Vāmadeva, Bhava, and Udbhava,
along with Ekaliṅga, Īkṣaṇeśāna, and the various worlds, each distinct from one another.
Those gods are the size of a thumb and are designated as having the thumb as their essence;
they are liberated through Māyā and Jñāna, and they possess the power of the Supreme Lord.

In that very place, the person (puruṣa) is to be known as resting upon the veil called passion (rāga); [therein are] the six elements consisting of the skin, the elements, and the objects of the senses. (3-203)
The intellect, the mind, the ego, and especially the three qualities—endowed with these, the Puruṣa remains established on earth within the principle of the Self (ātmatattva). (3.204)
Beyond that, the principle of Vidyā is a hundred times more powerful than Rāga;
it consists of Vāmadeva, Aghora, Bhīma, and likewise Ugra. (3.205)
Śarva, Īśāna, Ekavīra, Īśvara, Pracaṇḍadhṛt, Umābhakta, Ajeśa, and Ānanda. (3.206)
For from that [level], Śiva alone resides, supported by the veil of knowledge (vidyāvaraṇa);
above that, the principle of time (kālatattva) occurs, exceeding [the level of] knowledge by a hundredfold.
Ucchra, Śuṣka, Ambara, Mātaṅga, Ghorarūpaka,
Yāmya, Halāhala, Krodheśa, and Vasavāmukha.
Sthūlarudra, Varṣarudra, Rudra, and likewise Rudragalaguru—
these twelve of great prowess are situated within the Kalā-āvaraṇa.
Above this, there is Māyā, which exceeds [the previous] by one hundred [levels].
Within the pair of enclosures (saṃpuṭa), Māyā is established with twelve Rudras. (3.210)
One should know that in the lower casket is the Vidyā, and in the upper casket is the supreme upward breath;
likewise, in the Gahana [casket] are the Praśasta, the Avyaya, and the Lord Harihara.
Daśeśāna, as well as Trikāla and Gopati, and Adhomāyā at the end of the Puṭa—these are proclaimed as the six Rudras. (3.212)
Kṣemīśa, Brahmācārī, Vidyeśāna, Viśveśvara, Śiva, and Ananta—these indeed are the six. (3.213)
Those which extend upwards to the edges of the petals are proclaimed as the Rudras;
in their midst is the Blessed One, Ananteśa, the Lord of the World. (3.214)
Having brought about their manifestation, the Lord acts according to his own will;
those Rudras who are established in succession, beginning with Māyā and ending with the Earth.
There, those whose minds are gladdened by enjoyments and the like partake of them in various places;
subsequently, having resorted to knowledge, they take refuge in the principle of Śiva (śivatattva).
The characteristic ending with Māyā has been declared; now hear the characteristic that follows it.
Above Māyā, however, there is Ātman, whose stability is increased a hundredfold. (3-217)
Then that self is stainless and pure through qualities such as omniscience;
it should be known as this supreme seed of the world, which brings about the manifestation of Śiva. (3-218)

For the Self is indeed enveloped by Māyā, yet it exists for the sake of manifesting Śiva; likewise, the state of being the Lord of Paśus and Pāśas, as well as the three Guṇas, are found therein. || 3-219 ||
The Self is to be known in this way; now hear likewise concerning the reality of knowledge (vidyā-tattva).
The reality of knowledge is established as a thousandth part of the Self. (3.220)
Īśvara is established there, accompanied by Brahmā, Aṅga, and the others;
and above that is Sādākhya, where Sadāśiva resides.
Above that is the principle of the Bindu; above that is indeed the Nāda;
above that is the Śakti-principle, and further above is the Primordial Śakti.
Above that is the principle of Śiva (śivatattva), situated above all principles;
by its splendor, it pervades everything from Śivā down to the earth.
Earth, water, fire, air, and space as well; ego-sense, intellect, the qualities, and the unmanifest as well. (3.224)
From that [Śakti] comes passion (rāga), and from that, the five and ten faculties;
likewise, knowledge (vidyā), time (kāla), limited agency (kalā), illusion (māyā), and the self (ātman). (3.225)
Śuddhavidyā, Sādākhya, as well as Bindu and Nāda;
the second is the principle of Śakti, and the first is Śakti itself. (3.226)
These thirty-six principles here originate from the Śiva-principle.
The cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) is to be known as earth, and the water [contained] within it is remembered as primordial nature (prakṛti). (3.227)
Thus, fire extends up to Vidyā; wind extends up to Sadāśiva;
and ether extends up to Śakti—these indeed reside within the five elements.
These five principles (tattvas) are established within the principle of Sūtra;
the principles ending with Māyā are proclaimed as the principle of Śiva.

The Self alone is remembered as the sovereign lord of all principles (tattvas) within the reality of the Self; that which begins with the principle of Knowledge (vidyā-tattva) and ends with the power (śakti) is remembered as the principle of Knowledge. (3.230)
